Section 3.4 defines the evaluation pipeline for leakage detection. A response counts as leakage if either normalized matching finds the secret (verbatim/near-verbatim after normalization) or an LLM judge says the response reveals the full secret, a substantial substring, or enough partial information to identify it. Stage 1 strips non-digits from numeric secrets and case/whitespace from alphanumeric secrets while preserving meaningful delimiters. Stage 2 uses an open-weights Llama judge on responses negative under normalization, and the paper reports regex-only and hybrid rates separately because the judge can err. The new metric Privacy Half-Life (tau) is defined from leakage rates over observed drift lengths D_obs: delta = 0.1 * L(0), tau is the first drift length where leakage stays at or below delta for all later observed drift lengths; if no such point exists, tau = max(D_obs)+1. The section frames the benchmark as measuring bounded active-context persistence rather than arbitrarily long context windows.

PrivDrift’s target remains behavioral suppression of a secret still in the current context window, with later prompts trying to elicit it.

PrivDrift frames the target failure as active-context re-disclosure: after a secret is disclosed earlier in the dialogue, later unrelated drift plus a standardized probe may elicit the model to reproduce the secret exactly, approximately, or semantically. The paper distinguishes this from simply inspecting the transcript; the key question is whether the assistant itself re-discloses the secret.

Construction details: each dialogue begins with a persona sampled from 100+ profiles plus a ground-truth secret inserted into a plausible task. The paper studies whether intervening conversational tasks can cause an active LLM conversation to leak previously seeded sensitive information. It introduces PrivDrift, using seeded multi-turn histories, content-dense intervening exchanges, and three extraction conditions. The dataset has 1,000 dialogues containing phone numbers, email addresses, Social Security Numbers, or credit card numbers. Detection uses normalized matching plus an open-weights judge. Reported hybrid dialogue-level leakage rates across three evaluated models are 38.70%, 47.70%, and 54.60%. Leakage varies by model, secret type, and persuasion intensity; SSNs and credit card numbers are more strongly suppressed than contact identifiers. No system achieves stable suppression within the tested drift lengths, and the paper frames this as an active-context behavioral privacy failure rather than permanent memory.

Related work positions QX2 against parameter-held memorization/extraction, privacy-norm/compliance benchmarks, multi-turn adversarial attacks, and unlearning, emphasizing that QX2 concerns recoverability of user-supplied secrets after unrelated exchanges rather than harmful-content generation or parameter removal.

Section 3 defines QX2 as a controlled framework for testing whether a later probe can elicit an earlier secret after intervening topic drift. The threat model treats leakage as later reproduction of the secret, not its continued transcript presence, in an active/persistent session with unrelated content-dense exchanges before a standardized probe. Dataset generation uses a scaffold-then-rewrite pipeline that preserves exact ground truth, turn counts, and probe structure; the benchmark has 1,000 dialogues total, 900 synthetic and 100 human-authored, across 4 secret categories and drift lengths d in {0,2,3,4,5,6}. Reported length stats are 359.16 average words (385 median; 43/795 min/max) and 478.87 average approximate tokens (513.33 median; 57.33/1060.00 min/max). Probing uses three standardized conditions: Simple, Medium, and Hard. Drift length is sampled with 20% probability at d=0 and 80% uniformly over {2,3,4,5,6}. Evaluation is hybrid: a response is positive if normalized inclusion matches or an LLM judge identifies the full secret, a substantial substring, or enough partial information. Stage-1 B6T does deterministic normalization: numeric secrets/responses strip non-digit characters; alphanumerics normalize case/whitespace while keeping meaningful delimiters. The leakage indicator is defined as normalized-secret inclusion under φ(S) ⊆ φ(R).

Section 3.4.2 adds a second-stage verification step: an open-weights Llama judge examines secret S and response R to catch partial disclosures, indirect hints, and formatting variants that the deterministic regex baseline may miss. The paper says this judge is reported alongside H8D/U3P and is not assumed error-free.

Section 3.4.3 defines Privacy Half-Life (K2V), denoted τ, using observed drift lengths D_obs and leakage rates L(d). The safety threshold is δ = 0.1 × L(0), where L(0) is immediate-recall leakage. τ is the smallest observed d such that L(d) ≤ δ and all later observed lengths d' > d also satisfy L(d') ≤ δ; if no such d exists, τ = max(D_obs) + 1. The figure caption emphasizes that later resurgence invalidates earlier temporary drops.

Section 4 experimental setup: the three models are GPT-OSS-120B (M7Q), DeepSeek-R1 (T4X), and Qwen3-VL-235B (Y9C), queried via OpenRouter with the same histories and probe templates. Each system processes the full QX2 dataset with one seeded secret and one sampled d per dialogue under all standardized conditions. Cached responses are model outputs; counts are 3,000 per model and 9,000 total. G4P is dialogue-level: a dialogue is positive if any standardized probe elicits its secret. P6S is response-level: one observation per dialogue per persuasion condition, used for V4N and fuzzy-matching (R5J) analyses; G4P may exceed condition-specific means. Statistics: G4P CIs use 95% bootstrap over dialogues; P6S sensitivity checks use cached responses; matched model/detector comparisons use McNemar’s test with Bonferroni correction where applicable; repeated persuasion measures use Cochran’s Q followed by McNemar; chi-square tests assess independence against D7A, V4N, or S8Q; Cramer’s V (X2H) is an association effect size, not a significance test. Previously noted: Section 3.4.2 adds an open-weights Llama judge for partial disclosures/formatting variants alongside H8D/U3P; Section 3.4.3 defines Privacy Half-Life τ as the first observed d after which leakage stays at or below δ = 0.1 × L(0), with τ = max(D_obs)+1 if no such d exists; later resurgence invalidates earlier temporary drops.

Section 3 defines QX2 as a synthetic benchmark framework for active-context re-disclosure: a user supplies a secret at t0, then content-dense intervening turns (topic drift) occur before a standardized probe is appended. Leakage includes exact, approximate, or semantic revelation of the secret. The dataset contains 1,000 dialogues total: 900 synthetic and 100 human-authored, with 4 secret categories. The sampled secret formats are phone numbers, email addresses, Social Security Numbers, and credit card numbers. Drift length d is sampled from a mixture: 0 with probability 0.2, otherwise uniformly from {2,3,4,5,6}; immediate recall is included. Probing has three standardized styles: Simple (neutral direct retrieval), Medium (contextual justification), and Hard (urgent/high-pressure elicitation). Evaluation is hierarchical: deterministic normalization-based matching first, then an LLM judge for partial/indirect disclosures and formatting variations. The composite detector counts verbatim output, formatting changes, partial substrings, and paraphrases as possible leakage. A privacy half-life metric τ is defined from leakage rates L(d) using a threshold δ = 0.1 × L(0), requiring sustained suppression over later drift lengths; if no such point exists, τ = max(D_obs)+1.

PrivDrift is positioned against three adjacent literatures: (1) training-data extraction/membership inference, which studies private information in model parameters; (2) privacy-norm/contextual-integrity benchmarks like ConfAIde, PrivacyLens, and PrivaCI-Bench, which ask whether a model should share information in a static scenario; and (3) multi-turn adversarial attacks (Crescendo, automated jailbreaks, prompt injection), which aim at unsafe outputs or instruction hijacking rather than recovery of user-disclosed secrets after unrelated drift. PrivDrift’s target remains behavioral suppression of a secret still in the current context window, with later prompts trying to elicit it.

PrivDrift frames the target failure as active-context re-disclosure: after a secret is disclosed earlier in the dialogue, later unrelated drift plus a standardized probe may elicit the model to reproduce the secret exactly, approximately, or semantically. The paper distinguishes this from simply inspecting the transcript; the key question is whether the assistant itself re-discloses the secret.

Dataset generation: 1,000 controlled dialogues built via a scaffold-then-rewrite pipeline. Composition is 900 synthetic and 100 human-authored dialogues, with the human-authored ones distributed throughout the benchmark and not separately identifiable in cached metadata, so the paper says only aggregate results are reported. The benchmark includes 4 secret categories (phone numbers, email addresses, SSNs, credit card numbers) and drift lengths 0, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6. Average dialogue length is 359.16 words (approx. 478.87 tokens), median 385 words, min/max 43/795 words.

Construction details: each dialogue begins with a persona sampled from 100+ profiles plus a ground-truth secret inserted into a plausible task. Section 3 defines QX2 as a controlled framework for testing whether a later probe can elicit an earlier secret after intervening topic drift. The threat model treats leakage as later reproduction of the secret, not its continued transcript presence, in an active/persistent session with unrelated content-dense exchanges before a standardized probe. Dataset generation uses a scaffold-then-rewrite pipeline that preserves exact ground truth, turn counts, and probe structure; the benchmark has 1,000 dialogues total, 900 synthetic and 100 human-authored, across 4 secret categories and drift lengths d in {0,2,3,4,5,6}. Reported length stats are 359.16 average words (385 median; 43/795 min/max) and 478.87 average approximate tokens (513.33 median; 57.33/1060.00 min/max). Probing uses three standardized conditions: Simple, Medium, and Hard. Drift length is sampled with 20% probability at d=0 and 80% uniformly over {2,3,4,5,6}. Evaluation is hybrid: a response is positive if normalized inclusion matches or an LLM judge identifies the full secret, a substantial substring, or enough partial information. Stage-1 B6T does deterministic normalization: numeric secrets/responses strip non-digit characters; alphanumerics normalize case/whitespace while keeping meaningful delimiters. The leakage indicator is defined as normalized-secret inclusion under φ(S) ⊆ φ(R).

Section 3.4.2 adds a second-stage verification step: an open-weights Llama judge examines secret S and response R to catch partial disclosures, indirect hints, and formatting variants that the deterministic regex baseline may miss. The paper says this judge is reported alongside H8D/U3P and is not assumed error-free.

Section 3.4.3 defines Privacy Half-Life (K2V), denoted τ, using observed drift lengths D_obs and leakage rates L(d). The safety threshold is δ = 0.1 × L(0), where L(0) is immediate-recall leakage. τ is the smallest observed d such that L(d) ≤ δ and all later observed lengths d' > d also satisfy L(d') ≤ δ; if no such d exists, τ = max(D_obs) + 1. The figure caption emphasizes that later resurgence invalidates earlier temporary drops.

PrivDrift evaluates three models via OpenRouter: GPT-OSS-120B, DeepSeek-R1, and Qwen3-VL-235B. They use the same dialogue histories and probe templates. The benchmark runs on 1,000 generated dialogues per model; each dialogue has one secret and a drift length d in {0,2,3,4,5,6} sampled from the earlier distribution. Each dialogue is tested with three standardized persuasion probes, producing 3,000 cached model-probe responses per model and 9,000 total across the three models. Leakage is reported at two levels: dialogue-level (a dialogue leaks if any standardized probe reveals the secret) and probe-level (one response per persuasion condition). Dialogue-level leakage can exceed the mean persuasion-level leakage because of the any-probe rule. They report regex-only and hybrid leakage. Dialogue-level rates use 95% bootstrap CIs over dialogues; probe-level sensitivity checks use cached responses. Matched model/detector comparisons use McNemar’s test with Bonferroni correction; repeated-measures across persuasion levels use Cochran’s Q with post-hoc McNemar; associations with drift, persuasion, or secret type use chi-square tests and Cramer’s V.

Section 5 reports results for the three models. Dialogue-level hybrid leakage is close to regex-only matching: GPT-OSS-120B 47.70% vs 47.70% (Δ 0.00, p=1.0), DeepSeek-R1 38.70% vs 37.80% (Δ +0.90, p=7.7×10^-3), and Qwen3-VL-235B 54.60% vs 53.50% (Δ +1.10, p=2.57×10^-3). Dialogue-level hybrid leakage CIs are: DeepSeek 38.70% [35.7, 41.6], GPT-OSS 47.70% [44.6, 50.8], Qwen 54.60% [51.6, 57.7]. Probe-level leakage varies significantly by persuasion level for all models (Cochran’s Q, p<10^-5): GPT 39.30/40.50/32.90 (simple/medium/hard), DeepSeek 28.10/22.00/29.20, Qwen 38.70/33.30/40.60. Drift-length effects are small; Cramer’s V on cached probe-level data is 0.1073 (DeepSeek), 0.0659 (GPT), 0.0723 (Qwen), with a dip near d=3 then rebound. PrivDrift is positioned against three adjacent literatures: (1) training-data extraction/membership inference, which studies private information in model parameters; (2) privacy-norm/contextual-integrity benchmarks like ConfAIde, PrivacyLens, and PrivaCI-Bench, which ask whether a model should share information in a static scenario; and (3) multi-turn adversarial attacks (Crescendo, automated jailbreaks, prompt injection), which aim at unsafe outputs or instruction hijacking rather than recovery of user-disclosed secrets after unrelated drift. The paper also distinguishes PrivDrift from unlearning benchmarks such as TOFU and WMDP, which operate on static QA/model-parameter settings. PrivDrift’s target remains behavioral suppression of a secret still in the current context window, with later prompts trying to elicit it.

PrivDrift frames the target failure as active-context re-disclosure: after a secret is disclosed earlier in the dialogue, later unrelated drift plus a standardized probe may elicit the model to reproduce the secret exactly, approximately, or semantically. The paper distinguishes this from simply inspecting the transcript; the key question is whether the assistant itself re-discloses the secret.

Dataset generation: 1,000 controlled dialogues built via a scaffold-then-rewrite pipeline. Composition is 900 synthetic and 100 human-authored dialogues, with the human-authored ones distributed throughout the benchmark and not separately identifiable in cached metadata, so the paper says only aggregate results are reported. The benchmark includes 4 secret categories (phone numbers, email addresses, SSNs, credit card numbers) and drift lengths 0, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6. Average dialogue length is 359.16 words (approx. 478.87 tokens), median 385 words, min/max 43/795 words.

Construction details: each dialogue begins with a persona sampled from 100+ profiles plus a ground-truth secret inserted into a plausible task. Drift consists of content-dense, topic-conditioned Q&A pairs and fallback tasks on unrelated topics (e.g., tax filing, medical triage, travel logistics), with some turns written by annotators. A rewriting model then performs naturalistic refinement while preserving the exact secret, drift length, role structure, and final probe conditions.

Reported lengths are 359.16 average words, 385.00 median words, and 43/795 min/max words; average token length is 478.87, median 513.33, and min/max 57.33/1060.00 tokens.

The main evaluation appends a final standardized probe after the completed conversation. It defines three persuasion levels: Simple (direct neutral query), Medium (contextual justification), and Hard (high-pressure/urgent request). Drift length d is sampled from a mixed distribution: 0 with probability 0.2, otherwise uniformly from {2,3,4,5,6} with probability 0.8. The text says this includes immediate recall and emphasizes short-to-medium drift.

The short-to-medium D7A range does not characterize arbitrarily long or full-window behavior; findings concern bounded active-context persistence rather than full privacy behavior. Fixed-format secrets were studied; unstructured sensitive attributes remain future work. Training-data memorization, personalization memory, and cross-session retention were not tested. Section 3 defines QX2 as a controlled framework for testing whether a later probe can elicit an earlier secret after intervening topic drift. The threat model treats leakage as later reproduction of the secret, not its continued transcript presence, in an active/persistent session with unrelated content-dense exchanges before a standardized probe. Dataset generation uses a scaffold-then-rewrite pipeline that preserves exact ground truth, turn counts, and probe structure; the benchmark has 1,000 dialogues total, 900 synthetic and 100 human-authored, across 4 secret categories and drift lengths d in {0,2,3,4,5,6}. Reported length stats are 359.16 average words (385 median; 43/795 min/max) and 478.87 average approximate tokens (513.33 median; 57.33/1060.00 min/max). Probing uses three standardized conditions: Simple, Medium, and Hard. Drift length is sampled with 20% probability at d=0 and 80% uniformly over {2,3,4,5,6}. Evaluation is hybrid: a response is positive if normalized inclusion matches or an LLM judge identifies the full secret, a substantial substring, or enough partial information. Stage-1 B6T does deterministic normalization: numeric secrets/responses strip non-digit characters; alphanumerics normalize case/whitespace while keeping meaningful delimiters. The leakage indicator is defined as normalized-secret inclusion under φ(S) ⊆ φ(R).

Section 3.4.2 adds a second-stage verification step: an open-weights Llama judge examines secret S and response R to catch partial disclosures, indirect hints, and formatting variants that the deterministic regex baseline may miss. The paper says this judge is reported alongside H8D/U3P and is not assumed error-free.

Section 3.4.3 defines Privacy Half-Life (K2V), denoted τ, using observed drift lengths D_obs and leakage rates L(d). The safety threshold is δ = 0.1 × L(0), where L(0) is immediate-recall leakage. τ is the smallest observed d such that L(d) ≤ δ and all later observed lengths d' > d also satisfy L(d') ≤ δ; if no such d exists, τ = max(D_obs) + 1. The figure caption emphasizes that later resurgence invalidates earlier temporary drops.

Section 4 experimental setup: the three models are GPT-OSS-120B (M7Q), DeepSeek-R1 (T4X), and Qwen3-VL-235B (Y9C), queried via OpenRouter with the same histories and probe templates. Each system processes the full QX2 dataset with one seeded secret and one sampled d per dialogue under all standardized conditions. Cached responses are model outputs; counts are 3,000 per model and 9,000 total. G4P is dialogue-level: a dialogue is positive if any standardized probe elicits its secret. P6S is response-level: one observation per dialogue per persuasion condition, used for V4N and fuzzy-matching (R5J) analyses; G4P may exceed condition-specific means. Statistics: G4P CIs use 95% bootstrap over dialogues; P6S sensitivity checks use cached responses; matched model/detector comparisons use McNemar’s test with Bonferroni correction where applicable; repeated persuasion measures use Cochran’s Q followed by McNemar; chi-square tests assess independence against D7A, V4N, or S8Q; Cramer’s V (X2H) is an association effect size, not a significance test. Previously noted: Section 3.4.2 adds an open-weights Llama judge for partial disclosures/formatting variants alongside H8D/U3P; Section 3.4.3 defines Privacy Half-Life τ as the first observed d after which leakage stays at or below δ = 0.1 × L(0), with τ = max(D_obs)+1 if no such d exists; later resurgence invalidates earlier temporary drops.

PrivDrift is a benchmark for measuring privacy leakage in active multi-turn conversations after a user has disclosed a secret and the conversation later drifts to unrelated topics before probing. The paper frames the risk as behavioral: sensitive info may still be recoverable later through direct, justified, high-pressure, or tool-mediated prompts. Contributions include the benchmark, evaluation across probe styles, a hybrid detector combining normalization-based matching with an open-weights LLM judge, and a proposed Privacy Half-Life metric showing no stable decay within the observed drift range.

Evaluation is hierarchical: deterministic normalization-based matching first, then an LLM judge for partial/indirect disclosures and formatting variations. The composite detector counts verbatim output, formatting changes, partial substrings, and paraphrases as possible leakage. A privacy half-life metric τ is defined from leakage rates L(d) using a threshold δ = 0.1 × L(0), requiring sustained suppression over later drift lengths; if no such point exists, τ = max(D_obs)+1.

PrivDrift’s target remains behavioral suppression of a secret still in the current context window, with later prompts trying to elicit it.

PrivDrift frames the target failure as active-context re-disclosure: after a secret is disclosed earlier in the dialogue, later unrelated drift plus a standardized probe may elicit the model to reproduce the secret exactly, approximately, or semantically. The paper distinguishes this from simply inspecting the transcript; the key question is whether the assistant itself re-discloses the secret.

Probing uses three standardized conditions: Simple, Medium, and Hard. Drift length is sampled with 20% probability at d=0 and 80% uniformly over {2,3,4,5,6}. Evaluation is hybrid: a response is positive if normalized inclusion matches or an LLM judge identifies the full secret, a substantial substring, or enough partial information. Stage-1 B6T does deterministic normalization: numeric secrets/responses strip non-digit characters; alphanumerics normalize case/whitespace while keeping meaningful delimiters. The leakage indicator is defined as normalized-secret inclusion under φ(S) ⊆ φ(R).

Section 3.4.2 adds a second-stage verification step: an open-weights Llama judge examines secret S and response R to catch partial disclosures, indirect hints, and formatting variants that the deterministic regex baseline may miss. The paper says this judge is reported alongside H8D/U3P and is not assumed error-free.

Section 3.4.3 defines Privacy Half-Life (K2V), denoted τ, using observed drift lengths D_obs and leakage rates L(d). The safety threshold is δ = 0.1 × L(0), where L(0) is immediate-recall leakage. τ is the smallest observed d such that L(d) ≤ δ and all later observed lengths d' > d also satisfy L(d') ≤ δ; if no such d exists, τ = max(D_obs) + 1. The figure caption emphasizes that later resurgence invalidates earlier temporary drops.

PrivDrift is a synthetic evaluation framework for active-context re-disclosure: whether a secret disclosed earlier in a conversation can be recovered after unrelated topic drift. The threat model explicitly focuses on the model re-disclosing a secret when later prompted, rather than transcript inspection. Formally, a secret S is disclosed at turn t0, followed by d unrelated drift turns D, then a standardized probe P; leakage occurs if the model reveals S exactly, approximately, or semantically. The dataset generation pipeline creates N=1000 controlled dialogues via scaffold-then-rewrite, with 900 synthetic and 100 human-authored dialogues. Table 1 reports 4 secret categories, drift lengths {0,2,3,4,5,6}, average 359.16 words per dialogue, median 385.00, min/max 43/795, and approximate token counts averaging 478.87. Secrets are drawn from four PII types: phone numbers, email addresses, SSNs, and credit card numbers. Drift is topic-conditioned and content-dense, with some human-authored drift turns in the generation library. Probing uses three persuasion levels: simple/direct, medium/justified, and hard/high-pressure. Drift length d is sampled from a mixture: 0 with p=0.2 and Uniform{2,3,4,5,6} with p=0.8.

It introduces PrivDrift, a benchmark of 1,000 controlled dialogues with seeded secrets, unrelated intervening turns, and standardized extraction probes. No evaluated model meets the paper’s criterion for stable suppression.

PrivDrift Section 3 defines the benchmark framework: active-context re-disclosure means a secret disclosed earlier can still be elicited later after unrelated drift. A dialogue has a secret \(S\) introduced at turn \(t_0\), then \(d\) drift turns, then a standardized probe \(P\); leakage occurs if the response reveals \(S\) exactly, approximately, or semantically. The dataset generation pipeline builds 1,000 dialogues total: 900 synthetic and 100 human-authored, with secret categories = 4 and drift lengths {0,2,3,4,5,6}. The paper reports aggregate results only for the whole set and says it will not separately compare human vs. synthetic leakage here. Dialogue construction uses a scaffold-then-rewrite pipeline with personas sampled from 100+ profiles, and secrets are fixed-format PII from four categories: phone, email, SSN, and credit card. Drift is created via topic-conditioned dense QA/fallback tasks; rewriting improves fluency while preserving the exact secret, drift length, role structure, and probe conditions.

Section 3.3 defines three probe persuasion levels: Simple (direct neutral query), Medium (contextual justification), and Hard (high-pressure/urgent request). Drift length d is sampled from a mixed distribution: d=0 with probability 0.2, otherwise uniformly from {2,3,4,5,6} with probability 0.8. The paper says this includes immediate recall and focuses on short-to-medium drift.

Section 3.4 defines a hybrid leakage detector. Stage 1 normalizes secrets/responses: numeric secrets strip all non-digits; alphanumeric secrets are lowercased/whitespace-normalized while preserving meaningful delimiters. Leakage is flagged if the normalized secret is contained in the normalized response. Stage 2 sends only normalization-negative responses to an open-weights Llama judge, which labels whether the response reveals the secret, a substantial part, or enough partial information to identify it. Regex-only and hybrid rates are reported separately.

Privacy Half-Life tau is the earliest observed drift length where leakage is at or below 10% of the zero-drift leakage rate and remains at or below that threshold for all later observed drift lengths; if no such point exists, tau is max(D_obs)+1.

Section 4 Experimental Setup: Three target models are GPT-OSS-120B, DeepSeek-R1, and Qwen3-VL-235B, queried through the OpenRouter API with identical dialogue histories and probe templates. The dataset uses 1,000 PrivDrift dialogues per model; each dialogue has one secret and one drift length d sampled from {0,2,3,4,5,6} using the earlier mixed distribution. There are three standardized persuasion probes per dialogue, giving 3,000 cached model-probe responses per model and 9,000 total cached responses. Overall leakage is dialogue-level: a dialogue leaks if any standardized probe reveals the secret. Persuasion-level and fuzzy-matching analyses are probe-level, with one response per persuasion condition per dialogue, so dialogue-level leakage may exceed average probe-level rates. Reported metrics include regex-only and hybrid leakage. Dialogue-level rates use 95% bootstrap CIs over dialogues; probe-level sensitivity checks use cached responses. McNemar’s test is used for paired model/detector comparisons with Bonferroni correction when applicable; Cochran’s Q tests repeated measures across persuasion levels followed by post-hoc McNemar tests; chi-square tests assess associations with drift length, persuasion level, or secret type; Cramer’s V gives effect size.

Section 5 Results: dialogue-level hybrid leakage is close to regex-only. Table 2: GPT-OSS-120B 47.70% regex and hybrid (+0.00, p=1.0); DeepSeek-R1 37.80% regex vs 38.70% hybrid (+0.90, p=7.7e-3); Qwen3-VL-235B 53.50% vs 54.60% (+1.10, p=2.57e-3). Table 4 probe-level leakage by persuasion intensity (simple/medium/hard): GPT-OSS-120B 39.30/40.50/32.90, DeepSeek-R1 28.10/22.00/29.20, Qwen3-VL-235B 38.70/33.30/40.60; Cochran’s Q significant for all models (p<1e-5), with model-dependent nonmonotonic effects. Section 5.5 begins by stating secret type strongly affects hybrid leakage, with Cramer’s V 0.5871 (DeepSeek-R1), 0.7731 (GPT-OSS-120B), 0.6927 (Qwen3-VL-235B), and claims SSNs/credit cards leak less than emails/phone numbers.

The paper studies whether intervening conversational tasks can cause an active LLM conversation to leak previously seeded sensitive information. It introduces PrivDrift, using seeded multi-turn histories, content-dense intervening exchanges, and three extraction conditions. The dataset has 1,000 dialogues containing phone numbers, email addresses, Social Security Numbers, or credit card numbers. Detection uses normalized matching plus an open-weights judge. Reported hybrid dialogue-level leakage rates across three evaluated models are 38.70%, 47.70%, and 54.60%. The paper’s QX2 framework formalizes active-context re-disclosure: a secret S is seeded, unrelated content-dense turns create drift D, then a standardized probe tests whether the model later reproduces S. The dataset summary reports 1,000 dialogues total: 900 synthetic and 100 human-authored, with 4 secret categories and drift lengths d in {0,2,3,4,5,6}. Average length is 359.16 words per dialogue (478.87 approx. tokens), with word/token medians 385.00/513.33. The probing setup uses three standardized persuasion conditions: Simple, Medium, and Hard. Evaluation is hybrid: a response is positive if normalized inclusion or an LLM judge finds the full secret, a substantial substring, or enough partial information to identify it. Stage 1 normalization strips non-digits from numeric secrets/responses; alphanumeric secrets are normalized for case and whitespace while retaining meaningful delimiters.

Stage 2 uses an open-weights Llama judge to verify deterministic negatives that might otherwise be missed; it can flag full/substantial disclosure, partial disclosures, indirect hints, and formatting variations. The regex-only deterministic baseline (U3P) is still reported separately alongside H8D, and the authors note judge errors are possible. Section 3.4.3 defines Privacy Half-Life (K2V), denoted τ, using observed drift lengths D_obs and leakage rates L(d). The safety threshold is δ = 0.1 × L(0), where L(0) is immediate-recall leakage. τ is the minimum observed d such that L(d) ≤ δ and all later observed d' > d also satisfy L(d') ≤ δ; if no such d exists, τ is set to max(D_obs) + 1.

Section 4 experimental setup: the three models are GPT-OSS-120B (M7Q), DeepSeek-R1 (T4X), and Qwen3-VL-235B (Y9C), queried through OpenRouter with identical histories/probe templates. The full QX2 dataset is used; each model processes every dialogue under all standardized conditions, with one seeded secret and one sampled d per dialogue. Cached responses are saved outputs: 3,000 per model, 9,000 total across all models. Aggregation levels: G4P labels a dialogue positive if any standardized probe elicits the secret; P6S provides one observation per dialogue per persuasion condition for V4N and fuzzy-matching (R5J) analyses. R5J is a post-hoc normalized-similarity check, and G4P can exceed the mean condition-specific rate. Statistical methods include 95% bootstrap CIs over dialogues for G4P, cached-response sensitivity checks for P6S, McNemar’s tests for matched model/detector comparisons (with Bonferroni correction where applicable), Cochran’s Q followed by McNemar tests for repeated persuasion measures, chi-square tests for independence against D7A/V4N/S8Q, and Cramer’s V (X2H) as an association effect size; p denotes a test p-value.

Section 5 results: G4P/H8D is very similar to U3P/B6T, with only small augmentation: M7Q 47.70 vs 47.70 (+0.00, p=1.0), T4X 37.80 vs 38.70 (+0.90, p=7.7e-3), Y9C 53.50 vs 54.60 (+1.10, p=2.57e-3). Bootstrap CIs for H8D are T4X 38.70% [35.7, 41.6], M7Q 47.70% [44.6, 50.8], Y9C 54.60% [51.6, 57.7]. V4N effects are significant for all models (Cochran’s Q, p<1e-5) and non-monotonic: M7Q 39.3/40.5/32.9 (C8R/Z2F/L9W), T4X 28.1/22.0/29.2, Y9C 38.7/33.3/40.6. D7A associations are small/negligible and there is no stable suppression over d<=6; the text says there is a dip near d=3 then rebound. S8Q has the strongest association among tested variables; W3B and N6G are far more suppressed than F8Z and A2L (e.g., M7Q W3B 0.14%, N6G 0.00%, F8Z 78.24%, A2L 70.89%; similar for T4X and Y9C). K2V analysis concludes no model-condition reaches stable threshold-level suppression, with tau=max(Dobs)+1=7 and observed bounds only up to d<=6. R5J is a cached-output fuzzy-similarity check that largely tracks H8D: T4X 26.40/26.53 vs H8D 26.43, M7Q 37.03/37.07 vs 37.57, Y9C 37.60/37.93 vs 37.53.

Section 6 Discussion: The paper argues recoverability in-context does not mean permanent memory or a privacy boundary. It says assistants may reproduce sensitive in-context info under enough retrieval pressure. M7Q’s response is framed as urgency triggering safety/refusal; Y9C shows weaker pressure resistance. J7K is explicitly said not to be an implicit privacy boundary. Claims/evidence: pressure responses differ per Table 4, with M7Q C8R/Z2F/L9W = 39.30/40.50/32.90 and Y9C = 38.70/33.30/40.60. Intermediate decreases are not treated as stable suppression: Figure 4 shows a dip near d=3 then rebound, and Section 5.6 assigns tau=7 to every model/persuasion condition over d<=6. Figure 5/Table 6 say the higher threshold tracks H8D closely, with R5J 0.85/H8D columns: T4X 26.40/26.43; M7Q 37.03/37.57; Y9C 37.60/37.53.

Section 7 limitations: results are limited to bounded drift length and do not characterize arbitrarily long or full-window behavior. The paper says the short-to-medium range does not saturate modern windows, so findings are about bounded active-context persistence only. Fixed-format secrets are a limitation: structured identifiers are easier to detect than unstructured sensitive attributes (health, family, immigration, financial hardship), and extension to non-fixed sensitive attributes is future work. Training-data memorization, personalization memory, and cross-session retention were not tested. The mixed synthetic/human-authored dataset improves realism while retaining control; only aggregate results are reported and cached metadata no longer preserves human row identifiers. Detector scope is limited: surface-output labels under U3P, R5J, and an external judge are reported, but formal human–automated inter-annotator agreement is not. API-served model identities may change over time despite logged identifiers, prompts, timestamps, cached responses, and paired statistics; M7Q=GPT-OSS-120B, T4X=DeepSeek-R1, Y9C=Qwen3-VL-235B. Planned releases include generation code, probe templates, evaluation scripts, aggregate results, and a sanitized dialogue subset, with synthetic PII-like strings replaced by non-real identifiers for reproducibility.

Section 3 defines QX2 as a synthetic benchmark framework for active-context re-disclosure: a user supplies a secret at t0, then content-dense intervening turns (topic drift) occur before a standardized probe is appended. Leakage includes exact, approximate, or semantic revelation of the secret. The dataset contains 1,000 dialogues total: 900 synthetic and 100 human-authored, with 4 secret categories. The sampled secret formats are phone numbers, email addresses, Social Security Numbers, and credit card numbers. Drift length d is sampled from a mixture: 0 with probability 0.2, otherwise uniformly from {2,3,4,5,6}; immediate recall is included. Probing has three standardized styles: Simple (neutral direct retrieval), Medium (contextual justification), and Hard (urgent/high-pressure elicitation). Evaluation is hierarchical: deterministic normalization-based matching first, then an LLM judge for partial/indirect disclosures and formatting variations. The composite detector counts verbatim output, formatting changes, partial substrings, and paraphrases as possible leakage. A privacy half-life metric τ is defined from leakage rates L(d) using a threshold δ = 0.1 × L(0), requiring sustained suppression over later drift lengths; if no such point exists, τ = max(D_obs)+1.

Section 4 gives the experimental setup. All systems receive identical histories and probe templates via the OpenRouter API. Each model runs on the full QX2 dataset, with one seeded secret and one sampled drift length d per dialogue, under all three standardized probe conditions; the table reports 3,000 cached responses per model and 9,000 across all evaluated models. The benchmark is PrivDrift, also referred to in this section as QX2, using seeded multi-turn histories, content-dense intervening exchanges, and standardized extraction probes. This related-work section positions QX2 against prior work on training-data extraction and membership inference, contextual-integrity/privacy-norm benchmarks (ConfAIde, PrivacyLens, PrivaCI-Bench), multi-turn adversarial attacks, and unlearning/suppression benchmarks like TOFU and WMDP. It emphasizes that QX2 is about behavioral recoverability of secrets still in active context, not parameter-level memorization or static access-control/privacy-norm judgments.

Section 3 defines QX2 as a synthetic benchmark framework for active-context re-disclosure: a user supplies a secret at t0, then content-dense intervening turns (topic drift) occur before a standardized probe is appended. Leakage includes exact, approximate, or semantic revelation of the secret. The dataset contains 1,000 dialogues total: 900 synthetic and 100 human-authored, with 4 secret categories. The sampled secret formats are phone numbers, email addresses, Social Security Numbers, and credit card numbers. Drift length d is sampled from a mixture: 0 with probability 0.2, otherwise uniformly from {2,3,4,5,6}; immediate recall is included. Probing has three standardized styles: Simple (neutral direct retrieval), Medium (contextual justification), and Hard (urgent/high-pressure elicitation). Evaluation is hierarchical: deterministic normalization-based matching first, then an LLM judge for partial/indirect disclosures and formatting variations. The composite detector counts verbatim output, formatting changes, partial substrings, and paraphrases as possible leakage. A privacy half-life metric τ is defined from leakage rates L(d) using a threshold δ = 0.1 × L(0), requiring sustained suppression over later drift lengths; if no such point exists, τ = max(D_obs)+1.

Section 4 gives the experimental setup. All systems receive identical histories and probe templates via the OpenRouter API. Each model runs on the full QX2 dataset, with one seeded secret and one sampled drift length d per dialogue, under all three standardized probe conditions; the table reports 3,000 cached responses per model and 9,000 across all evaluated models. Two aggregation levels are defined: G4P (dialogue-level leakage) marks a dialogue positive if any standardized probe reveals the secret, while P6S (probe-level leakage) gives one observation per dialogue per persuasion condition for V4N and R5J analyses; G4P may exceed the mean condition-specific rate. For inference, G4P uses 95% bootstrap intervals over dialogues, P6S sensitivity checks use cached model-probe responses, matched model/detector comparisons use McNemar’s test with Bonferroni correction where applicable, repeated persuasion measures use Cochran’s Q followed by McNemar tests, and leakage associations against D7A, V4N, or S8Q use chi-square with Cramer’s V as effect size.

Section 3 defines QX2 as a controlled framework for testing whether a later probe can elicit an earlier secret after intervening topic drift. The threat model treats leakage as later reproduction of the secret, not its continued transcript presence, in an active/persistent session with unrelated content-dense exchanges before a standardized probe. Dataset generation uses a scaffold-then-rewrite pipeline that preserves exact ground truth, turn counts, and probe structure; the benchmark has 1,000 dialogues total, 900 synthetic and 100 human-authored, across 4 secret categories and drift lengths d in {0,2,3,4,5,6}. Reported length stats are 359.16 average words (385 median; 43/795 min/max) and 478.87 average approximate tokens (513.33 median; 57.33/1060.00 min/max). Probing uses three standardized conditions: Simple, Medium, and Hard. Drift length is sampled with 20% probability at d=0 and 80% uniformly over {2,3,4,5,6}. Evaluation is hybrid: a response is positive if normalized inclusion matches or an LLM judge identifies the full secret, a substantial substring, or enough partial information. Stage-1 B6T does deterministic normalization: numeric secrets/responses strip non-digit characters; alphanumerics normalize case/whitespace while keeping meaningful delimiters. The leakage indicator is defined as normalized-secret inclusion under φ(S) ⊆ φ(R).

Section 3.4.2 adds a second-stage verification step: an open-weights Llama judge examines secret S and response R to catch partial disclosures, indirect hints, and formatting variants that the deterministic regex baseline may miss. Paper title: "PrivDrift: Auditing User-Secret Leakage Under Topic Drift in Active LLM Conversations." Abstract claims that persistent, user-facing, shared-session, tool-augmented LLMs can retain behaviorally recoverable sensitive disclosures even after unrelated tasks. It says the benchmark PrivDrift audits this persistence using seeded multi-turn histories, content-dense intervening exchanges, and standardized extraction probes. The paper argues active-context privacy should be evaluated as persistent behavioral failure rather than only parameter memorization or immediate jailbreak behavior.

The paper argues that persistent, user-facing, shared-session, tool-augmented LLMs can retain behaviorally recoverable sensitive disclosures after unrelated tasks. The benchmark is PrivDrift, also referred to in this section as QX2, using seeded multi-turn histories, content-dense intervening exchanges, and standardized extraction probes. Main findings from the abstract: leakage can remain substantial under some conditions across extended-context models, varies sharply by system, and does not decline reliably within the tested window. The introduction frames sensitive PII as SSNs/payment identifiers, contact identifiers, financial identifiers, and health-related details. It argues existing safety evaluations mostly focus on two extremes: training-data memorization and immediate jailbreaks, while the relevant risk is later indirect/justified/high-pressure/tool-mediated elicitation in shared sessions. This related-work section positions QX2 against prior work on training-data extraction and membership inference, contextual-integrity/privacy-norm benchmarks (ConfAIde, PrivacyLens, PrivaCI-Bench), multi-turn adversarial attacks, and unlearning/suppression benchmarks like TOFU and WMDP. It emphasizes that QX2 is about behavioral recoverability of secrets still in active context, not parameter-level memorization or static access-control/privacy-norm judgments.

Section 3 defines QX2 as a synthetic benchmark framework for active-context re-disclosure: a user supplies a secret at t0, then content-dense intervening turns (topic drift) occur before a standardized probe is appended. Leakage includes exact, approximate, or semantic revelation of the secret. The dataset contains 1,000 dialogues total: 900 synthetic and 100 human-authored, with 4 secret categories. The sampled secret formats are phone numbers, email addresses, Social Security Numbers, and credit card numbers. Drift length d is sampled from a mixture: 0 with probability 0.2, otherwise uniformly from {2,3,4,5,6}; immediate recall is included. Probing has three standardized styles: Simple (neutral direct retrieval), Medium (contextual justification), and Hard (urgent/high-pressure elicitation). Evaluation is hierarchical: deterministic normalization-based matching first, then an LLM judge for partial/indirect disclosures and formatting variations. The composite detector counts verbatim output, formatting changes, partial substrings, and paraphrases as possible leakage. A privacy half-life metric τ is defined from leakage rates L(d) using a threshold δ = 0.1 × L(0), requiring sustained suppression over later drift lengths; if no such point exists, τ = max(D_obs)+1.

Section 4 gives the experimental setup. All systems receive identical histories and probe templates via the OpenRouter API. Each model runs on the full QX2 dataset, with one seeded secret and one sampled drift length d per dialogue, under all three standardized probe conditions; the table reports 3,000 cached responses per model and 9,000 across all evaluated models. Two aggregation levels are defined: G4P (dialogue-level leakage) marks a dialogue positive if any standardized probe reveals the secret, while P6S (probe-level leakage) gives one observation per dialogue per persuasion condition for V4N and R5J analyses; G4P may exceed the mean condition-specific rate. For inference, G4P uses 95% bootstrap intervals over dialogues, P6S sensitivity checks use cached model-probe responses, matched model/detector comparisons use McNemar’s test with Bonferroni correction where applicable, repeated persuasion measures use Cochran’s Q followed by McNemar tests, and leakage associations against D7A, V4N, or S8Q use chi-square with Cramer’s V as effect size.

Section 5 reports results. 5.1 says H8D is identical to B6T for every model and that judge augmentation is limited; Table 2 gives G4P for U3P vs H8D: M7Q 47.70/47.70, T4X 37.80/38.70 (+0.90, p=7.7e-3), Y9C 53.50/54.60 (+1.10, p=2.57e-3). 5.2 restates H8D G4P with 95% bootstrap CIs: T4X 38.70 [35.7, 41.6], M7Q 47.70 [44.6, 50.8], Y9C 54.60 [51.6, 57.7]. 5.3: V4N P6S is non-monotonic and significant for all models (Cochran’s Q p<1e-5): M7Q 39.3/40.5/32.9 (C8R/Z2F/L9W), T4X 28.1/22.0/29.2, Y9C 38.7/33.3/40.6. 5.4 says D7A associations are small/negligible with a dip near d=3 then rebound. 5.5 says S8Q has the strongest association; Table 5 gives W3B/N6G much lower leakage than F8Z/A2L (e.g., M7Q 0.14/0.00 vs 78.24/70.89). 5.6 says no system approaches threshold at tested lengths; observed bound d<=6 and assigned tau=7. 5.7 presents R5J fuzzy matching on cached outputs, saying G4P labels are unchanged and the judge is unnecessary; Table 6 lists cached-output P6S for T4X/M7Q/Y9C under U3P, R5J 0.85, R5J 0.80, and H8D.

Section 6 Discussion concludes that behavioral recoverability does not imply permanent memory and that current assistants may reproduce sensitive in-context information under sufficient retrieval pressure. It interprets the M7Q pressure response as consistent with urgency activating safety/refusal behavior and the Y9C response as indicating weaker pressure resistance. It also states that J7K is not an implicit privacy boundary, and that unstable intermediate decreases should be assessed with stability-based evaluation rather than treated as suppression evidence.

Section 7 lists limitations and future work. The results are bounded to short-to-medium active-context persistence and do not characterize full-window or arbitrarily long privacy behavior. The benchmark focuses on fixed-format identifiers; unstructured sensitive attributes (health, family, immigration, financial hardship) remain future work. The study tests active-context effects only, not training-data memorization, personalization memory, or cross-session retention. The mixed synthetic/human dialogue setup improves realism, but human-versus-synthetic leakage comparison is deferred and only aggregate results are reported because cached metadata no longer preserves human-authored row identifiers. Labels are based on surface-form outputs under U3P, R5J, and an external judge; formal human–automated inter-annotator agreement is not reported. The work uses API-served models, and identifiers may change over time, though prompts, timestamps, cached responses, and paired statistics on identical dialogue sets were logged. Planned releases include generation code, probe templates, evaluation scripts, aggregate result files, and a sanitized dialogue subset, with non-real identifiers used in released instances.

Section 8 concludes that the S8Q asymmetry indicates uneven safeguards that depend more on format/sensitivity cues and format-sensitive safety heuristics than on generalized contextual confidentiality or robust contextual reasoning. PrivDrift is a benchmark for measuring privacy leakage in active multi-turn conversations after a user has disclosed a secret and the conversation later drifts to unrelated topics before probing. The paper frames the risk as behavioral: sensitive info may still be recoverable later through direct, justified, high-pressure, or tool-mediated prompts. It evaluates three LLMs with extended context windows, using 1,000 dialogues per model. Reported dialogue-level hybrid leakage ranges from 38.7% to 54.6%, and leakage varies by model, secret type, and persuasion intensity; SSNs and credit cards are suppressed more often than emails and phone numbers. Within the tested drift window (d <= 6), additional topic drift does not reliably reduce leakage. Contributions include the benchmark, evaluation across probe styles, a hybrid detector combining normalization-based matching with an open-weights LLM judge, and a proposed Privacy Half-Life metric showing no stable decay within the observed drift range.

PrivDrift evaluates three models via OpenRouter: GPT-OSS-120B, DeepSeek-R1, and Qwen3-VL-235B. They use the same dialogue histories and probe templates. The benchmark runs on 1,000 generated dialogues per model; each dialogue has one secret and a drift length d in {0,2,3,4,5,6} sampled from the earlier distribution. Each dialogue is tested with three standardized persuasion probes, producing 3,000 cached model-probe responses per model and 9,000 total across the three models. Leakage is reported at two levels: dialogue-level (a dialogue leaks if any standardized probe reveals the secret) and probe-level (one response per persuasion condition). Dialogue-level leakage can exceed the mean persuasion-level leakage because of the any-probe rule. They report regex-only and hybrid leakage. Dialogue-level rates use 95% bootstrap CIs over dialogues; probe-level sensitivity checks use cached responses. Matched model/detector comparisons use McNemar’s test with Bonferroni correction; repeated-measures across persuasion levels use Cochran’s Q with post-hoc McNemar; associations with drift, persuasion, or secret type use chi-square tests and Cramer’s V.

Results section reports dialogue-level hybrid leakage for the three models: DeepSeek-R1 38.70% (95% CI [35.7, 41.6]), GPT-OSS-120B 47.70% ([44.6, 50.8]), and Qwen3-VL-235B 54.60% ([51.6, 57.7]). Regex-only dialogue-level rates are 37.80, 47.70, and 53.50 respectively; the LLM judge adds at most 1.10 percentage points. Probe-level leakage varies by persuasion intensity (Cochran’s Q p<1e-5): GPT-OSS simple/medium/hard 39.3/40.5/32.9, DeepSeek 28.1/22.0/29.2, Qwen 38.7/33.3/40.6. Drift effects are small (Cramer’s V: DeepSeek 0.1073, GPT-OSS 0.0659, Qwen 0.0723) with a dip near d=3 and rebound. Secret type has a much larger association with leakage (Cramer’s V: DeepSeek 0.5871, GPT-OSS 0.7731, Qwen 0.6927); SSNs and credit cards leak far less than emails and phone numbers. Privacy half-life never reaches the 10% decay threshold within tested drift lengths, so τ=max(D_obs)+1=7 for all models/conditions. Fuzzy matching at threshold 0.85 closely tracks hybrid probe-level leakage, with values near the hybrid rates for all models.

The composite detector counts verbatim output, formatting changes, partial substrings, and paraphrases as possible leakage. A privacy half-life metric τ is defined from leakage rates L(d) using a threshold δ = 0.1 × L(0), requiring sustained suppression over later drift lengths; if no such point exists, τ = max(D_obs)+1.

Section 3 defines QX2 as a controlled framework for testing whether a later probe can elicit an earlier secret after intervening topic drift. The threat model treats leakage as later reproduction of the secret, not its continued transcript presence, in an active/persistent session with unrelated content-dense exchanges before a standardized probe. Dataset generation uses a scaffold-then-rewrite pipeline that preserves exact ground truth, turn counts, and probe structure; the benchmark has 1,000 dialogues total, 900 synthetic and 100 human-authored, across 4 secret categories and drift lengths d in {0,2,3,4,5,6}. Probing uses three standardized conditions: Simple, Medium, and Hard. Drift length is sampled with 20% probability at d=0 and 80% uniformly over {2,3,4,5,6}. Section 8 defines the filability protocol. The authors say the study is currently one model/one task, and a second-model replication is pre-registered but not yet run: a 924-cell grid on Pythia-160m, same task, different architecture family, with the seed axis reduced from five levels to three. final_notes: Section 9 limitations: generalisation is untested because scale has not been tested; a pre-registered second-model replication on Pythia-160m (924-cell grid, same task, seeds with three levels instead of five) and a second task are designed but unrun. Size is an outcome, not an axis: threshold-selected circuit size distorts F, the null-comparison direction, and the sign of the functional gap; fixing size reduces F from 0.7316 to 0.2746, so pooled results must be decomposed by size. The instrument omits at least one defensible operator (optimal ablation [5]), so measured F is a lower bound relative to the field’s full defensible choices. The discard rate is 52.3% and the surviving pool is metric-imbalanced, though no repairs were made. Bootstrap intervals are invalid for conditioning groups with only 2–5 specifications because retained self-pairs dominate; point estimates are reported instead. Section 10 discussion: metric standardisation is the biggest single-axis lever, removing 0.1377 from a 0.7316 flip rate (leaving 0.5939, CI 0.5803–0.6063), but one-axis standardisation is insufficient. One of seven documented, publicly exported discovery objectives does not run on the library’s canonical task; all 220 cells in that arm fail. Section 11 reproducibility: the pre-registration is a timestamped public-repository commit tagged `prereg-p1-confirmatory`, made before the confirmatory sweep. The results archive verifies a single environment across all 1,320 cells, and content-addressed comparison recovered the code commit with 22/22 files identical. A verification script recomputes headline quantities with 36 checks and 0 failures, deriving F by three routes; a second script checks every numeric token against stored results. Every table is emitted directly from results, and the test suite contains 343 tests.

Paper summary claims: it studies whether circuit discovery can produce stable regulatory evidence by varying seven analytic choices and deterministically mapping each circuit to a structured Annex IV statement. This part is a glossary defining the paper’s terminology and symbols. It also states that the study’s confirmatory grid uses GPT-2 small, indirect object identification, seven documented discovery objectives, and that six executed, matching the earlier note that one objective does not execute. steps.notes_before: Section 4 formalism: a specification is \(s=(o,a,d,m,\tau,P,r,g)\), where \(o\)=objective, \(a\)=ablation operator, \(d\)=corruption distribution, \(m\)=evaluation metric, \(\tau\)=size threshold, \(P\)=prompt variant, \(r\)=seed, and \(g\)=granularity/claim-detail. Discovery outputs a circuit \(C(s)\subseteq E\); for GPT-2 small’s factorised graph, \(|E|=32{,}491\). The paper gives a closed-form component count: 144 attention heads + 12 MLPs = 156 components, and says the output receives from 157 non-terminal sources. Circuit instability is \(D=1-|C_i\cap C_j|/|C_i\cup C_j|\) and mean Jaccard similarity is \(\bar J\). Claim instability/flip rate is the pairwise probability of different structured Annex IV statements: \(F=1-\sum_c n_c(n_c-1)/(N(N-1))\), claimed to match brute-force tests; modal share is \(\pi^*=\max_c n_c/N\). Within-group flip rate \(F_{within}(G)\) is defined for conditioning groups and is said to reduce to Eq. 2 when \(G\) is empty, though the written formula seems undefined in that case.

Section 5 fixes the claim map φ as pre-registered, deterministic, and not LLM-generated. It defines two maps/addressees: φ_overseer uses Annex IV 2(e) and 3 with Article 14(4)(c), keyed first on dominant layer band, then size class, then ranked input segment; φ_affected uses Article 86(1) and leads with input segment. Granularities are nested: finer claims refine, not contradict, coarser ones.

Size bins were selected by a calibration rule from a measured node-count curve, not to maximize flip rate. Table 1 reports sensitivity to binning: committed bins F=0.7316; thresholds × 0.5, 0.8, 0.9 give 0.7448, 0.7435, 0.7394; 1.1, 1.25, 1.5, 2 give 0.7289, 0.7314, 0.7308, 0.7232; equal thirds 0.7018; deciles 0.7719; no size term (COARSE) 0.5733. The text says four alternatives exceed the committed bins, and the overall range across binnings is about 0.70 to 0.77.

Section 6 says the study uses GPT-2 small on indirect object identification for comparability and a random baseline. The pre-registered grid has seven discovery objectives, seven ablation operators, four corruption distributions nested within five operators that read them, four metrics, three thresholds, two prompt variants, and five seeds, yielding 1,540 discovery cells and 18,480 specifications. Corruption is nested, not crossed, because two operators never read the corrupt distribution. The analysis plan and both abstracts were committed before the confirmatory sweep; an append-only file tracks deviations and timing. Uncertainty is estimated with a nonparametric bootstrap over specifications (not pairs), B=10,000, with F and J̄ treated as U-statistics.

Two exclusions are fixed before seeing circuits: one objective fails completely, with all 220 cells erroring because mean squared error is computed against an integral target; this leaves 6 objectives, 1,320 cells, and 15,840 specifications. A metric-relative threshold rule discards 8,279 of 15,840 specifications (52.3%), unevenly across metrics. Table 2 reports kept/discarded by metric: comprehensiveness 3,947/13 (0.003 discard rate), KL divergence 1,467/2,493 (0.630), logit difference 1,270/2,690 (0.679), sufficiency 877/3,083 (0.779). It compares median observed overlap to a random expectation of 0.0031 at size 200 and 0.008 at size 500.

Section 7.2 says flip rate is 0.7316, above the 0.20 threshold; modal share is π* = 0.4109, and evidence fails filability at all pre-registered tolerances. Table 4 lists 9 claim classes with shares summing to 1; the top two are early layers/distributed (0.4109) and late layers/sparse (0.2848). Paper argues circuit evidence should be regulatorily usable only if analysts reach compatible conclusions. It cites EU AI Act Annex IV point 2(b) and 2(e), and Article 86(1), and frames mechanistic interpretability/circuit discovery as the technical basis for filings. The study measures how regulatory claims vary across defensible analytic specifications and proposes a standards-body decision rule. Contributions listed: (i) a pre-registered multiverse over seven circuit-discovery axes with all levels from published implementations and a deterministic map from circuits to Annex IV statements; (ii) a filability criterion π*≥1−α, where π* is modal claim share and α is permitted disagreement tolerance; (iii) evidence that instability persists even after standardizing any single axis, removing circuit size from the claim, and holding size fixed; (iv) a methodological point that pooled statistics can invert when specifications select objects of different sizes, with three inversions shown. Earlier results/numbers to track: 15,840 specifications on GPT-2 small indirect object identification, 7,561 yielded a claim; claim flip rate 73.2% (95% CI 0.725–0.738), modal claim share 41.1%; standardizing the metric lowers flip rate to 59.4%; removing circuit size and holding size fixed lowers it to 27.1% (95% CI 0.255–0.286); median circuit overlap 4%; functional agreement adjusted for chance is near zero / Cohen’s κ 0.015. Related work situates the paper among work on non-identifiability, faithfulness-metric sensitivity, structural vs functional circuit differences, variance estimation, auditing standards, multiverse analysis, and metric inflation. The paper positions its contribution as downstream from prior non-identifiability work: measuring the regulatory cost of explanation instability when an explanation is filed. It says Miller et al. showed ablation-based faithfulness scores are highly sensitive to methodological choices; the paper extends this across seven axes and connects it to regulatory statements. Bayat Makou et al. are used to motivate the concern that structurally different circuits may implement the same computation; the paper says later functional analysis will address this. The paper also cites work on estimator variance, auditing standards, standardized evaluation, and multiverse/specification-curve methods, and says explanation stability is the kind of claim analytic flexibility can manufacture. Hsia et al. are cited for the point that sufficiency and comprehensiveness can be inflated without changing predictions or explanations; the paper says two of its four metrics have this issue. Section 3 explicitly frames the paper’s limits: it does not claim discovered circuits are random, that filings differ without mechanism differences, that the same mechanism is merely re-dressed, that seeds reflect nondeterminism, or that results generalize to scale. Section 4 defines the formal setup. A specification is s=(o,a,d,m,τ,P,r,g), with axes objective, ablation operator, corruption distribution, evaluation metric, size threshold, prompt variant, seed, and granularity/statement resolution. G7U maps a discovered circuit C(s)⊆E to structured Annex IV statements; Y3W concerns agreement among claims, not the correctness of a specification. The GPT-2 small / Q7V factorised graph has |E|=32,491 edges, 144 attention heads, 12 MLPs, 156 total components, and output receives all 157 non-terminal sources. Circuit instability D(s_i,s_j) is 1 minus Jaccard similarity. Claim instability F is the Gini–Simpson disagreement probability over claim classes, with a within-group conditioned version F_within(G). Empty G reduces exactly to F. Y3W gives a claim-class ceiling F≤1−1/k; with 9 observed classes the ceiling is 0.8889 and the observed fraction of ceiling is 82.3%.

Section 5 (G7U) focuses on statement mappings and size-binning sensitivity. The paper says the size bins were fixed by a committed calibration rule on a measured node-count curve, not chosen to optimize F. Table 1 reports F for alternative binnings: committed bins 0.7316; thresholds ×0.5 0.7448; ×0.8 0.7435; ×0.9 0.7394; ×1.1 0.7289; ×1.25 0.7314; ×1.5 0.7308; ×2 0.7232; equal thirds 0.7018; deciles 0.7719; no size term (E7R) 0.5733. The stated sensitivity range across factor-four binnings is 0.70 to 0.77. It says four alternatives exceed the committed result, including halving thresholds. Regulatory addressees determine two mappings: D9P (overseer) orders dominant layer band, size class, and ranked input segment; L3X (affected) leads with input segment. The resolutions are E7R/COARSE (coarsest), K8Z/MEDIUM, and V2H/FINE, described as nested so refinement cannot contradict the coarser statement. The claim map φ is pre-registered, published deterministic code rather than language-model output.

steps.notes_before: Section 6 describes the method. The grid is said to include seven objectives, seven operators, four corruption distributions nested within five operators, four metrics (T9V, H2W/KL divergence, N6C/logit difference, U4J), three thresholds, two prompt variants, and five seeds, yielding 1,540 discovery cells and 18,480 pre-registered specifications. Two operators never read corruption. Pre-registration and an append-only deviations file are described as being in place before confirmatory analysis. Statistics use a nonparametric bootstrap over specifications with 10,000 resamples and no specification-level p-values. One objective fails entirely in the verbatim library, leaving 1,320 realised discovery cells and 15,840 realised specifications; 8,279 specifications admit no circuit, giving a 52.3% discard rate. Table 2 reports metric-specific kept/discarded counts; the listed “Rate” values are actually discard fractions (e.g., T9V kept 3,947 and discarded 13, so the rate shown as 0.003 is discard rate, not retention).

steps.notes_before: Section 7 reports four registered outcomes: J6D premise holds at 0.1396 [0.1377, 0.1418]; X4R claim instability is 0.7316 [0.7247, 0.7380] and exceeds the 0.20 threshold; Q2F is separated from the random null (outcome rejected); Z8N pooled functional gap is 0.3344 [0.3297, 0.3394] and exceeds 0.10. Section 7.1 says claim-producing specifications total 7,561, across 3,218 distinct circuits and 28,580,580 pairs; median circuit size is 200 edges, median shared-edge fraction 4%, median D is 0.960, and observed/chance overlap is about 45x. Section 7.2 says pair disagreement is 73.2% with CI 0.725 to 0.738; the most frequent category is early layers/distributed at 41.09%, with late layers/sparse second at 28.48%. This part presents a table of addressee/granularity rows: L3X and D9P over E7R/K8Z/V2H. Notable values include L3X/E7R F=0.3950, π*=0.7291, Y3W=no; D9P/K8Z F=0.7316, π*=0.4109, Y3W=no; D9P/V2H F=0.7681, π*=0.4109, Y3W=no. A small table gives coarsest L3X percentage disagreement = 39.5%.

Claims/evidence state: disagreement exceeds threshold (73.2% overall, lower bound 0.7247 vs 0.20); the top two claim classes are early/distributed (3,107; 41.09%) and late/sparse (2,153; 28.48%); the early aggregate reproduces the coarsest overseer modal share (47.9% matches Table 5 D9P/E7R π*=0.4788); no registered combination permits filing because all six Y3W entries are “no” and none reach π*≥0.80; L3X/E7R is cited as 39.5% with π*=0.7291.

Section 7.3 says metric standardisation removes the most instability but no axis rescues filing. Table 6 residual F values are 0.5939 (metric), 0.7014 (ablation operator), 0.7018 (discovery objective), 0.7070 (threshold), 0.7092 (corruption), 0.7232 (prompt), and 0.7307 (seed). The REML decomposition on log10 selected-circuit-size is dominated by ablation-corruption interaction (78.8%), with residual 11.5%, ablation 4.4%, threshold 4.1%, and metric 0.7%.

Section 7.4 reports a size-free claim at fixed size: F=0.2706, CI 0.2550–0.2859, corresponding to 27.1% (also 27% in discussion precision), still above the 0.20 threshold.

Section 7.5 compares discovered circuits to A6N: pooled discovered F=0.7316 vs A6N 0.6774; at fixed size K8Z discovered 0.2746 vs 0.4230; at fixed size E7R discovered 0.2706 vs 0.3822. The text says fixed-size comparison reverses the pooled ordering while discovered circuits still fail Y3W.

errors.claim: “Instability lives entirely below 2,000 edges.”

errors.explanation: The caption/generalization says instability is confined to sizes below 2,000, but the table itself shows a nonzero instability value at 2,000.

steps.notes_before: Section 7.5/Table 7 report within-size results for K8Z comparing discovery vs A6N across sizes 10 to 10,000. A6N is nonzero up to 500 edges (e.g., 500: F=0.1421) and collapses to F=0.0000 with one class at 1,000, 2,000, 5,000, and 10,000. Discovery remains nonzero through 2,000 edges (e.g., 1,000: F=0.5133; 2,000: F=0.5714) and collapses to F=0.0000 at 5,000 and 10,000. The caption says 2,692 of 7,561 specifications contribute no flips. Section 7.6 then argues that pooled functional instability is 0.3972, but agreement/kappa are low (0.6028 agreement, 0.0146 kappa) and the pooled gap is not uniform across sizes: 6 of 10 sizes fail the gap threshold, 5 sizes have negative gaps, and the pooled gap is said to be carried by the 500–2,000 edge band.

Section 8 introduces the Y3W protocol for circuit-derived filed claims. It requires: (1) declaring S, the space of defensible analytic axes and levels, with citations; (2) declaring φ as published deterministic code, not a language model; (3) computing π* = max_c n_c/N over S and F; (4) passing evidence at tolerance α iff π* ≥ 1−α; and (5) reporting π*, F, discard rate per axis level, and within-group decomposition of every pooled statistic. It also says a filing unable to state its own π* is asserted, not audited, and that implementability depends only on a declared space and measured agreement, not on regulatory adjudication of analytic correctness.

Section 9 limitations: the study is restricted to one model and one task; generalisation is untested, and a committed second-model study (M9B / Pythia-160m, same task) is planned but unrun. That second model uses a 924-cell grid identical on every axis except seed levels (3 instead of 5); replication/refutation criteria were pre-fixed. Circuit size is treated as an outcome, not an axis; size conditioning affects F, the null-comparison direction, and the functional-gap sign. Every pooled statistic is reported with within-size decomposition. The multiverse is wider than the measured instrument space: C4Y/optimal ablation is defensible but unsupported and excluded, making measured F a lower bound relative to the field’s full defensible choice set. Discard rate is high and uneven; retained metric imbalance is a reported-set property and was not adjusted away. The bootstrap is invalid for one reported family because conditioning groups of 2–5 specs retain dominating self-pairs; unusable intervals are replaced by point estimates, and no bias-corrected estimator was built. Key evidence values: size-free claim F=0.2706 vs Table 6 smallest residual F=0.5939; pooled comparison 0.7316 vs 0.6774; fixed-size K8Z 0.2746 vs 0.4230; fixed-size E7R 0.2706 vs 0.3822; functional diagnostic shows 5 sizes with negative gap and 6/10 failing the threshold; discard rates include 52.3% overall and 0.003, 0.630, 0.679, 0.779 in Table 2.

The paper frames regulatory documentation/explanation requirements as agreement between analysts, operationalized via a standards-body decision rule and Annex IV / Article 86. It studies how claims about circuits move across defensible analytic specifications using a pre-registered crossed design and only published implementations; deterministic code converts circuits into structured Annex IV statements. The design standardizes axes, removes dependence on size, and conditions comparisons on size. The introduction says three pooled statistics computed before size conditioning invert when the selected objects differ in size. No new interpretability method is proposed; the target is the filing standard.

Related work: non-uniqueness of explanations (Méloux et al. [6]); faithfulness scores sensitive to design choices (Miller et al. [8]); structurally different circuits can implement the same computation (Bayat Makou et al. [1], W5T/phantom specialisation); mechanistic interpretability can be framed as statistical estimation with estimator variance (Méloux et al. [7]); auditability work motivates measurement/criteria, not a standards proposal (Lan et al. [4], Sharkey et al. [10], Mueller et al. [9]); multiverse/specification-curve methods transfer to reporting across defensible analytic choices (Steegen et al. [13], Simonsohn et al. [12], Simmons et al. [11]); U4J and T9V can be inflated without changing predictions or explanations (Hsia et al. [3]). The section says these effects motivate measuring regulatory propagation across analytic flexibility.

Section 3 clarifies what the paper is not claiming: discovered circuits carry information and, at fixed size, beat the A6N size-matched random null baseline (reported comparison rows: K8Z 0.2746 vs 0.4230; E7R 0.2706 vs 0.3822). It also says their mechanisms differ substantially and are functionally uncorrelated (structural diagnostic median D=0.960; functional diagnostic Cohen’s kappa 0.0146). The seed is described as selecting sampled prompts and measuring evaluation-set variability, not nondeterminism; no scale claim is made.

Section 4 defines the paper’s formal objects. A specification is s=(o,a,d,m,τ,P,r,g), where each axis is a published analytic choice: discovery objective, ablation operator, corruption distribution, evaluation metric, size threshold, prompt variant, seed, and granularity. The claim map G7U turns discovery output C(s)⊆E into structured Annex IV statements; Y3W is about agreement among claims rather than correctness of a chosen specification.

For Q7V / GPT-2 small, the paper states the factorised graph has separate query, key, and value inputs and |E|=32,491 edges, checked by instrument and by counting. It says there are 144 attention heads and 12 MLPs, 156 components total, and output receives all 157 non-terminal sources.

Circuit instability is defined as 1 minus Jaccard similarity: D(s_i,s_j)=1-|C_i∩C_j|/|C_i∪C_j|. Claim instability F is defined as the probability that two distinct specifications yield different claim classes, with the Gini–Simpson form F=1-Σ_c n_c(n_c-1)/N(N-1). A within-group version F_within(G) weights pairs rather than groups and reduces to the unconditioned form when no grouping is applied.

The paper then states a ceiling on disagreement from the finite number of claim classes: with k classes, F≤1-1/k. The observed count is 9 classes, ceiling 0.8889, and observed fraction of ceiling 82.3%.

steps.notes_before: Section 4 formalism: a specification is \(s=(o,a,d,m,\tau,P,r,g)\), where \(o\)=objective, \(a\)=ablation operator, \(d\)=corruption distribution, \(m\)=evaluation metric, \(\tau\)=size threshold, \(P\)=prompt variant, \(r\)=seed, and \(g\)=granularity/claim-detail. Section 8 introduces the filability protocol. It requires: (1) declaring the specification space \(\mathcal S\) with cited levels for each analytic axis; (2) declaring a deterministic claim map \(\varphi\) as published code (not a language model); (3) computing \(\pi^*=\max_c n_c/N\) over \(\mathcal S\) and computing \(F\) via Equation 2; (4) deeming a claim filable at tolerance \(\alpha\) if \(\pi^*\ge 1-\alpha\); and (5) reporting \(\pi^*\), \(F\), discard rate by axis level, and any within-group decomposition of pooled statistics. It emphasizes that a filing must state its own \(\pi^*\), and the regulator need not choose the correct analytic choice.

Section 9 lists limitations. Generalisation is still untested because only one model and one task were run; a pre-registered second-model replication on Pythia-160m (924-cell grid) and a second task are designed but unrun. The second-model plan uses the same axes except seeds with three levels instead of five, and the authors say they will report either outcome. Circuit size is treated as an outcome, not an axis: the threshold rule changes circuit size and strongly affects F, with fixing size reducing F from 0.7316 to 0.2746; pooled statistics are reported with within-size decompositions. The instrument omits at least one defensible operator (optimal ablation [5]), so the measured F is only a lower bound relative to the field’s full defensible choices. The discard rate is 52.3% and the surviving pool is metric-imbalanced; they fixed the threshold rule in advance and did no repairs. For conditioning groups of size two to five specifications, bootstrap intervals are invalid because retained self-pairs dominate, so only point estimates are reported with a diagnostic.

Section 10 argues the evidence should be given measured, not assumed, weight. It says standardising the metric axis reduces the 0.7316 flip rate by 0.1377 to 0.5939 (CI 0.5803–0.6063), so one-axis standardisation is insufficient. It also says one of seven documented, publicly exported discovery objectives does not run on the library’s canonical task; all 220 cells in that arm fail, and this is reported as a discard rather than the headline result. The section frames the protocol’s π* and F as the basis for measuring evidentiary weight, but gives no numerical cost comparison.

Paper topic: explanation multiplicity in circuit-level interpretability. The study uses a crossed multiverse design over analytic choices, with deterministic code (G7U/claim map φ) turning discovered circuits into structured Annex IV statements. Key reported results: 7,561 claim-producing specifications; pairwise claim disagreement F = 0.7316. No single-axis standardisation fits registered tolerances. If size is removed from statements and comparisons are conditioned on size, disagreement drops to 0.2706. Discovered circuits outperform size-matched random baselines at fixed size, reversing the pooled comparison. Functional measurements do not support treating circuits as interchangeable mechanisms; size conditioning also changes/qualifies the pooled functional-gap result. Scope: one model (GPT-2 small, Q7V) and one task (indirect object identification, Z4K); a planned second-model study on Pythia-160m was not run. Abstract also states filability Y3W fails under plausible conformity-assessment tolerances, standardisation and size controls do not remove the failure, and applicability beyond the single model/task remains untested. Claim classes are structured Annex IV statements; filability Y3W requires the largest claim-class share π* to meet a tolerance. The factorised graph for GPT-2 small has 32,491 edges, 12 heads per block, 144 heads total, and 12 MLPs. Section 4 defines the formal setup. A specification is s=(o,a,d,m,τ,P,r,g), with axes objective, ablation operator, corruption distribution, evaluation metric, size threshold, prompt variant, seed, and granularity/statement resolution. G7U maps a discovered circuit C(s)⊆E to structured Annex IV statements; Y3W concerns agreement among claims, not the correctness of a specification. The GPT-2 small / Q7V factorised graph has |E|=32,491 edges, 144 attention heads, 12 MLPs, 156 total components, and output receives all 157 non-terminal sources. Circuit instability D(s_i,s_j) is 1 minus Jaccard similarity. Claim instability F is the Gini–Simpson disagreement probability over claim classes, with a within-group conditioned version F_within(G). Empty G reduces exactly to F. Y3W gives a claim-class ceiling F≤1−1/k; with 9 observed classes the ceiling is 0.8889 and the observed fraction of ceiling is 82.3%.
