Section 8 defines the Y3W filing protocol. For a circuit-derived filed claim c, a filer must declare the defensible analytic space \(\mathcal S\), publish deterministic code \(\varphi\), compute \(\pi^*=\max_c n_c/N\) over \(\mathcal S\) and F, and evidence passes only if \(\pi^* \ge 1-\alpha\). Required reporting includes \(\pi^*\), F, discard rate per axis level, and within-group decomposition of every pooled statistic. It also says a filing that cannot state its own \(\pi^*\) is asserted rather than audited, and that implementability depends on a declared space plus measured agreement, not on adjudicating analytic correctness.

Section 9 says the study’s conclusions are limited by scope, instrument, exclusions, and some bootstrap intervals. It emphasizes one model/one task; generalisation is untested. A committed second-model study is planned but unrun: M9B/Pythia-160m, same task, 924-cell grid, identical except three vs five seed levels, with replication/refutation criteria fixed in advance. A second task is also designed but unrun. Circuit size is treated as an outcome, not an axis; size conditioning affects F, null-comparison direction, and functional-gap sign. Every pooled statistic is reported with within-size decomposition. Unsupported defensible choices such as C4Y/optimal ablation are outside the measured space, so measured F is a lower bound on the broader defensible choice set. The retained metric imbalance is reported, not adjusted away; the threshold was fixed in advance and no failed item was repaired. For bootstrap families with conditioning groups of only 2–5 specifications, dominating self-pairs make intervals unusable; these are replaced by point estimates with diagnostics, and no bias-corrected estimator was built. Evidence cited: size-free claim fixed-size F=0.2706 vs Table 6 smallest residual F=0.5939; null-comparison direction changes in Section 7.5; functional-gap sign varies across 5 sizes and 6/10 fail the threshold; discard rates 52.3% and 0.003/0.630/0.679/0.779; bootstrap groups of size 2–5.

Section 10 argues for measured evidentiary weight rather than presumed reliability. It says standardising one metric axis is insufficient: complete metric standardisation does not resolve the filing problem, and no single knob suffices. The instrument has execution and retention issues: the failed objective is documented/exported but cannot execute on the library’s canonical task, and the discard rate reflects tooling maturity. The discussion frames interpretability evidence as having measurable weight. Evidence cited: Table 6 best residual F=0.5939 (95% CI 0.5803–0.6063; 59.4%); the Grid consequence table with 220 failed objective cells, 8,279 specifications admitting no circuit, and 52.3% discard rate; Section 7.5 Comparison table with fixed-size K8Z 0.2746 vs random 0.4230 and fixed-size E7R 0.2706 vs random 0.3822. It asserts measurement is cheap relative to discovery, but supplies no numerical cost comparison.

steps.notes_before: Section 4 formalism: a specification is \(s=(o,a,d,m,\tau,P,r,g)\), where \(o\)=objective, \(a\)=ablation operator, \(d\)=corruption distribution, \(m\)=evaluation metric, \(\tau\)=size threshold, \(P\)=prompt variant, \(r\)=seed, and \(g\)=granularity/claim-detail. Discovery outputs a circuit \(C(s)\subseteq E\); for GPT-2 small’s factorised graph, \(|E|=32{,}491\). The paper gives a closed-form component count: 144 attention heads + 12 MLPs = 156 components, and says the output receives from 157 non-terminal sources. Circuit instability is \(D=1-|C_i\cap C_j|/|C_i\cup C_j|\) and mean Jaccard similarity is \(\bar J\). Claim instability/flip rate is the pairwise probability of different structured Annex IV statements: \(F=1-\sum_c n_c(n_c-1)/(N(N-1))\), claimed to match brute-force tests; modal share is \(\pi^*=\max_c n_c/N\). Section 5 fixes the claim map φ as pre-registered, deterministic, and not LLM-generated. It defines two maps/addressees: φ_overseer uses Annex IV 2(e) and 3 with Article 14(4)(c), keyed first on dominant layer band, then size class, then ranked input segment; φ_affected uses Article 86(1) and leads with input segment. Granularities are nested: finer claims refine, not contradict, coarser ones.

Size bins were selected by a calibration rule from a measured node-count curve, not to maximize flip rate. Table 1 reports sensitivity to binning: committed bins F=0.7316; thresholds × 0.5, 0.8, 0.9 give 0.7448, 0.7435, 0.7394; 1.1, 1.25, 1.5, 2 give 0.7289, 0.7314, 0.7308, 0.7232; equal thirds 0.7018; deciles 0.7719; no size term (COARSE) 0.5733. The text says four alternatives exceed the committed bins, and the overall range across binnings is about 0.70 to 0.77.

Section 6 says the study uses GPT-2 small on indirect object identification for comparability and a random baseline. The pre-registered grid has seven discovery objectives, seven ablation operators, four corruption distributions nested within five operators that read them, four metrics, three thresholds, two prompt variants, and five seeds, yielding 1,540 discovery cells and 18,480 specifications. Corruption is nested, not crossed, because two operators never read the corrupt distribution. The analysis plan and both abstracts were committed before the confirmatory sweep; an append-only file tracks deviations and timing. Uncertainty is estimated with a nonparametric bootstrap over specifications (not pairs), B=10,000, with F and J̄ treated as U-statistics.

Two exclusions are fixed before seeing circuits: one objective fails completely, with all 220 cells erroring because mean squared error is computed against an integral target; this leaves 6 objectives, 1,320 cells, and 15,840 specifications. Section 4 defines the formal setup. A specification is s=(o,a,d,m,τ,P,r,g), with axes objective, ablation operator, corruption distribution, evaluation metric, size threshold, prompt variant, seed, and granularity/statement resolution. G7U maps a discovered circuit C(s)⊆E to structured Annex IV statements; Y3W concerns agreement among claims, not the correctness of a specification. Circuit instability D(s_i,s_j) is 1 minus Jaccard similarity. Claim instability F is the Gini–Simpson disagreement probability over claim classes, with a within-group conditioned version F_within(G). Paper claims to study whether mechanistic-interpretability evidence survives defensible analytic variation in circuit discovery. It pre-registers a crossed grid of seven analytic axes, using levels from a published implementation, on GPT-2 small and the indirect object identification task. Across 15,840 pre-registered specifications, 7,561 produced a claim; the derived statement flips across 73.2% of specification pairs (95% CI 0.725–0.738), and the modal claim covers 41.1% of the space. Standardising the evaluation metric reduces the flip rate to 49.4%. Removing circuit size from the claim and fixing it leaves 27.1% (95% CI 0.255–0.286), still above the pre-registered threshold. The circuits are structurally near-disjoint (median Jaccard overlap 4%) and functionally uncorrelated (Cohen’s kappa 0.015). The paper also says one of seven documented discovery objectives does not execute on the library’s canonical task, and that the study is limited to one model and one task.

The paper frames auditability as two auditors reaching the same conclusion and argues mechanistic interpretability/circuit discovery could supply the technical content needed for regulatory filings only if a second analyst using the same system and tool would produce a compatible account. Contributions: (i) a pre-registered multiverse over seven analytic axes of circuit discovery, with levels from a published implementation and a deterministic map from circuits to Annex IV statements; (ii) a filability criterion, π* ≥ 1−α, with a measured value on a canonical task; (iii) evidence that instability persists under strong controls, including standardising one axis, removing circuit size from the claim, and fixing size; (iv) a methodological point that pooled statistics can invert when specifications select objects of different sizes. Prior notes: study uses GPT-2 small and the indirect object identification task; across 15,840 specifications, 7,561 produced a claim; the derived statement flips across 73.2% of specification pairs (95% CI 0.725–0.738), modal claim covers 41.1% of space; standardising the evaluation metric reduces flip rate to 49.4%; removing circuit size from the claim and fixing it leaves 27.1% (95% CI 0.255–0.286), still above the pre-registered threshold; circuits are structurally near-disjoint (median Jaccard overlap 4%) and functionally uncorrelated (Cohen’s kappa 0.015); one of seven documented discovery objectives does not execute on the library’s canonical task; the study is limited to one model and one task.

Related-work positioning: the paper cites prior work on non-identifiability (Méloux et al. 6), metric sensitivity in ablation-based faithfulness (Miller et al. 8), structure-vs-function/phantom specialisation (Bayat Makou et al. 1), variance as estimation (Méloux et al. 7), auditability/standardisation (Lan et al. 4; Mueller et al. 9; Sharkey et al. 10), multiverse/specification-curve methods (Steegen et al. 13; Simonsohn et al. 12; Simmons et al. 11), and explanation metrics under optimisation pressure (Hsia et al. 3). The paper’s response to the structure-vs-function objection is that Section 7.6 uses a functional measurement and concludes the circuits are not functionally interchangeable. It also notes that two of the four evaluation metrics are sufficiency and comprehensiveness, motivating reporting discard rates per metric rather than pooling silently.

The paper’s Section 3 says it is not claiming: discovered circuits are no better than random; instead at fixed size they are more stable than size-matched random null (0.2746 vs 0.4230). It also says mechanisms differ substantially, with functional instability 0.3972 pooled and 0.4777 at the smallest circuits. Cohen’s kappa is 0.0146, implying functionally uncorrelated circuits. Random seeds are not blamed; the seed only affects which prompts are sampled, so variability is in the evaluation set rather than nondeterminism. The paper remains about one model and one task.

Section 4 formalizes a specification as s=(o,a,d,m,τ,P,r,g): objective, ablation operator, corruption distribution, evaluation metric, size threshold, prompt variant, seed, and granularity; each axis level comes from a published implementation. Circuit discovery returns C(s)⊆E. For GPT-2 small with the factorised graph and separate Q/K/V inputs, |E|=32,491, confirmed both instrumentally and by a closed-form count. The model has 144 attention heads and 12 MLPs, so 156 components total. Circuit instability is defined by Jaccard distance D(s_i,s_j)=1−|C_i∩C_j|/|C_i∪C_j|, with mean Jaccard similarity ̄J over unordered pairs. Claim instability uses flip rate F as the unbiased Gini–Simpson probability that two draws without replacement differ; within-group version F_within(G) weights all pairs equally and reduces to Equation 2 when G is empty. Filability at tolerance α means π*≥1−α. The paper notes the ceiling F≤1−1/k for k claim classes; with nine observed classes the ceiling is 0.8889, and observed F=0.7316, i.e. 82.3% of the ceiling.

Section 5 defines the claim map φ as fixed in preregistration, deterministic, and published; it is not language-model generated. There are two versions: φ_overseer, based on Annex IV 2(e) and 3 plus Article 14(4)(c), keyed on dominant layer band, then size class, then ranked input segment; and φ_affected, based on Article 86(1), keyed first on input segment. Three granularities are nested so finer claims refine coarser ones. The paper defends the chosen size bins as coming from a committed calibration rule, not being tuned to maximize instability.

Table 1 reports flip rate F under alternative size binnings. Committed bins give F=0.7316. Alternatives: thresholds ×0.5 gives 0.7448; ×0.8, 0.7435; ×0.9, 0.7394; ×1.1, 0.7289; ×1.25, 0.7314; ×1.5, 0.7308; ×2, 0.7232; equal thirds, 0.7018; deciles, 0.7719; no size term (COARSE), 0.5733. The text says four alternative binnings are higher than the committed bins, and the range across binnings differing by a factor of four is 0.70 to 0.77.

Section 6 uses GPT-2 small on indirect object identification. The pre-registered grid is described as 7 discovery objectives, 7 ablation operators, 4 corruption distributions nested within 5 operators that read them, 4 metrics, 3 thresholds, 2 prompt variants, and 5 seeds, totaling 1,540 discovery cells and 18,480 specifications. Discovery uses edge attribution patching and integrated edge gradients; the four corruption levels come from Wang et al. The analysis plan was committed and tagged before the confirmatory sweep, with deviations logged append-only.

Inference uses no p-values; uncertainty comes from a nonparametric bootstrap over specifications with B=10,000 because F and J̄ are U-statistics over dependent pairs. One discovery objective fails entirely: all 220 of its cells runtime-error in the library, leaving a realized grid of 6 objectives, 1,320 cells, and 15,840 specifications. Table 4 has nine overseer claim classes: top shares are early distributed 0.4109 and late sparse 0.2848; aggregated by layer the shares are 47.9% early, 43.6% late, 8.5% middle. The section defines the paper’s formal setup. A specification is s=(o,a,d,m,τ,P,r,g), where the components are discovery objective, ablation operator, corruption distribution, metric, size threshold, prompt variant, seed, and granularity; all levels are said to come from published implementations. Discovery returns a circuit C(s)⊆E. For GPT-2 small’s factorised graph, |E|=32,491, and the text claims an independent count confirms this using closed-form graph counts: 156 components total (144 attention heads + 12 MLPs), with 157 non-terminal sources feeding the output.

Circuit instability D(s_i,s_j) is defined as 1 minus edge-set Jaccard similarity. Claim instability F is defined as the pairwise probability that two specifications yield different structured claims, via the unbiased Gini–Simpson formula. The paper also defines modal share π* and within-group flip rate F_within(G), which reduces exactly to F when G is empty.

Filability is defined by modal share meeting a tolerance α: evidence is filable iff π*≥1−α. The maximum possible flip rate is stated as 1−1/k for k classes; with nine observed classes the ceiling is 0.8889, and the observed F is 0.7316, i.e. 82.3% of that ceiling.

Section 4 defines the formal setup. A specification is s=(o,a,d,m,τ,P,r,g), with axes objective, ablation operator, corruption distribution, evaluation metric, size threshold, prompt variant, seed, and granularity/statement resolution. G7U maps a discovered circuit C(s)⊆E to structured Annex IV statements; Y3W concerns agreement among claims, not the correctness of a specification. The GPT-2 small / Q7V factorised graph has |E|=32,491 edges, 144 attention heads, 12 MLPs, 156 total components, and output receives all 157 non-terminal sources. Circuit instability D(s_i,s_j) is 1 minus Jaccard similarity. Claim instability F is the Gini–Simpson disagreement probability over claim classes, with a within-group conditioned version F_within(G). Empty G reduces exactly to F. Y3W gives a claim-class ceiling F≤1−1/k; with 9 observed classes the ceiling is 0.8889 and the observed fraction of ceiling is 82.3%.

Section 5 (G7U) focuses on statement mappings and size-binning sensitivity. The paper says the size bins were fixed by a committed calibration rule on a measured node-count curve, not chosen to optimize F. Paper title: “Explanation Multiplicity: Circuit-Level Interpretability.” Abstract claims that circuit-derived regulatory evidence fails Y3W across defensible analytic variation/tolerances acceptable to a conformity-assessment body. It says competent analysts using the same system and tool can reach incompatible statements under different defensible settings. Standardisation and size controls do not remove the failure; structural and functional disagreement rule out merely reworded mechanisms. The abstract also states applicability beyond one model and one task has not been tested. Introduction adds that an audit requires two auditors to reach the same conclusion; EU AI Act documentation/explanation requirements are the regulatory target. Mechanistic interpretability’s mature instrument is circuit discovery, which returns a subgraph said to explain behaviour. The study uses a pre-registered crossed design with published implementations only; circuits are turned into structured Annex IV statements deterministically. Controls standardise axes, remove claim-size dependence, and condition on size. Three pooled statistics invert when selected objects differ in size. No improved discovery method is proposed; the objection is to the standard presumed by filing current evidence, not to interpretability itself.

Part 4 (What this paper is not claiming): The paper clarifies that discovered circuits carry information and, at fixed size, outperform a size-matched random null baseline (A6N), but the underlying mechanisms differ substantially and are functionally uncorrelated. It also says the seed changes the sampled prompts, so this is evaluation-set variability rather than nondeterminism, and that there is no scale claim.

Part 4 (Formalism): A specification is s=(o,a,d,m,τ,P,r,g): discovery objective, ablation operator, corruption distribution, evaluation metric, size threshold, prompt variant, seed, granularity; all axis levels are from published implementations. A circuit-to-statement transformation (G7U: claim map) maps discovery output C(s)⊆E, and admissibility (Y3W: filability) is about agreement among claims, not choosing the correct specification. For Q7V’s factorised graph with separate query/key/value inputs, |E|=32,491; the count is said to be independently verified by computation-order counting. Components are 144 attention heads and 12 MLPs, 156 total; output receives all 157 non-terminal sources. Circuit instability is D(s_i,s_j)=1-|C_i∩C_j|/|C_i∪C_j|, with mean Jaccard similarity ̄J over unordered pairs. Claim instability uses F=1-Σ_c n_c(n_c-1)/N(N-1), described as an unbiased Gini–Simpson disagreement probability for distinct draws without replacement. A within-axis version F_within(G) weights pairs equally and reduces exactly to F when G is empty. Y3W notes a ceiling F≤1-1/k depending on available claim classes; the table reports 9 observed classes, ceiling 0.8889, and observed fraction of ceiling 82.3%.

Section 4 defines the formal setup. A specification is s=(o,a,d,m,τ,P,r,g), with axes objective, ablation operator, corruption distribution, evaluation metric, size threshold, prompt variant, seed, and granularity/statement resolution. G7U maps a discovered circuit C(s)⊆E to structured Annex IV statements; Y3W concerns agreement among claims, not the correctness of a specification. The GPT-2 small / Q7V factorised graph has |E|=32,491 edges, 144 attention heads, 12 MLPs, 156 total components, and output receives all 157 non-terminal sources. Circuit instability D(s_i,s_j) is 1 minus Jaccard similarity. Claim instability F is the Gini–Simpson disagreement probability over claim classes, with a within-group conditioned version F_within(G). Empty G reduces exactly to F. Y3W gives a claim-class ceiling F≤1−1/k; with 9 observed classes the ceiling is 0.8889 and the observed fraction of ceiling is 82.3%.

Section 5 (G7U) focuses on statement mappings and size-binning sensitivity. The paper says the size bins were fixed by a committed calibration rule on a measured node-count curve, not chosen to optimize F. Table 1 reports F for alternative binnings: committed bins 0.7316; thresholds ×0.5 0.7448; ×0.8 0.7435; ×0.9 0.7394; ×1.1 0.7289; ×1.25 0.7314; ×1.5 0.7308; ×2 0.7232; equal thirds 0.7018; deciles 0.7719; no size term (E7R) 0.5733. The stated sensitivity range across factor-four binnings is 0.70 to 0.77. It says four alternatives exceed the committed result, including halving thresholds. Regulatory addressees determine two mappings: D9P (overseer) orders dominant layer band, size class, and ranked input segment; L3X (affected) leads with input segment. The resolutions are E7R/COARSE (coarsest), K8Z/MEDIUM, and V2H/FINE, described as nested so refinement cannot contradict the coarser statement. The claim map φ is pre-registered, published deterministic code rather than language-model output.

steps.notes_before: Section 7.5/Table 7 report within-size results for K8Z comparing discovery vs A6N across sizes 10 to 10,000. Discovery remains nonzero through 2,000 edges (e.g., 1,000: F=0.5133; 2,000: F=0.5714) and collapses to F=0.0000 at 5,000 and 10,000. The caption says 2,692 of 7,561 specifications contribute no flips. Section 7.6 then argues that pooled functional instability is 0.3972, but agreement/kappa are low (0.6028 agreement, 0.0146 kappa) and the pooled gap is not uniform across sizes: 6 of 10 sizes fail the gap threshold, 5 sizes have negative gaps, and the pooled gap is said to be carried by the 500–2,000 edge band.

Section 8 introduces the Y3W protocol for circuit-derived filed claims. It requires: (1) declaring S, the space of defensible analytic axes and levels, with citations; (2) declaring φ as published deterministic code, not a language model; (3) computing π* = max_c n_c/N over S and F; (4) passing evidence at tolerance α iff π* ≥ 1−α; and (5) reporting π*, F, discard rate per axis level, and within-group decomposition of every pooled statistic. It also says a filing unable to state its own π* is asserted, not audited, and that implementability depends only on a declared space and measured agreement, not on regulatory adjudication of analytic correctness.

Section 9 limitations: the study is restricted to one model and one task; generalisation is untested, and a committed second-model study (M9B / Pythia-160m, same task) is planned but unrun. That second model uses a 924-cell grid identical on every axis except seed levels (3 instead of 5); replication/refutation criteria were pre-fixed. Circuit size is treated as an outcome, not an axis; size conditioning affects F, the null-comparison direction, and the functional-gap sign. Every pooled statistic is reported with within-size decomposition. The multiverse is wider than the measured instrument space: C4Y/optimal ablation is defensible but unsupported and excluded, making measured F a lower bound relative to the field’s full defensible choice set. Discard rate is high and uneven; retained metric imbalance is a reported-set property and was not adjusted away. final_notes: Section 11 claims strong reproducibility: the pre-registration is a timestamped commit tagged prereg-p1-confirmatory made before the confirmatory sweep; every reported number traces to a config, seed, and environment fingerprint. The confirmatory sweep used a single environment across all 1,320 cells, verified from the results archive. The code commit was recovered by content-addressed comparison of the uploaded archive with the git tree, with 22 of 22 files identical. The analysis layer runs without a GPU. A verification script recomputes all headline quantities from raw results and matches them with 36 checks and 0 failures, including F computed three ways. errors.claim: “With G empty, it reduces exactly to Equation 2.”
errors.evidence: Equation 3 is \(F_{\text{within}}(G)=1-\frac{\sum_g\sum_c n_{g,c}(n_{g,c}-1)}{\sum_g n_g(n_g-1)}\). If \(G\) is empty, both sums over \(g\) have no terms, so the expression is undefined as written rather than equal to Equation 2.
errors.explanation: The text asserts an exact reduction in the empty-\(G\) case, but the displayed formula has no defined value when there are no conditioning groups unless an extra convention is added.

steps.notes_before: Section 4 formalism: a specification is \(s=(o,a,d,m,\tau,P,r,g)\), where \(o\)=objective, \(a\)=ablation operator, \(d\)=corruption distribution, \(m\)=evaluation metric, \(\tau\)=size threshold, \(P\)=prompt variant, \(r\)=seed, and \(g\)=granularity/claim-detail. Discovery outputs a circuit \(C(s)\subseteq E\); for GPT-2 small’s factorised graph, \(|E|=32{,}491\). The paper gives a closed-form component count: 144 attention heads + 12 MLPs = 156 components, and says the output receives from 157 non-terminal sources. Circuit instability is \(D=1-|C_i\cap C_j|/|C_i\cup C_j|\) and mean Jaccard similarity is \(\bar J\). Claim instability/flip rate is the pairwise probability of different structured Annex IV statements: \(F=1-\sum_c n_c(n_c-1)/(N(N-1))\), claimed to match brute-force tests; modal share is \(\pi^*=\max_c n_c/N\). Within-group flip rate \(F_{within}(G)\) is defined for conditioning groups and is said to reduce to Eq. 2 when \(G\) is empty, though the written formula seems undefined in that case.

Section 5 fixes the claim map φ as pre-registered, deterministic, and not LLM-generated. It defines two maps/addressees: φ_overseer uses Annex IV 2(e) and 3 with Article 14(4)(c), keyed first on dominant layer band, then size class, then ranked input segment; φ_affected uses Article 86(1) and leads with input segment. Granularities are nested: finer claims refine, not contradict, coarser ones.

Size bins were selected by a calibration rule from a measured node-count curve, not to maximize flip rate. Table 1 reports sensitivity to binning: committed bins F=0.7316; thresholds × 0.5, 0.8, 0.9 give 0.7448, 0.7435, 0.7394; 1.1, 1.25, 1.5, 2 give 0.7289, 0.7314, 0.7308, 0.7232; equal thirds 0.7018; deciles 0.7719; no size term (COARSE) 0.5733. The text says four alternatives exceed the committed bins, and the overall range across binnings is about 0.70 to 0.77.

Section 6 says the study uses GPT-2 small on indirect object identification for comparability and a random baseline. The pre-registered grid has seven discovery objectives, seven ablation operators, four corruption distributions nested within five operators that read them, four metrics, three thresholds, two prompt variants, and five seeds, yielding 1,540 discovery cells and 18,480 specifications. Corruption is nested, not crossed, because two operators never read the corrupt distribution. The analysis plan and both abstracts were committed before the confirmatory sweep; an append-only file tracks deviations and timing. Uncertainty is estimated with a nonparametric bootstrap over specifications (not pairs), B=10,000, with F and J̄ treated as U-statistics.

Two exclusions are fixed before seeing circuits: one objective fails completely, with all 220 cells erroring because mean squared error is computed against an integral target; this leaves 6 objectives, 1,320 cells, and 15,840 specifications. A metric-relative threshold rule discards 8,279 of 15,840 specifications (52.3%), unevenly across metrics. Table 2 reports kept/discarded by metric: comprehensiveness 3,947/13 (0.003 discard rate), KL divergence 1,467/2,493 (0.630), logit difference 1,270/2,690 (0.679), sufficiency 877/3,083 (0.779). The surviving pool is 52% comprehensiveness versus 25% by design. Unevenness was disclosed before lock from a six-cell validation slice.

Section 7 reports pre-registered results. Table 3 maps outcomes to results: P0 ̄J = 0.1396 [0.1377, 0.1418], H2 F = 0.7316 [0.7247, 0.7380], H3 is rejected because the data are separated from the random null, and H4 = 0.3344 [0.3297, 0.3394].

Section 7.1 says overlap is low but above chance: mean Jaccard 0.1396 over all 28,580,580 pairs among 7,561 specifications and 3,218 distinct circuits; D quantiles 0.196, 0.788, 0.960, 0.998; median pair shares 4% of edges; 1% of pairs exceed Jaccard 0.8. It compares median observed overlap to a random expectation of 0.0031 at size 200 and 0.008 at size 500.

Section 7.2 says flip rate is 0.7316, above the 0.20 threshold; modal share is π* = 0.4109, and evidence fails filability at all pre-registered tolerances. Table 4 lists 9 claim classes with shares summing to 1; the top two are early layers/distributed (0.4109) and late layers/sparse (0.2848). Aggregated layer shares are 47.9% early, 43.6% late, 8.5% middle; Table 5 says all six addressee-granularity combinations reject filability.

Section 7.3 reports residual flip rates after standardising each axis (Table 6). Residual F values are: evaluation metric 0.5939 (CI 0.5803–0.6063, removes 0.1377), ablation operator 0.7014, discovery objective 0.7018, threshold 0.7070, corruption 0.7092, prompt variant 0.7232, and seed 0.7307. The metric is the largest single reduction but still leaves F well above the 0.20 threshold. The text also says structural variance is mostly from ablation-corruption interaction (78.8%), with 11.5% residual, 4.4% ablation, 4.1% threshold, and 0.7% metric, while claim variance is said to be largest for the metric.

Section 7.4 says that after removing circuit size from the claim and holding size fixed, the result is F=0.2706 (95% CI 0.2550–0.2859), still above the 0.20 threshold.

The part includes Table 5 with addressee/granularity combinations: affected COARSE 0.3950/0.7291, affected MEDIUM 0.6597/0.4875, affected FINE 0.6744/0.4786, overseer COARSE 0.5733/0.4788, overseer MEDIUM 0.7316/0.4109, overseer FINE 0.7681/0.4109; all are marked not filable. Figure 1 captions the overseer-medium specification curve and says the pooled random comparison is confounded by circuit size, to be discussed in Section 7.5.

Section 4 defines the formal setup. errors.claim: “With G empty, it reduces exactly to Equation 2.”
errors.evidence: Equation 3 is \(F_{\text{within}}(G)=1-\frac{\sum_g\sum_c n_{g,c}(n_{g,c}-1)}{\sum_g n_g(n_g-1)}\). If \(G\) is empty, both sums over \(g\) have no terms, so the expression is undefined as written rather than equal to Equation 2.
errors.explanation: The text asserts an exact reduction in the empty-\(G\) case, but the displayed formula has no defined value when there are no conditioning groups unless an extra convention is added.

steps.notes_before: Section 4 formalism: a specification is \(s=(o,a,d,m,\tau,P,r,g)\), where \(o\)=objective, \(a\)=ablation operator, \(d\)=corruption distribution, \(m\)=evaluation metric, \(\tau\)=size threshold, \(P\)=prompt variant, \(r\)=seed, and \(g\)=granularity/claim-detail. Discovery outputs a circuit \(C(s)\subseteq E\); for GPT-2 small’s factorised graph, \(|E|=32{,}491\). The paper gives a closed-form component count: 144 attention heads + 12 MLPs = 156 components, and says the output receives from 157 non-terminal sources. Circuit instability is \(D=1-|C_i\cap C_j|/|C_i\cup C_j|\) and mean Jaccard similarity is \(\bar J\). Claim instability/flip rate is the pairwise probability of different structured Annex IV statements: \(F=1-\sum_c n_c(n_c-1)/(N(N-1))\), claimed to match brute-force tests; modal share is \(\pi^*=\max_c n_c/N\). Within-group flip rate \(F_{within}(G)\) is defined for conditioning groups and is said to reduce to Eq. 2 when \(G\) is empty, though the written formula seems undefined in that case.

Section 5 fixes the claim map φ as pre-registered, deterministic, and not LLM-generated. It defines two maps/addressees: φ_overseer uses Annex IV 2(e) and 3 with Article 14(4)(c), keyed first on dominant layer band, then size class, then ranked input segment; φ_affected uses Article 86(1) and leads with input segment. Granularities are nested: finer claims refine, not contradict, coarser ones.

Size bins were selected by a calibration rule from a measured node-count curve, not to maximize flip rate. Table 1 reports sensitivity to binning: committed bins F=0.7316; thresholds × 0.5, 0.8, 0.9 give 0.7448, 0.7435, 0.7394; 1.1, 1.25, 1.5, 2 give 0.7289, 0.7314, 0.7308, 0.7232; equal thirds 0.7018; deciles 0.7719; no size term (COARSE) 0.5733. The text says four alternatives exceed the committed bins, and the overall range across binnings is about 0.70 to 0.77.

Section 6 says the study uses GPT-2 small on indirect object identification for comparability and a random baseline. The pre-registered grid has seven discovery objectives, seven ablation operators, four corruption distributions nested within five operators that read them, four metrics, three thresholds, two prompt variants, and five seeds, yielding 1,540 discovery cells and 18,480 specifications. Corruption is nested, not crossed, because two operators never read the corrupt distribution. The analysis plan and both abstracts were committed before the confirmatory sweep; an append-only file tracks deviations and timing. Uncertainty is estimated with a nonparametric bootstrap over specifications (not pairs), B=10,000, with F and J̄ treated as U-statistics.

Two exclusions are fixed before seeing circuits: one objective fails completely, with all 220 cells erroring because mean squared error is computed against an integral target; this leaves 6 objectives, 1,320 cells, and 15,840 specifications. A metric-relative threshold rule discards 8,279 of 15,840 specifications (52.3%), unevenly across metrics. Table 2 reports kept/discarded by metric: comprehensiveness 3,947/13 (0.003 discard rate), KL divergence 1,467/2,493 (0.630), logit difference 1,270/2,690 (0.679), sufficiency 877/3,083 (0.779). The surviving pool is 52% comprehensiveness versus 25% by design. Unevenness was disclosed before lock from a six-cell validation slice.

Section 7 reports pre-registered results. Table 3 maps outcomes to results: P0 ̄J = 0.1396 [0.1377, 0.1418], H2 F = 0.7316 [0.7247, 0.7380], H3 is rejected because the data are separated from the random null, and H4 = 0.3344 [0.3297, 0.3394].

Section 7.1 says overlap is low but above chance: mean Jaccard 0.1396 over all 28,580,580 pairs among 7,561 specifications and 3,218 distinct circuits; D quantiles 0.196, 0.788, 0.960, 0.998; median pair shares 4% of edges; 1% of pairs exceed Jaccard 0.8. It compares median observed overlap to a random expectation of 0.0031 at size 200 and 0.008 at size 500.

Section 7.2 says flip rate is 0.7316, above the 0.20 threshold; modal share is π* = 0.4109, and evidence fails filability at all pre-registered tolerances. Table 4 lists 9 claim classes with shares summing to 1; the top two are early layers/distributed (0.4109) and late layers/sparse (0.2848). Aggregated layer shares are 47.9% early, 43.6% late, 8.5% middle; Table 5 says all six addressee-granularity combinations reject filability.

Section 7.3 reports residual flip rates after standardising each axis (Table 6). Residual F values are: evaluation metric 0.5939 (CI 0.5803–0.6063, removes 0.1377), ablation operator 0.7014, discovery objective 0.7018, threshold 0.7070, corruption 0.7092, prompt variant 0.7232, and seed 0.7307. The metric is the largest single reduction but still leaves F well above the 0.20 threshold. The text also says structural variance is mostly from ablation-corruption interaction (78.8%), with 11.5% residual, 4.4% ablation, 4.1% threshold, and 0.7% metric, while claim variance is said to be largest for the metric.

Section 7.4 says that after removing circuit size from the claim and holding size fixed, the result is F=0.2706 (95% CI 0.2550–0.2859), still above the 0.20 threshold.

The part includes Table 5 with addressee/granularity combinations: affected COARSE 0.3950/0.7291, affected MEDIUM 0.6597/0.4875, affected FINE 0.6744/0.4786, overseer COARSE 0.5733/0.4788, overseer MEDIUM 0.7316/0.4109, overseer FINE 0.7681/0.4109; all are marked not filable. Figure 1 captions the overseer-medium specification curve and says the pooled random comparison is confounded by circuit size, to be discussed in Section 7.5.

Cohen’s kappa is 0.0146; size-specific kappa stays 0.016–0.047, raw agreement rises 0.52–0.92, and accuracy 0.51–0.95. The pooled gap fails to generalize across sizes: 6/10 sizes miss 0.10, 5 are negative, and the pooled result is carried by the 500–2,000 edge band.

Section 7 overview claims: P0 holds with J̄=0.1396 [0.1377, 0.1418]. H2 is confirmed with F=0.7316 [0.7247, 0.7380]. H3 is rejected: pooled distributions are separated with disjoint intervals, but this is qualified by a within-size reversal (the size artefact noted in Section 7.5). H4 is supported with gap 0.3344 [0.3297, 0.3394], but this does not generalize well across sizes: 6 of 10 sizes miss the 0.10 threshold and 5 sizes have negative gaps, so the pooled result is driven by the 500–2,000 edge band.

Section 8 defines the filability protocol: a claim must declare a specification space S (analytic axes and defensible levels with citations), declare a deterministic claim map φ as published code, compute π* = max_c n_c/N over S and F from Eq. 2, and is filable at tolerance α if π* ≥ 1−α. The filer should report π*, F, discard rate by axis level, and within-group decomposition of any pooled statistic. It argues a filing that cannot state its own π* is asserted, not audited, and that the regulator need not decide which analytic choice is correct.

Section 9 limitations: generalisation remains untested because the planned replications have not run. One pre-registered second-model replication is a 924-cell grid on Pythia-160m; it uses the same task, same axes except seeds have 3 levels instead of 5, and criteria distinguishing replication from refutation were timestamped. A second task is designed but unrun.

Circuit size is treated as an outcome, not an axis: the threshold rule selects size and size distorts F, the null-comparison direction, and the sign of the functional gap. Fixing size lowers F from 0.7316 to 0.2746, and the paper says it reports within-size decompositions for pooled statistics.

The instrument omits at least one defensible operator: optimal ablation [5], so the measured F is a lower bound relative to the field’s full defensible choices.

Discard rate is high and uneven: 52.3%, with metric imbalance; the rule was fixed in advance and no failing item was repaired.

Bootstrap intervals are invalid for one reported family: conditioning groups of 2 to 5 specifications are dominated by retained self-pairs, so the paper reports point estimates with a diagnostic instead of naive intervals.

final_notes:
Section 9 lists limitations. The study is framed as one model and one task, but generalisation is untested; a committed second-model plan (M9B/Pythia-160m, same task) is timestamped and unrun, with a 924-cell grid identical on all axes except having three seed levels instead of five, plus a second unrun task. Circuit size is treated as an outcome, not an axis; size conditioning is said to alter F, the null-comparison direction, and the functional-gap sign, and every pooled statistic is reported with within-size decomposition. The multiverse is wider than the measured library because optimal ablation (C4Y) is defensible but outside the instrument’s space, making measured F a lower bound on the field’s full defensible set. Discard rate is high and uneven; the retained metric imbalance is reported rather than adjusted away, with threshold fixed in advance and no repaired failures. Bootstrap intervals are invalid for one family: tiny conditioning groups (2–5 specs) retain self-pairs, so point estimates replace unusable intervals; no bias-corrected estimator was built. Evidence cited includes size-conditioning F=0.2706 vs residual F=0.5939, discard rate 52.3%, and axis-level rates 0.003, 0.630, 0.679, and 0.779.

Section 10 discussion argues for measured evidentiary weight rather than presumed filing reliability. It says standardising one axis does not resolve instability; Table 6 reports best residual F=0.5939 (95% CI 0.5803–0.6063). It reiterates execution/retention problems: 220 failed objective cells, 8,279 specifications admitting no circuit, and a 52.3% discard rate. It also says discovered circuits retain information, citing fixed-size vs random comparisons (K8Z 0.2746 vs 0.4230; E7R 0.2706 vs 0.3822), and notes that measurement is cheap relative to discovery but gives no numbers.

Section 11 says the public timestamped commit is `prereg-p1-confirmatory`; every reported number traces to a configuration, seed and environment fingerprint; archive verification establishes one environment across all 1,320 confirmatory cells; the uploaded archive matches the git tree exactly (22/22 files identical); one script recomputes headline quantities with 36 checks and 0 failures; another checks every manuscript numeric token; and the suite contains 343 tests.

Section 4 defines the formal setup. A specification is s=(o,a,d,m,τ,P,r,g), with axes objective, ablation operator, corruption distribution, evaluation metric, size threshold, prompt variant, seed, and granularity/statement resolution. G7U maps a discovered circuit C(s)⊆E to structured Annex IV statements; Y3W concerns agreement among claims, not the correctness of a specification. Circuit instability D(s_i,s_j) is 1 minus Jaccard similarity. Claim instability F is the Gini–Simpson disagreement probability over claim classes, with a within-group conditioned version F_within(G). A second-model replication is pre-registered but not yet run: a 924-cell grid on Pythia-160m (same task, same axes except seed has 3 levels instead of 5), with analysis plan and criteria timestamped before execution; a second task is designed but not run. Section 10 emphasizes that standardizing one axis only removes 0.1377 of a 0.7316 flip rate, identifies one of seven documented public discovery objectives as not running on the library’s canonical task, and argues evidentiary weight should be treated as measurable and cheap to assess relative to the original sweep. Abstract notes: GPT-2 small on indirect object identification, 15,840 pre-registered specifications, 7,561 produced a claim, claim flip rate 73.2% (95% CI 0.725 to 0.738), modal claim covers 41.1% of the space, 59.4% flip rate after standardising the evaluation metric, 27.1% (95% CI 0.255 to 0.286) after removing size from the claim and fixing size, median pairwise Jaccard overlap 4%, Cohen’s kappa 0.015, and one of seven documented discovery objectives does not execute on the library’s canonical task, leaving six executed objectives.

Related work claims: prior work shows explanations need not be unique; faithfulness metrics are sensitive to methodological choices; structurally different circuits can implement the same computation; estimator variance matters; auditing standards and standardised evaluation are needed; multiverse analysis exposes analytic flexibility; and sufficiency/comprehensiveness can be inflated without changing predictions or explanations.

This section adds: discovered circuits are more stable than a size-matched random null (0.2746 vs 0.4230); functional instability is 0.3972 pooled and 0.4777 at the smallest circuits; Cohen’s kappa is 0.0146; and the seed refers to sampled prompts, not nondeterminism.

errors.explanation: The text asserts an exact reduction in the empty-\(G\) case, but the displayed formula has no defined value when there are no conditioning groups unless an extra convention is added.

steps.notes_before: Section 4 formalism: a specification is \(s=(o,a,d,m,\tau,P,r,g)\), where \(o\)=objective, \(a\)=ablation operator, \(d\)=corruption distribution, \(m\)=evaluation metric, \(\tau\)=size threshold, \(P\)=prompt variant, \(r\)=seed, and \(g\)=granularity/claim-detail. Discovery outputs a circuit \(C(s)\subseteq E\); for GPT-2 small’s factorised graph, \(|E|=32{,}491\). The paper gives a closed-form component count: 144 attention heads + 12 MLPs = 156 components, and says the output receives from 157 non-terminal sources. Circuit instability is \(D=1-|C_i\cap C_j|/|C_i\cup C_j|\) and mean Jaccard similarity is \(\bar J\). Claim instability/flip rate is the pairwise probability of different structured Annex IV statements: \(F=1-\sum_c n_c(n_c-1)/(N(N-1))\), claimed to match brute-force tests; modal share is \(\pi^*=\max_c n_c/N\). Within-group flip rate \(F_{within}(G)\) is defined for conditioning groups and is said to reduce to Eq. 2 when \(G\) is empty, though the written formula seems undefined in that case.

Section 5 fixes the claim map φ as pre-registered, deterministic, and not LLM-generated. It defines two maps/addressees: φ_overseer uses Annex IV 2(e) and 3 with Article 14(4)(c), keyed first on dominant layer band, then size class, then ranked input segment; φ_affected uses Article 86(1) and leads with input segment. Granularities are nested: finer claims refine, not contradict, coarser ones.

Size bins were selected by a calibration rule from a measured node-count curve, not to maximize flip rate. Table 1 reports sensitivity to binning: committed bins F=0.7316; thresholds × 0.5, 0.8, 0.9 give 0.7448, 0.7435, 0.7394; 1.1, 1.25, 1.5, 2 give 0.7289, 0.7314, 0.7308, 0.7232; equal thirds 0.7018; deciles 0.7719; no size term (COARSE) 0.5733. The text says four alternatives exceed the committed bins, and the overall range across binnings is about 0.70 to 0.77.

Section 6 says the study uses GPT-2 small on indirect object identification for comparability and a random baseline. The pre-registered grid has seven discovery objectives, seven ablation operators, four corruption distributions nested within five operators that read them, four metrics, three thresholds, two prompt variants, and five seeds, yielding 1,540 discovery cells and 18,480 specifications. Corruption is nested, not crossed, because two operators never read the corrupt distribution. The analysis plan and both abstracts were committed before the confirmatory sweep; an append-only file tracks deviations and timing. Uncertainty is estimated with a nonparametric bootstrap over specifications (not pairs), B=10,000, with F and J̄ treated as U-statistics.

Two exclusions are fixed before seeing circuits: one objective fails completely, with all 220 cells erroring because mean squared error is computed against an integral target; this leaves 6 objectives, 1,320 cells, and 15,840 specifications. A metric-relative threshold rule discards 8,279 of 15,840 specifications (52.3%), unevenly across metrics. Table 2 reports kept/discarded by metric: comprehensiveness 3,947/13 (0.003 discard rate), KL divergence 1,467/2,493 (0.630), logit difference 1,270/2,690 (0.679), sufficiency 877/3,083 (0.779). The surviving pool is 52% comprehensiveness versus 25% by design. Unevenness was disclosed before lock from a six-cell validation slice.

Section 7 reports pre-registered results. Table 3 maps outcomes to results: P0 ̄J = 0.1396 [0.1377, 0.1418], H2 F = 0.7316 [0.7247, 0.7380], H3 is rejected because the data are separated from the random null, and H4 = 0.3344 [0.3297, 0.3394].

Section 7.1 says overlap is low but above chance: mean Jaccard 0.1396 over all 28,580,580 pairs among 7,561 specifications and 3,218 distinct circuits; D quantiles 0.196, 0.788, 0.960, 0.998; median pair shares 4% of edges; 1% of pairs exceed Jaccard 0.8. It compares median observed overlap to a random expectation of 0.0031 at size 200 and 0.008 at size 500.

Section 7.2 says flip rate is 0.7316, above the 0.20 threshold; modal share is π* = 0.4109, and evidence fails filability at all pre-registered tolerances. Table 4 lists 9 claim classes with shares summing to 1; the top two are early layers/distributed (0.4109) and late layers/sparse (0.2848). Aggregated layer shares are 47.9% early, 43.6% late, 8.5% middle; Table 5 says all six addressee-granularity combinations reject filability.

Section 7.3 reports residual flip rates after standardising each axis (Table 6). Residual F values are: evaluation metric 0.5939 (CI 0.5803–0.6063, removes 0.1377), ablation operator 0.7014, discovery objective 0.7018, threshold 0.7070, corruption 0.7092, prompt variant 0.7232, and seed 0.7307. The metric is the largest single reduction but still leaves F well above the 0.20 threshold. The text also says structural variance is mostly from ablation-corruption interaction (78.8%), with 11.5% residual, 4.4% ablation, 4.1% threshold, and 0.7% metric, while claim variance is said to be largest for the metric.

Section 7.4 says that after removing circuit size from the claim and holding size fixed, the result is F=0.2706 (95% CI 0.2550–0.2859), still above the 0.20 threshold.

The part includes Table 5 with addressee/granularity combinations: affected COARSE 0.3950/0.7291, affected MEDIUM 0.6597/0.4875, affected FINE 0.6744/0.4786, overseer COARSE 0.5733/0.4788, overseer MEDIUM 0.7316/0.4109, overseer FINE 0.7681/0.4109; all are marked not filable. Figure 1 captions the overseer-medium specification curve and says the pooled random comparison is confounded by circuit size, to be discussed in Section 7.5.

H4 is supported with gap 0.3344 [0.3297, 0.3394], but this does not generalize well across sizes: 6 of 10 sizes miss the 0.10 threshold and 5 sizes have negative gaps, so the pooled result is driven by the 500–2,000 edge band. Section 8 defines the filability protocol: declare the specification space, use a deterministic published-code claim map, compute π* = max_c n_c/N and F, and deem a claim filable if π* ≥ 1-α; report π*, F, discard rate by axis level, and within-group decomposition. It concludes that all high-risk AI systems fail filability under defensible analytic variation.

Section 9 limitations says generalisation remains untested because only one model and one task have been run; the pre-registered Pythia-160m replication (924-cell grid, same task, 3 seed levels) and a second task are still unrun. It also says the instrument omits at least one defensible operator (optimal ablation [5]), so the measured F is a lower bound relative to full defensible choices. The discard rate is 52.3% and the retained pool is metric-imbalanced. Finally, the bootstrap is invalid for conditioning groups of 2–5 specifications because retained self-pairs dominate; for that family the paper reports point estimates with diagnostics instead of intervals.

Section 10 argues for measured evidentiary weight. It claims standardising one axis is insufficient: the metric is the biggest lever, removing 0.1377 from a 0.7316 flip rate, leaving 0.5939 (CI 0.5803 to 0.6063). It says one of seven documented, publicly exported discovery objectives does not run on the library’s canonical task, and all 220 cells in that arm fail. The section frames this as a discard and a tooling-maturity issue, not the headline. It concludes interpretability evidence is not worthless, but its evidentiary weight is measurable rather than assumed, and that measurement is cheap relative to the sweep that produced the circuit.

Abstract claims that circuit-derived regulatory evidence fails Y3W across tolerances plausibly acceptable to a conformity-assessment body; competent analysts using the same system/tool can reach incompatible statements under different defensible settings. The paper says it proposes no improved discovery method and instead challenges the standard assumed by currently produced evidence.

Section 4 formalizes the setup. A circuit-to-statement transformation (G7U / claim map) maps discovery output C(s)⊆E, and Y3W (filability) is about agreement among resulting claims, not whether the specification is correct. Paper summary claims: it studies whether circuit discovery can produce stable regulatory evidence by varying seven analytic choices and deterministically mapping each circuit to a structured Annex IV statement. On GPT-2 small and indirect object identification, 7,561 of 15,840 specifications produce a claim. Reported instability metrics: claim flip rate 73.2%; most common claim covers 41.1% of specifications; standardising the evaluation metric leaves a 59.4% flip rate; removing circuit size from the claim and holding size fixed leaves 27.1%; median circuit overlap is 4%; functional agreement adjusted for chance is near zero. One documented discovery objective does not execute. Scope caveat: one model and one task; generalisation to scale is untested.

This part is a glossary defining the paper’s terminology and symbols. It confirms key concepts from the summary: circuit discovery returns a circuit for each specification; a claim is a deterministic structured Annex IV statement produced by the claim map; claim flip rate is the probability two distinct specifications yield different statements; circuit instability is one minus Jaccard similarity; functional agreement concerns per-example correct/incorrect verdicts; and the paper’s main statistical objects include modal claim share, within-group flip rate, mean Jaccard similarity, and the random null. It also states that the study’s confirmatory grid uses GPT-2 small, indirect object identification, seven documented discovery objectives, and that six executed, matching the earlier note that one objective does not execute. No inconsistencies appear in this section.

This part is the paper title/abstract/summary. It frames the study as testing whether circuit-derived regulatory statements survive defensible analytic variation. Key reported results: 15,840 pre-registered specifications on GPT-2 small and the indirect object identification task; 7,561 produced a claim; claim flip rate 73.2% (95% CI 0.725 to 0.738); modal claim share 41.1%; removing metric standardisation leaves a 59.4% flip rate; removing circuit size and holding size fixed leaves a 27.1% flip rate (95% CI 0.255 to 0.286); median pairwise Jaccard overlap is 4%; Cohen’s kappa is 0.015. It also says one of seven documented discovery objectives does not execute on the library’s canonical task, and claims non-filability across model families and tasks. No internal inconsistency is visible yet.

This section frames the paper’s motivation and contributions. It defines an audit as two auditors reaching the same conclusion, and argues that circuit-level regulatory filings are only useful if a second analyst, given the same system and tool, would produce a compatible filing. It cites EU AI Act documentation/explanation requirements and positions mechanistic interpretability as the technical basis for such filings. Contributions listed: (i) a pre-registered multiverse over seven circuit-discovery axes with a deterministic map from circuits to Annex IV statements; (ii) a filability criterion π* ≥ 1-α, where π* is modal claim share, measured on a canonical task; (iii) evidence of instability even after standardizing one axis, removing circuit size, or holding size fixed; and (iv) a methodological warning that pooled statistics can invert when specifications select objects of different sizes, with three inversions shown.

This section situates the paper among related work. It argues that mechanistic explanations can be non-identifiable, ablation-based faithfulness scores are sensitive to methodological choices, and structurally different circuits can implement the same behavior. It also cites work treating mechanistic interpretability as statistical estimation, prior calls for auditing standards and standardized evaluation, and multiverse-analysis methods for exposing analytic flexibility. Finally, it notes that sufficiency and comprehensiveness can be inflated without changing predictions or explanations, motivating reporting discard rates by metric rather than pooling them. No numerical results are presented in this section.

This section explicitly states what the paper is not claiming. It says the results do not imply random circuits, equivalent mechanisms, seed nondeterminism, or generalization to scale. Key reported evidence: discovered circuits are more stable than a size-matched random null at fixed size (0.2746 vs 0.4230); functional instability (one minus agreement on per-example verdicts) is 0.3972 pooled and 0.4777 for the smallest circuits; Cohen’s kappa is 0.0146, supporting the claim that circuits are functionally uncorrelated. It also clarifies that the seed refers to sampled prompts / evaluation-set variability rather than nondeterminism, and that the study is limited to one model and one task.

Section 8 defines the filability protocol for interpretability claims derived from a circuit. A filer must (1) declare the specification space S, i.e., the analytic axes and defensible levels for each with citations; (2) declare the claim map φ as deterministic published code, not a language model; (3) compute π* = max_c n_c/N over S and F by Equation 2; (4) deem the claim filable at tolerance α if π* ≥ 1−α; and (5) report π*, F, discard rates per axis level, and any within-group decomposition of pooled statistics. The section emphasizes that a filing that cannot state its own π* is not audited, only asserted, and that the protocol does not require the regulator to decide which analytic choice is correct.

Section 9 lists limitations. A second-model replication is pre-registered but not yet run: a 924-cell grid on Pythia-160m, a different architecture family doing the same task, identical on every axis except the seed axis (3 levels instead of 5); the plan and refutation/replication criteria were timestamped before any cell ran, and a second task is designed but not run. Circuit size is an outcome, not an axis: thresholding it changes pooled quantities, and fixing it drops F from 0.7316 to 0.2746, a larger reduction than standardising any pre-registered axis. The multiverse is limited to the library of implemented choices, not all literature choices; optimal ablation is defensible but not implemented, so measured F is a lower bound relative to the field’s full defensible space. The discard rate is 52.3% and the surviving pool is metric imbalanced. The bootstrap is invalid for one reported family because conditioning groups with only two to five specifications make retained self-pairs dominate; those results are reported as point estimates with diagnostics.

Section 10 Discussion argues that standardising one axis is insufficient: the metric is the biggest lever and only removes 0.1377 of a 0.7316 flip rate. It reiterates that one of seven documented, publicly exported discovery objectives does not run on the library’s own canonical task; this is reported as a discard and as evidence that the tooling is immature, not as a criticism of the library itself. The takeaway for regulators is that interpretability evidence has measurable evidentiary weight, and that estimating it is cheap relative to the sweep that produced the circuit.

steps.notes_before: Section 4 formalism: a specification is \(s=(o,a,d,m,\tau,P,r,g)\), where \(o\)=objective, \(a\)=ablation operator, \(d\)=corruption distribution, \(m\)=evaluation metric, \(\tau\)=size threshold, \(P\)=prompt variant, \(r\)=seed, and \(g\)=granularity/claim-detail. Discovery outputs a circuit \(C(s)\subseteq E\); for GPT-2 small’s factorised graph, \(|E|=32{,}491\). The paper gives a closed-form component count: 144 attention heads + 12 MLPs = 156 components, and says the output receives from 157 non-terminal sources. Circuit instability is \(D=1-|C_i\cap C_j|/|C_i\cup C_j|\) and mean Jaccard similarity is \(\bar J\). Claim instability/flip rate is the pairwise probability of different structured Annex IV statements: \(F=1-\sum_c n_c(n_c-1)/(N(N-1))\), claimed to match brute-force tests; modal share is \(\pi^*=\max_c n_c/N\). Within-group flip rate \(F_{within}(G)\) is defined for conditioning groups and is said to reduce to Eq. 2 when \(G\) is empty, though the written formula seems undefined in that case.

Section 5 fixes the claim map φ as pre-registered, deterministic, and not LLM-generated. It defines two maps/addressees: φ_overseer uses Annex IV 2(e) and 3 with Article 14(4)(c), keyed first on dominant layer band, then size class, then ranked input segment; φ_affected uses Article 86(1) and leads with input segment. Granularities are nested: finer claims refine, not contradict, coarser ones.

Size bins were selected by a calibration rule from a measured node-count curve, not to maximize flip rate. Section 6 says the study uses GPT-2 small on indirect object identification for comparability and a random baseline. The pre-registered grid has seven discovery objectives, seven ablation operators, four corruption distributions nested within five operators that read them, four metrics, three thresholds, two prompt variants, and five seeds, yielding 1,540 discovery cells and 18,480 specifications. Corruption is nested, not crossed, because two operators never read the corrupt distribution. The analysis plan and both abstracts were committed before the confirmatory sweep; an append-only file tracks deviations and timing. Key reported results: 7,561 claim-producing specifications; pairwise claim disagreement F = 0.7316. No single-axis standardisation fits registered tolerances. If size is removed from statements and comparisons are conditioned on size, disagreement drops to 0.2706. Discovered circuits outperform size-matched random baselines at fixed size, reversing the pooled comparison. Functional measurements do not support treating circuits as interchangeable mechanisms; size conditioning also changes/qualifies the pooled functional-gap result. Scope: one model (GPT-2 small, Q7V) and one task (indirect object identification, Z4K); a planned second-model study on Pythia-160m was not run.

Overseer/affected mappings order dominant layer band, size class, and ranked input segment (with some provisions leading with input segment). Section 4 defines the formal setup. A specification is s=(o,a,d,m,τ,P,r,g), with axes objective, ablation operator, corruption distribution, evaluation metric, size threshold, prompt variant, seed, and granularity/statement resolution. G7U maps a discovered circuit C(s)⊆E to structured Annex IV statements; Y3W concerns agreement among claims, not the correctness of a specification. The GPT-2 small / Q7V factorised graph has |E|=32,491 edges, 144 attention heads, 12 MLPs, 156 total components, and output receives all 157 non-terminal sources. Circuit instability D(s_i,s_j) is 1 minus Jaccard similarity. Claim instability F is the Gini–Simpson disagreement probability over claim classes, with a within-group conditioned version F_within(G). Empty G reduces exactly to F. Y3W gives a claim-class ceiling F≤1−1/k; with 9 observed classes the ceiling is 0.8889 and the observed fraction of ceiling is 82.3%.

Section 5 (G7U) focuses on statement mappings and size-binning sensitivity. The paper says the size bins were fixed by a committed calibration rule on a measured node-count curve, not chosen to optimize F. Table 1 reports F for alternative binnings: committed bins 0.7316; thresholds ×0.5 0.7448; ×0.8 0.7435; ×0.9 0.7394; ×1.1 0.7289; ×1.25 0.7314; ×1.5 0.7308; ×2 0.7232; equal thirds 0.7018; deciles 0.7719; no size term (E7R) 0.5733. The stated sensitivity range across factor-four binnings is 0.70 to 0.77. It says four alternatives exceed the committed result, including halving thresholds. Regulatory addressees determine two mappings: D9P (overseer) orders dominant layer band, size class, and ranked input segment; L3X (affected) leads with input segment. The resolutions are E7R/COARSE (coarsest), K8Z/MEDIUM, and V2H/FINE, described as nested so refinement cannot contradict the coarser statement. The claim map φ is pre-registered, published deterministic code rather than language-model output.

steps.notes_before: Section 6 describes the method. The grid is said to include seven objectives, seven operators, four corruption distributions nested within five operators, four metrics (T9V, H2W/KL divergence, N6C/logit difference, U4J), three thresholds, two prompt variants, and five seeds, yielding 1,540 discovery cells and 18,480 pre-registered specifications. Two operators never read corruption. Pre-registration and an append-only deviations file are described as being in place before confirmatory analysis. Statistics use a nonparametric bootstrap over specifications with 10,000 resamples and no specification-level p-values. One objective fails entirely in the verbatim library, leaving 1,320 realised discovery cells and 15,840 realised specifications; 8,279 specifications admit no circuit, giving a 52.3% discard rate. Table 2 reports metric-specific kept/discarded counts; the listed “Rate” values are actually discard fractions (e.g., T9V kept 3,947 and discarded 13, so the rate shown as 0.003 is discard rate, not retention).

Section 7 reports registered outcomes and says the decision rules were fixed on 6 Aug 2026 before the sweep. Table 3 lists four outcomes: J6D/premise holds with 0.1396 [0.1377, 0.1418]; X4R/claim instability confirmed with 0.7316 [0.7247, 0.7380] against 0.20; Q2F/random comparison rejected, with separated intervals but no numeric interval shown; Z8N/functional gap supported with 0.3344 [0.3297, 0.3394] against 0.10. Section 7.1 says claim-producing specifications are 7,561, yielding 3,218 distinct circuits and 28,580,580 specification pairs; circuits are mostly disjoint (median shared-edge fraction 4%, median D 0.960, only 1% of pairs exceed Jaccard 0.8), with median size 200 edges and observed overlap about 45× chance. Section 7.2 says claims flip on 73.2% of pairs; the modal addressee-resolution class is early layers, distributed (3,107; 41.09%), followed by late layers, sparse (2,153; 28.48%). The table also reports 95% CI 0.725 to 0.738 for disagreement and size-aggregated early/late/middle shares of 47.9%/43.6%/8.5%. The loosest tolerance α=0.20 and required π* ≥ 0.80 are stated for Table 5.

final_notes: Section 9 limitations/robustness: the study covers one model and one task; a pre-registered Pythia-160m replication (924-cell grid, same task, different architecture family, same axes except seed levels) is not yet run, and a second task is designed but not run. Circuit size is an outcome, not a pre-registered axis; fixing it reportedly reduces F from 0.7316 to 0.2746 and distorts pooled quantities including the null comparison and functional-gap sign. The declared multiverse omits optimal ablation because the instrument does not implement it, so measured F is a lower bound relative to the full set of defensible choices. Discard rate is 52.3% with uneven/metric-imbalanced survivors; the threshold rule was fixed in advance. For one reported family, bootstrap intervals are invalid because conditioning groups have only 2–5 specifications, so those quantities are reported as point estimates with diagnostics. Section 10 discussion says standardising one axis buys less than it appears; it claims the metric is the biggest lever, and also notes one of seven documented discovery objectives does not run on the library’s canonical task and is treated as a discard. Section 11 reproducibility says the pre-registration is a timestamped commit tagged prereg-p1-confirmatory in the public repository, made before the confirmatory sweep began; every reported number traces to a config, seed, and environment fingerprint. The confirmatory sweep ran under a single environment across all 1,320 cells, the code commit was recovered by archive-to-git content comparison with 22/22 files identical, the analysis layer runs without a GPU, and verification scripts report 36 checks with 0 failures, plus a separate script checking numeric tokens, with tables emitted directly from stored results. The test suite has 343 tests.

Section 8 defines the filability protocol for an interpretability claim derived from a circuit. A filer must: (1) declare the specification space S (analytic axes and defensible levels, each cited); (2) declare the claim map φ as deterministic published code, not a language model; (3) compute π* = max_c n_c/N over S and F by Equation 2; (4) call the claim filable at tolerance α if π* ≥ 1−α; and (5) report π*, F, discard rate per axis level, and within-group decomposition of any pooled statistic. The section emphasizes that if a filing cannot state its own π*, it is not audited, and that the regulator is not asked to decide which analytic choice is correct, only to quantify agreement across the declared space.

Section 9 lists limitations and robustness caveats. The study currently covers one model and one task; a second-model replication on Pythia-160m is pre-registered but not yet run (924-cell grid, same task, different architecture family, identical axes except seed has 3 levels instead of 5), and a second task is designed but not run. Circuit size is treated as an outcome, not a pre-registered axis; fixing it reduces F from 0.7316 to 0.2746, and the paper says it distorts pooled quantities including the null comparison and functional-gap sign. The declared multiverse omits optimal ablation because the instrument does not implement it, so the measured F is described as a lower bound relative to the field’s full set of defensible choices. final_notes:
Part 11 (limitations): The study uses one model and one task, but there is a committed, timestamped second-model plan (M9B: Pythia-160m) that is unrun, plus a second task designed but unrun. Circuit size is treated as an outcome rather than an axis; threshold-selected size can distort F, the null-comparison direction, and the functional-gap sign, so pooled stats are decomposed by size. The multiverse is limited to the library’s operators, making the measured F a lower bound relative to the field’s full defensible choice set, with C4Y optimal ablation explicitly excluded. The retained metric imbalance is fixed in advance and not repaired. The bootstrap is invalid for one reported family because groups with only two to five specifications retain dominating self-pairs; unusable intervals are replaced by point estimates with diagnostics, and no bias-corrected estimator was constructed after naive intervals disagreed.

Part 12 (Discussion): The paper argues that standardising one axis is insufficient and that a single knob cannot justify declaring resolution. It says the failed objective is documented and publicly exported but cannot execute on the library’s canonical task. It concludes interpretability evidence is not worthless and that evidentiary weight is measurable rather than presumed.

Part 13 (Reproducibility): The public timestamped commit is tagged `prereg-p1-confirmatory`. Reported numbers trace to configuration, seed, and environment fingerprint; archive verification says all 1,320 confirmatory cells ran in one environment and the uploaded archive matches the git tree (22/22 files identical). One script recomputes headline quantities from raw results and asserts reported values via 36 checks with 0 failures, including F through three routes; another checks every manuscript numeric token. The suite has 343 tests, and tables are emitted directly rather than transcribed.

Section 4 defines the formal setup. A specification is s=(o,a,d,m,τ,P,r,g), with axes objective, ablation operator, corruption distribution, evaluation metric, size threshold, prompt variant, seed, and granularity/statement resolution. G7U maps a discovered circuit C(s)⊆E to structured Annex IV statements; Y3W concerns agreement among claims, not the correctness of a specification. The GPT-2 small / Q7V factorised graph has |E|=32,491 edges, 144 attention heads, 12 MLPs, 156 total components, and output receives all 157 non-terminal sources. Circuit instability D(s_i,s_j) is 1 minus Jaccard similarity. Claim instability F is the Gini–Simpson disagreement probability over claim classes, with a within-group conditioned version F_within(G). Empty G reduces exactly to F. Y3W gives a claim-class ceiling F≤1−1/k; with 9 observed classes the ceiling is 0.8889 and the observed fraction of ceiling is 82.3%.

Section 5 (G7U) focuses on statement mappings and size-binning sensitivity. The paper says the size bins were fixed by a committed calibration rule on a measured node-count curve, not chosen to optimize F. Table 1 reports F for alternative binnings: committed bins 0.7316; thresholds ×0.5 0.7448; ×0.8 0.7435; ×0.9 0.7394; ×1.1 0.7289; ×1.25 0.7314; ×1.5 0.7308; ×2 0.7232; equal thirds 0.7018; deciles 0.7719; no size term (E7R) 0.5733. The stated sensitivity range across factor-four binnings is 0.70 to 0.77. It says four alternatives exceed the committed result, including halving thresholds. Regulatory addressees determine two mappings: D9P (overseer) orders dominant layer band, size class, and ranked input segment; L3X (affected) leads with input segment. The resolutions are E7R/COARSE (coarsest), K8Z/MEDIUM, and V2H/FINE, described as nested so refinement cannot contradict the coarser statement. The claim map φ is pre-registered, published deterministic code rather than language-model output.

steps.notes_before: Section 6 describes the method. The grid is said to include seven objectives, seven operators, four corruption distributions nested within five operators, four metrics (T9V, H2W/KL divergence, N6C/logit difference, U4J), three thresholds, two prompt variants, and five seeds, yielding 1,540 discovery cells and 18,480 pre-registered specifications. Two operators never read corruption. Pre-registration and an append-only deviations file are described as being in place before confirmatory analysis. Statistics use a nonparametric bootstrap over specifications with 10,000 resamples and no specification-level p-values. One objective fails entirely in the verbatim library, leaving 1,320 realised discovery cells and 15,840 realised specifications; 8,279 specifications admit no circuit, giving a 52.3% discard rate. Table 2 reports metric-specific kept/discarded counts; the listed “Rate” values are actually discard fractions (e.g., T9V kept 3,947 and discarded 13, so the rate shown as 0.003 is discard rate, not retention).

Table 5 starts addressee-resolution combinations, with loosest tolerance alpha=0.20 and required pi*>=0.80.

Section 7.2/7.3 add more results. Coarsest L3X percentage disagreement is 39.5%. The section claims all Y3W entries are no at required pi* >= 0.80. Section 7.3 says metric standardisation gives the lowest residual F: evaluation metric 0.5939 (removes 0.1377), ablation operator 0.7014, discovery objective 0.7018, threshold 0.7070, corruption 0.7092, prompt variant 0.7232, seed 0.7307. REML structural variance on log10 selected circuit size is ablation-corruption interaction 78.8%, residual 11.5%, ablation 4.4%, threshold 4.1%, metric 0.7%. Metric-standardised percentage disagreement is 59.4%.

Section 7.4 reports size-free claim, fixed size: F=0.2706 with 95% CI 0.2550 to 0.2859; abstract precision 27.1% (CI 0.255 to 0.286), discussion precision 27%.

Section 7.5 compares discovered vs A6N: pooled 0.7316 vs 0.6774; fixed size K8Z 0.2746 vs 0.4230; fixed size E7R 0.2706 vs 0.3822. It says fixed-size comparison reverses the pooled ordering and discovered circuits still fail Y3W.

steps.notes_before: Section 7.5 / Table 7: K8Z within-size results. A6N uses R=1,000 null multiverses and collapses at and above 1,000 edges. Discovery collapses at 5,000 and 10,000 edges. Table 7 rows: size 10 n=2,492 discovered F=0.4543 classes 3; 20 n=489 F=0.3380 classes 4; 50 n=519 F=0.4639 classes 3; 100 n=242 F=0.5792 classes 3; 200 n=199 F=0.5122 classes 4; 500 n=236 F=0.4258 classes 3; 1,000 n=380 F=0.5133 classes 3; 2,000 n=312 F=0.5714 classes 3; 5,000 n=625 F=0.0000 classes 1; 10,000 n=2,067 F=0.0000 classes 1. The caption says 2,692 of 7,561 specifications contribute no flips. Claims/evidence also state pooled discovery is less stable than A6N (0.7316 vs 0.6774), fixed-size comparison reverses ordering (K8Z 0.2746 vs 0.4230; E7R 0.2706 vs 0.3822), and the null collapses at and above 1,000 edges.

Section 8 introduces the Y3W protocol for circuit-derived filed claims. It requires: (1) declaring the space S of defensible analytic axes and levels, each cited; (2) declaring φ as published deterministic code, not a language model; (3) computing π* = max_c n_c/N over S and F; (4) evidence passes Y3W at tolerance α iff π* ≥ 1−α; and (5) reporting π*, F, discard rate per axis level, and within-group decomposition of every pooled statistic. It states that a filing unable to state its own π* is asserted, not audited, and that implementability needs only a declared space and measured agreement, not regulatory adjudication of analytic correctness.

Section 9 lists limitations and supporting evidence. It says the study is limited by one model/one task; a committed second-model replication/refutation study on M9B (Pythia-160m) is planned but unrun, with a 924-cell grid identical on all axes except having three rather than five seed levels and fixed pre-run criteria. It says circuit size is not an axis but an outcome, and size conditioning changes three pooled conclusions: it distorts F, the null-comparison direction, and the functional-gap sign. It argues the multiverse is wider than the instrumented space because C4Y/optimal ablation is defensible but outside the measured set, making measured F a lower bound on the full defensible choice set. It also says discard rates are high and uneven, and that no failed item was repaired. The bootstrap is said to be invalid for one reported family because very small conditioning groups (2–5 specs) retain dominating self-pairs; these intervals were replaced by point estimates with diagnostics. Evidence cited includes size-conditioning vs Table 6 F values, comparison-table reversals, functional-gap counts, discard rates (52.3% and table rates 0.003/0.630/0.679/0.779), and the bootstrap-group issue.

Section 10 Discussion argues for measured rather than presumed evidentiary weight. It says complete metric standardisation, or standardising one axis, does not resolve the filing/instability problem; no single knob suffices. It frames the instrument as having execution and retention problems: the failed objective is publicly documented but cannot run on the library’s canonical task, and the grid shows 220 failed objective cells, 8,279 specifications with no circuit, and a 52.3% discard rate. It also says discovered circuits retain information, citing Section 7.5 comparison results: fixed-size K8Z 0.2746 vs random 0.4230, and fixed-size E7R 0.2706 vs random 0.3822. It reiterates Table 6’s best residual F=0.5939 (95% CI 0.5803–0.6063; 59.4%). It asserts measurement is cheap relative to discovery but provides no numerical cost comparison.
