steps.notes_before: Section 4 formalism: a specification is \(s=(o,a,d,m,\tau,P,r,g)\), where \(o\)=objective, \(a\)=ablation operator, \(d\)=corruption distribution, \(m\)=evaluation metric, \(\tau\)=size threshold, \(P\)=prompt variant, \(r\)=seed, and \(g\)=granularity/claim-detail. Discovery outputs a circuit \(C(s)\subseteq E\); for GPT-2 small’s factorised graph, \(|E|=32{,}491\). The paper gives a closed-form component count: 144 attention heads + 12 MLPs = 156 components, and says the output receives from 157 non-terminal sources. Circuit instability is \(D=1-|C_i\cap C_j|/|C_i\cup C_j|\) and mean Jaccard similarity is \(\bar J\). Claim instability/flip rate is the pairwise probability of different structured Annex IV statements: \(F=1-\sum_c n_c(n_c-1)/(N(N-1))\), claimed to match brute-force tests; modal share is \(\pi^*=\max_c n_c/N\). Within-group flip rate \(F_{within}(G)\) is defined for conditioning groups and is said to reduce to Eq. 2 when \(G\) is empty, though the written formula seems undefined in that case.

Section 5 fixes the claim map φ as pre-registered, deterministic, and not LLM-generated. It defines two maps/addressees: φ_overseer uses Annex IV 2(e) and 3 with Article 14(4)(c), keyed first on dominant layer band, then size class, then ranked input segment; φ_affected uses Article 86(1) and leads with input segment. Granularities are nested: finer claims refine, not contradict, coarser ones.

Size bins were selected by a calibration rule from a measured node-count curve, not to maximize flip rate. Table 1 reports sensitivity to binning: committed bins F=0.7316; thresholds × 0.5, 0.8, 0.9 give 0.7448, 0.7435, 0.7394; 1.1, 1.25, 1.5, 2 give 0.7289, 0.7314, 0.7308, 0.7232; equal thirds 0.7018; deciles 0.7719; no size term (COARSE) 0.5733. The text says four alternatives exceed the committed bins, and the overall range across binnings is about 0.70 to 0.77.

Section 6 says the study uses GPT-2 small on indirect object identification for comparability and a random baseline. The pre-registered grid has seven discovery objectives, seven ablation operators, four corruption distributions nested within five operators that read them, four metrics, three thresholds, two prompt variants, and five seeds, yielding 1,540 discovery cells and 18,480 specifications. Corruption is nested, not crossed, because two operators never read the corrupt distribution. The analysis plan and both abstracts were committed before the confirmatory sweep; an append-only file tracks deviations and timing. Uncertainty is estimated with a nonparametric bootstrap over specifications (not pairs), B=10,000, with F and J̄ treated as U-statistics.

Two exclusions are fixed before seeing circuits: one objective fails completely, with all 220 cells erroring because mean squared error is computed against an integral target; this leaves 6 objectives, 1,320 cells, and 15,840 specifications. A metric-relative threshold rule discards 8,279 of 15,840 specifications (52.3%), unevenly across metrics. Table 2 reports kept/discarded by metric: comprehensiveness 3,947/13 (0.003 discard rate), KL divergence 1,467/2,493 (0.630), logit difference 1,270/2,690 (0.679), sufficiency 877/3,083 (0.779). Section 8 defines the filability protocol: a claim must declare a specification space S (analytic axes and defensible levels with citations), declare a deterministic claim map φ as published code, compute π* = max_c n_c/N over S and F from Eq. 2, and is filable at tolerance α if π* ≥ 1−α. The filer should report π*, F, discard rate by axis level, and within-group decomposition of any pooled statistic. It argues a filing that cannot state its own π* is asserted, not audited, and that the regulator need not decide which analytic choice is correct.

Section 9 limitations: generalisation is untested because scale has not been tested; a pre-registered second-model replication on Pythia-160m (924-cell grid, same task, seeds with three levels instead of five) and a second task are designed but unrun. Size is an outcome, not an axis: threshold-selected circuit size distorts F, the null-comparison direction, and the sign of the functional gap; fixing size reduces F from 0.7316 to 0.2746, so pooled results must be decomposed by size. The instrument omits at least one defensible operator (optimal ablation [5]), so measured F is a lower bound relative to the field’s full defensible choices. The discard rate is 52.3% and the surviving pool is metric-imbalanced, though no repairs were made. Bootstrap intervals are invalid for conditioning groups with only 2–5 specifications because retained self-pairs dominate; point estimates are reported instead.

Section 4 defines the formal setup. A specification is s=(o,a,d,m,τ,P,r,g), with axes objective, ablation operator, corruption distribution, evaluation metric, size threshold, prompt variant, seed, and granularity/statement resolution. G7U maps a discovered circuit C(s)⊆E to structured Annex IV statements; Y3W concerns agreement among claims, not the correctness of a specification. The GPT-2 small / Q7V factorised graph has |E|=32,491 edges, 144 attention heads, 12 MLPs, 156 total components, and output receives all 157 non-terminal sources. Circuit instability D(s_i,s_j) is 1 minus Jaccard similarity. Claim instability F is the Gini–Simpson disagreement probability over claim classes, with a within-group conditioned version F_within(G). Empty G reduces exactly to F. Y3W gives a claim-class ceiling F≤1−1/k; with 9 observed classes the ceiling is 0.8889 and the observed fraction of ceiling is 82.3%.

Section 5 (G7U) focuses on statement mappings and size-binning sensitivity. The paper says the size bins were fixed by a committed calibration rule on a measured node-count curve, not chosen to optimize F. Table 1 reports F for alternative binnings: committed bins 0.7316; thresholds ×0.5 0.7448; ×0.8 0.7435; ×0.9 0.7394; ×1.1 0.7289; ×1.25 0.7314; ×1.5 0.7308; ×2 0.7232; equal thirds 0.7018; deciles 0.7719; no size term (E7R) 0.5733. The stated sensitivity range across factor-four binnings is 0.70 to 0.77. It says four alternatives exceed the committed result, including halving thresholds. Regulatory addressees determine two mappings: D9P (overseer) orders dominant layer band, size class, and ranked input segment; L3X (affected) leads with input segment. The resolutions are E7R/COARSE (coarsest), K8Z/MEDIUM, and V2H/FINE, described as nested so refinement cannot contradict the coarser statement. The claim map φ is pre-registered, published deterministic code rather than language-model output.

On GPT-2 small and indirect object identification, 7,561 of 15,840 specifications produce a claim. This part is a glossary defining the paper’s terminology and symbols. It confirms key concepts from the summary: circuit discovery returns a circuit for each specification; a claim is a deterministic structured Annex IV statement produced by the claim map; claim flip rate is the probability two distinct specifications yield different statements; circuit instability is one minus Jaccard similarity; functional agreement concerns per-example correct/incorrect verdicts; and the paper’s main statistical objects include modal claim share, within-group flip rate, mean Jaccard similarity, and the random null. It also states that the study’s confirmatory grid uses GPT-2 small, indirect object identification, seven documented discovery objectives, and that six executed, matching the earlier note that one objective does not execute. No inconsistencies appear in this section.

This part is the abstract and summary. The study asks whether circuit-derived regulatory statements survive defensible analytic variation. It uses GPT-2 small on the indirect object identification task and a crossed grid of seven analytic axes, with every level taken from a published implementation. Across 15,840 pre-registered specifications, 7,561 produced a claim. The claim flip rate is 73.2% (95% CI 0.725 to 0.738), and the modal claim covers 41.1% of the space. Standardising the evaluation metric still leaves a 59.4% flip rate; removing circuit size from the claim and fixing size leaves 27.1% (95% CI 0.255 to 0.286). Median pairwise Jaccard overlap is 4%, and Cohen’s kappa is 0.015. The abstract also says one of seven documented discovery objectives does not execute on the library’s canonical task, implying six execute.

The introduction frames the paper as testing whether circuit-level regulatory claims remain compatible across analysts/specifications. It cites EU AI Act documentation/explanation duties and argues that circuit discovery only has regulatory value if a second analyst would produce a compatible filing. Section 5 fixes the deterministic, preregistered claim map φ and says it is not generated by a language model. There are two addressee-specific maps: φ_overseer (Annex IV 2(e) and 3 with Article 14(4)(c), keyed by dominant layer band → size class → ranked input segment) and φ_affected (Article 86(1), keyed first on input segment). The three granularities are nested, so finer claims refine coarser ones.

The section then studies sensitivity to size binning. Table 1 reports the committed bins at F=0.7316, with higher F under thresholds×0.5 (0.7448), 0.8 (0.7435), 0.9 (0.7394), and deciles (0.7719); other alternatives are 1.1 (0.7289), 1.25 (0.7314), 1.5 (0.7308), 2 (0.7232), equal thirds (0.7018). Removing size entirely (COARSE) gives F=0.5733. Claims made: committed bins do not maximize F; sensitivity stays in roughly the 0.70–0.77 range; removing size does not eliminate instability.

Section 6 describes the method. The model is GPT-2 small on indirect object identification, chosen for comparability and a size-matched random baseline. The preregistered grid includes seven discovery objectives, seven ablation operators, four corruption distributions nested within five operators that read them, four metrics, three thresholds, two prompt variants, and five seeds, yielding 1,540 discovery cells and 18,480 specifications. Corruption is nested rather than crossed because two operators never read the corrupt distribution.

The plan and both abstract directions were committed before the confirmatory sweep; an append-only file records deviations and their timing. Uncertainty is estimated with a nonparametric bootstrap over specifications (not pairs) using 10,000 resamples; no p-values are computed because the grid is designed rather than sampled.

Two preregistered exclusions are reported. First, one objective fails entirely: all 220 of its cells raise a runtime error in the library, leaving a realised grid of six objectives, 1,320 cells, and 15,840 specifications. Second, the metric-relative threshold rule discards 8,279 of 15,840 specifications (52.3%), unevenly across metrics. Table 2 reports kept/discarded counts for comprehensiveness (3,947/13), KL divergence (1,467/2,493), logit difference (1,270/2,690), and sufficiency (877/3,083); the surviving pool is 52% comprehensiveness versus 25% by design.

Section 7 reports preregistered results. Table 3 maps outcomes to results: P0 (structural premise) has mean Jaccard overlap 0.1396 [0.1377, 0.1418] and is treated as holding; H2 (claim instability / flip rate) is 0.7316 [0.7247, 0.7380], above the 0.20 threshold and confirmed; H3 (separation from the random null) is reported as separated with disjoint intervals and rejected; H4 (gap between claim instability and functional instability) is 0.3344 [0.3297, 0.3394] and supported. Decision rules and thresholds were fixed before the confirmatory sweep.

Section 7.1 says the Jaccard mean is computed exactly over all 28,580,580 specification pairs from 7,561 specifications and 3,218 distinct circuits. The pairwise D quantiles are 0.196 (1%), 0.788 (25%), 0.960 (median), and 0.998 (75%); the median pair shares 4% of edges. Overlap is much higher than the random-line expectation (median-size 200 gives 0.0031, about 45× chance; at 500 edges expected overlap is 0.008).

Section 7.2 reports flip rate F=0.7316 and modal share π*=0.4109; the evidence fails all preregistered filability tolerances (0.95, 0.90, 0.80). Table 4 lists nine claim classes at medium granularity; top shares are early/distributed 0.4109 and late/sparse 0.2848, with early/middle/late layer shares aggregating to 47.9%/43.6%/8.5% across size classes. All six addressee-granularity combinations reject filability.

Section 7.2’s addressee/granularity table (Table 5) shows filability fails for all six combinations: affected COARSE 0.3950/π*=0.7291, MEDIUM 0.6597/0.4875, FINE 0.6744/0.4786; overseer COARSE 0.5733/0.4788, MEDIUM 0.7316/0.4109, FINE 0.7681/0.4109, all marked no. The text reiterates that H2 is confirmed at F=0.7316 (95% CI 0.7247–0.7380) against the 0.20 threshold, and that early/distributed and late/sparse are the dominant claim classes (3,107 at 0.4109; 2,153 at 0.2848), with layer shares 47.9% early, 43.6% late, 8.5% middle.

Section 7.3: standardising one axis leaves substantial instability. Residual flip rates are 0.5939 (metric, biggest reduction 0.1377), 0.7014 (ablation), 0.7018 (objective), 0.7070 (threshold), 0.7092 (corruption), 0.7232 (prompt), and 0.7307 (seed). REML decomposition of log10 selected circuit size attributes 78.8% of structural variance to ablation-corruption interaction, 11.5% residual, 4.4% ablation, 4.1% threshold, 0.7% metric.

Section 7.4: removing all circuit-size information still leaves F=0.2706 (95% CI 0.2550–0.2859), above the preregistered 0.20 threshold.

Section 7.5 starts by stating that the pooled random comparison reverses when circuit size is held fixed; details are not yet shown.

final_notes:
Section 9 (Limitations): Scope/instrument/exclusions/bootstrap intervals limit conclusions. Generalisation is untested; a committed second-model study is still unrun. The planned second model is M9B/Pythia-160m, same task, 924-cell grid, identical on every axis except three seed levels; replication/refutation criteria were pre-fixed. The second task is also designed but unrun. Circuit size is an outcome, not an axis: size conditioning affects F, null-comparison direction, and the sign of the functional gap; pooled stats are reported with within-size decomposition. The space of defensible choices is wider than the measured space because C4Y/optimal ablation is defensible but excluded, so measured F is a lower bound on the full choice set. Discard rate is high and uneven; the retained metric imbalance is reported, not adjusted away. One bootstrap family is invalid for very small conditioning groups (2–5 specs): dominating self-pairs remain, so point estimates with diagnostics replace unusable intervals; no bias-corrected estimator was built.

Section 10 (Discussion): The paper argues measured evidentiary weight rather than presumed filing reliability. Complete metric standardisation does not resolve the filing problem; no single knob suffices, and declaring resolution after standardising one axis would be mistaken. The instrument’s discard rate is used as evidence of tooling maturity, not the headline. Claims/evidence listed: Table 6 best residual F=0.5939 (95% CI 0.5803–0.6063; 59.4%); Grid consequence table has 220 failed objective cells, 8,279 specifications admitting no circuit, and 52.3% discard rate; Section 7.5 Comparison table reports fixed-size K8Z 0.2746 vs random 0.4230 and fixed-size E7R 0.2706 vs random 0.3822. Measurement is said to be cheap relative to discovery, but no numerical cost comparison is given.

Section 11 (Reproducibility): Public commit `prereg-p1-confirmatory`; every reported number traces to config/seed/environment fingerprint. Archive verification says one environment across all 1,320 confirmatory cells; code commit recovered from archive matches git tree with 22/22 files identical. One script recomputes headline quantities with 36 checks, 0 failures, including F via three routes; another checks every manuscript numeric token. The suite contains 343 tests.

errors.claim: “With G empty, it reduces exactly to Equation 2.”
errors.evidence: Equation 3 is \(F_{\text{within}}(G)=1-\frac{\sum_g\sum_c n_{g,c}(n_{g,c}-1)}{\sum_g n_g(n_g-1)}\). If \(G\) is empty, both sums over \(g\) have no terms, so the expression is undefined as written rather than equal to Equation 2.

steps.notes_before: Section 4 formalism: a specification is \(s=(o,a,d,m,\tau,P,r,g)\), where \(o\)=objective, \(a\)=ablation operator, \(d\)=corruption distribution, \(m\)=evaluation metric, \(\tau\)=size threshold, \(P\)=prompt variant, \(r\)=seed, and \(g\)=granularity/claim-detail. Discovery outputs a circuit \(C(s)\subseteq E\); for GPT-2 small’s factorised graph, \(|E|=32{,}491\). The paper gives a closed-form component count: 144 attention heads + 12 MLPs = 156 components, and says the output receives from 157 non-terminal sources. Circuit instability is \(D=1-|C_i\cap C_j|/|C_i\cup C_j|\) and mean Jaccard similarity is \(\bar J\). Claim instability/flip rate is the pairwise probability of different structured Annex IV statements: \(F=1-\sum_c n_c(n_c-1)/(N(N-1))\), claimed to match brute-force tests; modal share is \(\pi^*=\max_c n_c/N\). Within-group flip rate \(F_{within}(G)\) is defined for conditioning groups and is said to reduce to Eq. 2 when \(G\) is empty, though the written formula seems undefined in that case.

Section 5 fixes the claim map φ as pre-registered, deterministic, and not LLM-generated. It defines two maps/addressees: φ_overseer uses Annex IV 2(e) and 3 with Article 14(4)(c), keyed first on dominant layer band, then size class, then ranked input segment; φ_affected uses Article 86(1) and leads with input segment. Granularities are nested: finer claims refine, not contradict, coarser ones.

Size bins were selected by a calibration rule from a measured node-count curve, not to maximize flip rate. Table 1 reports sensitivity to binning: committed bins F=0.7316; thresholds × 0.5, 0.8, 0.9 give 0.7448, 0.7435, 0.7394; 1.1, 1.25, 1.5, 2 give 0.7289, 0.7314, 0.7308, 0.7232; equal thirds 0.7018; deciles 0.7719; no size term (COARSE) 0.5733. The text says four alternatives exceed the committed bins, and the overall range across binnings is about 0.70 to 0.77.

Section 6 says the study uses GPT-2 small on indirect object identification for comparability and a random baseline. The pre-registered grid has seven discovery objectives, seven ablation operators, four corruption distributions nested within five operators that read them, four metrics, three thresholds, two prompt variants, and five seeds, yielding 1,540 discovery cells and 18,480 specifications. Corruption is nested, not crossed, because two operators never read the corrupt distribution. The analysis plan and both abstracts were committed before the confirmatory sweep; an append-only file tracks deviations and timing. Uncertainty is estimated with a nonparametric bootstrap over specifications (not pairs), B=10,000, with F and J̄ treated as U-statistics.

Two exclusions are fixed before seeing circuits: one objective fails completely, with all 220 cells erroring because mean squared error is computed against an integral target; this leaves 6 objectives, 1,320 cells, and 15,840 specifications. A metric-relative threshold rule discards 8,279 of 15,840 specifications (52.3%), unevenly across metrics. Table 2 reports kept/discarded by metric: comprehensiveness 3,947/13 (0.003 discard rate), KL divergence 1,467/2,493 (0.630), logit difference 1,270/2,690 (0.679), sufficiency 877/3,083 (0.779). The surviving pool is 52% comprehensiveness versus 25% by design. Unevenness was disclosed before lock from a six-cell validation slice.

Section 7 reports pre-registered results. Table 3 maps outcomes to results: P0 ̄J = 0.1396 [0.1377, 0.1418], H2 F = 0.7316 [0.7247, 0.7380], H3 is rejected because the data are separated from the random null, and H4 = 0.3344 [0.3297, 0.3394].

Section 7.1 says overlap is low but above chance: mean Jaccard 0.1396 over all 28,580,580 pairs among 7,561 specifications and 3,218 distinct circuits; D quantiles 0.196, 0.788, 0.960, 0.998; median pair shares 4% of edges; 1% of pairs exceed Jaccard 0.8. It compares median observed overlap to a random expectation of 0.0031 at size 200 and 0.008 at size 500.

Section 7.2 says flip rate is 0.7316, above the 0.20 threshold; modal share is π* = 0.4109, and evidence fails filability at all pre-registered tolerances. Table 4 lists 9 claim classes with shares summing to 1; the top two are early layers/distributed (0.4109) and late layers/sparse (0.2848). Aggregated layer shares are 47.9% early, 43.6% late, 8.5% middle; Table 5 says all six addressee-granularity combinations reject filability.

Section 7.3 reports residual flip rates after standardising each axis (Table 6). Residual F values are: evaluation metric 0.5939 (CI 0.5803–0.6063, removes 0.1377), ablation operator 0.7014, discovery objective 0.7018, threshold 0.7070, corruption 0.7092, prompt variant 0.7232, and seed 0.7307. The metric is the largest single reduction but still leaves F well above the 0.20 threshold. The text also says structural variance is mostly from ablation-corruption interaction (78.8%), with 11.5% residual, 4.4% ablation, 4.1% threshold, and 0.7% metric, while claim variance is said to be largest for the metric.

Section 7.4 says that after removing circuit size from the claim and holding size fixed, the result is F=0.2706 (95% CI 0.2550–0.2859), still above the 0.20 threshold.

The part includes Table 5 with addressee/granularity combinations: affected COARSE 0.3950/0.7291, affected MEDIUM 0.6597/0.4875, affected FINE 0.6744/0.4786, overseer COARSE 0.5733/0.4788, overseer MEDIUM 0.7316/0.4109, overseer FINE 0.7681/0.4109; all are marked not filable. Figure 1 captions the overseer-medium specification curve and says the pooled random comparison is confounded by circuit size, to be discussed in Section 7.5.

Section 8 defines the filability protocol: a claim must declare a specification space S (analytic axes and defensible levels with citations), declare a deterministic claim map φ as published code, compute π* = max_c n_c/N over S and F from Eq. 2, and is filable at tolerance α if π* ≥ 1−α. The filer should report π*, F, discard rate by axis level, and within-group decomposition of any pooled statistic. It argues a filing that cannot state its own π* is asserted, not audited, and that the regulator need not decide which analytic choice is correct.

Section 9 limitations: generalisation is untested because scale has not been tested; a pre-registered second-model replication on Pythia-160m (924-cell grid, same task, seeds with three levels instead of five) and a second task are designed but unrun. Size is an outcome, not an axis: threshold-selected circuit size distorts F, the null-comparison direction, and the sign of the functional gap; fixing size reduces F from 0.7316 to 0.2746, so pooled results must be decomposed by size. The instrument omits at least one defensible operator (optimal ablation [5]), so measured F is a lower bound relative to the field’s full defensible choices. The discard rate is 52.3% and the surviving pool is metric-imbalanced, though no repairs were made. Bootstrap intervals are invalid for conditioning groups with only 2–5 specifications because retained self-pairs dominate; point estimates are reported instead.

Paper summary claims: it studies whether circuit discovery can produce stable regulatory evidence by varying seven analytic choices and deterministically mapping each circuit to a structured Annex IV statement. On GPT-2 small and indirect object identification, 7,561 of 15,840 specifications produce a claim. Reported instability metrics: claim flip rate 73.2%; most common claim covers 41.1% of specifications; standardising the evaluation metric leaves a 59.4% flip rate; removing circuit size from the claim and holding size fixed leaves 27.1%; median circuit overlap is 4%; functional agreement adjusted for chance is near zero. One documented discovery objective does not execute. Scope caveat: one model and one task; generalisation to scale is untested.

This part is a glossary defining the paper’s terminology and symbols. It confirms key concepts from the summary: circuit discovery returns a circuit for each specification; a claim is a deterministic structured Annex IV statement produced by the claim map; claim flip rate is the probability two distinct specifications yield different statements; circuit instability is one minus Jaccard similarity; functional agreement concerns per-example correct/incorrect verdicts; and the paper’s main statistical objects include modal claim share, within-group flip rate, mean Jaccard similarity, and the random null. It also states that the study’s confirmatory grid uses GPT-2 small, indirect object identification, seven documented discovery objectives, and that six executed, matching the earlier note that one objective does not execute. No inconsistencies appear in this section.

This part is the abstract. It states the paper studies whether circuit-derived regulatory statements survive defensible analytic variation, using GPT-2 small on the indirect object identification task. It pre-registers 15,840 specifications across seven analytic axes, of which 7,561 produce a claim. The main results reported here are: claim flip rate 73.2% (95% CI 0.725–0.738), modal claim share 41.1%, metric-standardised flip rate 59.4%, and flip rate 27.1% (95% CI 0.255–0.286) after removing size from the claim and fixing size. Structural similarity is low, with median pairwise Jaccard overlap 4%, and functional agreement is very low, with Cohen’s kappa 0.015. The abstract also says the evidence fails the filability criterion at any plausible tolerance, and notes that one of seven documented discovery objectives does not execute on the library’s canonical task. No internal inconsistency is evident here.

This part frames the paper’s motivation: a circuit-level regulatory filing is only useful if a second analyst, using the same system and tool, would produce a compatible filing. It cites EU AI Act documentation/explanation requirements and says the paper does not propose a better discovery method, only assesses whether current evidence meets the presumed standard. Contributions listed: (i) a pre-registered multiverse over seven circuit-discovery axes, with every level from a published implementation and a deterministic map from circuits to Annex IV statements; (ii) a filability criterion π* ≥ 1−α, where π* is modal claim share and α is disagreement tolerance; (iii) evidence that instability remains after standardising any single axis, removing circuit size from the claim, and holding size fixed; (iv) three examples where pooled statistics invert when specifications select objects of different sizes. Earlier abstract results: 15,840 specifications across seven axes; 7,561 yield a claim; claim flip rate 73.2% (95% CI 0.725–0.738), modal claim share 41.1%, metric-standardised flip rate 59.4%, flip rate 27.1% (95% CI 0.255–0.286) after removing size from the claim and fixing size; median pairwise Jaccard overlap 4%; Cohen’s kappa 0.015; evidence fails the filability criterion at any plausible tolerance; one of seven documented discovery objectives does not execute on the library’s canonical task.

This part is related work. It frames prior literature along six themes: non-identifiability of mechanistic explanations; sensitivity of ablation-based faithfulness metrics to methodological choices; distinction between structure and function (phantom specialisation); estimator variance; auditing/standardisation; multiverse analysis; and metric inflation under optimisation pressure. It argues prior work motivates the paper’s question, but does not answer it. Specific cited claims: explanations need not be unique; faithfulness scores can depend strongly on analytic choices; structurally different circuits can implement the same computation; standardised evaluation is needed for comparison/auditing; and sufficiency/comprehensiveness can be inflated without changing predictions or explanations. The section says the paper’s contribution is downstream from non-identifiability: measuring the cost when an explanation is filed rather than published. It also says the paper uses a released library from Miller et al. and adapts multiverse/specification-curve ideas to a machine-learning evidentiary question. It emphasizes that the study reports discard rates by metric rather than pooling because some metrics can be inflated.

This section clarifies what the paper is not claiming. It says the results do not imply that discovered circuits are random, that different filers/mechanisms are equivalent, that seed effects are due to nondeterminism, or that results generalize to scale. It reports that discovered circuits are more stable than a size-matched random null (flip rates 0.2746 vs 0.4230), that functional instability is 0.3972 pooled and 0.4777 for the smallest circuits, and that Cohen’s kappa is 0.0146, indicating weak functional association. It also states that the seed corresponds to sampled prompts/evaluation-set variability, not random initialization, and that the study is limited to one model and one task.

Section 4 defines the formalism. A specification is s=(o,a,d,m,τ,P,r,g), covering objective, ablation operator, corruption distribution, evaluation metric, size threshold, prompt variant, seed, and granularity; all levels come from published implementations. Discovery returns a circuit C(s)⊆E. For GPT-2 small’s factorised graph, |E|=32,491; the paper says this is independently confirmed by a closed-form count, with 156 components total (144 attention heads and 12 MLPs). steps.notes_before: Section 5 introduces the claim map φ as pre-registered, deterministic, and not LLM-generated. There are two regulation-based addressees: overseer map φ_overseer (Annex IV 2(e) and 3 with Article 14(4)(c), keyed by dominant layer band → size class → ranked input segment) and affected-person map φ_affected (Article 86(1), keyed first on input segment). The paper says the three granularities are nested, with finer claims refining coarser ones. Table 1 reports sensitivity of flip rate F to size binning: committed bins 0.7316; thresholds ×0.5 0.7448; ×0.8 0.7435; ×0.9 0.7394; ×1.1 0.7289; ×1.25 0.7314; ×1.5 0.7308; ×2 0.7232; equal thirds 0.7018; deciles 0.7719; no size term (COARSE) 0.5733. The section’s claims assert that committed bins are not maximal, that removing size still leaves substantial instability, and that COARSE is the coarsest granularity.

Section 6 says the study uses GPT-2 small on indirect object identification. The pre-registered grid contains seven discovery objectives, seven ablation operators, four corruption distributions nested within five operators that use them, four metrics, three thresholds, two prompt variants, and five seeds, yielding 1,540 discovery cells and 18,480 specifications. Corruption is nested rather than crossed because two operators never read the corrupt distribution. The analysis plan and both abstracts were committed before the confirmatory sweep. Uncertainty is estimated by a nonparametric bootstrap over specifications (10,000 resamples), not p-values; F and J̄ are U-statistics over dependent pairs. Table 2 reports kept/discarded counts and rates for comprehensiveness, KL divergence, logit difference, and sufficiency, and says the unevenness was disclosed before lock.

Section 7 reports pre-registered outcomes. The paper reports four evaluation metrics: comprehensiveness, KL divergence, logit difference, and sufficiency. Hypotheses: H2 claim instability (F > 0.20 with CI lower bound above it), H3 no separation from random null, H4 functional gap > 0.10. Section 6 Method: one model/task (GPT-2 small Q7V on indirect object identification Z4K). The grid crosses analytic choices with 7 objectives, 7 operators, 4 corruption distributions nested within 5 operators, 4 metrics, 3 thresholds, 2 prompt variants, and 5 seeds, yielding 1,540 discovery cells and 18,480 pre-registered specifications. Discovery uses edge attribution patching (R8X) and integrated edge gradients (B3Q). Pre-registration included a committed plan, directional abstracts, and an append-only deviations file.

Statistics: no specification-level p-values; bootstrap over specifications with B=10,000; F and J̄ are pairwise U-statistics; CIs condition on the grid.

Exclusions: one objective fails entirely in the library, removing 220 cells and leaving 6 objectives, 1,320 discovery cells, and 15,840 realised specifications. A metric-relative threshold rule then excludes 8,279 specifications with no circuit, leaving 7,561 claim-producing specifications (discard rate 52.3%). Z8N/H4 functional gap is 0.3344 [0.3297, 0.3394] vs 0.10.

Section 7.1: claim-producing pool has 7,561 specifications, 3,218 distinct circuits, and 28,580,580 specification pairs. Circuits are described as almost disjoint: median D 0.960, median shared-edge fraction 4%, only 1% of pairs exceed Jaccard 0.8, median circuit size 200 edges, observed/chance overlap about 45x, expected random overlap for a 500-edge circuit 0.008, with analytic random line k/(2|E|-k).

Section 7.2: pair disagreement is 73.2% (95% CI 0.725 to 0.738). Modal pair attribute is early layers/distributed at 41.1%; second is late layers/sparse at 28.5%. Paper title: "Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection." Authors: Daniel Yoo and Adrians Skapars. Abstract claims linear probes on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct activations may fail OOD, but projecting activations onto a small subset of principal components from the training distribution enables cross-domain transfer close to probes trained directly on the test distribution. The paper also claims PC interpretations can identify transferable PCs: an LLM judge scores each PC by whether its most/least activating examples imply a transferable deception direction; probing the highest-scoring PCs closes the baseline-to-oracle gap by 78% on Insider Trading Report and 25% on Sandbagging. It argues source-probe weights encode source-specific surface features, while transferable directions encode the same contrast more abstractly and can be described in natural language. Main thesis: OOD robustness of probes is largely determined by subspace selection.

Paper title: "Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection." Authors: Daniel Yoo and Adrians Skapars. Core claim: linear probes on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct activations can fail OOD, but projecting activations onto a small subset of principal components from the training distribution yields better cross-domain transfer. The paper studies deception probes trained on a single source dataset (Roleplaying deception scenarios) and evaluated on three held-out targets: Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, and Sandbagging. Main thesis: OOD robustness of probes is largely determined by subspace selection in the source PCA basis, not the full representation.

Abstract-level claims: a small transferable subspace exists; an LLM judge can score PCs by whether their most/least activating examples indicate a transferable deception direction; probing the highest-scoring PCs closes the baseline-to-oracle gap by 78% on Insider Trading Report and 25% on Sandbagging. The paper argues source-probe weights can reflect source-specific surface features, while transferable directions are more abstract and can be described in natural language.

Introduction/contributions so far: they propose working in the basis of source-domain principal components rather than raw activations, then selecting a subset of PCs that avoids spurious correlations. They claim (1) a target-supervised greedy search over source PCs finds 8–15 components on which a source-trained probe nearly matches a target-trained probe; (2) source-side and target-side ranking by probe weights fails to recover a better-transfering subspace than the full representation baseline; (3) an LLM judge partially recovers the subspace without target data by identifying PCs likely to encode transferable behavioral contrast.

Related work frames the paper among three strands: (1) linear concept directions/subspaces in activation space, including work on truth/falsehood, honesty, emotion, refusal, and assistant-like behavior; (2) linear probes and their limitations, especially concerns about high accuracy, surface correlates, and uneven OOD generalization; and (3) natural-language interpretation of internal features via LLM-generated explanations, sparse autoencoder feature labeling, and concept ablation. No new empirical results yet, but the section motivates the paper’s focus on robust safety probes and interpretable subspace selection.

Section 3 defines the experimental setup. The paper uses 4 deception datasets from Goldowsky-Dill et al. Section 3 specifies the experimental setup. The model is Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (E6), using layer 15 residual-stream activations and averaging over assistant-response tokens only. The datasets are one source dataset (Roleplaying: V8) and three held-out targets: Insider Trading Report (C2R), Insider Trading Confirm (W6), and Sandbagging (J9). The labeler is GPT-4o (K8), with labels honest=0, ambiguous=-1, deceptive=1; ambiguous responses are dropped. Activations are standardized using source mean/variance, and those source statistics are applied to targets. PCA (N4D) keeps the leading 100 PCs (Q7), and a subset S is used for projection before training/evaluation. All classifiers are logistic regression with λ=10, while the full-representation baseline (B8Q) trains on all standardized activations. The 100-PC choice is for interpretability comparability, not because lower-index components generalize better; alignment with U9 decreases with PC index.

Section 4 reports experiments on transfer/generalization across the three held-out targets. Baselines: W6 transfer is reasonably good, C2R moderate, J9 poor. Source-trained probes in the retained source PCA subspace separate deceptive vs honest on every target, but the source-trained direction itself does not generalize well. Greedy selection over the leading 100 source PCs, using target labels only to choose directions (not fit weights), finds transferable subspaces; this is an upper bound because selection uses target folds. Small source-trained subspaces can nearly match target-trained probes, especially on C2R and J9, while variance-based selection only works well on easy W6 and fails on harder C2R/J9. Hypothesis-driven rankings (source-PCA probe T6 and target-PCA probe M9) do not recover the transferable subspace or beat the baseline; T6 is about as good as B8Q, M9 is good on C2R, worse than H2 on W6, and below random on J9. Section 4.4 uses an LLM judge (C7) to score each leading source direction via examples and OOD generalization ratings (R5), keeping all directions tied for the max score. Section 4.5 defines the interpretation-selected PC probe L2, with controls A7 (complement) and Y4 (equal-sized variance-ranked subset); L2 improves over B8Q on all targets and over A7 everywhere, with substantial gains on C2R and J9 but little headroom on W6.

Paper studies OOD deception detection via selecting principal components (PCs) from a source activation basis. It trains linear probes on one source dataset and evaluates on 3 held-out target datasets. Main reported methods/results: (1) a target-supervised greedy search that adds PCs by target performance finds 8–15 PCs and nearly matches probes trained on target data; (2) ranking PCs by source- or target-probe weights does not recover the transferable subspace; (3) an LLM judge scores natural-language PC descriptions without target data, and selecting 19 PCs with the maximum observed score in both runs improves transfer on all 3 targets. The summary says this selection closes 78% and 25% of the gap between the full-representation baseline and the greedy oracle on two targets.

Glossary confirms the paper’s terminology: source = Roleplaying, target = held-out deception datasets, probes are logistic regression on standardized activations, and PCA is done on scaled source activations. Token activations are averaged over the assistant response before probing. OOD/judge scoring uses a 1–10 scale; the maximum observed OOD score is 6, and the interp-selected set consists of the 19 PCs that received that maximum score in both scoring runs. Cross-validation is described as using 5 target folds. The glossary also notes that inference-time ablation/causal validation was not performed.

This related-work section frames the paper around linear concept directions, limitations of probes, and natural-language feature explanations, emphasizing that probe accuracy may not indicate robust concepts.

Section 3 defines the experimental setup. The paper uses four deception datasets: Roleplaying as the source domain and Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, and Sandbagging as target test sets. GPT-4o labels responses as honest (0), ambiguous (-1), or deceptive (1), and ambiguous responses are removed. Probes use layer 15 residual-stream activations from Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, averaged over the assistant’s response; layer 15 was chosen because it had the highest cross-domain AUROC in prior work. Activations are standardized using source-domain mean and variance, and those same statistics are applied to targets. PCA is fit on the standardized source activations and the top 100 PCs are retained. All probes are logistic-regression classifiers with λ=10. PC-based probes train/evaluate on subsets of the top 100 PCs, while baseline probes use the full standardized representation. The paper says the 100-PC subspace is kept because lower-index PCs align better with SAE decoder features and are more interpretable, but explicitly does not claim they generalize better.

Section 4 begins the experiments. Figure 2 shows that source-trained probes transfer unevenly from the source domain to targets: Insider Trading Confirm is relatively strong (0.874 AUROC), Insider Trading Report is moderate (0.706), and Sandbagging is poor (0.606). Training/evaluating within the top-100 source-PC subspace on target data via 5-fold CV yields much higher AUROCs (0.936 / 0.950 / 0.869 across the three targets), so the subspace itself contains enough target-discriminative information; the issue is the source-learned direction not generalizing.

Section 4.2 introduces a greedy PC-selection procedure that searches among the top 100 source PCs and uses labeled target examples only for subset selection. With 5-fold target CV, the selected source-trained probe is evaluated on held-out target folds. Selection stops when no added PC improves AUROC by more than 0.001; the resulting subsets average 15 PCs for Report, 8 for Confirm, and 14 for Sandbagging. This greedy method is treated as an upper bound / oracle transfer estimate, not an unbiased OOD estimate. A variance-matched control selects the top-k PCs by variance with k matched to greedy. Greedy nearly matches target-trained performance on Report and Sandbagging, improving baseline AUROC by 0.22 and 0.23, while variance-matched selection only matches greedy on Confirm and is much worse on Report and Sandbagging.

Section 4.3 sets up two hypotheses about why transferable PCs are selected: either they are individually strong target separators, or they are PCs the source probe already weights heavily; the section then tests whether source- or target-probe coefficient rankings can recover greedy performance.

Section 4.3 tests whether transferable PCs are recoverable by ranking PCs with a standardized coefficient (|probe weight| times PC std dev). Two rankings are compared: source-PCA probe rankings use source-trained weights; target-PCA probe rankings use target-trained weights. For transfer evaluation, the probe is still trained on source data projected onto the top-k PCs in each ranking. To choose k, greedy is rerun on the full target data (not foldwise), giving stable set sizes k=13 for Report, 7 for Confirm, and 14 for Sandbagging; these differ slightly from the 5-fold CV greedy results in Section 4.2.

Both ranking hypotheses fail. The source-PCA ranking transfers about as well as the full-representation baseline, implying the source probe emphasizes non-generalizing PCs. The target-PCA ranking does well on Report, but is worse than greedy on Confirm and below random on Sandbagging. The greedy-selected and target-ranked PC sets have small overlaps (Jaccard 0.182 / 0.077 / 0.167).

Section 4.4 uses LLM-based interpretations of the top 100 source PCs. For each PC, the authors inspect 8 most-activating and 8 least-activating source examples, and a judge assigns an OOD score from 1–10. No PC scores above 6, so 6 is the maximum observed score. PCs scoring 6 in both runs are retained, yielding 19 interp-selected PCs. Among the 5 PCs selected by greedy for more than one target, 3 receive score 6; among the top 5 source-PCA-probe PCs, only 1 receives 6.

Section 4.5 then evaluates the 19-PC interpretation-selected subspace against three controls: full-representation baseline, top-19 PCs by variance, and the 81-PC interp-ablated remainder.

Section 6 concludes that robust deception probing depends on selecting where the behavioral signal is represented, not just linear accessibility. It claims a small source-PC subspace can nearly match target-trained performance (8–15 components), that source- and target-side separability alone does not recover this subset, and that an LLM judge’s interpretation score over PCs partly recovers it without target data. The section restates that full-representation probes may mix general behavioral features with dataset-specific surface cues, and frames OOD probing as representation selection. It summarizes the evidence: small source-PC subspace nearly matches target-trained performance; separability alone does not recover it; interpretation recovers 78% of the Report gap and 25% of the Sandbagging gap, with no causal validation or inference-time ablation.

Appendix A lists the four deception datasets and their label distributions, with labels ordered ambiguous (-1), honest (0), deceptive (1): Roleplaying 371 (140/59/172); Insider Trading Report 473 (218/194/61); Insider Trading Confirm 151 (29/38/84); Sandbagging 1000 (379/375/246).

Appendix B gives the GPT-5-mini prompt used to interpret PC directions. It asks for the positive pole, negative pole, shared direction, and an OOD deception usefulness score (1–10), based on high-positive and high-negative token-activation examples from a roleplay setup where the model has a strategic chance to lie.

Appendix C reports that lower-index PCs align more strongly with SAE decoder features. Decoder alignment is defined as the match between a PC and an SAE decoder feature, using Spearman rho versus PC index. Figure 6 reports negative correlations: rho = -0.857 for the best-matching SAE feature and rho = -0.917 for the mean of the top 10 features.

Appendix D compares PC sets selected by source-only probe weights, greedy transfer selection, and target separability ranking. It says greedy and target-pca overlap little, and Table 2 lists selected PCs for each method and target.

Target-trained entries are measured inside the leading-100 source subspace. AUROC F3 values: B8Q = C2R 0.706, W6 0.874, J9 0.606; target-trained F3 = 0.936, 0.950, 0.869. H2 improvement over B8Q is 0.22 for C2R and 0.23 for J9 (W6 not reported), with H2 F3 used for recovery comparison 0.929 and 0.832. L2 F3 is 0.881 on C2R and 0.662 on J9, recovering 78% and 25% of the B8Q–H2 gap, respectively. Mean H2 subset size under target CV is 15 (C2R), 8 (W6), 14 (J9); full-target H2 k is 13, 7, 14. Additional observations: small H2 subset range 8–15; decoder alignment Spearman rho values are -0.857 for the best-matching feature and -0.917 for the mean of the top 10 features. Appendix B introduces the LLM judge prompt: GPT-5-mini (P2), with prompt instructions to interpret a bipolar Q7 direction from positive/negative token-activation examples and output Positive pole, Negative pole, Shared direction, and R5 (1-10). Appendix C states that lower-index Q7 directions align more strongly with decoder vectors/U9 features, using both best-matching-feature and mean-top-10-feature measures, and repeats the Spearman values -0.857 and -0.917. Appendix D reports low overlap between H2 transfer selection and M9 target-separation ranking: Jaccard D3 = 0.182 (C2R), 0.077 (W6), 0.167 (J9), with selected Q7 indices listed for T6 source, H2, and M9 on C2R/W6/J9. Appendix E: two scoring runs retained 19 directions at max R5=6, leaving 81 for A7. Five directions were selected by H2 for more than one target, and 3/5 of those were max-rated; 1 of the top 5 T6 selections was max-rated. Table 3 lists shared-H2 directions 62, 57, 9, 81, 86 with R5 6,6,3,3,6, emphasizing transferable denial/hedging but also lexical/domain brittleness. Table 4 lists 7, 8, 11, 12, 4 with R5 3,4,3,3,6, again mostly surface cues with transfer caveats.

The paper studies OOD deception detection in language-model representations, comparing probes trained on full representations versus selected subspaces/directions. One selection method uses target labels to choose directions without fitting probe weights on them; another uses natural-language interpretations without target data. The summary claims: small target-guided subspaces nearly match target-trained probes; source-weights, target-class separation, and explained variance do not recover the same transferable subspaces; interpretation-based selection improves over the full-representation baseline on all targets but with sharply varying recovery. The study uses one model and one source dataset, and its interpretations are descriptive rather than causal.

The paper studies OOD deception detection in Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct layer-15 residual-stream activations. The source dataset is Roleplaying (V8); held-out targets are Insider Trading Report (C2R), Insider Trading Confirm (W6), and Sandbagging (J9). Labels are -1 ambiguous, 0 honest, 1 deceptive; ambiguous examples are removed. Activations are standardized with source statistics, and PCA/N4D keeps the top 100 source directions. All classifiers are logistic regression with λ=10, and performance is AUROC with 95% CIs. The full-representation baseline (B8Q) uses all standardized activations; Y4 uses top-k PCs by variance. H2 is a target-guided greedy selection using target labels for direction choice but source-trained probe weights; it is treated as a transfer upper bound. T6/M9 are source- and target-trained ranking probes. X4 is the standardized coefficient magnitude. R5 is GPT-5-mini's OOD usefulness rating, used to build L2 (interp-selected PC probe) and A7 (its complement). The paper also measures SAE decoder alignment using the `andyrdt/saes-llama-3.1-8b-instruct` resource and Jaccard overlap among selected directions.

Baseline transfer varies: B8Q F3 is W6 0.874, C2R 0.706, J9 0.606. Target-trained probes on the retained source subspace separate honest vs deceptive on every target: C2R 0.936, W6 0.950, J9 0.869. Target-guided greedy selection (H2) starts from an empty subset over the 100 source PCs, adding directions that most improve target F3; it uses target labels for subset selection but not probe fitting. Mean H2 subset sizes under target CV are C2R 15, W6 8, J9 14; full-target H2 k values are C2R 13, W6 7, J9 14. H2 improves over B8Q by 0.22 on C2R and 0.23 on J9 (F3 0.929 and 0.832). Variance selection Y4 only matches H2 on W6. Source-ranking T6 transfers about like B8Q; target-ranking M9 does well on C2R, worse than H2 on W6, and below random on J9. H2 and M9 select different directions (H2–M9 D3: C2R 0.182, W6 0.077, J9 0.167).

errors.claim: “H2 improvement over B8Q, F3 points” is 0.22 for C2R and 0.23 for J9.
errors.evidence: In the same table, the listed values are B8Q F3 = 0.706 and H2 F3 used for recovery comparison = 0.929 for C2R, and B8Q F3 = 0.606 and H2 F3 used for recovery comparison = 0.832 for J9.
errors.explanation: These differences are 0.223 and 0.226 if using the recovery-comparison H2 values, not 0.22 and 0.23 as stated. They also do not match the gains implied by the later L2 row versus B8Q (0.175 and 0.056).

errors.explanation: The stated D3 values do not match the overlaps implied by the direction sets listed in the same part.

final_notes:
Appendix D compares Q7 direction sets. It states H2 and M9 overlap is low under Jaccard D3 and gives values C2R 0.182, W6 0.077, J9 0.167, but the listed indices imply different Jaccards (C2R 0.167, W6 0.100, J9 0.154). Target-guided greedy selection (H2) starts from an empty subset and greedily adds among the leading 100 source directions; it uses target labels for selection but not probe-weight fitting, and is treated as a transfer upper bound. H2 finds small subspaces (about 8–15 directions) that nearly match target-trained performance, especially on C2R and J9; its F3 is 0.929 on C2R and 0.832 on J9. Source-side and target-side coefficient rankings are compared using standardized coefficients (X4): source-PCA ranking T6, target-PCA ranking M9. Paper title: "Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection." Authors: Daniel Yoo and Adrians Skapars. Core claim: linear probes on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct activations can fail OOD, but projecting activations onto a small subset of principal components from the training distribution yields better cross-domain transfer. The paper studies deception probes trained on a single source dataset (Roleplaying deception scenarios) and evaluated on three held-out targets: Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, and Sandbagging. Main thesis: OOD robustness of probes is largely determined by subspace selection in the source PCA basis, not the full representation.

Abstract-level claims: a small transferable subspace exists; an LLM judge can score PCs by whether their most/least activating examples indicate a transferable deception direction; probing the highest-scoring PCs closes the baseline-to-oracle gap by 78% on Insider Trading Report and 25% on Sandbagging. The paper argues source-probe weights can reflect source-specific surface features, while transferable directions are more abstract and can be described in natural language.

Introduction/contributions so far: they propose working in the basis of source-domain principal components rather than raw activations, then selecting a subset of PCs that avoids spurious correlations. They claim (1) a target-supervised greedy search over source PCs finds 8–15 components on which a source-trained probe nearly matches a target-trained probe; (2) source-side and target-side ranking by probe weights fails to recover a better-transfering subspace than the full representation baseline; (3) an LLM judge partially recovers the subspace without target data by identifying PCs likely to encode transferable behavioral contrast.

Related work frames the paper among three strands: (1) linear concept directions/subspaces in activation space, including work on truth/falsehood, honesty, emotion, refusal, and assistant-like behavior; (2) linear probes and their limitations, especially concerns about high accuracy, surface correlates, and uneven OOD generalization; and (3) natural-language interpretation of internal features via LLM-generated explanations, sparse autoencoder feature labeling, and concept ablation. No new empirical results yet, but the section motivates the paper’s focus on robust safety probes and interpretable subspace selection.

Section 3 defines the experimental setup. The paper uses 4 deception datasets from Goldowsky-Dill et al. (2025): Roleplaying as the source domain and Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, and Sandbagging as target test sets. Labels are honest (0), ambiguous (-1), or deceptive (1) from GPT-4o, with ambiguous examples removed. Activations come from layer 15 residual stream of Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, chosen because Ying et al. (2026) found it had the highest cross-domain AUROC. For each prompt, activations are averaged over the assistant’s response. Source activations are standardized to zero mean and unit variance, and the same statistics are applied to targets. PCA is fit on source activations and the top 100 PCs are retained. Probes are logistic regression classifiers with lambda=10; subset experiments project onto selected PCs before training/evaluation, while baselines use the full standardized activations. The top 100 PCs are justified by decreasing alignment with SAE decoder features as PC index increases, making lower PCs more interpretable, but the authors explicitly say this is not a claim about better generalization.

Section 4 reports experiments on the same 3 target datasets. Source-trained probes on full representations transfer unevenly: AUROC is 0.874 on Insider Trading Confirm, 0.706 on Insider Trading Report, and 0.606 on Sandbagging. To verify the 100-PC subspace is not the bottleneck, the authors train probes directly on target data within that subspace using 5-fold CV and obtain 0.936 / 0.950 / 0.869 AUROC (Report / Confirm / Sandbagging), showing the subspace contains enough signal. They then use greedy PC selection guided by target-fold AUROC while fitting probe weights on source data; this converges to small subsets on average (15 PCs for Report, 8 for Confirm, 14 for Sandbagging) and substantially improves transfer, nearly matching target-trained probes for Report and Sandbagging. A variance-matched top-k baseline is much weaker, matching greedy only on Confirm. Section 4.3 asks whether transferable PCs are those individually discriminative on target or those with high source-probe weight, and compares PC rankings based on standardized coefficients from probes trained in the source-PCA basis.

Paper title: "Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection." Authors: Daniel Yoo and Adrians Skapars. Abstract claims linear probes on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct activations may fail OOD, but projecting activations onto a small subset of principal components from the training distribution enables cross-domain transfer close to probes trained directly on the test distribution. The paper also claims PC interpretations can identify transferable PCs: an LLM judge scores each PC by whether its most/least activating examples imply a transferable deception direction; probing the highest-scoring PCs closes the baseline-to-oracle gap by 78% on Insider Trading Report and 25% on Sandbagging. Main thesis: OOD robustness of probes is largely determined by subspace selection.

Paper title: "Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection." Authors: Daniel Yoo and Adrians Skapars. Core claim: linear probes on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct activations can fail OOD, but projecting activations onto a small subset of principal components from the training distribution yields better cross-domain transfer. The paper studies deception probes trained on a single source dataset (Roleplaying deception scenarios) and evaluated on three held-out targets: Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, and Sandbagging. Main thesis: OOD robustness of probes is largely determined by subspace selection in the source PCA basis, not the full representation.

Abstract-level claims: a small transferable subspace exists; an LLM judge can score PCs by whether their most/least activating examples indicate a transferable deception direction; probing the highest-scoring PCs closes the baseline-to-oracle gap by 78% on Insider Trading Report and 25% on Sandbagging. The paper argues source-probe weights can reflect source-specific surface features, while transferable directions are more abstract and can be described in natural language.

Introduction/contributions so far: they propose working in the basis of source-domain principal components rather than raw activations, then selecting a subset of PCs that avoids spurious correlations. They claim (1) a target-supervised greedy search over source PCs finds 8–15 components on which a source-trained probe nearly matches a target-trained probe; (2) source-side and target-side ranking by probe weights fails to recover a better-transfering subspace than the full representation baseline; (3) an LLM judge partially recovers the subspace without target data by identifying PCs likely to encode transferable behavioral contrast.

Related work frames the paper among three strands: (1) linear concept directions/subspaces in activation space, including work on truth/falsehood, honesty, emotion, refusal, and assistant-like behavior; (2) linear probes and their limitations, especially concerns about high accuracy, surface correlates, and uneven OOD generalization; and (3) natural-language interpretation of internal features via LLM-generated explanations, sparse autoencoder feature labeling, and concept ablation. No new empirical results yet, but the section motivates the paper’s focus on robust safety probes and interpretable subspace selection.

Section 3 defines the experimental setup. The paper uses 4 deception datasets from Goldowsky-Dill et al. (2025): Roleplaying as the source domain and Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, and Sandbagging as target test sets. Labels are honest (0), ambiguous (-1), or deceptive (1) from GPT-4o, with ambiguous examples removed. Activations come from layer 15 residual stream of Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, chosen because Ying et al. (2026) found it had the highest cross-domain AUROC. For each prompt, activations are averaged over the assistant’s response. Source activations are standardized to zero mean and unit variance, and the same statistics are applied to targets. PCA is fit on source activations and the top 100 PCs are retained. Probes are logistic regression classifiers with lambda=10; subset experiments project onto selected PCs before training/evaluation, while baselines use the full standardized activations. The top 100 PCs are justified by decreasing alignment with SAE decoder features as PC index increases, making lower PCs more interpretable, but the authors explicitly say this is not a claim about better generalization.

Section 4 reports experiments on the same 3 target datasets. Source-trained probes on full representations transfer unevenly: AUROC is 0.874 on Insider Trading Confirm, 0.706 on Insider Trading Report, and 0.606 on Sandbagging. To verify the 100-PC subspace is not the bottleneck, the authors train probes directly on target data within that subspace using 5-fold CV and obtain 0.936 / 0.950 / 0.869 AUROC (Report / Confirm / Sandbagging), showing the subspace contains enough signal. They then use greedy PC selection guided by target-fold AUROC while fitting probe weights on source data; this converges to small subsets on average (15 PCs for Report, 8 for Confirm, 14 for Sandbagging) and substantially improves transfer, nearly matching target-trained probes for Report and Sandbagging. Section 4.3 asks whether transferable PCs are those individually discriminative on target or those with high source-probe weight, and compares PC rankings based on standardized coefficients from probes trained in the source-PCA basis.

Section 4.3 compares two PC-ranking hypotheses using source-PCA coordinates: a source-PCA probe ranks PCs by weights from a probe trained on source data, and a target-PCA probe ranks PCs by weights from a probe trained on target data, but in both cases the evaluated probes are trained on source data restricted to the top k PCs from the chosen ranking. For this comparison, k is set by running greedy selection on the full target dataset (not CV): k=13 for Insider Trading Report, 7 for Insider Trading Confirm, and 14 for Sandbagging. Results: the source-PCA probe performs about like the full-representation baseline; the target-PCA probe is good on Report but worse than greedy on Confirm and below random on Sandbagging.

For each of the top 100 source PCs, the authors use the 8 most/least activating source examples and an LLM to describe the PC; an LLM judge assigns OOD/generalizability scores from 1–10. No PC scores above 6, so 6 is treated as the maximum observed score; PCs with that score in both runs are kept, yielding 19 interp-selected PCs. Of the 5 PCs that appear in greedy selections for more than one target, 3 receive the maximum OOD score.

Section 4.5 evaluates the 19 interp-selected PCs against three controls: full representation, top-19 PCs by variance, and the 81 PCs remaining after ablating the interp-selected set.

Paper studies OOD deception detection using principal components (PCs) of source activations from Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct. It uses four datasets from Goldowsky-Dill et al. (2025): Roleplaying as the source domain, and Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, and Sandbagging as target test sets. GPT-4o labels responses honest (0), ambiguous (-1), or deceptive (1); ambiguous responses are removed. Probes use layer 15 residual-stream activations averaged over the assistant’s response, following Ying et al. (2026). Activations are standardized with source mean/variance and the same statistics are applied to targets. PCA is run on the scaled source activations, and the top 100 PCs are retained. All probes are logistic-regression classifiers with parameter λ=10; PC-based probes train/evaluate on subsets of these 100 source PCs, while baselines use the full standardized representation. The paper says layer 15 had the highest cross-domain AUROC in prior analysis and that the 100-PC subspace still preserves enough information for source/target distinction.

Section 4 reports experiments on the 100-PC source subspace. In 4.1, source-trained full-representation probes transfer unevenly to the three targets: Insider Trading Confirm 0.874 AUROC, Insider Trading Report 0.706, and Sandbagging 0.606. Target-trained probes evaluated within the 100-PC subspace via 5-fold CV achieve 0.936 / 0.950 / 0.869 AUROC on Report / Confirm / Sandbagging, showing the subspace retains enough class information and that transfer failure is due to the learned direction, not missing information.

In 4.2, the paper introduces a greedy PC-selection algorithm that starts empty, iteratively adds the source PC that most improves target AUROC, and trains logistic-regression weights on source data only. Subset selection uses labeled target examples in non-held-out folds, so this is an oracle/upper bound rather than an unbiased OOD estimate. Selection stops when no PC improves AUROC by more than 0.001. Mean selected subset sizes are 15 PCs (Report), 8 (Confirm), and 14 (Sandbagging). Greedy nearly matches target-trained performance on Report and Sandbagging, improving baseline AUROC by 0.22 and 0.23, while variance-ranked top-k PCs only match greedy on Confirm and lag on the harder tasks.

In 4.3, the paper tests two hypotheses about transferable PCs: (1) PCs that individually separate target classes well; (2) PCs most important to the source probe. Figure 4 compares rankings by source-probe weights, target-probe weights, and greedy oracle selection across the three targets.

Section 4.3 compares two PC rankings using standardized coefficients (|weight| × PC std) on source-PCA activations: one from source-trained weights and one from target-trained weights. For transfer evaluation, source-trained logistic probes are fit on the top-k PCs in each ranking. To choose k, greedy is run on the full target dataset (not CV), giving stable sets of k=13 for Insider Trading Report, 7 for Confirm, and 14 for Sandbagging; these differ slightly from Section 4.2 because they use the full dataset. Result: both hypotheses fail. The source-PCA ranking transfers about as well as the full-representation baseline, while the target-PCA ranking works on Report but is worse than greedy on Confirm and below random on Sandbagging. Jaccard overlap between greedy and target-ranked sets is low (0.182 / 0.077 / 0.167).

Section 4.4 interprets top source PCs with LLM descriptions of positive/negative poles and an OOD score from 1–10. No PC scores above 6, so 6 is the maximum observed score. Scoring twice and keeping PCs that score 6 both times yields 19 interp-selected PCs. Of the 5 PCs selected by greedy for more than one target, 3 receive the maximum score, suggesting some recovery of transferable directions; only 1 of the top 5 source-PCA-probe PCs gets the maximum score.

Section 4.5 uses the 19 interp-selected PCs as a transfer subspace and compares them to top-19 variance PCs and an ablated 81-PC complement. The claim is that interpretation-based selection improves transfer without target data, with different gains across targets.

Section 6 concludes that robust deception probing requires choosing where a behavioral signal is represented, not just whether it is linearly accessible. It argues that a small subset of source PCs can nearly match target-trained probes for cross-domain transfer, while source-side or target-side separability alone does not identify the right subset. Paper title: "Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection." Authors: Daniel Yoo and Adrians Skapars. Core claim: linear probes on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct activations can fail OOD, but projecting activations onto a small subset of principal components from the training distribution yields better cross-domain transfer. The paper studies deception probes trained on a single source dataset (Roleplaying deception scenarios) and evaluated on three held-out targets: Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, and Sandbagging. Main thesis: OOD robustness of probes is largely determined by subspace selection in the source PCA basis, not the full representation.

Abstract-level claims: a small transferable subspace exists; an LLM judge can score PCs by whether their most/least activating examples indicate a transferable deception direction; probing the highest-scoring PCs closes the baseline-to-oracle gap by 78% on Insider Trading Report and 25% on Sandbagging. The paper argues source-probe weights can reflect source-specific surface features, while transferable directions are more abstract and can be described in natural language.

Introduction/contributions so far: they propose working in the basis of source-domain principal components rather than raw activations, then selecting a subset of PCs that avoids spurious correlations. They claim (1) a target-supervised greedy search over source PCs finds 8–15 components on which a source-trained probe nearly matches a target-trained probe; (2) source-side and target-side ranking by probe weights fails to recover a better-transfering subspace than the full representation baseline; (3) an LLM judge partially recovers the subspace without target data by identifying PCs likely to encode transferable behavioral contrast.

Related work frames the paper among three strands: (1) linear concept directions/subspaces in activation space, including work on truth/falsehood, honesty, emotion, refusal, and assistant-like behavior; (2) linear probes and their limitations, especially concerns about high accuracy, surface correlates, and uneven OOD generalization; and (3) natural-language interpretation of internal features via LLM-generated explanations, sparse autoencoder feature labeling, and concept ablation. No new empirical results yet, but the section motivates the paper’s focus on robust safety probes and interpretable subspace selection.

Section 3 defines the experimental setup. The paper uses 4 deception datasets from Goldowsky-Dill et al. (2025): Roleplaying as the source domain and Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, and Sandbagging as target test sets. Labels are honest (0), ambiguous (-1), or deceptive (1) from GPT-4o, with ambiguous examples removed. Activations come from layer 15 residual stream of Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, chosen because Ying et al. (2026) found it had the highest cross-domain AUROC. For each prompt, activations are averaged over the assistant’s response. Source activations are standardized to zero mean and unit variance, and the same statistics are applied to targets. PCA is fit on source activations and the top 100 PCs are retained. Probes are logistic regression classifiers with lambda=10; subset experiments project onto selected PCs before training/evaluation, while baselines use the full standardized activations. The top 100 PCs are justified by decreasing alignment with SAE decoder features as PC index increases, making lower PCs more interpretable, but the authors explicitly say this is not a claim about better generalization.

Section 4 reports experiments on the same 3 target datasets. Source-trained probes on full representations transfer unevenly: AUROC is 0.874 on Insider Trading Confirm, 0.706 on Insider Trading Report, and 0.606 on Sandbagging. To verify the 100-PC subspace is not the bottleneck, the authors train probes directly on target data within that subspace using 5-fold CV and obtain 0.936 / 0.950 / 0.869 AUROC (Report / Confirm / Sandbagging), showing the subspace contains enough signal. They then use greedy PC selection guided by target-fold AUROC while fitting probe weights on source data; this converges to small subsets on average (15 PCs for Report, 8 for Confirm, 14 for Sandbagging) and substantially improves transfer, nearly matching target-trained probes for Report and Sandbagging. A variance-matched top-k baseline is much weaker, matching greedy only on Confirm. Section 4.3 asks whether transferable PCs are those individually discriminative on target or those with high source-probe weight, and compares PC rankings based on standardized coefficients from probes trained in the source-PCA basis.

Section 4.3 compares two PC-ranking hypotheses using source-PCA coordinates: a source-PCA probe ranks PCs by weights from a probe trained on source data, and a target-PCA probe ranks PCs by weights from a probe trained on target data, but in both cases the evaluated probes are trained on source data restricted to the top k PCs from the chosen ranking. For this comparison, k is set by running greedy selection on the full target dataset (not CV): k=13 for Insider Trading Report, 7 for Insider Trading Confirm, and 14 for Sandbagging. Results: the source-PCA probe performs about like the full-representation baseline; the target-PCA probe is good on Report but worse than greedy on Confirm and below random on Sandbagging.

Section 4.4 asks whether the transferable subspace is human-interpretable. For each of the top 100 source PCs, the authors use the 8 most/least activating source examples and an LLM to describe the PC; an LLM judge assigns OOD/generalizability scores from 1–10. No PC scores above 6, so 6 is treated as the maximum observed score; PCs with that score in both runs are kept, yielding 19 interp-selected PCs. Of the 5 PCs that appear in greedy selections for more than one target, 3 receive the maximum OOD score.

Section 4.5 evaluates the 19 interp-selected PCs against three controls: full representation, top-19 PCs by variance, and the 81 PCs remaining after ablating the interp-selected set.

Then PCA on the standardized source activations retains the top 100 principal components (Q7), and a selected subset S is projected before training and evaluation. All classifiers use logistic regression with λ=10; the full-representation baseline trains directly on all standardized activations. The choice of 100 PCs is for interpretability comparability, because alignment with U9 decreases with index, rather than for better low-index generalization. Error bars are 95% CIs.

Section 4 reports results for several probes/subspaces. Baselines: source-trained full rep (B8Q) and source-trained leading-100 PC probe; target-trained probe on the retained source subspace separates honest vs deceptive on all targets, but the source-trained direction does not generalize. Target performance is W6 reasonably good, C2R moderate, J9 poor. Greedy target-guided selection over the leading 100 source PCs is an upper bound: it uses target labels for subset search only, with source-trained logistic weights, and yields H2. Small source-trained subspaces can nearly match target-trained probes, especially on C2R and J9, but variance-ranked PCs (Y4) only match H2 on W6 and otherwise fall behind. Source-side and target-side ranking methods use standardized coefficient X4 (abs coefficient times source PC std) on source-projected activations; source-PCA ranking (T6) and target-PCA ranking (M9) do not recover a basis better than B8Q. M9 is good on C2R, worse than H2 on W6, and below random on J9. Interpretation-based selection (L2) uses an LLM judge over the 8 most- and least-activating examples per source PC, retains directions with maximal OOD score, and then trains a source probe on the selected intersection; its controls are the complement (A7) and a variance-matched subset (Y4). J9 is described as the weakest and most out-of-distribution target; its gains are modest, while C2R’s improvement is more robust. The method is fully linear (N4D projection plus logistic regression), and the paper notes this may make transferable subspaces unsurprising.
