Paper studies OOD deception detection using principal components (PCs) of source activations from Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct. It uses four datasets from Goldowsky-Dill et al. (2025): Roleplaying as the source domain, and Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, and Sandbagging as target test sets. GPT-4o labels responses honest (0), ambiguous (-1), or deceptive (1); ambiguous responses are removed. Probes use layer 15 residual-stream activations averaged over the assistant’s response, following Ying et al. (2026). Activations are standardized with source mean/variance and the same statistics are applied to targets. PCA is run on the scaled source activations, and the top 100 PCs are retained. All probes are logistic-regression classifiers with parameter λ=10; PC-based probes train/evaluate on subsets of these 100 source PCs, while baselines use the full standardized representation. The paper says layer 15 had the highest cross-domain AUROC in prior analysis and that the 100-PC subspace still preserves enough information for source/target distinction.

Section 4 reports experiments on the 100-PC source subspace. In 4.1, source-trained full-representation probes transfer unevenly to the three targets: Insider Trading Confirm 0.874 AUROC, Insider Trading Report 0.706, and Sandbagging 0.606. Target-trained probes evaluated within the 100-PC subspace via 5-fold CV achieve 0.936 / 0.950 / 0.869 AUROC on Report / Confirm / Sandbagging, showing the subspace retains enough class information and that transfer failure is due to the learned direction, not missing information.

In 4.2, the paper introduces a greedy PC-selection algorithm that starts empty, iteratively adds the source PC that most improves target AUROC, and trains logistic-regression weights on source data only. Subset selection uses labeled target examples in non-held-out folds, so this is an oracle/upper bound rather than an unbiased OOD estimate. Selection stops when no PC improves AUROC by more than 0.001. Mean selected subset sizes are 15 PCs (Report), 8 (Confirm), and 14 (Sandbagging). Greedy nearly matches target-trained performance on Report and Sandbagging, improving baseline AUROC by 0.22 and 0.23, while variance-ranked top-k PCs only match greedy on Confirm and lag on the harder tasks.

In 4.3, the paper tests two hypotheses about transferable PCs: (1) PCs that individually separate target classes well; (2) PCs most important to the source probe. Figure 4 compares rankings by source-probe weights, target-probe weights, and greedy oracle selection across the three targets.

Section 4.3 compares two PC rankings using standardized coefficients (|weight| × PC std) on source-PCA activations: one from source-trained weights and one from target-trained weights. For transfer evaluation, source-trained logistic probes are fit on the top-k PCs in each ranking. To choose k, greedy is run on the full target dataset (not CV), giving stable sets of k=13 for Insider Trading Report, 7 for Confirm, and 14 for Sandbagging; these differ slightly from Section 4.2 because they use the full dataset. Result: both hypotheses fail. The source-PCA ranking transfers about as well as the full-representation baseline, while the target-PCA ranking works on Report but is worse than greedy on Confirm and below random on Sandbagging. Jaccard overlap between greedy and target-ranked sets is low (0.182 / 0.077 / 0.167).

Section 4.4 interprets top source PCs with LLM descriptions of positive/negative poles and an OOD score from 1–10. No PC scores above 6, so 6 is the maximum observed score. Scoring twice and keeping PCs that score 6 both times yields 19 interp-selected PCs. Of the 5 PCs selected by greedy for more than one target, 3 receive the maximum score, suggesting some recovery of transferable directions; only 1 of the top 5 source-PCA-probe PCs gets the maximum score.

Section 4.5 uses the 19 interp-selected PCs as a transfer subspace and compares them to top-19 variance PCs and an ablated 81-PC complement. The claim is that interpretation-based selection improves transfer without target data, with different gains across targets.

Paper title: "Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection." Authors: Daniel Yoo and Adrians Skapars. Abstract claims linear probes on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct activations may fail OOD, but projecting activations onto a small subset of principal components from the training distribution enables cross-domain transfer close to probes trained directly on the test distribution. The paper also claims PC interpretations can identify transferable PCs: an LLM judge scores each PC by whether its most/least activating examples imply a transferable deception direction; probing the highest-scoring PCs closes the baseline-to-oracle gap by 78% on Insider Trading Report and 25% on Sandbagging. It argues source-probe weights encode source-specific surface features, while transferable directions encode the same contrast more abstractly and can be described in natural language. Main thesis: OOD robustness of probes is largely determined by subspace selection.

Paper title: "Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection." Authors: Daniel Yoo and Adrians Skapars. Core claim: linear probes on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct activations can fail OOD, but projecting activations onto a small subset of principal components from the training distribution yields better cross-domain transfer. The paper studies deception probes trained on a single source dataset (Roleplaying deception scenarios) and evaluated on three held-out targets: Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, and Sandbagging. Main thesis: OOD robustness of probes is largely determined by subspace selection in the source PCA basis, not the full representation.

Abstract-level claims: a small transferable subspace exists; an LLM judge can score PCs by whether their most/least activating examples indicate a transferable deception direction; probing the highest-scoring PCs closes the baseline-to-oracle gap by 78% on Insider Trading Report and 25% on Sandbagging. The paper argues source-probe weights can reflect source-specific surface features, while transferable directions are more abstract and can be described in natural language.

Introduction/contributions so far: they propose working in the basis of source-domain principal components rather than raw activations, then selecting a subset of PCs that avoids spurious correlations. They claim (1) a target-supervised greedy search over source PCs finds 8–15 components on which a source-trained probe nearly matches a target-trained probe; (2) source-side and target-side ranking by probe weights fails to recover a better-transfering subspace than the full representation baseline; (3) an LLM judge partially recovers the subspace without target data by identifying PCs likely to encode transferable behavioral contrast.

Related work frames the paper among three strands: (1) linear concept directions/subspaces in activation space, including work on truth/falsehood, honesty, emotion, refusal, and assistant-like behavior; (2) linear probes and their limitations, especially concerns about high accuracy, surface correlates, and uneven OOD generalization; and (3) natural-language interpretation of internal features via LLM-generated explanations, sparse autoencoder feature labeling, and concept ablation. No new empirical results yet, but the section motivates the paper’s focus on robust safety probes and interpretable subspace selection.

Section 3 defines the experimental setup. The paper uses 4 deception datasets from Goldowsky-Dill et al. (2025): Roleplaying as the source domain and Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, and Sandbagging as target test sets. Labels are honest (0), ambiguous (-1), or deceptive (1) from GPT-4o, with ambiguous examples removed. Activations come from layer 15 residual stream of Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, chosen because Ying et al. (2026) found it had the highest cross-domain AUROC. For each prompt, activations are averaged over the assistant’s response. Source activations are standardized to zero mean and unit variance, and the same statistics are applied to targets. PCA is fit on source activations and the top 100 PCs are retained. Probes are logistic regression classifiers with lambda=10; subset experiments project onto selected PCs before training/evaluation, while baselines use the full standardized activations. The top 100 PCs are justified by decreasing alignment with SAE decoder features as PC index increases, making lower PCs more interpretable, but the authors explicitly say this is not a claim about better generalization.

steps.notes_before: Section 4 reports the main experiments. In 4.1, source-trained probes on full source representations transfer to the three targets with AUROC 0.706 (Insider Trading Report), 0.874 (Insider Trading Confirm), and 0.606 (Sandbagging). Target-trained probes evaluated within the top-100-PC subspace using 5-fold CV achieve 0.936 / 0.950 / 0.869 AUROC across the three targets, showing the subspace contains enough information. In 4.2, the authors introduce greedy PC selection using target-labeled folds to choose PCs while fitting probe weights on source data; it converges to small subsets (about 15 PCs for Report, 8 for Confirm, 14 for Sandbagging) and is described as an upper bound rather than an unbiased OOD estimate. They compare it to variance-ranked top-k PCs matched by the greedy subset size. Section 4.2 also contains a claimed improvement of 0.32 and 0.33 AUROC over the baseline for Report and Sandbagging, which appears numerically inconsistent with the reported baseline values.

Section 4.3 compares two alternative PC-ranking schemes for selecting source-PC subspaces: source-PCA probes rank PCs by weights from a source-trained probe, target-PCA probes rank PCs by weights from a target-trained probe; in both cases the final probe is trained on source data projected onto the selected source-PCA basis. To choose k, they rerun the greedy method on the full target dataset (not CV), getting stable subset sizes k=13 (Insider Trading Report), 7 (Confirm), and 14 (Sandbagging), slightly different from the earlier CV-based greedy sizes. Both alternatives fail to match greedy: source-PCA performs about as well as the full baseline, while target-PCA does well on Report but worse than greedy on Confirm and below random on Sandbagging.

Section 4.4 uses Bills/Casademunt-style interpretability on the top 100 source PCs. For each PC they take the 8 most/least activating source examples, ask an LLM to describe the poles and whole direction, and have a judge score generalizability from 1–10. No PC scores above 6; they treat 6 as the maximum observed OOD score and retain all PCs achieving it in both runs, yielding 19 interp-selected PCs. Among 5 PCs appearing in greedy selections for more than one target, 3 get the max OOD score; only 1 of the top 5 source-PCA-probe PCs does.

Section 4.5 tests whether these 19 interp-selected PCs recover greedy-like performance without target data. Controls are a top-19-by-variance probe and a probe on the remaining 81 PCs after ablating the selected PCs; Figure 5 reports AUROC across the three targets.

Section 4.5 evaluates the 19 interpretability-selected PCs against two controls: a top-19-by-variance probe and an ablated probe using the remaining 81 PCs. Figure 5 reports AUROC on the three targets. The interp-selected probe beats the baseline on all 3 targets and also beats the variance-selected control, with especially large gains on Insider Trading Report and Sandbagging; it also beats the ablated control on all 3. On Insider Trading Report, interp-selection closes 78% of the gap between baseline (0.706) and the greedy oracle (0.929). On Insider Trading Confirm, baseline performance is already near ceiling, so differences among selection methods are small and the result is said to be uninformative. On Sandbagging, interp-selection closes 25% of the gap to the greedy oracle. Overall, selecting PCs from natural-language descriptions yields a meaningful improvement over baseline without using target data.

Section 5 lists limitations: experiments use one model (Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, layer 15) and one source dataset (Roleplaying). Insider Trading Confirm is said to be uninformative because baseline transfer already reaches 0.874. Sandbagging is the weakest result: interpretability selection improves AUROC from 0.606 to 0.662, recovering 25% of the gap to the greedy upper bound (0.832). Insider Trading Report is the stronger result: 0.706 to 0.881, closing 78% of the gap to greedy at 0.929. The probe pipeline is fully linear (PCA plus logistic regression), so the transferable subspace result may be unsurprising; generalization to nonlinear probes or other readout locations is left open. The authors also note there is no causal validation: PC meanings are inferred descriptively from top-activating examples and LLM verbalizations, not from inference-time ablations.

Section 6 concludes that a small subset of source-domain PCs can enable cross-domain transfer that nearly matches target-trained probes, and that an LLM-based interpretability score over top-activating examples can partially recover this subspace without target data. The conclusion frames OOD probing as a representation-selection problem: identify not just whether behavior is linearly accessible, but where it is represented most robustly, since full linear probes may rely on dataset-specific surface cues that harm transfer.

Paper studies OOD deception detection with linear probes. Main thesis from the abstract: directions heavily weighted by a source probe encode source-specific surface features, while transferable directions encode the same contrast more abstractly and can be expressed in natural language; probe OOD robustness is largely determined by subspace selection. Introduction says linear probes can expose semantically meaningful information in LM representations but may fail out of distribution despite strong in-distribution performance. The paper frames harmful-interaction monitoring as a setting where such unreliability is unacceptable. It also says working in source Q7 coordinates avoids privileging latent dimensions; these coordinates provide data-driven representation structure, and selecting dimensions is the key problem. Figure 1 is described as an OOD deception-probing pipeline: project into the source N4D basis, filter candidate Q7 directions, then train a probe in the selected low-dimensional subspace. Related work: linear concept directions can support readout/intervention (true/false, honesty, emotion, refusal, assistant axis), but stable concepts vs context-dependent correlations remain unresolved; linear probes have interpretability value but may learn tasks/surface correlates; natural-language feature explanations support interpretation and intervention.

The model is Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, and the paper uses layer 15 residual-stream activations averaged over assistant-response tokens. The datasets are one source task (Roleplaying) and three held-out targets: Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, and Sandbagging. Labels are honest=0, ambiguous=-1, deceptive=1, and ambiguous examples are removed. Source activations are standardized to zero mean/unit variance, with source statistics applied to targets as well. Then PCA on the standardized source activations retains the top 100 principal components (Q7), and a selected subset S is projected before training and evaluation. All classifiers use logistic regression with λ=10; the full-representation baseline trains directly on all standardized activations. The choice of 100 PCs is for interpretability comparability, because alignment with U9 decreases with index, rather than for better low-index generalization. Error bars are 95% CIs.

Section 4 reports results for several probes/subspaces. Baselines: source-trained full rep (B8Q) and source-trained leading-100 PC probe; target-trained probe on the retained source subspace separates honest vs deceptive on all targets, but the source-trained direction does not generalize. Target performance is W6 reasonably good, C2R moderate, J9 poor. Greedy target-guided selection over the leading 100 source PCs is an upper bound: it uses target labels for subset search only, with source-trained logistic weights, and yields H2. Small source-trained subspaces can nearly match target-trained probes, especially on C2R and J9, but variance-ranked PCs (Y4) only match H2 on W6 and otherwise fall behind. Source-side and target-side ranking methods use standardized coefficient X4 (abs coefficient times source PC std) on source-projected activations; source-PCA ranking (T6) and target-PCA ranking (M9) do not recover a basis better than B8Q. M9 is good on C2R, worse than H2 on W6, and below random on J9. Interpretation-based selection (L2) uses an LLM judge over the 8 most- and least-activating examples per source PC, retains directions with maximal OOD score, and then trains a source probe on the selected intersection; its controls are the complement (A7) and a variance-matched subset (Y4). L2 improves over B8Q and Y4 on all targets, with the biggest gains on C2R and J9; W6 has little headroom and methods are mostly tied.

Section 5 states the paper’s limitations: results are narrow to a single model/source, with W6’s high baseline making it less informative. J9 is described as the weakest and most out-of-distribution target; its gains are modest, while C2R’s improvement is more robust. The method is fully linear (N4D projection plus logistic regression), and the paper notes this may make transferable subspaces unsurprising. Claims about directions “encoding” are only descriptive, based on extreme-activation examples and C7 verbalizations; the directions have not been causally validated by ablation during inference.

The justification for keeping 100 PCs is interpretability/comparability: alignment with U9 decreases with component index, so lower-index directions are more amenable to natural-language interpretation.

Section 4 reports experiment results on three targets (W6, C2R, J9). Baselines: source-trained probes in the retained source PCA subspace transfer reasonably well overall, but a target-trained probe within the same source subspace separates honest vs deceptive responses on every target, showing the information is present and the source-trained direction itself does not generalize. Interpretation-based selection uses an LLM judge to score each leading source PC from activating examples; the chosen directions are those with maximal OOD/generalization scores, and the evaluated method is L2. Section 4 reports experiments on OOD deception detection with three comparison families: full representation B8Q, target-guided subspace selection H2, variance-based selection Y4, and ranking-based probes T6/M9. In 4.1, source-trained full-rep transfer AUROC is W6 0.874, C2R 0.706, J9 0.606, while target-trained probes in the retained source subspace reach C2R 0.936, W6 0.950, J9 0.869. In 4.2, H2 is a greedy target-guided search over the leading 100 source Q7 directions, stopping when no improvement >0.001; it uses target labels only for subset selection, not weight fitting. Mean H2 subset sizes are C2R 15, W6 8, J9 14 (range 8–15). H2 improves over B8Q by 0.22 on C2R and 0.23 on J9; its full-target AUROC is 0.929 (C2R) and 0.832 (J9), slightly below the target-trained values. Y4 matches H2 only on W6 and is much worse on C2R/J9. In 4.3, T6 and M9 rank directions by standardized coefficient X4 (abs coefficient × source Q7 std) on source-N4D-projected activations. T6 performs about like B8Q; M9 does well on C2R, worse than H2 on W6, and below random on J9. H2–M9 direction overlap is modest (D3: C2R 0.182, W6 0.077, J9 0.167). Full-target H2 k values are C2R 13, W6 7, J9 14. Section 4.4 says interpretations suggest more domain-stable transferable contrasts, but recovery is only partial.

Section 4.5 introduces interpretation-only selection (L2): an LLM judge sees the 8 most- and 8 least-activating source examples for each leading source direction, produces pole and whole-direction descriptions, and assigns an OOD/generalization score R5. Selection keeps directions that reach the maximum score in both scoring runs; Appendix E reports max R5 = 6, 2 runs, and 19 directions retained. Claims: L2 (intersection of retained directions) improves over B8Q on all targets and over the variance control Y4 and ablated complement A7 on all targets; exact W6 values are not given, but W6 is largely tied across methods except A7. On C2R, L2 reaches 0.881 vs B8Q 0.706, recovering 78% of the baseline–H2 gap; on J9, L2 reaches 0.662 vs 0.606, recovering 25% of the gap. The retained intersection defines L2; A7 is its complement, and both are equal-dimensional variance-ranked subsets trained as source probes. Earlier in Section 4, H2 was a target-guided greedy subspace search over the leading 100 source directions, using target labels only for subset selection. H2 mean subset sizes were C2R 15, W6 8, J9 14, and its full-target AUROC values were C2R 0.929 and J9 0.832.

Section 4 reports experiments on the 100-PC source subspace. In 4.1, source-trained full-representation probes transfer unevenly to the three targets: Insider Trading Confirm 0.874 AUROC, Insider Trading Report 0.706, and Sandbagging 0.606. Subset selection uses labeled target examples in non-held-out folds, so this is an oracle/upper bound rather than an unbiased OOD estimate. Selection stops when no PC improves AUROC by more than 0.001. Mean selected subset sizes are 15 PCs (Report), 8 (Confirm), and 14 (Sandbagging). Greedy nearly matches target-trained performance on Report and Sandbagging, improving baseline AUROC by 0.22 and 0.23, while variance-ranked top-k PCs only match greedy on Confirm and lag on the harder tasks.

In 4.3, the paper tests two hypotheses about transferable PCs: (1) PCs that individually separate target classes well; (2) PCs most important to the source probe. Figure 4 compares rankings by source-probe weights, target-probe weights, and greedy oracle selection across the three targets.

Section 4.3 compares two source-PCA-basis rankings using standardized coefficients (|coef| times PC SD): a source-PCA probe ranked by source-trained weights and a target-PCA probe ranked by target-trained weights. The paper studies OOD deception detection in language-model representations, comparing probes trained on full representations versus selected subspaces/directions. One selection method uses target labels to choose directions without fitting probe weights on them; another uses natural-language interpretations without target data. The summary claims: small target-guided subspaces nearly match target-trained probes; source-weights, target-class separation, and explained variance do not recover the same transferable subspaces; interpretation-based selection improves over the full-representation baseline on all targets but with sharply varying recovery. The study uses one model and one source dataset, and its interpretations are descriptive rather than causal.

The paper studies OOD deception detection in Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct layer-15 residual-stream activations. The source dataset is Roleplaying (V8); held-out targets are Insider Trading Report (C2R), Insider Trading Confirm (W6), and Sandbagging (J9). Labels are -1 ambiguous, 0 honest, 1 deceptive; ambiguous examples are removed. Activations are standardized with source statistics, and PCA/N4D keeps the top 100 source directions. All classifiers are logistic regression with λ=10, and performance is AUROC with 95% CIs. The full-representation baseline (B8Q) uses all standardized activations; Y4 uses top-k PCs by variance. H2 is a target-guided greedy selection using target labels for direction choice but source-trained probe weights; it is treated as a transfer upper bound. T6/M9 are source- and target-trained ranking probes. X4 is the standardized coefficient magnitude. R5 is GPT-5-mini's OOD usefulness rating, used to build L2 (interp-selected PC probe) and A7 (its complement). The paper also measures SAE decoder alignment using the `andyrdt/saes-llama-3.1-8b-instruct` resource and Jaccard overlap among selected directions.

The paper also states that lower-index PCA directions are more interpretable because alignment with sparse-autoencoder decoder features decreases with index.

Section 4 compares full representations, target-guided subspaces, coefficient rankings, and interpretation-based selection. Baseline transfer varies by target: source-trained full-representation B8Q AUROC is W6 0.874, C2R 0.706, J9 0.606. In contrast, target-trained probes evaluated within the retained source subspace perform well on all targets: C2R 0.936, W6 0.950, J9 0.869 (5-fold CV). H2 is a greedy target-guided search over the top 100 source PCs; it starts empty, adds the direction that most improves target F3, stops when no gain exceeds 0.001, and uses target labels only for subset selection, not weight fitting. H2 selects small subspaces (mean sizes C2R 15, W6 8, J9 14) and improves over B8Q by 0.22 on C2R and 0.23 on J9, with H2 F3 0.929 and 0.832 respectively. Variance selection Y4 matches H2 only on W6 and is worse on C2R/J9. The ranking methods T6 (source-PCA probe) and M9 (target-PCA probe) use standardized coefficient X4 = |weight| × source-PC standard deviation on source-N4D-projected activations; both train source logistic regression on top-k ranked directions. T6 performs about like B8Q; M9 does well on C2R, worse than H2 on W6, and below random on J9. Full-target H2 uses target-specific k values C2R 13, W6 7, J9 14; its numbers differ slightly from CV. Section 4.4 begins the interpretation analysis and states recovery is only partial.

Section 4.5 introduces interpretation-only selection. For each leading source direction, an LLM judge (C7) sees the 8 most-activating and 8 least-activating source examples, produces positive-pole, negative-pole, and whole-direction descriptions, and assigns a generalization/OOD score R5. Selection keeps directions that reach the maximum score in both scoring runs; the observed maximum R5 is 6, there are 2 scoring runs, and 19 directions meet that max in both runs.

Claims/evidence: H2 interpretations include potentially transferable contrasts and explicit limits: Q7 directions 62, 57, and 86 have R5 6; Q7 9 and 81 have R5 3. Recovery is partial: among shared H2 selections, 3/5 are max-rated; among the top T6 selections, 1/5 is max-rated.

L2 is the intersection of directions retained across both scoring runs. Its controls are A7 (the complement) and Y4 (equal-dimensional variance-ranked subset). L2 is trained as a source probe, improves over B8Q on C2R and J9, and exceeds B8Q, Y4, and A7 on all targets; W6 has little headroom and methods are roughly tied except A7. Reported gains: C2R 0.881 vs B8Q 0.706, J9 0.662 vs 0.606; baseline–H2 gap recovered by L2 is 78% on C2R and 25% on J9. L2 and A7 are complementary subsets of sizes 19 and 81.

Section 5 (Limitations) says the paper’s results are narrow in scope: only one model and one source dataset are studied, so other models/datasets remain open. W6 already has a high baseline (0.874 in Appendix A), so its results are described as uninformative. J9 is the weakest and most out-of-distribution target; its improvement is modest and likely due to distribution shift, while C2R’s improvement is more robust. The pipeline is fully linear (N4D projection + logistic regression), which may make transferable-subspace existence less surprising; extensions to nonlinear probes or other readout locations are left open. Interpretations of what directions “encode” are only descriptive, based on extreme-activation examples and C7 verbalizations, and no inference-time ablation has been reported to causally verify them.

Paper title: "Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection." Authors: Daniel Yoo and Adrians Skapars. Core claim: linear probes on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct activations can fail OOD, but projecting activations onto a small subset of principal components from the training distribution yields better cross-domain transfer. The paper studies deception probes trained on a single source dataset (Roleplaying deception scenarios) and evaluated on three held-out targets: Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, and Sandbagging. Main thesis: OOD robustness of probes is largely determined by subspace selection in the source PCA basis, not the full representation.

Abstract-level claims: a small transferable subspace exists; an LLM judge can score PCs by whether their most/least activating examples indicate a transferable deception direction; probing the highest-scoring PCs closes the baseline-to-oracle gap by 78% on Insider Trading Report and 25% on Sandbagging. The paper argues source-probe weights can reflect source-specific surface features, while transferable directions are more abstract and can be described in natural language.

Introduction/contributions so far: they propose working in the basis of source-domain principal components rather than raw activations, then selecting a subset of PCs that avoids spurious correlations. They claim (1) a target-supervised greedy search over source PCs finds 8–15 components on which a source-trained probe nearly matches a target-trained probe; (2) source-side and target-side ranking by probe weights fails to recover a better-transfering subspace than the full representation baseline; (3) an LLM judge partially recovers the subspace without target data by identifying PCs likely to encode transferable behavioral contrast.

Related work frames the paper among three strands: (1) linear concept directions/subspaces in activation space, including work on truth/falsehood, honesty, emotion, refusal, and assistant-like behavior; (2) linear probes and their limitations, especially concerns about high accuracy, surface correlates, and uneven OOD generalization; and (3) natural-language interpretation of internal features via LLM-generated explanations, sparse autoencoder feature labeling, and concept ablation. No new empirical results yet, but the section motivates the paper’s focus on robust safety probes and interpretable subspace selection.

Section 3 defines the experimental setup. The paper uses 4 deception datasets from Goldowsky-Dill et al. (2025): Roleplaying as the source domain and Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, and Sandbagging as target test sets. Labels are honest (0), ambiguous (-1), or deceptive (1) from GPT-4o, with ambiguous examples removed. Activations come from layer 15 residual stream of Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, chosen because Ying et al. (2026) found it had the highest cross-domain AUROC. For each prompt, activations are averaged over the assistant’s response. Source activations are standardized to zero mean and unit variance, and the same statistics are applied to targets. PCA is fit on source activations and the top 100 PCs are retained. Probes are logistic regression classifiers with lambda=10; subset experiments project onto selected PCs before training/evaluation, while baselines use the full standardized activations. The top 100 PCs are justified by decreasing alignment with SAE decoder features as PC index increases, making lower PCs more interpretable, but the authors explicitly say this is not a claim about better generalization.

Section 4 reports experiments on the same 3 target datasets. Source-trained probes on full representations transfer unevenly: AUROC is 0.874 on Insider Trading Confirm, 0.706 on Insider Trading Report, and 0.606 on Sandbagging. To verify the 100-PC subspace is not the bottleneck, the authors train probes directly on target data within that subspace using 5-fold CV and obtain 0.936 / 0.950 / 0.869 AUROC (Report / Confirm / Sandbagging), showing the subspace contains enough signal. They then use greedy PC selection guided by target-fold AUROC while fitting probe weights on source data; this converges to small subsets on average (15 PCs for Report, 8 for Confirm, 14 for Sandbagging) and substantially improves transfer, nearly matching target-trained probes for Report and Sandbagging. A variance-matched top-k baseline is much weaker, matching greedy only on Confirm. Section 4.3 asks whether transferable PCs are those individually discriminative on target or those with high source-probe weight, and compares PC rankings based on standardized coefficients from probes trained in the source-PCA basis.

Section 4.3 compares two PC-ranking hypotheses using source-PCA coordinates: a source-PCA probe ranks PCs by weights from a probe trained on source data, and a target-PCA probe ranks PCs by weights from a probe trained on target data, but in both cases the evaluated probes are trained on source data restricted to the top k PCs from the chosen ranking. For this comparison, k is set by running greedy selection on the full target dataset (not CV): k=13 for Insider Trading Report, 7 for Insider Trading Confirm, and 14 for Sandbagging. Results: the source-PCA probe performs about like the full-representation baseline; the target-PCA probe is good on Report but worse than greedy on Confirm and below random on Sandbagging.

Section 4.4 asks whether the transferable subspace is human-interpretable. For each of the top 100 source PCs, the authors use the 8 most/least activating source examples and an LLM to describe the PC; an LLM judge assigns OOD/generalizability scores from 1–10. No PC scores above 6, so 6 is treated as the maximum observed score; PCs with that score in both runs are kept, yielding 19 interp-selected PCs. Of the 5 PCs that appear in greedy selections for more than one target, 3 receive the maximum OOD score.

Section 4.5 evaluates the 19 interp-selected PCs against three controls: full representation, top-19 PCs by variance, and the 81 PCs remaining after ablating the interp-selected set.

Section 4.5 evaluates the 19 interp-selected PCs against three controls: full representation (baseline), top-19 PCs by variance, and the 81 PCs remaining after ablating the interp-selected set. The interp-selected PC probe outperforms the baseline on all 3 targets and also beats the source-variance-selected control; it also outperforms the interp-ablated control on all 3 targets. The reported recovery varies by dataset: on Insider Trading Report, interp-selection closes 78% of the gap between baseline (0.706) and the greedy oracle (0.929); on Insider Trading Confirm, the baseline is lower than on Sandbagging and the selection methods (except interp-ablated) are roughly similar; on Sandbagging, interp-selection closes 25% of the gap to the greedy oracle (oracle score 0.832). Overall, natural-language-based PC selection improves generalization without target data.

Section 5 lists limitations: all experiments use one model (Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, layer 15) and one source dataset (Roleplaying); generalization to other models/datasets is open. Paper studies OOD deception detection using principal components (PCs) of source activations from Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct. It uses four datasets from Goldowsky-Dill et al. (2025): Roleplaying as the source domain, and Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, and Sandbagging as target test sets. GPT-4o labels responses honest (0), ambiguous (-1), or deceptive (1); ambiguous responses are removed. Probes use layer 15 residual-stream activations averaged over the assistant’s response, following Ying et al. (2026). Activations are standardized with source mean/variance and the same statistics are applied to targets. PCA is run on the scaled source activations, and the top 100 PCs are retained. All probes are logistic-regression classifiers with parameter λ=10; PC-based probes train/evaluate on subsets of these 100 source PCs, while baselines use the full standardized representation. The paper says layer 15 had the highest cross-domain AUROC in prior analysis and that the 100-PC subspace still preserves enough information for source/target distinction.

Section 4 reports experiments on the 100-PC source subspace. In 4.1, source-trained full-representation probes transfer unevenly to the three targets: Insider Trading Confirm 0.874 AUROC, Insider Trading Report 0.706, and Sandbagging 0.606. Target-trained probes evaluated within the 100-PC subspace via 5-fold CV achieve 0.936 / 0.950 / 0.869 AUROC on Report / Confirm / Sandbagging, showing the subspace retains enough class information and that transfer failure is due to the learned direction, not missing information.

In 4.2, the paper introduces a greedy PC-selection algorithm that starts empty, iteratively adds the source PC that most improves target AUROC, and trains logistic-regression weights on source data only. Subset selection uses labeled target examples in non-held-out folds, so this is an oracle/upper bound rather than an unbiased OOD estimate. Selection stops when no PC improves AUROC by more than 0.001. Mean selected subset sizes are 15 PCs (Report), 8 (Confirm), and 14 (Sandbagging). Greedy nearly matches target-trained performance on Report and Sandbagging, improving baseline AUROC by 0.22 and 0.23, while variance-ranked top-k PCs only match greedy on Confirm and lag on the harder tasks.

In 4.3, the paper tests two hypotheses about transferable PCs: (1) PCs that individually separate target classes well; (2) PCs most important to the source probe. Figure 4 compares rankings by source-probe weights, target-probe weights, and greedy oracle selection across the three targets.

Section 4.3 compares two PC rankings using standardized coefficients (|weight| × PC std) on source-PCA activations: one from source-trained weights and one from target-trained weights. For transfer evaluation, source-trained logistic probes are fit on the top-k PCs in each ranking. To choose k, greedy is run on the full target dataset (not CV), giving stable sets of k=13 for Insider Trading Report, 7 for Confirm, and 14 for Sandbagging; these differ slightly from Section 4.2 because they use the full dataset. Result: both hypotheses fail. The source-PCA ranking transfers about as well as the full-representation baseline, while the target-PCA ranking works on Report but is worse than greedy on Confirm and below random on Sandbagging. Jaccard overlap between greedy and target-ranked sets is low (0.182 / 0.077 / 0.167).

Section 4.4 interprets top source PCs with LLM descriptions of positive/negative poles and an OOD score from 1–10. No PC scores above 6, so 6 is the maximum observed score. Scoring twice and keeping PCs that score 6 both times yields 19 interp-selected PCs. Of the 5 PCs selected by greedy for more than one target, 3 receive the maximum score, suggesting some recovery of transferable directions; only 1 of the top 5 source-PCA-probe PCs gets the maximum score.

Section 4.5 uses the 19 interp-selected PCs as a transfer subspace and compares them to top-19 variance PCs and an ablated 81-PC complement. The claim is that interpretation-based selection improves transfer without target data, with different gains across targets.

Section 6’s conclusion remains that only a small subset of source-domain PCs seems to transfer, and OOD probing is framed as a representation-selection problem rather than simple linear decodability. The experimental setup described earlier is still one model (Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, layer 15) with Roleplaying as the source dataset; Sandbagging is the weakest target and Insider Trading Report the stronger one. Appendix A defines the datasets: Roleplaying (371; 140/59/172), Insider Trading Report (473; 218/194/61), Insider Trading Confirm (151; 29/38/84), and Sandbagging (1000; 379/375/246). Appendix B uses GPT-5-mini to interpret top Roleplaying PCs and score their OOD deception usefulness, without causal validation.

Appendix C reports that lower PCs show stronger decoder alignment with SAE features, with Spearman rho values of -0.857 for the best-matching SAE feature and -0.917 for the mean of the top 10 features. Appendix D compares PC sets from source-only probe weights, greedy transfer selection, and target separability ranking across Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, and Sandbagging. The Jaccard overlaps between greedy and target-PCA sets are low: 0.182, 0.077, and 0.167, respectively, supporting the claim that the transferable subspace is not simply the most discriminative part of the source or target representation space. Appendix E gives LLM-judged interpretability scores for selected PCs, including PC62/57/9 for Insider Trading Report + Sandbagging and PC81/86 for Insider Trading Confirm + Sandbagging, with OOD scores ranging from 3 to 6, and also Table 4 scores for PCs 7, 8, 11, 12, and 4 (scores 3, 4, 3, 3, 6).

Paper title: "Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection." Authors: Daniel Yoo and Adrians Skapars. Abstract claims linear probes on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct activations may fail OOD, but projecting activations onto a small subset of principal components from the training distribution enables cross-domain transfer close to probes trained directly on the test distribution. The paper also claims PC interpretations can identify transferable PCs: an LLM judge scores each PC by whether its most/least activating examples imply a transferable deception direction; probing the highest-scoring PCs closes the baseline-to-oracle gap by 78% on Insider Trading Report and 25% on Sandbagging. It argues source-probe weights encode source-specific surface features, while transferable directions encode the same contrast more abstractly and can be described in natural language. Main thesis: OOD robustness of probes is largely determined by subspace selection.

Paper title: "Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection." Authors: Daniel Yoo and Adrians Skapars. The paper studies linear deception probes on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct activations under OOD shift. Core claim: probes trained on source activations can fail OOD because they learn spurious correlations, but selecting a small transferable subspace in the source PCA basis can yield much better transfer. The setup uses a single source dataset (Roleplaying deception scenarios) and three held-out target datasets: Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, and Sandbagging.

Main contributions stated in the introduction: (1) a small transferable subspace exists; a target-supervised greedy search over source PCs finds about 8–15 components where a source-trained probe nearly matches a target-trained probe. (2) Source-side and target-side rankings do not recover this subspace; ranking PCs by either source or target probe weights does not beat the full-representation baseline. (3) An LLM judge can partially recover transferable PCs without target data by identifying PCs whose most/least activating examples suggest a transferable behavioral contrast.

Overall thesis from the abstract/intro: OOD robustness of probes is largely determined by subspace selection, and transferable directions can be identified and sometimes described in natural language.

The paper’s related work frames the contribution in three adjacent areas: (1) linear concept directions/subspaces in activation space, citing work on linear representation hypotheses and population-level directions for properties like honesty, emotion, refusal, and assistant-like behavior; (2) linear probes and their known limitations, including concerns that high in-distribution probe accuracy may reflect spurious correlates and may not transfer OOD; and (3) natural-language interpretation of features, via LLM-generated explanations for neurons/features and their use in intervention/ablation.

These sections support the paper’s motivation that probing can be unstable OOD and that interpretability methods may help identify transferable subspaces or directions.

Section 3 setup: Uses 4 deception datasets from Goldowsky-Dill et al. (2025): Roleplaying (source) plus three targets (Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, Sandbagging). Labels are honest (0), ambiguous (-1), deceptive (1); ambiguous examples are removed. Model is Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, using layer 15 residual stream activations, chosen because it had the highest cross-domain AUROC in Ying et al. (2026). Activations are averaged over the assistant’s response. For probes, source activations are standardized to zero mean/unit variance and the same source statistics are applied to targets. PCA is fit on source and top 100 PCs are retained. Probes are logistic regression with λ=10. Subset-S experiments project onto chosen PCs before training/eval; baseline uses full standardized activations. Authors justify 100 PCs because alignment with SAE decoder features decreases with PC index, making lower PCs more interpretable, but they explicitly say this is not a claim that low-index PCs generalize better; they later say the 100-PC subspace retains enough information to separate deceptive from honest responses on every target.

Section 4 results: Source-trained probes on full representations transfer to targets with AUROC 0.874 (Insider Trading Confirm), 0.706 (Insider Trading Report), and 0.606 (Sandbagging). Training/evaluating directly within the top-100 source PC subspace via target 5-fold CV gives 0.936 / 0.950 / 0.869 AUROC, supporting the claim that the 100-PC subspace retains enough signal to separate deceptive vs honest responses on all targets. 

Greedy PC selection: starting from no PCs, iteratively add from the top 100 PCs the one that most improves target AUROC, training the probe on source data projected to the selected subset. Selection uses target labels within CV folds, so it is an upper bound rather than unbiased OOD estimate. The greedy search converges to small subsets on average: 15 PCs (Insider Trading Report), 8 (Insider Trading Confirm), 14 (Sandbagging). The setup uses Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (E6) and extracts layer-15 residual-stream activations, averaged over assistant-response tokens. The datasets are Goldowsky-Dill et al. (2025): one source dataset, Roleplaying (V8), and three held-out targets: Insider Trading Report (C2R), Insider Trading Confirm (W6), and Sandbagging (J9). Labels are honest=0, ambiguous=-1, deceptive=1, and ambiguous examples are removed. Source activations are standardized to zero mean/unit variance, and the same source statistics are used to standardize targets. PCA then keeps the leading 100 principal components, and the classifier is logistic regression with lambda=10; the full-representation baseline trains on all standardized activations. The paper says the 100-component choice is for interpretability comparability rather than best low-index generalization, because alignment with U9 decreases with index and lower indices are more interpretable.

Section 4 presents the main experimental comparisons. Baseline: source-trained full representations transfer unevenly across targets; W6 is reasonably good, C2R moderate, J9 poor. However, when training within the retained source subspace, target-trained probes separate deceptive from honest on every target, showing the relevant information exists but the source-trained direction does not generalize. 

A transferable subspace search is then evaluated: starting from no directions, the method greedily adds one of the leading 100 source-ranked directions to improve target F3, using target labels only for subset selection (not weight fitting). This is a transfer upper bound, not an unbiased OOD estimate. Small source-trained subspaces nearly match target-trained probes, especially on C2R and J9. Variance-based selection only matches the greedy oracle on easy W6 and performs much worse on C2R/J9; explained variance is not predictive.

Hypothesis tests compare source-side ranking (source-PCA probe: T6) and target-side ranking (target-PCA probe: M9). Neither recovers the transferable subspace or beats the variance baseline consistently. T6 is about as good as the variance baseline. M9 does well on C2R, is worse than H2 on W6, and falls below random on J9. Both ranking schemes use standardized coefficient magnitude (absolute coefficient times corresponding PC standard deviation).

Interpretation-based selection: an LLM judge (C7) scores leading source directions from activating examples and assigns an OOD generalization score (R5); all directions tied for maximum score in both runs are retained. The resulting language-only selected subspace (L2) improves over the variance baseline on all targets, especially C2R and J9, and also beats the ablated control (A7). The equal-dimensional variance-ranked control is Y4. W6 remains largely uninformative because methods are mostly tied there.

Section 4 compares methods on transfer AUROC (F3). Baseline source-trained full representations B8Q perform at W6 0.874, C2R 0.706, J9 0.606. Target-trained probes evaluated within the retained source subspace are much stronger: C2R 0.936, W6 0.950, J9 0.869, showing that relevant information exists in the source subspace even when source-trained transfer is poor. H2 is a target-guided greedy subset search over the leading 100 source Q7 directions, using target labels only for subset choice and source-trained logistic weights; it is treated as an upper bound. H2 nearly matches target-trained performance, with mean subset sizes 15 (C2R), 8 (W6), 14 (J9), and full-target H2 k values 13, 7, 14. H2 F3 is 0.929 on C2R and 0.832 on J9, improving over B8Q by 0.22 and 0.23 respectively. Variance-based Y4 matches H2 only on W6 and lags on C2R and J9. T6 (source-side PCA ranking) and M9 (target-side ranking) use X4 = |coefficient| × Q7 std on source-N4D-projected activations. T6 performs about like B8Q; M9 does well on C2R, worse than H2 on W6, and below random on J9. Figure 4 compares T6, M9, and H2.

Section 4.5 introduces interpretation-only subspace selection (L2). For each leading source direction, an LLM judge sees the eight most- and eight least-activating source examples, generates positive-pole, negative-pole, and whole-direction descriptions, and assigns an OOD/generalization score R5. Paper title: "Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection." Authors: Daniel Yoo and Adrians Skapars. Core claim: linear probes on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct activations can fail OOD, but projecting activations onto a small subset of principal components from the training distribution yields better cross-domain transfer. The paper studies deception probes trained on a single source dataset (Roleplaying deception scenarios) and evaluated on three held-out targets: Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, and Sandbagging. Main thesis: OOD robustness of probes is largely determined by subspace selection in the source PCA basis, not the full representation.

Abstract-level claims: a small transferable subspace exists; an LLM judge can score PCs by whether their most/least activating examples indicate a transferable deception direction; probing the highest-scoring PCs closes the baseline-to-oracle gap by 78% on Insider Trading Report and 25% on Sandbagging. The paper argues source-probe weights can reflect source-specific surface features, while transferable directions are more abstract and can be described in natural language.

Introduction/contributions so far: they propose working in the basis of source-domain principal components rather than raw activations, then selecting a subset of PCs that avoids spurious correlations. They claim (1) a target-supervised greedy search over source PCs finds 8–15 components on which a source-trained probe nearly matches a target-trained probe; (2) source-side and target-side ranking by probe weights fails to recover a better-transfering subspace than the full representation baseline; (3) an LLM judge partially recovers the subspace without target data by identifying PCs likely to encode transferable behavioral contrast.

Related work frames the paper among three strands: (1) linear concept directions/subspaces in activation space, including work on truth/falsehood, honesty, emotion, refusal, and assistant-like behavior; (2) linear probes and their limitations, especially concerns about high accuracy, surface correlates, and uneven OOD generalization; and (3) natural-language interpretation of internal features via LLM-generated explanations, sparse autoencoder feature labeling, and concept ablation. No new empirical results yet, but the section motivates the paper’s focus on robust safety probes and interpretable subspace selection.

Section 3 defines the experimental setup. The paper uses 4 deception datasets from Goldowsky-Dill et al. (2025): Roleplaying as the source domain and Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, and Sandbagging as target test sets. Labels are honest (0), ambiguous (-1), or deceptive (1) from GPT-4o, with ambiguous examples removed. Activations come from layer 15 residual stream of Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, chosen because Ying et al. (2026) found it had the highest cross-domain AUROC. For each prompt, activations are averaged over the assistant’s response. Source activations are standardized to zero mean and unit variance, and the same statistics are applied to targets. PCA is fit on source activations and the top 100 PCs are retained. Probes are logistic regression classifiers with lambda=10; subset experiments project onto selected PCs before training/evaluation, while baselines use the full standardized activations. The top 100 PCs are justified by decreasing alignment with SAE decoder features as PC index increases, making lower PCs more interpretable, but the authors explicitly say this is not a claim about better generalization.

Section 4 reports experiments on the same 3 target datasets. Source-trained probes on full representations transfer unevenly: AUROC is 0.874 on Insider Trading Confirm, 0.706 on Insider Trading Report, and 0.606 on Sandbagging. To verify the 100-PC subspace is not the bottleneck, the authors train probes directly on target data within that subspace using 5-fold CV and obtain 0.936 / 0.950 / 0.869 AUROC (Report / Confirm / Sandbagging), showing the subspace contains enough signal. They then use greedy PC selection guided by target-fold AUROC while fitting probe weights on source data; this converges to small subsets on average (15 PCs for Report, 8 for Confirm, 14 for Sandbagging) and substantially improves transfer, nearly matching target-trained probes for Report and Sandbagging. A variance-matched top-k baseline is much weaker, matching greedy only on Confirm. Section 4.3 asks whether transferable PCs are those individually discriminative on target or those with high source-probe weight, and compares PC rankings based on standardized coefficients from probes trained in the source-PCA basis.

Section 4.3 compares two PC-ranking hypotheses using source-PCA coordinates: a source-PCA probe ranks PCs by weights from a probe trained on source data, and a target-PCA probe ranks PCs by weights from a probe trained on target data, but in both cases the evaluated probes are trained on source data restricted to the top k PCs from the chosen ranking. For this comparison, k is set by running greedy selection on the full target dataset (not CV): k=13 for Insider Trading Report, 7 for Insider Trading Confirm, and 14 for Sandbagging. Results: the source-PCA probe performs about like the full-representation baseline; the target-PCA probe is good on Report but worse than greedy on Confirm and below random on Sandbagging.

Section 4.4 asks whether the transferable subspace is human-interpretable. For each of the top 100 source PCs, the authors use the 8 most/least activating source examples and an LLM to describe the PC; an LLM judge assigns OOD/generalizability scores from 1–10. No PC scores above 6, so 6 is treated as the maximum observed score; PCs with that score in both runs are kept, yielding 19 interp-selected PCs. Of the 5 PCs that appear in greedy selections for more than one target, 3 receive the maximum OOD score.

Section 4.5 evaluates the 19 interp-selected PCs against three controls: full representation, top-19 PCs by variance, and the 81 PCs remaining after ablating the interp-selected set.

Section 4.5 evaluates the 19 interp-selected PCs against three controls: the full representation baseline, the top-19 PCs by source variance, and the 81 PCs remaining after ablating the interp-selected set. The interp-selected PC probe outperforms the baseline on all 3 targets and also beats the source-variance-selected control, with especially large gains on Insider Trading Report and Sandbagging. Paper studies OOD deception detection using principal components (PCs) of source activations from Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct. It uses four datasets from Goldowsky-Dill et al. (2025): Roleplaying as the source domain, and Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, and Sandbagging as target test sets. GPT-4o labels responses honest (0), ambiguous (-1), or deceptive (1); ambiguous responses are removed. Probes use layer 15 residual-stream activations averaged over the assistant’s response, following Ying et al. (2026). Activations are standardized with source mean/variance and the same statistics are applied to targets. PCA is run on the scaled source activations, and the top 100 PCs are retained. All probes are logistic-regression classifiers with parameter λ=10; PC-based probes train/evaluate on subsets of these 100 source PCs, while baselines use the full standardized representation. The paper says layer 15 had the highest cross-domain AUROC in prior analysis and that the 100-PC subspace still preserves enough information for source/target distinction.

Section 4 reports experiments on the 100-PC source subspace. In 4.1, source-trained full-representation probes transfer unevenly to the three targets: Insider Trading Confirm 0.874 AUROC, Insider Trading Report 0.706, and Sandbagging 0.606. Target-trained probes evaluated within the 100-PC subspace via 5-fold CV achieve 0.936 / 0.950 / 0.869 AUROC on Report / Confirm / Sandbagging, showing the subspace retains enough class information and that transfer failure is due to the learned direction, not missing information.

In 4.2, the paper introduces a greedy PC-selection algorithm that starts empty, iteratively adds the source PC that most improves target AUROC, and trains logistic-regression weights on source data only. Subset selection uses labeled target examples in non-held-out folds, so this is an oracle/upper bound rather than an unbiased OOD estimate. Selection stops when no PC improves AUROC by more than 0.001. Mean selected subset sizes are 15 PCs (Report), 8 (Confirm), and 14 (Sandbagging). Greedy nearly matches target-trained performance on Report and Sandbagging, improving baseline AUROC by 0.22 and 0.23, while variance-ranked top-k PCs only match greedy on Confirm and lag on the harder tasks.

In 4.3, the paper tests two hypotheses about transferable PCs: (1) PCs that individually separate target classes well; (2) PCs most important to the source probe. Figure 4 compares rankings by source-probe weights, target-probe weights, and greedy oracle selection across the three targets.

Section 4.3 compares two PC rankings using standardized coefficients (|weight| × PC std) on source-PCA activations: one from source-trained weights and one from target-trained weights. For transfer evaluation, source-trained logistic probes are fit on the top-k PCs in each ranking. To choose k, greedy is run on the full target dataset (not CV), giving stable sets of k=13 for Insider Trading Report, 7 for Confirm, and 14 for Sandbagging; these differ slightly from Section 4.2 because they use the full dataset. Result: both hypotheses fail. The source-PCA ranking transfers about as well as the full-representation baseline, while the target-PCA ranking works on Report but is worse than greedy on Confirm and below random on Sandbagging. Jaccard overlap between greedy and target-ranked sets is low (0.182 / 0.077 / 0.167).

Section 4.4 interprets top source PCs with LLM descriptions of positive/negative poles and an OOD score from 1–10. No PC scores above 6, so 6 is the maximum observed score. Scoring twice and keeping PCs that score 6 both times yields 19 interp-selected PCs. Of the 5 PCs selected by greedy for more than one target, 3 receive the maximum score, suggesting some recovery of transferable directions; only 1 of the top 5 source-PCA-probe PCs gets the maximum score.

Section 4.5 uses the 19 interp-selected PCs as a transfer subspace and compares them to top-19 variance PCs and an ablated 81-PC complement. The claim is that interpretation-based selection improves transfer without target data, with different gains across targets.

The summary claims: small target-guided subspaces nearly match target-trained probes; source-weights, target-class separation, and explained variance do not recover the same transferable subspaces; interpretation-based selection improves over the full-representation baseline on all targets but with sharply varying recovery. The study uses one model and one source dataset, and its interpretations are descriptive rather than causal.

The paper studies OOD deception detection in Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct layer-15 residual-stream activations. The source dataset is Roleplaying (V8); held-out targets are Insider Trading Report (C2R), Insider Trading Confirm (W6), and Sandbagging (J9). Labels are -1 ambiguous, 0 honest, 1 deceptive; ambiguous examples are removed. Activations are standardized with source statistics, and PCA/N4D keeps the top 100 source directions. All classifiers are logistic regression with λ=10, and performance is AUROC with 95% CIs. The full-representation baseline (B8Q) uses all standardized activations; Y4 uses top-k PCs by variance. H2 is a target-guided greedy selection using target labels for direction choice but source-trained probe weights; it is treated as a transfer upper bound. T6/M9 are source- and target-trained ranking probes. X4 is the standardized coefficient magnitude. R5 is GPT-5-mini's OOD usefulness rating, used to build L2 (interp-selected PC probe) and A7 (its complement). The paper also measures SAE decoder alignment using the `andyrdt/saes-llama-3.1-8b-instruct` resource and Jaccard overlap among selected directions.

final_notes:
Appendix B describes the LLM judge prompt for interpreting PCA directions. It uses GPT-5-mini and asks for bipolar interpretations (positive pole, negative pole, shared direction) plus an OOD deception usefulness score from 1 to 10. The examples are from a roleplay-style dataset setup with a strategic opportunity to lie; no inconsistency was noted with earlier appendix descriptions.

Appendix C says lower PCs show stronger decoder alignment, for both the best-matching SAE feature and the mean of the top 10 features, with Spearman rho = -0.857 and -0.917.

Appendix D compares PC sets from source probe weights, greedy selection, and target separability ranking. Jaccard overlaps between greedy and target-pca are 0.182 (Insider Trading Report), 0.077 (Insider Trading Confirm), and 0.167 (Sandbagging), summarized as less than a fifth of selections agreeing. The table lists selected PCs for each method and dataset, and concludes that the transferable subspace is neither the most discriminative on the source nor the target.

Appendix E lists LLM-judged interpretations and OOD scores for PCs. Table 3 shows PC62 and PC57 as most transferable (score 6) for Insider Trading Report + Sandbagging, while PC9 and PC81 are lower-confidence (score 3), and PC86 is moderate (score 6) for Insider Trading Confirm + Sandbagging. Table 4 gives additional PC scores: PC7=3, PC8=4, PC11=3, PC12=3, PC4=6, with explanations emphasizing mostly surface-level denial/admission cues and varying brittleness out of distribution.

Paper title: "Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection." Authors: Daniel Yoo and Adrians Skapars. Abstract claims linear probes on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct activations may fail OOD, but projecting activations onto a small subset of principal components from the training distribution enables cross-domain transfer close to probes trained directly on the test distribution. The paper also claims PC interpretations can identify transferable PCs: an LLM judge scores each PC by whether its most/least activating examples imply a transferable deception direction; probing the highest-scoring PCs closes the baseline-to-oracle gap by 78% on Insider Trading Report and 25% on Sandbagging. It argues source-probe weights encode source-specific surface features, while transferable directions encode the same contrast more abstractly and can be described in natural language. Main thesis: OOD robustness of probes is largely determined by subspace selection.

Paper title: "Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection." Authors: Daniel Yoo and Adrians Skapars. Core claim: linear probes on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct activations can fail OOD, but projecting activations onto a small subset of principal components from the training distribution yields better cross-domain transfer. The paper studies deception probes trained on a single source dataset (Roleplaying deception scenarios) and evaluated on three held-out targets: Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, and Sandbagging. Main thesis: OOD robustness of probes is largely determined by subspace selection in the source PCA basis, not the full representation.

Abstract-level claims: a small transferable subspace exists; an LLM judge can score PCs by whether their most/least activating examples indicate a transferable deception direction; probing the highest-scoring PCs closes the baseline-to-oracle gap by 78% on Insider Trading Report and 25% on Sandbagging. The paper argues source-probe weights can reflect source-specific surface features, while transferable directions are more abstract and can be described in natural language.

Introduction/contributions so far: they propose working in the basis of source-domain principal components rather than raw activations, then selecting a subset of PCs that avoids spurious correlations. They claim (1) a target-supervised greedy search over source PCs finds 8–15 components on which a source-trained probe nearly matches a target-trained probe; (2) source-side and target-side ranking by probe weights fails to recover a better-transfering subspace than the full representation baseline; (3) an LLM judge partially recovers the subspace without target data by identifying PCs likely to encode transferable behavioral contrast.

Related work frames the paper among three strands: (1) linear concept directions/subspaces in activation space, including work on truth/falsehood, honesty, emotion, refusal, and assistant-like behavior; (2) linear probes and their limitations, especially concerns about high accuracy, surface correlates, and uneven OOD generalization; and (3) natural-language interpretation of internal features via LLM-generated explanations, sparse autoencoder feature labeling, and concept ablation. No new empirical results yet, but the section motivates the paper’s focus on robust safety probes and interpretable subspace selection.

Section 3 defines the experimental setup. The paper uses 4 deception datasets from Goldowsky-Dill et al. (2025): Roleplaying as the source domain and Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, and Sandbagging as target test sets. Labels are honest (0), ambiguous (-1), or deceptive (1) from GPT-4o, with ambiguous examples removed. Activations come from layer 15 residual stream of Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, chosen because Ying et al. (2026) found it had the highest cross-domain AUROC. For each prompt, activations are averaged over the assistant’s response. Source activations are standardized to zero mean and unit variance, and the same statistics are applied to targets. PCA is fit on source activations and the top 100 PCs are retained. Probes are logistic regression classifiers with lambda=10; subset experiments project onto selected PCs before training/evaluation, while baselines use the full standardized activations. The top 100 PCs are justified by decreasing alignment with SAE decoder features as PC index increases, making lower PCs more interpretable, but the authors explicitly say this is not a claim about better generalization.

Section 4 reports experiments on the same 3 target datasets. Source-trained probes on full representations transfer unevenly: AUROC is 0.874 on Insider Trading Confirm, 0.706 on Insider Trading Report, and 0.606 on Sandbagging. To verify the 100-PC subspace is not the bottleneck, the authors train probes directly on target data within that subspace using 5-fold CV and obtain 0.936 / 0.950 / 0.869 AUROC (Report / Confirm / Sandbagging), showing the subspace contains enough signal. They then use greedy PC selection guided by target-fold AUROC while fitting probe weights on source data; this converges to small subsets on average (15 PCs for Report, 8 for Confirm, 14 for Sandbagging) and substantially improves transfer, nearly matching target-trained probes for Report and Sandbagging. A variance-matched top-k baseline is much weaker, matching greedy only on Confirm. Section 4.3 asks whether transferable PCs are those individually discriminative on target or those with high source-probe weight, and compares PC rankings based on standardized coefficients from probes trained in the source-PCA basis.

Section 4.3 compares two PC-ranking hypotheses using probes trained on source data projected onto the source-PCA basis: (i) source-PCA probe ranks PCs by coefficients from a source-trained probe; (ii) target-PCA probe ranks PCs by coefficients from a target-trained probe. To compare with greedy selection, they rerun greedy on the full target datasets (not CV) to get one stable PC set: k=13 for Insider Trading Report, 7 for Insider Trading Confirm, and 14 for Sandbagging. Both hypotheses fail to match greedy: source-PCA performs about like the full-representation baseline, while target-PCA does well on Report but is worse than greedy on Confirm and below random on Sandbagging.

Section 4.4 uses the Bills/Casademunt interpretability method on the top 100 source PCs: for each PC they find 8 most/least activating source examples and ask an LLM to describe the poles/direction, then score generalizability on a 1–10 OOD scale. No PC scores above 6, so 6 is treated as the maximum observed score. Repeating scoring twice and keeping PCs with max score in both runs yields 19 PCs. Five PCs appear in greedy selections of more than one target; 3/5 of those get the max OOD score, while only 1 of the top 5 source-PCA-probe PCs does.

Section 4.5 evaluates the 19 interp-selected PCs against full representation, top-19 variance PCs, and the ablation of the 19 PCs (remaining 81 PCs).

Section 4.5 evaluates 19 interp-selected PCs against the full representation, top-19 variance PCs, and the ablation of those 19 PCs (remaining 81 PCs). The interp-selected PC probe outperforms the baseline on all 3 targets and also beats the source-variance-selected control; gains are described as wide on Insider Trading Report and Sandbagging. It also outperforms the interp-ablated PC probe on all 3 targets. For Insider Trading Report, interp-selection closes 78% of the gap between baseline (0.706) and the greedy oracle (0.929). For Insider Trading Confirm, baseline transfer is already near ceiling, so comparisons are said to be uninformative and all selection methods except interp-ablated perform similarly. For Sandbagging, interp-selection closes 25% of the gap to the greedy oracle (0.832). Overall claim: selecting PCs by natural-language descriptions yields meaningful improvement over baseline without target data.

Section 5 lists limitations: the work uses one model (Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, layer 15) and one source dataset (Roleplaying). Section 4 reports experiments on the 100-PC source subspace. The paper studies OOD deception detection in Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct layer-15 residual-stream activations. The source dataset is Roleplaying (V8); held-out targets are Insider Trading Report (C2R), Insider Trading Confirm (W6), and Sandbagging (J9). Labels are -1 ambiguous, 0 honest, 1 deceptive; ambiguous examples are removed. Activations are standardized with source statistics, and PCA/N4D keeps the top 100 source directions. All classifiers are logistic regression with λ=10, and performance is AUROC with 95% CIs. The full-representation baseline (B8Q) uses all standardized activations; Y4 uses top-k PCs by variance. H2 is a target-guided greedy selection using target labels for direction choice but source-trained probe weights; it is treated as a transfer upper bound. T6/M9 are source- and target-trained ranking probes. X4 is the standardized coefficient magnitude. R5 is GPT-5-mini's OOD usefulness rating, used to build L2 (interp-selected PC probe) and A7 (its complement). The paper also measures SAE decoder alignment using the `andyrdt/saes-llama-3.1-8b-instruct` resource and Jaccard overlap among selected directions.

Activations are standardized with source statistics, and N4D is the PCA transformation retaining the top 100 source principal components (Q7). All classifiers are logistic regression with λ=10, and performance is AUROC with 95% CIs. The model and setup follow prior work noting layer 15 has strong cross-domain discrimination. The paper also states that lower-index PCA directions are more interpretable because alignment with sparse-autoencoder decoder features decreases with index.

Section 4 compares full representations, target-guided subspaces, coefficient rankings, and interpretation-based selection. Baseline transfer of source-trained full representations B8Q varies by target: W6 0.874, C2R 0.706, J9 0.606 AUROC. Target-trained probes within the retained source subspace achieve high target-CV AUROC on all targets: C2R 0.936, W6 0.950, J9 0.869. The paper concludes that the source-trained direction/generalization is weak, but relevant information exists in the source subspace.

Target-guided greedy H2 selection starts from an empty subset over the leading 100 source PCs, adds directions that improve target F3, and stops when improvement is <0.001. Target labels are used only for subset selection, not weight fitting. H2 uses small subsets (mean sizes C2R 15, W6 8, J9 14; range 8–15) and improves over B8Q by about 0.22 on C2R and 0.23 on J9, with H2 F3 around 0.929 and 0.832 versus target-trained F3 0.936 and 0.869. Variance-based Y4 matches H2 only on W6, not on C2R or J9.

For rankings, T6 is the source-PCA probe and M9 the target-PCA probe; both rank directions by standardized coefficient (absolute coefficient × Q7 std) on source-N4D-projected activations, then train source probes on top-k directions. T6 performs about like B8Q. M9 does well on C2R, worse than H2 on W6, and below random on J9. The paper argues source-side and target-side rankings recover different directions. Section 4.4 begins interpreting H2-selected directions as more domain-stable contrasts, with only partial recovery.

Section 4.5 introduces interpretation-only selection. For each leading source direction, an LLM judge (C7) is shown the eight most-activating and eight least-activating source examples, produces positive-pole, negative-pole, and whole-direction descriptions, and assigns a generalization/OOD score R5. Selection keeps directions that achieve the maximum R5 in both scoring runs; the reported maximum is R5=6, with 2 runs and 19 directions meeting that threshold in both. Example interpretations include several directions with R5=6 and some with R5=3, showing scores are noisy and can encode both transferable contrasts and limitations.

The resulting language-only probe L2 uses the intersection of retained directions; A7 is the complement and Y4 is an equal-dimensional variance-ranked control. All are trained as source probes. L2 improves generalization without target data: it exceeds B8Q on all targets and also beats Y4 and A7. The gains are strongest on C2R and J9 (e.g., 0.881 vs 0.706 on C2R; 0.662 vs 0.606 on J9), recovering 78% of the baseline–H2 gap on C2R and 25% on J9. W6 has little headroom, so methods there are mostly tied except A7.

Section 5 states the paper’s main limitations: results are narrow in model/dataset scope, with only one model and one source, and the direction interpretations are descriptive rather than causally verified. It emphasizes that W6 has a high baseline (0.874), leaving little headroom and making its results less informative. J9 is described as the weakest and most out-of-distribution target; its improvement is modest (0.606 to 0.662, 25% recovery), while C2R improves more robustly (0.706 to 0.881, 78% recovery). The method is fully linear (N4D projection plus logistic regression), so transferable-subspace existence may be unsurprising. There is no inference-time ablation; interpretations come from extreme-activation examples and C7 verbalizations.
