Paper title: "Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection." Authors: Daniel Yoo and Adrians Skapars. Core claim: linear probes on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct activations can fail OOD, but projecting activations onto a small subset of principal components from the training distribution yields better cross-domain transfer. The paper studies deception probes trained on a single source dataset (Roleplaying deception scenarios) and evaluated on three held-out targets: Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, and Sandbagging. Main thesis: OOD robustness of probes is largely determined by subspace selection in the source PCA basis, not the full representation.

Abstract-level claims: a small transferable subspace exists; an LLM judge can score PCs by whether their most/least activating examples indicate a transferable deception direction; probing the highest-scoring PCs closes the baseline-to-oracle gap by 78% on Insider Trading Report and 25% on Sandbagging. The paper argues source-probe weights can reflect source-specific surface features, while transferable directions are more abstract and can be described in natural language.

Introduction/contributions so far: they propose working in the basis of source-domain principal components rather than raw activations, then selecting a subset of PCs that avoids spurious correlations. They claim (1) a target-supervised greedy search over source PCs finds 8–15 components on which a source-trained probe nearly matches a target-trained probe; (2) source-side and target-side ranking by probe weights fails to recover a better-transfering subspace than the full representation baseline; (3) an LLM judge partially recovers the subspace without target data by identifying PCs likely to encode transferable behavioral contrast.

Related work frames the paper among three strands: (1) linear concept directions/subspaces in activation space, including work on truth/falsehood, honesty, emotion, refusal, and assistant-like behavior; (2) linear probes and their limitations, especially concerns about high accuracy, surface correlates, and uneven OOD generalization; and (3) natural-language interpretation of internal features via LLM-generated explanations, sparse autoencoder feature labeling, and concept ablation. No new empirical results yet, but the section motivates the paper’s focus on robust safety probes and interpretable subspace selection.

Section 3 defines the experimental setup. The paper uses 4 deception datasets from Goldowsky-Dill et al. (2025): Roleplaying as the source domain and Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, and Sandbagging as target test sets. Labels are honest (0), ambiguous (-1), or deceptive (1) from GPT-4o, with ambiguous examples removed. Activations come from layer 15 residual stream of Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, chosen because Ying et al. (2026) found it had the highest cross-domain AUROC. For each prompt, activations are averaged over the assistant’s response. Source activations are standardized to zero mean and unit variance, and the same statistics are applied to targets. PCA is fit on source activations and the top 100 PCs are retained. Probes are logistic regression classifiers with lambda=10; subset experiments project onto selected PCs before training/evaluation, while baselines use the full standardized activations. The top 100 PCs are justified by decreasing alignment with SAE decoder features as PC index increases, making lower PCs more interpretable, but the authors explicitly say this is not a claim about better generalization.

Section 4 begins the experiments. Figure 2 compares source-trained probes on full standardized activations vs top-100 source PCs, and also target-trained probes on the top-100 source PCs with 5-fold CV. Reported source-transfer AUROC is 0.874 on Insider Trading Confirm, 0.706 on Insider Trading Report, and 0.606 on Sandbagging. Target-trained probes in the same PC subspace reach 0.936 / 0.950 / 0.869 AUROC, supporting the claim that the subspace contains enough information and that the transfer gap is not due to missing information.

Section 4.2 introduces greedy PC selection: starting from no PCs, iteratively add one of the top 100 PCs that best improves target AUROC, training logistic regression on source projections. Subset selection uses target labels, so this is an upper bound rather than an unbiased OOD estimate. The greedy method uses small subsets on average: 15 PCs (Insider Trading Report), 8 (Insider Trading Confirm), and 14 (Sandbagging). It nearly matches target-trained probes for Report and Sandbagging, improving over the full baseline by 0.22 and 0.23 AUROC respectively. Variance-based PC selection only matches greedy on Insider Trading Confirm and is worse on the other two.

Section 4.3 tests two hypotheses for transferable PCs: that they are individually good on target, or that they are the PCs most relied on by the source probe. The paper plans to compare rankings based on standardized coefficients from a probe trained on source-PCA-projected activations.

Section 4.3 compares two ranking schemes for transferable PCs. The source-PCA probe ranks PCs by weights from a probe trained on source data; the target-PCA probe ranks PCs by weights from a probe trained on target data. In both cases, the evaluated probe is trained on source data projected onto the source-PCA basis, using the top-k PCs from the chosen ranking. To choose k, they rerun greedy selection on the full target dataset (not CV), getting stable sets of k=13 for Insider Trading Report, 7 for Insider Trading Confirm, and 14 for Sandbagging. Both hypotheses fail: the source-PCA probe performs about like the full-representation baseline, while the target-PCA probe is good on Report but worse than greedy on Confirm and below random on Sandbagging.

Section 4.4 interprets PCs using Bills et al./Casademunt et al.-style LLM descriptions. For each of the top 100 source PCs, they take the 8 most and 8 least activating source examples, have an LLM describe the PC, and score its OOD generalizability on a 1–10 scale. No PC scores above 6; they treat 6 as the maximum observed OOD score and keep PCs that hit this score in both runs, yielding 19 PCs. Of 5 PCs appearing in greedy selections for more than one target, 3 get the max OOD score; only 1 of the top 5 source-PCA-probe PCs does.

Section 4.5 evaluates these 19 interpretability-selected PCs as a probe subspace against a full baseline, top-19 variance PCs, and the ablation control of the remaining 81 PCs.

Paper studies out-of-distribution (OOD) deception detection using linear probes on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct activations. Main claim: projecting activations onto a small subset of principal components (PCs) from the training distribution can improve cross-domain transfer and nearly match probes trained directly on the test distribution. They evaluate on 3 held-out deception detection datasets. They also claim that LLM-based interpretations of PCs can identify transferable PCs: scoring each PC by whether its most/least activating examples imply a transferable deception direction, then probing on the highest-scoring PCs. Reported improvements: this closes the baseline-to-oracle gap by 78% on Insider Trading Report and 25% on Sandbagging. The abstract argues that source-probe-weighted directions may capture source-specific surface features, while transferable directions capture a more abstract contrast, and that OOD robustness of probes is largely determined by subspace selection.

The paper studies OOD deception detection with linear probes on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct activations, using source-domain PCA coordinates rather than raw activations. Source training is on the Roleplaying deception scenarios dataset, and evaluation is on three held-out target datasets: Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, and Sandbagging. Main hypothesis: a small subset of source PCs can yield better cross-domain transfer than using the full representation, and the transferable subspace may be identifiable.

Stated contributions: (1) a small transferable subspace exists; a target-supervised greedy search over source PCs finds about 8–15 components where a source-trained probe nearly matches a target-trained probe. (2) Simple source-side or target-side weight rankings do not recover this subspace and do not beat the full-representation baseline. (3) An LLM judge can partially recover the transferable subspace without target data by selecting PCs that seem to encode a transferable behavioral contrast rather than surface patterns.

The introduction also frames prior work as suggesting that PC choice matters, and that probe robustness is determined largely by subspace selection.

The paper studies OOD deception detection with linear probes on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct activations. Source domain is Roleplaying; target test sets are Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, and Sandbagging. Labels are honest (0), ambiguous (-1), and deceptive (1), with ambiguous examples removed. The model uses layer 15 residual stream activations, averaged over the assistant’s response tokens. Source activations are standardized to zero mean/unit variance and the same source statistics are applied to targets. PCA is fit on source activations and the top 100 PCs are retained. Probes are logistic regression with λ=10; subset experiments project onto selected PCs, while baselines train on the full standardized activations. The 100-PC choice is motivated by decreasing alignment with SAE decoder features as PC index increases, to support interpretability-driven selection, not because lower PCs are claimed to generalize better.

Section 4 reports three evaluation settings on target datasets: source-trained probes on full standardized activations, source-trained probes on the top 100 source PCs, and target-trained probes within the same 100-PC subspace using 5-fold CV. The full source-trained probe transfers with AUROC 0.874 (Insider Trading Confirm), 0.706 (Insider Trading Report), and 0.606 (Sandbagging). Target-trained probes on the 100-PC subspace reach 0.936 / 0.950 / 0.869 AUROC, showing the subspace itself is sufficient.

They then define a greedy PC-selection procedure guided by target AUROC but training the probe on source data projected into the selected PCs. Using 5-fold CV over target folds and stopping when no candidate improves AUROC by more than 0.001, the greedy subsets average 15 PCs (Report), 8 PCs (Confirm), and 14 PCs (Sandbagging). Greedy improves over the source baseline by 0.22 and 0.23 AUROC on Report and Sandbagging, respectively; variance-based PC selection matches greedy only on Confirm and is much worse on the harder tasks.

Section 4.3 tests whether transferable PCs are identified by source-probe weights or target-probe weights. Both rankings use standardized coefficients (absolute weight times PC standard deviation) from probes on the source-PCA basis. Final probes are trained on source data projected onto top-k PCs selected by each ranking.

Section 4 shows experiments on transfer in the top-100-PC subspace. Section 4.2 introduces greedy target-guided PC selection within the top 100 PCs: start from empty set, add the PC that most improves target AUROC, train weights on source only, and in 5-fold CV use non-held-out target folds for selection and evaluate on held-out folds. Paper title: "Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection." Authors: Daniel Yoo and Adrians Skapars. Abstract claims linear probes on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct activations may fail OOD, but projecting activations onto a small subset of principal components from the training distribution enables cross-domain transfer close to probes trained directly on the test distribution. Paper title: "Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection." Authors: Daniel Yoo and Adrians Skapars. Core claim: linear probes on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct activations can fail OOD, but projecting activations onto a small subset of principal components from the training distribution yields better cross-domain transfer. The paper studies deception probes trained on a single source dataset (Roleplaying deception scenarios) and evaluated on three held-out targets: Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, and Sandbagging. Main thesis: OOD robustness of probes is largely determined by subspace selection in the source PCA basis, not the full representation.

Abstract-level claims: a small transferable subspace exists; an LLM judge can score PCs by whether their most/least activating examples indicate a transferable deception direction; probing the highest-scoring PCs closes the baseline-to-oracle gap by 78% on Insider Trading Report and 25% on Sandbagging. The paper argues source-probe weights can reflect source-specific surface features, while transferable directions are more abstract and can be described in natural language.

Introduction/contributions so far: they propose working in the basis of source-domain principal components rather than raw activations, then selecting a subset of PCs that avoids spurious correlations. They claim (1) a target-supervised greedy search over source PCs finds 8–15 components on which a source-trained probe nearly matches a target-trained probe; (2) source-side and target-side ranking by probe weights fails to recover a better-transfering subspace than the full representation baseline; (3) an LLM judge partially recovers the subspace without target data by identifying PCs likely to encode transferable behavioral contrast.

Related work frames the paper among three strands: (1) linear concept directions/subspaces in activation space, including work on truth/falsehood, honesty, emotion, refusal, and assistant-like behavior; (2) linear probes and their limitations, especially concerns about high accuracy, surface correlates, and uneven OOD generalization; and (3) natural-language interpretation of internal features via LLM-generated explanations, sparse autoencoder feature labeling, and concept ablation. No new empirical results yet, but the section motivates the paper’s focus on robust safety probes and interpretable subspace selection.

Section 3 defines the experimental setup. The paper uses 4 deception datasets from Goldowsky-Dill et al. (2025): Roleplaying as the source domain and Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, and Sandbagging as target test sets. Labels are honest (0), ambiguous (-1), or deceptive (1) from GPT-4o, with ambiguous examples removed. Activations come from layer 15 residual stream of Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, chosen because Ying et al. (2026) found it had the highest cross-domain AUROC. For each prompt, activations are averaged over the assistant’s response. Source activations are standardized to zero mean and unit variance, and the same statistics are applied to targets. PCA is fit on source activations and the top 100 PCs are retained. Probes are logistic regression classifiers with lambda=10; subset experiments project onto selected PCs before training/evaluation, while baselines use the full standardized activations. The top 100 PCs are justified by decreasing alignment with SAE decoder features as PC index increases, making lower PCs more interpretable, but the authors explicitly say this is not a claim about better generalization.

Section 4 reports experiments on the same 3 target datasets. Source-trained probes on full representations transfer unevenly: AUROC is 0.874 on Insider Trading Confirm, 0.706 on Insider Trading Report, and 0.606 on Sandbagging. To verify the 100-PC subspace is not the bottleneck, the authors train probes directly on target data within that subspace using 5-fold CV and obtain 0.936 / 0.950 / 0.869 AUROC (Report / Confirm / Sandbagging), showing the subspace contains enough signal. They then use greedy PC selection guided by target-fold AUROC while fitting probe weights on source data; this converges to small subsets on average (15 PCs for Report, 8 for Confirm, 14 for Sandbagging) and substantially improves transfer, nearly matching target-trained probes for Report and Sandbagging. A variance-matched top-k baseline is much weaker, matching greedy only on Confirm. Section 4.3 asks whether transferable PCs are those individually discriminative on target or those with high source-probe weight, and compares PC rankings based on standardized coefficients from probes trained in the source-PCA basis.

Section 4.3 compares two PC-ranking hypotheses using source-PCA coordinates: a source-PCA probe ranks PCs by weights from a probe trained on source data, and a target-PCA probe ranks PCs by weights from a probe trained on target data, but in both cases the evaluated probes are trained on source data restricted to the top k PCs from the chosen ranking. For this comparison, k is set by running greedy selection on the full target dataset (not CV): k=13 for Insider Trading Report, 7 for Insider Trading Confirm, and 14 for Sandbagging. Results: the source-PCA probe performs about like the full-representation baseline; the target-PCA probe is good on Report but worse than greedy on Confirm and below random on Sandbagging.

Section 4.4 asks whether the transferable subspace is human-interpretable. For each of the top 100 source PCs, the authors use the 8 most/least activating source examples and an LLM to describe the PC; an LLM judge assigns OOD/generalizability scores from 1–10. No PC scores above 6, so 6 is treated as the maximum observed score; PCs with that score in both runs are kept, yielding 19 interp-selected PCs. Of the 5 PCs that appear in greedy selections for more than one target, 3 receive the maximum OOD score.

Section 4.5 evaluates the 19 interp-selected PCs against three controls: full representation, top-19 PCs by variance, and the 81 PCs remaining after ablating the interp-selected set.

Section 4.5 evaluates the 19 interp-selected PCs against three controls: full representation, top-19 PCs by variance, and the 81 PCs remaining after ablating the interp-selected set. The interp-selected PC probe outperforms the baseline on all 3 targets and beats the source-variance-selected control, with large margins on Insider Trading Report and Sandbagging. It also outperforms the interp-ablated probe on all 3 targets. Report: interp-selection closes 78% of the gap between baseline (0.706) and the greedy oracle (0.929). Confirm: baseline transfer is near ceiling, so comparisons are uninformative; all methods except interp-ablated perform similarly. Sandbagging: interp-selection closes 25% of the gap to the greedy oracle (0.832). Overall, selecting PCs only from natural-language descriptions, without target data, reduces deceptive behavior across tasks.

Section 4.5 compares the 19 interp-selected PCs against three controls: full representation, top-19 PCs by variance, and the 81 PCs remaining after ablating the interp-selected set. The interp-selected PC probe outperforms the baseline on all 3 targets and beats the source-variance-selected control, with large margins on Insider Trading Report and Sandbagging. It also outperforms the interp-ablated probe on all 3 targets. Report: interp-selection closes 78% of the gap between baseline (0.706) and the greedy oracle (0.929), reaching 0.881. Confirm: baseline transfer is near ceiling, so comparisons are uninformative; baseline is 0.874 and all methods except interp-ablated perform similarly. Sandbagging: interp-selection raises AUROC from 0.606 to 0.662, closing 25% of the gap to the greedy oracle (0.832). The paper studies OOD deception detection in language-model representations, comparing probes trained on full representations versus selected subspaces/directions. One selection method uses target labels to choose directions without fitting probe weights on them; another uses natural-language interpretations without target data. The summary claims: small target-guided subspaces nearly match target-trained probes; source-weights, target-class separation, and explained variance do not recover the same transferable subspaces; interpretation-based selection improves over the full-representation baseline on all targets but with sharply varying recovery. The study uses one model and one source dataset, and its interpretations are descriptive rather than causal.

The paper studies OOD deception detection in Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct layer-15 residual-stream activations. The source dataset is Roleplaying (V8); held-out targets are Insider Trading Report (C2R), Insider Trading Confirm (W6), and Sandbagging (J9). Labels are -1 ambiguous, 0 honest, 1 deceptive; ambiguous examples are removed. Activations are standardized with source statistics, and PCA/N4D keeps the top 100 source directions. All classifiers are logistic regression with λ=10, and performance is AUROC with 95% CIs. The full-representation baseline (B8Q) uses all standardized activations; Y4 uses top-k PCs by variance. H2 is a target-guided greedy selection using target labels for direction choice but source-trained probe weights; it is treated as a transfer upper bound. T6/M9 are source- and target-trained ranking probes. X4 is the standardized coefficient magnitude. R5 is GPT-5-mini's OOD usefulness rating, used to build L2 (interp-selected PC probe) and A7 (its complement). The paper also measures SAE decoder alignment using the `andyrdt/saes-llama-3.1-8b-instruct` resource and Jaccard overlap among selected directions.

Paper title: "Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection." Abstract claims that linear probes on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct may not transfer well to out-of-distribution deception datasets, but projecting activations onto a small subset of principal components from the training distribution improves transfer and nearly matches probes trained directly on the test distribution. It further claims PC interpretations can identify transferable PCs via an LLM judge scoring each PC by whether its most/least activating examples imply a transferable deception direction. Using the highest-scoring PCs reportedly closes the baseline-to-oracle gap by 78% on Insider Trading Report and 25% on Sandbagging. The abstract also claims transferable directions are more abstract, while source-probe-heavy directions rely on source-specific surface features.

Paper studies OOD deception detection with linear probes on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct. Core idea: train probes in the source-domain PCA basis instead of raw activations, then select a transferable subset of principal components. Source training data is Roleplaying deception scenarios; target datasets are Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, and Sandbagging. The introduction claims three main findings: (1) a small transferable subspace exists, and a target-supervised greedy search over source PCs finds about 8–15 components where a source-trained probe nearly matches a target-trained probe; (2) ranking PCs by source or target probe weights does not recover a better-transfering basis than the full-representation baseline; (3) an LLM judge can partially recover the transferable subspace without target data by identifying PCs that encode transferable behavioral contrasts rather than surface patterns. The paper frames the problem as avoiding spurious correlations in probe training and asks which subset of PCs supports generalizable probe learning and how to identify it.

Core idea: train probes in the source-domain PCA basis instead of raw activations, then select a transferable subset of principal components. Source training data is Roleplaying deception scenarios; target datasets are Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, and Sandbagging. The introduction claims three main findings: (1) a small transferable subspace exists, and a target-supervised greedy search over source PCs finds about 8–15 components where a source-trained probe nearly matches a target-trained probe; (2) ranking PCs by source or target probe weights does not recover a better-transferring basis than the full-representation baseline; (3) an LLM judge can partially recover the transferable subspace without target data by identifying PCs that encode transferable behavioral contrasts rather than surface patterns. Setup details: use 4 datasets total (Roleplaying plus the 3 targets), remove ambiguous labels (-1), use layer 15 residual stream activations of Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct averaged over assistant tokens, standardize source activations and apply source stats to targets, run PCA on source and keep top 100 PCs, and train logistic regression probes with λ=10. The paper says the top-100-PC choice is motivated by decreasing alignment with SAE decoder features as PC index increases, and that the 100-PC subspace still retains enough information to separate deceptive from honest responses on every target.

Section 4 reports the main transfer results. On target datasets, source-trained probes transfer unevenly: Insider Trading Confirm AUROC 0.874, Insider Trading Report 0.706, Sandbagging 0.606. A target-trained probe within the top-100 source-PC subspace gets much higher AUROC: 0.936 / 0.950 / 0.869 on the three targets, showing the subspace itself is sufficient. The authors then introduce a greedy PC-selection procedure: starting from an empty set, at each step they search over the top 100 PCs and add the PC that most improves target AUROC, training the logistic regression probe on source projections but using target labels to choose subsets via 5-fold CV. The greedy search converges to small subsets averaging 15 PCs for Insider Trading Report, 8 for Insider Trading Confirm, and 14 for Sandbagging. It approaches target-trained performance for Report and Sandbagging, improving over the full-representation baseline by 0.22 and 0.23 AUROC, while a variance-based top-k control only matches greedy on Insider Trading Confirm and is worse on the harder tasks. The section concludes that a transferable subspace exists, and variance explained does not predict transfer usefulness. Next, they test two hypotheses for transferable PCs: either they are individually strong on target, or they are the PCs most heavily weighted by a source-trained probe. Figure 4 compares rankings by source-probe weights, target-probe weights, and greedy oracle selection.

Section 4.3 compares two hypotheses for which PCs transfer: PCs weighted highly by a source-trained probe vs PCs that are individually strong on target. The source-PCA probe ranks source PCs by source-probe weights; the target-PCA probe ranks them by target-probe weights, but both are evaluated by training on source data projected into the source-PCA basis. To compare them with the greedy oracle, the authors rerun greedy on the full target set (not CV), yielding stable greedy sizes k=13 (Insider Trading Report), 7 (Insider Trading Confirm), and 14 (Sandbagging), slightly different from the CV-selected subsets. Both hypotheses fail: source-PCA performs about like the full-representation baseline, while target-PCA is good on Report but worse than greedy on Confirm and below random on Sandbagging. 

Section 4.4 interprets PCs using an LLM-based OOD score. For each of the top 100 source PCs, they describe the positive/negative poles from 8 most and 8 least activating source examples. No PC scores above 6/10, so 6 is treated as the max observed OOD score; PCs reaching this max in both scoring runs are retained, giving 19 PCs. Of 5 PCs appearing in greedy selections for more than one target, 3 receive the max OOD score; only 1 of the top-5 source-PCA PCs does. 

Section 4.5 tests these 19 interpretability-selected PCs as a subspace, compared with the full baseline, top-19 variance PCs, and an ablation set of the remaining 81 PCs.

Section 4.5 evaluates the 19 PCs selected by LLM-based interpretability as a subspace against the full baseline, a source-variance-selected control (top-19 variance PCs), and an interp-ablated control (the remaining 81 PCs). The interp-selected PC probe outperforms the baseline on all 3 targets and also beats the source-variance-selected control, with especially large gains on Insider Trading Report and Sandbagging. It also outperforms the interp-ablated probe on all 3 targets. Recovery differs by dataset: on Insider Trading Report, interp-selection closes 78% of the gap between baseline (0.706) and the greedy oracle (0.929); on Insider Trading Confirm, baseline performance is near ceiling so comparisons are mostly uninformative and all selection methods except interp-ablated are roughly similar; on Sandbagging, interp-selection closes 25% of the gap to the greedy oracle (0.832). Overall, natural-language interpretation alone yields meaningful improvements over baseline on the generalization tasks.

Section 5 lists limitations and restates some key results. The paper uses a single model (Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, layer 15) and a single source dataset (Roleplaying). Insider Trading Confirm is described as uninformative because baseline transfer is already 0.874, so comparisons there are near ceiling. Sandbagging is the weakest target: interpretability selection improves AUROC from 0.606 to 0.662, recovering 25% of the gap to the greedy upper bound 0.832. Insider Trading Report is the stronger result: 0.706 to 0.881, closing 78% of the gap to greedy at 0.929. The method is fully linear (PCA + logistic regression), and the authors note they have not done causal ablations of the high-scoring PCs, so claims about what PCs encode are descriptive rather than causal.

The paper studies OOD deception detection in language-model representations, comparing probes trained on full representations versus selected subspaces/directions. One selection method uses target labels to choose directions without fitting probe weights on them; another uses natural-language interpretations without target data. The summary claims: small target-guided subspaces nearly match target-trained probes; source-weights, target-class separation, and explained variance do not recover the same transferable subspaces; interpretation-based selection improves over the full-representation baseline on all targets but with sharply varying recovery. The study uses one model and one source dataset, and its interpretations are descriptive rather than causal.

The paper studies OOD deception detection in Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct layer-15 residual-stream activations. The source dataset is Roleplaying (V8); held-out targets are Insider Trading Report (C2R), Insider Trading Confirm (W6), and Sandbagging (J9). Labels are -1 ambiguous, 0 honest, 1 deceptive; ambiguous examples are removed. Activations are standardized with source statistics, and PCA/N4D keeps the top 100 source directions. All classifiers are logistic regression with λ=10, and performance is AUROC with 95% CIs. The full-representation baseline (B8Q) uses all standardized activations; Y4 uses top-k PCs by variance. H2 is a target-guided greedy selection using target labels for direction choice but source-trained probe weights; it is treated as a transfer upper bound. T6/M9 are source- and target-trained ranking probes. X4 is the standardized coefficient magnitude. R5 is GPT-5-mini's OOD usefulness rating, used to build L2 (interp-selected PC probe) and A7 (its complement). The paper also measures SAE decoder alignment using the `andyrdt/saes-llama-3.1-8b-instruct` resource and Jaccard overlap among selected directions.

Section 4 compares several ways to find transferable directions in the retained source subspace. 4.1 reports baseline transfer AUROC (F3): B8Q source-trained full representations transfer best on W6 (0.874), moderately on C2R (0.706), and poorly on J9 (0.606). Yet target-trained probes on the retained source subspace separate classes well on all targets: C2R 0.936, W6 0.950, J9 0.869 (5-fold CV). 4.2 studies target-guided greedy selection H2, which uses target labels only to choose directions, not to fit probe weights, and is an upper bound rather than an unbiased OOD estimate. H2 finds small subsets (mean sizes C2R 15, W6 8, J9 14) and improves strongly over B8Q on C2R and J9; full-target H2 uses k = 13, 7, 14 respectively, with numbers slightly different from CV. Variance-based selection Y4 matches H2 only on W6 and is worse on C2R/J9. 4.3 tests ranking hypotheses with X4 = |coefficient| × source standard deviation on source-N4D-projected activations. T6 is source-side ranking, M9 target-side ranking. T6 performs about like B8Q; M9 is good on C2R, worse than H2 on W6, and below random on J9. The section concludes that neither source- nor target-separation rankings recover the transferable subspace. 4.4 begins interpretation-based analysis and says recovery is only partial and noisy.

Section 4.4/4.5 describes interpretation-based selection of source directions using an LLM judge (C7). For each leading source direction, it sees the eight most- and least-activating source examples, produces positive-pole, negative-pole, and whole-direction descriptions, then assigns an OOD/generalization rating R5. Selection keeps directions attaining the maximum R5 in both noisy scoring runs; the appendix reports max R5=6, two runs, and 19 directions retained in both. Evidence notes that some H2-selected directions have high R5 while others are lower, and that recovery is only partial (e.g., 3/5 of maximum-rated shared H2 selections, 1/5 among top T6 selections). Section 4.5 defines L2 as the intersection of retained directions across runs, with A7 as its complement and Y4 as an equal-sized variance-ranked control, all trained as source probes. L2 improves over B8Q on all targets, especially C2R (0.881 vs 0.706) and J9 (0.662 vs 0.606), and recovers 78% of the baseline–H2 gap on C2R but only 25% on J9. W6 has little headroom, with methods roughly tied except A7.

Section 5 emphasizes limitations: the work is narrow in scope (one model, one source, limited datasets) and the direction interpretations are descriptive rather than causally verified. It states that W6 has a high baseline (Appendix A, B8Q F3 = 0.874), making results less informative, while J9 is the weakest and most out-of-distribution target; its improvement is modest (0.606 to 0.662), whereas C2R improves more strongly (0.706 to 0.881). The recovery row reports 25% for J9 and 78% for C2R. The pipeline is fully linear (N4D projection + logistic regression), so the paper notes that transferable-subspace existence may be unsurprising. No inference-time ablation is reported; interpretations rely on extreme activations and C7 verbalizations.

Section 6 concludes that robust behavioral probing is not just about linear accessibility, but about selecting representations that preserve the intended behavior while filtering spurious correlations. It argues full-representation probes can mix general behavioral features with dataset-specific surface cues, yielding good in-distribution performance but poorer transfer, whereas sparse directional subspaces may isolate more general behavioral structure. It claims selected subspaces can outperform full representations in transfer, citing Appendix A rows for B8Q F3, H2 F3 used for recovery comparison, and L2 F3; the cited figures include C2R 0.706, 0.929, 0.881 and J9 0.606, 0.832, 0.662. It also says the interpretations of contrasts versus surface cues remain descriptive, consistent with Section 5.

Paper title: "Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection." Authors: Daniel Yoo and Adrians Skapars. Core claim: linear probes on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct activations can fail OOD, but projecting activations onto a small subset of principal components from the training distribution yields better cross-domain transfer. The paper studies deception probes trained on a single source dataset (Roleplaying deception scenarios) and evaluated on three held-out targets: Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, and Sandbagging. Main thesis: OOD robustness of probes is largely determined by subspace selection in the source PCA basis, not the full representation.

Abstract-level claims: a small transferable subspace exists; an LLM judge can score PCs by whether their most/least activating examples indicate a transferable deception direction; probing the highest-scoring PCs closes the baseline-to-oracle gap by 78% on Insider Trading Report and 25% on Sandbagging. The paper argues source-probe weights can reflect source-specific surface features, while transferable directions are more abstract and can be described in natural language.

Introduction/contributions so far: they propose working in the basis of source-domain principal components rather than raw activations, then selecting a subset of PCs that avoids spurious correlations. They claim (1) a target-supervised greedy search over source PCs finds 8–15 components on which a source-trained probe nearly matches a target-trained probe; (2) source-side and target-side ranking by probe weights fails to recover a better-transfering subspace than the full representation baseline; (3) an LLM judge partially recovers the subspace without target data by identifying PCs likely to encode transferable behavioral contrast.

Related work frames the paper among three strands: (1) linear concept directions/subspaces in activation space, including work on truth/falsehood, honesty, emotion, refusal, and assistant-like behavior; (2) linear probes and their limitations, especially concerns about high accuracy, surface correlates, and uneven OOD generalization; and (3) natural-language interpretation of internal features via LLM-generated explanations, sparse autoencoder feature labeling, and concept ablation. No new empirical results yet, but the section motivates the paper’s focus on robust safety probes and interpretable subspace selection.

Section 3 defines the experimental setup. The paper uses 4 deception datasets from Goldowsky-Dill et al. (2025): Roleplaying as the source domain and Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, and Sandbagging as target test sets. Labels are honest (0), ambiguous (-1), or deceptive (1) from GPT-4o, with ambiguous examples removed. Activations come from layer 15 residual stream of Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, chosen because Ying et al. (2026) found it had the highest cross-domain AUROC. For each prompt, activations are averaged over the assistant’s response. Source activations are standardized to zero mean and unit variance, and the same statistics are applied to targets. PCA is fit on source activations and the top 100 PCs are retained. Probes are logistic regression classifiers with lambda=10; subset experiments project onto selected PCs before training/evaluation, while baselines use the full standardized activations. The top 100 PCs are justified by decreasing alignment with SAE decoder features as PC index increases, making lower PCs more interpretable, but the authors explicitly say this is not a claim about better generalization.

Section 4 reports experiments on the same 3 target datasets. Source-trained probes on full representations transfer unevenly: AUROC is 0.874 on Insider Trading Confirm, 0.706 on Insider Trading Report, and 0.606 on Sandbagging. To verify the 100-PC subspace is not the bottleneck, the authors train probes directly on target data within that subspace using 5-fold CV and obtain 0.936 / 0.950 / 0.869 AUROC (Report / Confirm / Sandbagging), showing the subspace contains enough signal. They then use greedy PC selection guided by target-fold AUROC while fitting probe weights on source data; this converges to small subsets on average (15 PCs for Report, 8 for Confirm, 14 for Sandbagging) and substantially improves transfer, nearly matching target-trained probes for Report and Sandbagging. A variance-matched top-k baseline is much weaker, matching greedy only on Confirm. Section 4.3 asks whether transferable PCs are those individually discriminative on target or those with high source-probe weight, and compares PC rankings based on standardized coefficients from probes trained in the source-PCA basis.

Section 4.3 compares two PC-ranking hypotheses using source-PCA coordinates: a source-PCA probe ranks PCs by weights from a probe trained on source data, and a target-PCA probe ranks PCs by weights from a probe trained on target data, but in both cases the evaluated probes are trained on source data restricted to the top k PCs from the chosen ranking. For this comparison, k is set by running greedy selection on the full target dataset (not CV): k=13 for Insider Trading Report, 7 for Insider Trading Confirm, and 14 for Sandbagging. Results: the source-PCA probe performs about like the full-representation baseline; the target-PCA probe is good on Report but worse than greedy on Confirm and below random on Sandbagging.

Section 4.4 asks whether the transferable subspace is human-interpretable. For each of the top 100 source PCs, the authors use the 8 most/least activating source examples and an LLM to describe the PC; an LLM judge assigns OOD/generalizability scores from 1–10. No PC scores above 6, so 6 is treated as the maximum observed score; PCs with that score in both runs are kept, yielding 19 interp-selected PCs. Of the 5 PCs that appear in greedy selections for more than one target, 3 receive the maximum OOD score.

Section 4.5 evaluates the 19 interp-selected PCs against three controls: full representation, top-19 PCs by variance, and the 81 PCs remaining after ablating the interp-selected set.

GPT-4o labels responses honest (0), ambiguous (-1), or deceptive (1); ambiguous responses are removed. Paper title: "Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection." Authors: Daniel Yoo and Adrians Skapars. Core claim: linear probes on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct activations can fail OOD, but projecting activations onto a small subset of principal components from the training distribution yields better cross-domain transfer. The paper studies deception probes trained on a single source dataset (Roleplaying deception scenarios) and evaluated on three held-out targets: Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, and Sandbagging. Main thesis: OOD robustness of probes is largely determined by subspace selection in the source PCA basis, not the full representation.

Abstract-level claims: a small transferable subspace exists; an LLM judge can score PCs by whether their most/least activating examples indicate a transferable deception direction; probing the highest-scoring PCs closes the baseline-to-oracle gap by 78% on Insider Trading Report and 25% on Sandbagging. The paper argues source-probe weights can reflect source-specific surface features, while transferable directions are more abstract and can be described in natural language.

Introduction/contributions so far: they propose working in the basis of source-domain principal components rather than raw activations, then selecting a subset of PCs that avoids spurious correlations. They claim (1) a target-supervised greedy search over source PCs finds 8–15 components on which a source-trained probe nearly matches a target-trained probe; (2) source-side and target-side ranking by probe weights fails to recover a better-transfering subspace than the full representation baseline; (3) an LLM judge partially recovers the subspace without target data by identifying PCs likely to encode transferable behavioral contrast.

Related work frames the paper among three strands: (1) linear concept directions/subspaces in activation space, including work on truth/falsehood, honesty, emotion, refusal, and assistant-like behavior; (2) linear probes and their limitations, especially concerns about high accuracy, surface correlates, and uneven OOD generalization; and (3) natural-language interpretation of internal features via LLM-generated explanations, sparse autoencoder feature labeling, and concept ablation. No new empirical results yet, but the section motivates the paper’s focus on robust safety probes and interpretable subspace selection.

Setup: The paper uses 4 deception-detection datasets from Goldowsky-Dill et al. (2025): Roleplaying, Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, and Sandbagging. Roleplaying is the source domain; the other three are target test sets. They retain 311 Roleplaying responses. Each response is labeled honest (0), ambiguous (-1), or deceptive (1) by GPT-4o, and ambiguous responses are removed for experiments. Model/activations: they use layer 15 residual stream activations from Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, averaging token activations over the assistant’s response. Probes: source activations are standardized to zero mean/unit variance, then the same source statistics are applied to targets; PCA is fit on source and the top 100 PCs are retained. Logistic regression probes use lambda=10. For subsets of PCs, activations are projected before training/evaluation; baseline probes use full standardized activations. The 100-PC choice is motivated by decreasing alignment with SAE decoder features for higher-index PCs, making low-index PCs more interpretable, not because they generalize better.

Experiments use Roleplaying as the source domain and Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, and Sandbagging as targets. In Fig. 2, source-trained probes on full source representations transfer with AUROC 0.874 (Confirm), 0.706 (Report), and 0.606 (Sandbagging). A probe trained directly on target data within the top-100 source-PC subspace (5-fold CV) reaches 0.936 / 0.950 / 0.869 AUROC across the three targets, showing the subspace itself is sufficient and the failure is the source direction, not missing information. 

Section 4.2 introduces greedy PC selection: starting from empty, iteratively add one of the top 100 PCs that most improves target AUROC when a logistic regression probe is trained on source data projected to the current subset. Selection is guided by labeled target folds in 5-fold CV, so the greedy method is an upper bound rather than an unbiased OOD estimate. The greedy search converges to small subsets on average: 15 PCs for Report, 8 for Confirm, and 14 for Sandbagging. It comes close to target-trained performance for Report and Sandbagging, improving over the full-representation baseline by 0.22 and 0.23 AUROC, respectively. A variance-only control (top-k PCs by variance, with k matched to greedy) matches greedy only on Confirm and is much worse on Report and Sandbagging.

Section 4.3 tests whether transferable PCs are those that are individually predictive on target data or those most weighted by the source probe. They compare PC rankings based on standardized coefficients from probes trained on source-PCA projections, using source-probe weights and target-probe weights.

Section 4.3 compares two PC-ranking hypotheses on the source-PCA basis: a source-PCA probe ranks PCs by a probe trained on source data, and a target-PCA probe ranks PCs by a probe trained on target data. For evaluation, the final probes are trained on source data projected onto the top-k PCs from each ranking. To choose k, they rerun greedy selection on the full target datasets (not CV), yielding k=13 for Insider Trading Report, 7 for Insider Trading Confirm, and 14 for Sandbagging; these differ slightly from the CV values in the previous section. Both hypotheses fail: the source-PCA probe is about as good as the full-representation baseline, while the target-PCA probe works well on Report but is worse than greedy on Confirm and below random on Sandbagging.

Section 4.4 interprets the transferable subspace. For each of the top 100 source PCs, they examine the 8 most and 8 least activating source examples and have an LLM describe the positive pole, negative pole, and whole direction. The judge gives OOD scores on a 1–10 scale; no PC scores above 6, so 6 becomes the maximum observed score. Repeating the scoring twice and keeping only PCs that hit this max in both runs yields 19 interp-selected PCs. Among the 5 PCs appearing in greedy selections for more than one target, 3 receive the maximum OOD score; only 1 of the source-PCA probe’s top 5 PCs does.

In the next evaluation, the interp-selected PC probe outperforms the baseline on all 3 targets and also beats the source-variance-selected control; it also outperforms the interp-ablated PC probe on all 3 targets. On Insider Trading Report, it closes 78% of the gap between baseline (0.706) and the greedy oracle (0.929). On Insider Trading Confirm, baseline transfer is already near ceiling, so differences among selection methods are small except for interp-ablated. On Sandbagging, interp-selection closes 25% of the gap to the greedy oracle (oracle score 0.832 mentioned here).

Section 5 lists limitations: results are based on a single model (Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, layer 15) and a single source dataset (Roleplaying). Insider Trading Confirm is described as uninformative because baseline transfer already reaches 0.874. Sandbagging is the weakest target: interpretability selection improves AUROC from 0.606 to 0.662, recovering 25% of the gap to the greedy upper bound/oracle of 0.832. Insider Trading Report improves from 0.706 to 0.881, closing 78% of the gap to the greedy oracle at 0.929. The method is fully linear (PCA + logistic regression), and the authors explicitly note they have not causally validated the high-scoring PCs by ablation.

Section 6 concludes that a small subset of source-domain principal components can enable cross-domain transfer that nearly matches target-trained probes, and that this subset cannot be identified by source-side or target-side separability alone. The paper frames interpretability scoring over each PC’s top-activating examples as a way to partially recover that subspace without target data. The main takeaway is that robust OOD probing should be treated as a representation-selection problem: find not just a linearly accessible signal, but the subspace where that behavioral signal is represented most robustly, avoiding dataset-specific surface cues that can boost in-distribution accuracy but hurt transfer.

Source activations are standardized to zero mean/unit variance and the same statistics are applied to targets. PCA is fit on source activations; the top 100 PCs are retained. Probes are logistic regression with λ=10. For subset experiments, activations are projected onto selected PCs before training/evaluation; baselines train on full standardized activations. The paper’s baseline results show source-trained probes on full standardized representations transfer unevenly to the three targets: Insider Trading Confirm 0.874 AUROC, Insider Trading Report 0.706, and Sandbagging 0.606. Section 4.3 compares two ranking schemes: the source-PCA probe ranks source-PCA directions by weights from a probe trained on source data, and the target-PCA probe ranks them by weights from a probe trained on target data; in both cases, probes are fit on source data projected onto the source-PCA basis, using the top-k PCs from the relevant ranking. Paper title: "Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection." Authors: Daniel Yoo and Adrians Skapars. Abstract claims linear probes on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct activations may fail OOD, but projecting activations onto a small subset of principal components from the training distribution enables cross-domain transfer close to probes trained directly on the test distribution. The paper also claims PC interpretations can identify transferable PCs: an LLM judge scores each PC by whether its most/least activating examples imply a transferable deception direction; probing the highest-scoring PCs closes the baseline-to-oracle gap by 78% on Insider Trading Report and 25% on Sandbagging. Main thesis: OOD robustness of probes is largely determined by subspace selection.

Paper title: "Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection." Authors: Daniel Yoo and Adrians Skapars. Core claim: linear probes on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct activations can fail OOD, but projecting activations onto a small subset of principal components from the training distribution yields better cross-domain transfer. The paper studies deception probes trained on a single source dataset (Roleplaying deception scenarios) and evaluated on three held-out targets: Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, and Sandbagging. Main thesis: OOD robustness of probes is largely determined by subspace selection in the source PCA basis, not the full representation.

Abstract-level claims: a small transferable subspace exists; an LLM judge can score PCs by whether their most/least activating examples indicate a transferable deception direction; probing the highest-scoring PCs closes the baseline-to-oracle gap by 78% on Insider Trading Report and 25% on Sandbagging. The paper argues source-probe weights can reflect source-specific surface features, while transferable directions are more abstract and can be described in natural language.

Introduction/contributions so far: they propose working in the basis of source-domain principal components rather than raw activations, then selecting a subset of PCs that avoids spurious correlations. They claim (1) a target-supervised greedy search over source PCs finds 8–15 components on which a source-trained probe nearly matches a target-trained probe; (2) source-side and target-side ranking by probe weights fails to recover a better-transfering subspace than the full representation baseline; (3) an LLM judge partially recovers the subspace without target data by identifying PCs likely to encode transferable behavioral contrast.

Related work frames the paper among three strands: (1) linear concept directions/subspaces in activation space, including work on truth/falsehood, honesty, emotion, refusal, and assistant-like behavior; (2) linear probes and their limitations, especially concerns about high accuracy, surface correlates, and uneven OOD generalization; and (3) natural-language interpretation of internal features via LLM-generated explanations, sparse autoencoder feature labeling, and concept ablation. No new empirical results yet, but the section motivates the paper’s focus on robust safety probes and interpretable subspace selection.

Section 3 defines the experimental setup. The paper uses 4 deception datasets from Goldowsky-Dill et al. (2025): Roleplaying as the source domain and Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, and Sandbagging as target test sets. Labels are honest (0), ambiguous (-1), or deceptive (1) from GPT-4o, with ambiguous examples removed. Activations come from layer 15 residual stream of Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, chosen because Ying et al. (2026) found it had the highest cross-domain AUROC. For each prompt, activations are averaged over the assistant’s response. Source activations are standardized to zero mean and unit variance, and the same statistics are applied to targets. PCA is fit on source activations and the top 100 PCs are retained. Probes are logistic regression classifiers with lambda=10; subset experiments project onto selected PCs before training/evaluation, while baselines use the full standardized activations. The top 100 PCs are justified by decreasing alignment with SAE decoder features as PC index increases, making lower PCs more interpretable, but the authors explicitly say this is not a claim about better generalization.

Section 4 reports experiments on the same 3 target datasets. Source-trained probes on full representations transfer unevenly: AUROC is 0.874 on Insider Trading Confirm, 0.706 on Insider Trading Report, and 0.606 on Sandbagging. To verify the 100-PC subspace is not the bottleneck, the authors train probes directly on target data within that subspace using 5-fold CV and obtain 0.936 / 0.950 / 0.869 AUROC (Report / Confirm / Sandbagging), showing the subspace contains enough signal. They then use greedy PC selection guided by target-fold AUROC while fitting probe weights on source data; this converges to small subsets on average (15 PCs for Report, 8 for Confirm, 14 for Sandbagging) and substantially improves transfer, nearly matching target-trained probes for Report and Sandbagging. A variance-matched top-k baseline is much weaker, matching greedy only on Confirm. Section 4.3 asks whether transferable PCs are those individually discriminative on target or those with high source-probe weight, and compares PC rankings based on standardized coefficients from probes trained in the source-PCA basis.

Section 4.3 compares two PC-ranking hypotheses using source-PCA coordinates: a source-PCA probe ranks PCs by weights from a probe trained on source data, and a target-PCA probe ranks PCs by weights from a probe trained on target data, but in both cases the evaluated probes are trained on source data restricted to the top k PCs from the chosen ranking. For this comparison, k is set by running greedy selection on the full target dataset (not CV): k=13 for Insider Trading Report, 7 for Insider Trading Confirm, and 14 for Sandbagging. Results: the source-PCA probe performs about like the full-representation baseline; the target-PCA probe is good on Report but worse than greedy on Confirm and below random on Sandbagging.

Section 4.4 asks whether the transferable subspace is human-interpretable. For each of the top 100 source PCs, the authors use the 8 most/least activating source examples and an LLM to describe the PC; an LLM judge assigns OOD/generalizability scores from 1–10. No PC scores above 6, so 6 is treated as the maximum observed score; PCs with that score in both runs are kept, yielding 19 interp-selected PCs. Of the 5 PCs that appear in greedy selections for more than one target, 3 receive the maximum OOD score.

Section 4.5 evaluates the 19 interp-selected PCs against three controls: full representation, top-19 PCs by variance, and the 81 PCs remaining after ablating the interp-selected set.

Section 4.5 evaluates the 19 interp-selected PCs against three controls: the full representation baseline, the top-19 PCs by source variance, and the 81 PCs remaining after ablating the interp-selected set. The interp-selected PC probe outperforms the baseline on all 3 targets and also beats the source-variance-selected control, with especially large gains on Insider Trading Report and Sandbagging. (2025): Roleplaying as the source domain, and Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, and Sandbagging as target test sets. GPT-4o labels responses honest (0), ambiguous (-1), or deceptive (1); ambiguous responses are removed. Probes use layer 15 residual-stream activations averaged over the assistant’s response, following Ying et al. (2026). Activations are standardized with source mean/variance and the same statistics are applied to targets. PCA is run on the scaled source activations, and the top 100 PCs are retained. All probes are logistic-regression classifiers with parameter λ=10; PC-based probes train/evaluate on subsets of these 100 source PCs, while baselines use the full standardized representation. The paper says layer 15 had the highest cross-domain AUROC in prior analysis and that the 100-PC subspace still preserves enough information for source/target distinction.

Section 4 reports experiments on the 100-PC source subspace. In 4.1, source-trained full-representation probes transfer unevenly to the three targets: Insider Trading Confirm 0.874 AUROC, Insider Trading Report 0.706, and Sandbagging 0.606. Target-trained probes evaluated within the 100-PC subspace via 5-fold CV achieve 0.936 / 0.950 / 0.869 AUROC on Report / Confirm / Sandbagging, showing the subspace retains enough class information and that transfer failure is due to the learned direction, not missing information.

In 4.2, the paper introduces a greedy PC-selection algorithm that starts empty, iteratively adds the source PC that most improves target AUROC, and trains logistic-regression weights on source data only. Subset selection uses labeled target examples in non-held-out folds, so this is an oracle/upper bound rather than an unbiased OOD estimate. Selection stops when no PC improves AUROC by more than 0.001. Mean selected subset sizes are 15 PCs (Report), 8 (Confirm), and 14 (Sandbagging). Greedy nearly matches target-trained performance on Report and Sandbagging, improving baseline AUROC by 0.22 and 0.23, while variance-ranked top-k PCs only match greedy on Confirm and lag on the harder tasks.

In 4.3, the paper tests two hypotheses about transferable PCs: (1) PCs that individually separate target classes well; (2) PCs most important to the source probe. Figure 4 compares rankings by source-probe weights, target-probe weights, and greedy oracle selection across the three targets.

For transfer evaluation, source-trained logistic probes are fit on the top-k PCs in each ranking. To choose k, greedy is run on the full target dataset (not CV), giving stable sets of k=13 for Insider Trading Report, 7 for Confirm, and 14 for Sandbagging; these differ slightly from Section 4.2 because they use the full dataset. Result: both hypotheses fail. Jaccard overlap between greedy and target-ranked sets is low (0.182 / 0.077 / 0.167).

Section 4.4 interprets top source PCs with LLM descriptions of positive/negative poles and an OOD score from 1–10. No PC scores above 6, so 6 is the maximum observed score. Of the 5 PCs selected by greedy for more than one target, 3 receive the maximum score, suggesting some recovery of transferable directions; only 1 of the top 5 source-PCA-probe PCs gets the maximum score.

Section 4.5 uses the 19 interp-selected PCs as a transfer subspace and compares them to top-19 variance PCs and an ablated 81-PC complement. The claim is that interpretation-based selection improves transfer without target data, with different gains across targets.

The paper studies OOD deception detection in language-model representations, comparing probes trained on full representations versus selected subspaces/directions. One selection method uses target labels to choose directions without fitting probe weights on them; another uses natural-language interpretations without target data. The summary claims: small target-guided subspaces nearly match target-trained probes; source-weights, target-class separation, and explained variance do not recover the same transferable subspaces; interpretation-based selection improves over the full-representation baseline on all targets but with sharply varying recovery. The study uses one model and one source dataset, and its interpretations are descriptive rather than causal.

The paper studies OOD deception detection in Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct layer-15 residual-stream activations. The source dataset is Roleplaying (V8); held-out targets are Insider Trading Report (C2R), Insider Trading Confirm (W6), and Sandbagging (J9). Labels are -1 ambiguous, 0 honest, 1 deceptive; ambiguous examples are removed. Activations are standardized with source statistics, and PCA/N4D keeps the top 100 source directions. All classifiers are logistic regression with λ=10, and performance is AUROC with 95% CIs. The full-representation baseline (B8Q) uses all standardized activations; Y4 uses top-k PCs by variance. H2 is a target-guided greedy selection using target labels for direction choice but source-trained probe weights; it is treated as a transfer upper bound. T6/M9 are source- and target-trained ranking probes. X4 is the standardized coefficient magnitude. R5 is GPT-5-mini's OOD usefulness rating, used to build L2 (interp-selected PC probe) and A7 (its complement). The paper also measures SAE decoder alignment using the `andyrdt/saes-llama-3.1-8b-instruct` resource and Jaccard overlap among selected directions.

Paper: “Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting” (JMLR 2014). Main claim: dropout randomly drops units and their connections during training, causing an exponential number of thinned networks to be sampled; at test time, one can approximate averaging over them with a single unthinned network using smaller weights. Abstract says this reduces overfitting and improves supervised learning performance in vision, speech recognition, document classification, and computational biology, with state-of-the-art results on many benchmarks. Introduction frames dropout as a regularization method for deep nets, alongside early stopping and weight penalties (L1/L2, soft weight sharing). Figure 1 illustrates a standard neural net vs. a thinned net produced by dropout.

The paper motivates dropout as an approximation to Bayesian model averaging / geometric mean over an exponential number of shared-parameter networks, aiming for good performance with less computation. It argues that averaging many separately trained nets is expensive because diverse nets require different architectures or data and are costly to train/test. Dropout drops hidden and visible units (removing incoming/outgoing connections) at random during training; each unit is retained independently with probability p, typically 0.5 for many layers, while input units usually use p closer to 1. Figure 2 states that at test time all units are present and outgoing weights are multiplied by p, so the test-time network matches the expected training-time output.

Model description: for a network with L hidden layers, y^(0)=x, layer l has weights W^(l) and biases b^(l). Standard feedforward uses z^(l+1)=w^(l+1) y^(l)+b^(l+1), y^(l+1)=f(z^(l+1)). With dropout, a Bernoulli mask r^(l) with retention probability p is sampled for each layer, the thinned outputs y~^(l)=r^(l)*y^(l) are passed to the next layer, and this is done at every layer. Training backpropagates through the sampled subnetwork. At test time, dropout is removed and weights are scaled by p: W_test = p W^(l). Section 5.1: Dropout nets are trained with SGD by sampling a thinned network per training case; forward/backprop are run only on that thinned network, gradients are averaged over the mini-batch, and units not used contribute zero gradient. Usual SGD improvements (momentum, annealed learning rates, L2 decay) also help. A particularly useful regularizer is max-norm: constrain each hidden unit’s incoming weight vector w to satisfy ||w||2 ≤ c by projecting back onto the ball of radius c; c is tuned on validation. The paper says dropout + max-norm + large decaying learning rates + high momentum works better than dropout alone.

Section 5.2: Dropout can be used to fine-tune pretrained nets (RBMs, autoencoders, DBMs) without changing the pretraining procedure. Weights from pretraining should be scaled up by 1/p so the expected output under dropout matches pretraining. Smaller finetuning learning rates are needed; with them, pretrained information is retained and final generalization improves versus finetuning without dropout.

Section 6 begins experiments: they evaluate dropout on classification tasks across many domains and claim dropout improved generalization on all data sets compared to non-dropout neural nets. If r_j=0, hidden unit h_j is forced to 0; the joint distribution factorizes as P(r)P(h,v|r), and conditioned on r the model is an RBM with some hidden units removed. Section 7.3 studies the effect of dropout rate p on MNIST. In the first setting, the network architecture is fixed at 784-2048-2048-2048-10 with no input dropout; as p increases, test error decreases, is roughly flat for 0.4 ≤ p ≤ 0.8, and rises again near p = 1. Small p causes underfitting because few units are active during training. In the second setting, pn is held constant so smaller p uses larger layers; here pn = 256 for the first two hidden layers and 512 for the last. This reduces errors for small p (e.g., p=0.1 drops from 2.7% to 1.7% compared with fixed architecture), and the best p is around 0.6, with the usual 0.5 close to optimal.

Section 7.4 studies dataset size with dropout on MNIST using a 784-1024-1024-2048-10 network. Dataset sizes are 100, 500, 1K, 5K, 10K, and 50K. Dropout is p=0.5 on hidden layers and p=0.8 on the input layer. For extremely small datasets (100, 500), dropout does not help; as data size increases, the benefit grows and then declines, suggesting a sweet spot where the data are enough to avoid memorization but not so large that overfitting is absent.

Section 7.5 begins a comparison of test-time approximate model averaging by weight scaling versus Monte-Carlo averaging by sampling multiple dropout networks.

Section 7.5 compares test-time approximate model averaging by weight scaling with Monte-Carlo averaging over k sampled dropout networks on MNIST. The text says that as k→∞ Monte-Carlo approaches the true model average, and empirically around k=50 it becomes as good as the weight-scaling approximation; for larger k it is slightly better but within one standard deviation.

Section 8 introduces Dropout Restricted Boltzmann Machines (RBMs). An RBM has visible units v∈{0,1}^D and hidden units h∈{0,1}^F with parameters θ={W,a,b}. Dropout RBMs add binary mask variables r∈{0,1}^F, where each r_j=1 with probability p and, if r_j=0, hidden unit h_j is forced to 0 via g(h_j,r_j). The joint distribution is P(r,h,v;p,θ)=P(r;p)P(h,v|r;θ), and conditioned on r the model is equivalent to an RBM with the dropped hidden units removed. Hidden units are factorial conditioned on v,r, and visible units are factorial conditioned on h.

Learning uses standard RBM methods such as Contrastive Divergence; the only change is that r is sampled first and only retained hidden units are used. The experiments use CD-1 and sample a different r for each training case in every minibatch.

Section 8.3 begins an investigation of whether dropout improves RBM features. Figure 12 compares features learned by a 256-hidden-unit binary RBM without dropout versus a dropout RBM with p=0.5, ordered by L2 norm.

Section 8.4 studies sparsity in dropout RBMs. Figure 13 compares hidden-unit activations/means for a standard RBM vs a dropout RBM after training; the dropout RBM is described as having much sparser representations, with many activations near zero. The text also says dropout RBM features look coarser than standard RBM features and that there are very few dead units in the dropout RBM relative to the standard RBM.

Section 9 introduces marginalizing dropout noise to obtain deterministic versions of dropout. In linear regression, with input dropout mask R_ij ~ Bernoulli(p), the marginalized objective becomes ||y - pXw||^2 + p(1-p)||Γw||^2, where Γ = (diag(X^T X))^{1/2}; equivalently, with w̃ = pw, the regularization coefficient is (1-p)/p.

For logistic regression, Wang and Manning’s approximate marginalization assumes Gaussian distributions for inputs to the logistic unit and for gradients; it can be trained efficiently and is said to outperform Monte-Carlo dropout in training time and generalization, but the assumptions weaken for deep networks. The table reports test errors for Bernoulli vs Gaussian dropout: MNIST 1.08±0.04 vs 0.95±0.04, CIFAR-10 12.6±0.1 vs 12.5±0.1, favoring Gaussian dropout on both datasets.

Section 10 generalizes dropout to multiplicative Gaussian noise. Each activation hi can be perturbed as hi + hi r with r ~ N(0,1), equivalently hi r0 with r0 ~ N(1,1). More generally, r0 ~ N(1, σ^2) and σ is a tunable hyperparameter. The expected activation is unchanged, so no test-time weight scaling is needed in this formulation.

The paper contrasts the usual Bernoulli scaling view of dropout (multiply by 1/p with probability p, else 0) with Gaussian multiplicative noise. Matching first and second moments requires σ^2 = (1-p)/p. Under these constraints, the Gaussian has highest entropy and the Bernoulli lowest; the paper says both work well, with preliminary results suggesting the high-entropy Gaussian may do slightly better.

Table 10 compares Bernoulli vs Gaussian dropout on classification error. For MNIST, Bernoulli uses p = 0.5 for hidden units and p = 0.8 for inputs; for CIFAR-10, p = (0.9, 0.75, 0.75, 0.5, 0.5, 0.5) from input layer to top. Gaussian dropout uses σ chosen from the corresponding Bernoulli p values. Results are averaged over 10 random seeds, and Gaussian slightly outperforms Bernoulli on both MNIST and CIFAR-10.

Section 11/appendix concludes that dropout is broadly useful across many domains and can be extended to RBMs and other graphical models. It reiterates that dropout training is slower than standard nets: typically 2–3x longer, because each case trains a different random submodel and gradients are noisy; this stochasticity may help prevent overfitting. It suggests future work on marginalizing the noise to obtain a regularizer that approximates dropout in expectation, noting that for linear regression this yields a modified L2 regularizer.

Appendix A gives practical heuristics for training dropout networks. If a layer has n hidden units and keep probability p, expected active units are pn, so a good dropout net may need at least n/p units. Dropout often needs 10–100x the learning rate of a standard net and momentum around 0.95–0.99 (vs 0.9 common in standard nets). Max-norm regularization is recommended to prevent weight blow-up, with typical c around 3–4. Typical keep probabilities are 0.5–0.8 for hidden units and about 0.8 for real-valued inputs. Smaller p requires larger n and can slow training or underfit; p=1 means no dropout.

Appendix B gives experimental/data details. MNIST: 60k train/10k test, with 10k held out for validation. Hyperparameters were tuned so best validation error occurred after 1M weight updates; then validation was merged back into training and the model trained for 1M updates for test evaluation. MNIST architectures in Fig. 4 cover 2-, 3-, and 4-layer nets with 1024 or 2048 units; for all MNIST architectures (including Table 2) they used p=0.5 in hidden layers and p=0.8 in the input layer, with momentum 0.95 and max-norm c=2. Larger 4096/8192-unit nets were also tried; 2-layer nets improved as in Table 2, while 3-layer nets were slightly worse than 2-layer nets at the same dropout, and increasing dropout helped but not enough to beat 2-layer nets.

SVHN: about 600k training and 26k test images. The training set has standard and extra labeled parts; validation was built from both (400 per class from standard, 200 per class from extra, total 6000). Inputs were RGB normalized to zero mean/unit variance. Best model: 3 conv layers (96/128/256 filters), each 5x5 stride 1, each followed by 3x3 max pooling stride 2, then two fully connected layers of 2048 units; ReLU activations throughout. Dropout keep probabilities were (0.9, 0.75, 0.75, 0.5, 0.5, 0.5) from input through conv/FC layers, with max-norm c=4 and momentum 0.95. Validation was kept separate for final training/testing.

CIFAR-10/100: 50k train and 10k test each, with 5k validation. They tuned hyperparameters on validation then combined validation with training. Preprocessing used global contrast normalization per color channel and ZCA whitening.

Paper: "Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting" (JMLR 15, 2014, pp. 1929–1958). Authors: Nitish Srivastava, Geoffrey Hinton, Alex Krizhevsky, Ilya Sutskever, and Ruslan Salakhutdinov (University of Toronto); editor Yoshua Bengio. The paper map on the first pages lays out the structure across sections 2–11 plus appendices A and B. Abstract/intro claims: dropout randomly removes units and their connections during training, reducing co-adaptation and implicitly sampling exponentially many thinned networks; a single unthinned network with reduced weights approximates the averaged predictions. It claims dropout reduces overfitting and improves results across vision, speech recognition, document classification, and computational biology, often state of the art. Section 1 also says posterior-weighted averaging is the best regularization given unlimited computation, while dropout approximates an equally weighted geometric mean over exponentially many shared-parameter models. A network with n units corresponds to 2^n thinned networks and reuses O(n^2) or fewer parameters. The introduction contrasts dropout with stopping early, soft weight sharing, and L1/L2 penalties, and says model combination is powerful but expensive. It introduces the practical inference rule (weight scaling) versus Monte Carlo model averaging, and notes dropout extends to graphical models such as Boltzmann machines, including Restricted Boltzmann Machines and dropout RBMs. Figure 1 shows a standard two-hidden-layer net and a thinned version with crossed units removed.

Section 2 motivates dropout using analogies from evolution and robustness. It contrasts sexual vs asexual reproduction: recombination breaks co-adapted gene sets, suggesting a tension between individual-fitness optimization and the value of mixable, robust genes. The Livnat et al. view is that selection may favor gene sets that work with many partners; the paper maps this to hidden units trained with dropout, which must be useful with randomly selected partners and thus learn independently useful, robust features rather than depend on other units. It also uses a conspiracy analogy: smaller conspiracies are more robust to changing conditions than a larger one needing many correct participants. These examples support the claim that complex co-adaptations can fit training data yet generalize poorly, whereas simpler robust components may generalize better.

Section 3 surveys related work on noise-based regularization. It frames hidden-unit noise as a regularizer for QX2, connecting it to denoising autoencoders (Vincent et al. 2008, 2010): input corruption plus reconstruction, effective hidden-layer corruption, model averaging, supervised and unsupervised use, and applicability to other neuron-based architectures such as Boltzmann machines. A comparison table says typical best noise is 5% for S2H, while QX2 often works best at 20% input-unit removal or 50% hidden-unit removal. It contrasts stochastic noise training with adversarial removal methods (Globerson and Roweis 2006; Dekel et al. 2010), noting those have no hidden units. It also says analytically marginalizing QX2 yields deterministic regularizers in simple cases; related exponential-family input-noise regularizers (“blankout noise”) were studied by van der Maaten et al. (2013) for models without hidden layers. Chen et al. (2012) examined marginalization for denoising autoencoders, and Wang and Manning (2013) proposed marginalization to accelerate QX2.
