steps.notes_before: Section 4 defines QX2 as stochastic deletion (“dropout”) applied to every layer: each layer output vector is multiplied elementwise by an independent Bernoulli mask with retention probability \(p\). Training samples a subnetwork and backpropagates through it; both hidden and visible units can be removed. At test time, no units are removed and the outgoing weights are scaled by \(p\): \(\mathbf W^{(l)}_{	ext{test}}=p\mathbf W^{(l)}\). The section states that validation can choose \(p\), but the default is usually near optimal and input retention is often closer to 1. It also claims that the expected output under deletion matches test-time output, though the formulas only directly show this for the preactivation, not necessarily after a nonlinear activation.

Section 5 says QX2 training uses standard SGD on a per-case sampled thinned network: each case is forwarded/backpropagated through its own sampled subnetwork, gradients are averaged, and absent parameters contribute zero. It highlights that QX2 works well with high momentum, large decaying learning rates, and V9C max-norm regularization, where each incoming hidden-unit weight vector is constrained by ||w||_2 <= c and projected back onto the radius-c ball if it exceeds it. The section also notes that this constraint is a validation-tuned hyperparameter and can help deep-net training even without QX2. For unsupervised pretraining, the procedure is unchanged, but before QX2 finetuning pretrained weights are multiplied by 1/p so that expected random-removal output matches the pretrained output. Smaller finetuning learning rates are said to preserve pretrained information better than rates comparable to best randomly initialized-net rates.

Section 6 reports experimental results. It claims QX2 improved generalization over non-QX2 neural nets on every tested data set and that models attaining state of the art on all five vision collections use QX2. Table 1 lists datasets: H4Z/MNIST (784, 60K/10K), A2F/SVHN (3072, 600K/26K), J3V/W6R/CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 (3072, 60K/10K), K9D/ImageNet ILSVRC-2012 (65536, 1.2M/150K), N8Q/TIMIT (2520, 1.1M frames/58K frames), M5X/Reuters-RCV1 (2000, 200K/200K), and Z7P/Alternative Splicing (1014, 2932/733). In H4Z, QX2 improves over standard neural nets; ReLUs, max-norm regularization (V9C), larger architectures, and maxout (L8J) each improve further. Best H4Z listed result is E5Q + QX2 finetuning at 0.79% error; G6W + QX2 finetuning gets 0.92%, while E5Q + finetuning without QX2 is 0.96%. Figure 4 compares training trajectories with and without QX2 under fixed hyperparameters, yielding two separated error clusters. The A2F section says convolutional nets outperform other methods; adding QX2 to fully connected layers helps, adding it to convolutional layers helps more, and maxout helps further.

For logistic regression and deep networks, exact marginalization is difficult. The paper says approximate marginalization outperforms Monte-Carlo QX2 for logistic regression, and that under reasonable assumptions logistic-unit inputs and marginalized gradients are Gaussian with computable means/variances, but these assumptions become weaker with depth, so the results are not directly applicable to deep networks.

Paper: "Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting" (JMLR 15, 2014, pp. 1929–1958). Authors: Nitish Srivastava, Geoffrey Hinton, Alex Krizhevsky, Ilya Sutskever, Ruslan Salakhutdinov. Submitted 11/13; published 6/14. Front matter and abstract read so far. Abstract claims dropout randomly removes units and connections during training to inhibit co-adaptation and sample exponentially many thinned networks; a single unthinned network with reduced weights approximates the average prediction of these networks. It claims dropout substantially reduces overfitting and yields major improvements, with experiments in vision, speech recognition, document classification, and computational biology achieving state-of-the-art on many benchmarks. The page map lists the paper structure from p. 1930 through 1955, including sections 2–11, tables 1–10, figures 1–13, and appendices A and B.

Section 1 argues that, for a fixed-sized model with unlimited computation, posterior-weighted averaging over all parameter settings is the best regularization; dropout approximates an equally weighted geometric mean of exponentially many parameter-sharing thinned networks. An n-unit network corresponds to 2^n possible thinned networks while sharing O(n^2) or fewer parameters, and each sampled member is trained only rarely because a fresh thinned network is sampled for each training case. The section motivates dropout as an alternative to stopping, soft weight sharing, and L1/L2 penalties, and says model averaging usually helps but is expensive. It presents the practical inference rule as using one unthinned network with weight scaling instead of explicitly averaging many sampled networks, and notes a Monte-Carlo averaging alternative. It also states the method extends to graphical models, including Boltzmann machines, with Restricted Boltzmann Machines admitting a dropout variant. The paper map lists sections on motivation, previous work, formal model, training algorithm, experiments, network-property effects/hyperparameter interactions, RBMs, and marginalization, plus Appendix A on practical training guidance.

steps.notes_before: Section 4 defines the dropout model more formally. It says retention is random and usually independent with a common probability p; p can be chosen by validation, and the usual default is close to optimal, while input retention is often nearer complete retention. The network notation uses L hidden layers with activations y^(l), weights W^(l), and biases b^(l). Standard feed-forward computation is z_i^(l+1)=w_i^(l+1) y^(l)+b_i^(l+1), followed by y_i^(l+1)=f(z_i^(l+1)), where f can be any activation, including sigmoid. Dropout replaces this by sampling Bernoulli masks r_j^(l), forming masked outputs \tilde y^(l)=r^(l)*y^(l), and then computing the next layer from the masked activations. This can be applied at every layer, sampling a subnetwork each time, and both hidden and visible units may be removed. At inference, no units are dropped; instead outgoing weights are scaled by p: W_test^(l)=p W^(l). Figures 2 and 3 illustrate the training-time masking versus test-time weight scaling.

Section 5 discusses learning QX2 nets. It says QX2 combined with high momentum, large decaying learning rates, and incoming-weight max-norm constraint V9C yields additional gains, and V9C constrains each incoming hidden-unit weight vector to have L2 norm at most c via projection back onto the radius-c ball. Stochastic gradient descent uses a different sampled thinned network for each mini-batch case; gradients are averaged and unused parameters contribute zero. In unsupervised pretraining, the pretraining procedure itself is unchanged, but before QX2 finetuning pretrained weights are multiplied by 1/p so expected random-removal outputs match pretraining outputs. Smaller finetuning learning rates help preserve pretrained information; larger rates can erase it. Pretraining plus backprop finetuning is said to work with stacked U2L, autoencoders, and DBMs.

Section 8 introduces B8T, a mixture of exponentially many shared-weight U2L models formed by sampling a binary retention vector r for hidden units. Each h_j is retained independently with probability p; if r_j=0 then h_j is forced to 0. Conditional on r, the model is just an ordinary U2L with the dropped hidden units removed. The visible conditional remains the standard U2L form; the hidden conditional is factorial with P(h_j=1|r_j,v)=1(r_j=1)·σ(b_j+Σ_i W_ij v_i). Learning uses ordinary U2L methods such as CD, but with a fresh r sampled for each training case in each mini-batch; experiments use CD-1. Section 8.3 says B8T features are coarser than the sharply defined stroke-like U2L features and have very few dead units relative to U2L (Fig. 12, 256-hidden-unit H4Z models, ordinary U2L vs B8T with p=0.5). Section 8.4 says B8T learns much sparser representations than U2L even without an explicit sparsity regularizer, using test mini-batch activation histograms (Fig. 13): many activations near zero and very few high activations.

Section 9 discusses marginalizing QX2. Deterministic noise-marginalized models need no random bits and allow gradients of the marginalized loss, unlike standard Monte-Carlo QX2. Prior work cited: Globerson and Roweis (2006) on deterministic robustness to feature deletion; Srivastava (2013) on linear-regression QX2 marginalization; Wager et al. (2013) on QX2 as an adaptive regularizer.

For linear regression, retaining each input dimension with probability p gives an expected objective equivalent to ridge regression with a data-dependent penalty: minimize ||y - pXw||^2 + p(1-p)||Γw||^2, where Γ = diag(X^T X)^(1/2). With w~ = p w, this becomes ||y - Xw~||^2 + ((1-p)/p)||Γw~||^2.

For logistic regression and deep nets, the paper says approximate marginalization can outperform Monte-Carlo QX2 in training time and generalization for logistic regression (Wang and Manning, 2013). Closed-form marginalized models are difficult for logistic regression and deep nets; under reasonable assumptions, logistic-unit inputs and marginalized-model gradients are Gaussian with computable means/variances, but the assumptions get weaker with more layers, so the results are not directly applicable to deep networks.

Section 10 reports that multiplicative Gaussian noise (D4K) and Bernoulli dropout (P7V) have the same first and second moments under a suitable parameter match, but the Gaussian multiplier has higher entropy. Preliminary results slightly favor Gaussian noise: H4Z error is 1.08±0.04 for P7V vs 0.95±0.04 for D4K, and J3V error is 12.6±0.1 vs 12.5±0.1. For the reported settings, P7V retention is p=0.5 for H4Z hidden units, p=0.8 for H4Z input units, and p=(0.9,0.75,0.75,0.5,0.5,0.5) for J3V input-to-top layers. The corresponding Gaussian standard deviation per layer is σ=sqrt((1-p)/p). The section explains that Bernoulli multiplicative dropout can be viewed either as keeping activations during training and scaling outgoing weights by p at test time, or equivalently as multiplying retained training activations by 1/p. In that latter view, the Bernoulli multiplier r_b takes value 1/p with probability p and 0 otherwise, so E[r_b]=1 and Var[r_b]=(1-p)/p. A Gaussian multiplier r_g~N(1,σ^2) with σ^2=(1-p)/p matches these moments, giving E[r_g]=1 and Var[r_g]=(1-p)/p.

Abstract claims dropout randomly removes units during training, samples an exponential number of thinned networks, and uses one unthinned network with smaller weights at test time to approximate their average predictions. It says dropout reduces overfitting and improves supervised-learning performance on vision, speech recognition, document classification, and computational-biology tasks, with state-of-the-art results on many benchmarks. It also says dropout outperforms other regularization methods.

Introduction claims deep nets overfit limited data and reviews standard regularization (early stopping, L1/L2, soft weight sharing). The paper’s goal is to approximate Bayesian model averaging / an equally weighted geometric mean of predictions from exponentially many parameter-sharing models at low cost. Dropout randomly removes hidden or visible units during training; in the simplest case each unit is retained independently with probability p (often p=0.5 for hidden units, closer to 1 for inputs). A thinned network is sampled for each training case. At test time, dropout is turned off and outgoing weights are multiplied by p so expected training-time output matches test-time output. A network with n units represents 2^n thinned networks with shared weights, making explicit averaging infeasible. The paper claims dropout reduces generalization error and also applies to RBMs. Section roadmap: 2 motivation, 3 related work, 4 model, 5 training, 6 experiments, 7 network properties/hyperparameters, 8 Dropout RBMs, 9 marginalizing dropout, Appendix A practical guidance.

This part begins Section 2 (Motivation) and uses two analogies to explain why dropout should help: (1) sexual reproduction/mix-ability—useful genes must work with random partners, so hidden units trained with dropout should become robust and not rely on specific co-adaptations; and (2) conspiracies—smaller groups are more likely to keep working under changing conditions than one large tightly coordinated group. The section’s conclusion is that complex co-adaptations may fit training data but are more likely to fail on test data than several simpler co-adaptations.

Section 3 relates dropout to noisy autoencoders and robustness. It says dropout can be seen as regularization via noise in hidden states; Denoising Autoencoders add noise to unit states / inputs and reconstruct clean input. Dropout extends this idea to hidden layers and to supervised learning, and to other neuron-based architectures including Boltzmann Machines. It claims that although 5% noise is typical for DAEs, test-time weight scaling allows much higher noise, with 20% input dropout and 50% hidden dropout often optimal. Under dropout, each layer output is multiplied elementwise by an independent Bernoulli(p) mask r^(l) before being fed to the next layer, producing a sampled sub-network. Section 5 covers learning dropout nets. Training uses SGD on a sampled thinned network per mini-batch case; gradients are averaged and inactive parameters contribute zero gradient. Max-norm regularization constrains each hidden unit’s incoming weight vector to norm <= c and is especially useful with dropout; the paper claims dropout + max-norm beats dropout + L2 (Table 9: 1.05% vs 1.25%), and max-norm alone beats L2 (1.35% vs 1.62%).

Section 7 studies how dropout affects learned features, sparsity, and sensitivity to retention probability. In 7.1, the paper compares two otherwise identical MNIST autoencoders with 256 ReLU hidden units, one without dropout and one with hidden-layer dropout at p=0.5. It claims both have similar test reconstruction error, but dropout yields more interpretable features (edges, strokes, spots) and reduces co-adaptation. In 7.2, the same autoencoders are evaluated on a random test mini-batch: without dropout, mean activation is about 2.0 and activations have a large mass away from zero; with dropout, mean activation is about 0.7 and activations are sharply peaked at zero. Thus dropout makes activations sparser without an explicit sparsity penalty. In 7.3, the paper varies dropout rate on MNIST using architecture 784-2048-2048-2048-10, first with fixed network size and then with expected retained size pn fixed. For fixed size, error is high at small p, decreases as p increases, stays roughly flat for 0.4<=p<=0.8, and then rises again as p approaches 1. The second setting keeps expected retained units constant while changing actual network size.

For fixed architecture 784-2048-2048-2048-10, error is high at small p, falls as p increases, is roughly flat for 0.4<=p<=0.8, and rises again near p=1. A second experiment keeps expected retained units constant while changing actual network size; with retained sizes pn=256 for the first two hidden layers and pn=512 for the last, Figure 9b has much lower error at low p than Figure 9a (at p=0.1, 2.7% vs 1.7%). For these retained sizes, p around 0.6 is best and p=0.5 is close to optimal.

Section 7.4 varies MNIST training-set size using architecture 784-1024-1024-2048-10 with p=0.5 in all hidden layers and p=0.8 at the input. Training-set sizes are 100, 500, 1K, 5K, 10K, and 50K. Dropout gives no improvement at 100 and 500 cases, but its gain first increases and then declines as data size grows, suggesting an architecture- and dropout-dependent sweet spot.

Section 7.5 compares Monte-Carlo model averaging with weight scaling. Test-time averaging over k sampled dropout networks approaches the true model average as k increases. On MNIST, about k=50 samples match the weight-scaling approximation; beyond that, Monte-Carlo averaging is slightly better but within one standard deviation, so weight scaling is a good approximation.

Section 8 defines Dropout RBMs as a mixture over hidden-unit subsets. An RBM over v,h has standard energy-based joint P(h,v;θ). A dropout mask r∈{0,1}^F is sampled with independent retention probability p per hidden unit; if r_j=0 then h_j is constrained to 0 via a factor g(h_j,r_j). Conditioned on r, the model is just an RBM with the dropped hidden units removed, so the full model is a mixture of exponentially many RBMs sharing weights. Learning uses standard RBM methods (e.g., CD-1) after sampling a new mask for each training case in each mini-batch.

The section qualitatively compares standard and dropout RBMs on MNIST with 256 hidden units. Figure 12 shows dropout (p=0.5) learns coarser-looking features and appears to have fewer dead units than the standard RBM. Figure 13 suggests dropout also yields sparser hidden activations: many units near zero and few high-activation units, even without any explicit sparsity regularizer.

Section 9 studies deterministic models formed by marginalizing dropout noise. It notes prior related work on feature deletion, denoising autoencoders, linear regression, and adaptive regularization. For linear regression, with inputs X, targets y, and Bernoulli(p) masking of each input entry, the expected squared-loss objective becomes ||y-pXw||^2 + p(1-p)||Γw||^2, where Γ = diag(X^T X)^(1/2). After rescaling w via \tilde w = p w, the objective is ||y-X\tilde w||^2 + ((1-p)/p)||Γ\tilde w||^2, so the regularization strength increases as p decreases. The text interprets this as ridge regression with feature-dependent penalties proportional to input standard deviations. For logistic regression, exact marginalization is said to be difficult; Wang and Manning (2013) provide an approximation using Gaussian means/variances of unit inputs and gradients, which is claimed to improve training time and generalization over Monte-Carlo dropout. The paper also states that the approximation assumptions become weaker in deeper networks, so the result does not directly extend to deep models.

Section 10 generalizes dropout to multiplicative Gaussian noise. A unit activation h_i can be perturbed as h_i+h_i r with r~N(0,1), equivalently h_i r' with r'~N(1,1); more generally r'~N(1,σ^2). Because the mean is 1, no test-time weight scaling is needed. The section also describes the standard dropout rescaling equivalence: retaining units with probability p and scaling weights at test time is equivalent to scaling retained training activations by 1/p and leaving test weights unchanged. Under this rescaled view, the Bernoulli multiplier r_b is 1/p with probability p and 0 otherwise, with mean 1 and variance (1-p)/p. Matching Gaussian variance to σ^2=(1-p)/p makes Bernoulli and Gaussian multipliers share first two moments; Gaussian has higher entropy and Bernoulli lower entropy. Table 10 reports preliminary classification errors showing Gaussian dropout slightly better than Bernoulli on MNIST (0.95±0.04 vs 1.08±0.04) and CIFAR-10 (12.5±0.1 vs 12.6±0.1), using p values specified per layer and 10 random seeds.

Section 11 concludes that dropout reduces overfitting by breaking co-adaptations via random omission of hidden units. It claims dropout improves object classification, digit recognition, speech recognition, document classification, and computational-biology tasks, and that dropout methods achieve state-of-the-art results on SVHN, ImageNet, CIFAR-100, and MNIST. The conclusion says the approach extends to RBMs and other graphical models via repeated sampling/training of smaller sub-models, and that Dropout RBMs show desirable properties. It also states a drawback: training typically takes 2-3 times longer than a standard network because gradients come from a random architecture rather than the final test architecture. Finally, it notes that marginalizing noise can yield a modified L2 regularizer for linear regression, while analogous regularizers for more complex models are not obvious.

Section 11 concluded that dropout reduces overfitting by breaking co-adaptations via random omission of hidden units. It claimed dropout improves object classification, digit recognition, speech recognition, document classification, and computational-biology tasks, and reaches state-of-the-art on SVHN, ImageNet, CIFAR-100, and MNIST. It also said dropout extends to RBMs and other graphical models via repeated sampling/training of smaller sub-models, with desirable properties for Dropout RBMs. A noted drawback is training typically takes 2-3 times longer than a standard network because gradients come from a random architecture rather than the final test architecture. For linear regression, marginalizing noise yields a modified L2 regularizer, but analogous regularizers for more complex models are not obvious.

Appendix A gives practical dropout heuristics: because dropping units reduces capacity, a layer with n hidden units and retention probability p should often be scaled up to at least n/p units. Recommended dropout training settings include learning rates 10-100 times those used for standard networks and momentum around 0.95-0.99 instead of 0.9. Max-norm regularization is suggested to keep incoming hidden-unit weight norms bounded, with typical c values of 3 to 4. Typical hidden-unit retention probabilities are 0.5 to 0.8, while input retention for real-valued image patches or speech frames is around 0.8. The appendix stresses that p and n must be chosen together: smaller p needs larger n, which can slow training and cause underfitting, while larger p may under-regularize.

Appendix B gives experimental details and code availability. Implementations were GPU-based using cudamat and cuda-convnet.

MNIST: 60,000 training and 10,000 test images (28x28). They held out 10,000 training images for validation, selected hyperparameters so best validation error occurred after 1M updates, then retrained on combined train+validation for 1M updates. Figure 4 covers all 2-, 3-, and 4-hidden-layer nets with 1024 or 2048 units; these and Table 2 used hidden p=0.5, input p=0.8, final momentum 0.95, and max-norm c=2. They also tested larger 2- and 3-layer nets with 4096/8192 units; 2-layer nets improved, 3-layer nets were slightly worse, and more dropout did not beat the 2-layer nets.

SVHN: about 600,000 training and 26,000 test images. Validation set was 6000 examples: 400/class from standard labels and 200/class from extra labels. Inputs were RGB normalized to zero mean and unit variance; contrast normalization and ZCA whitening did not help. Best model: 3 conv layers (96, 128, 256 filters, each 5x5, stride 1), each followed by 3x3 max-pooling with stride 2, then two 2048-unit fully connected layers, all ReLU. Retention probabilities were (0.9, 0.75, 0.75, 0.5, 0.5, 0.5), with c=4 and momentum 0.95. Because training set was large, validation data was not merged back; test error is for the model with smallest validation error.

CIFAR-10/100: each has 50,000 train and 10,000 test color 32x32 images. They used 5000 validation images, then merged validation back into training after selection. Preprocessing: global contrast normalization separately per color channel, then ZCA whitening. Architecture and dropout matched SVHN except input-layer learning rates were smaller.

TIMIT begins with Kaldi log-filter-bank features, monophone forced alignment, 21-frame windows predicting the central frame, no speaker-dependent processing, and mean-centered/unit-variance inputs.

final_notes: Appendix B gives experiment details and implementation: GPU-based code using cudamat and cuda-convnet. MNIST: 60k train/10k test; 10k held out for validation, then train+validation reunited and trained for 1M updates. Figure 4 uses 2-, 3-, and 4-hidden-layer MLPs with 1024 or 2048 units per layer (6 architectures). For these and Table 2 models, hidden layers used p=0.5, input p=0.8, final momentum 0.95, and c=2. Larger 2-layer MNIST nets with 4096 and 8192 units were also tried; 2-layer models improved, deeper ones were slightly worse, and more dropout did not surpass them. SVHN: about 600k train and 26k test images; validation set of 6000 formed from 400 standard + 200 extra examples per class. Inputs were RGB normalized to zero mean and unit variance; global/local contrast normalization and ZCA whitening gave no noticeable gain. Best model: 3 conv layers with 96/128/256 filters (5x5, stride 1), each followed by 3x3 max-pooling with stride 2, then two 2048-unit ReLU fully connected layers. Dropout retention p=(0.9,0.75,0.75,0.5,0.5,0.5), momentum 0.95, c=4. Test error reported from the best validation model; final training did not add back validation data. Result noted: 2.55% error. CIFAR-10/100: 50k train/10k test, 5k validation, then validation merged back into training. Preprocessing: global contrast normalization per color channel and ZCA whitening. Architecture and dropout matched SVHN except input-layer learning rates were smaller. TIMIT / speech DBN: dropout finetuning used input retention p=0.8 and hidden p=0.5, max-norm c=4, momentum 0.95, and learning rate 0.1 with decay epsilon0(1+t/T)^-1. Pretraining used CD-1 Gaussian RBMs with input variance fixed to 1. Best dropout finetuning results required a smaller learning rate of about 0.01, and adding max-norm constraints gave no improvement. Table 7 reports dropout rows 21.8%, 19.7%, and 19.7%. Reuters: RCV1 subset of 402,738 articles with 2000-word vocabulary and 50 categories; each document has exactly one class and the subset was split equally into train/test. Dropout improved all tried architectures but less than on image and speech tasks; best-network comparison was 31.05% without dropout vs 29.62% with dropout.

This part is the title/author block and abstract. The paper presents dropout as a training method that randomly removes units and connections, sampling an exponential number of thinned subnetworks that share weights. At test time, a single unthinned network with scaled-down weights approximates the average of these subnetworks. The abstract claims dropout substantially reduces overfitting, outperforms other regularization methods, and improves performance on vision, speech recognition, document classification, and computational-biology tasks. It also claims state-of-the-art results on many benchmarks. The paper’s listed evidence here includes image results in Tables 2–6, TIMIT in Table 7, Reuters results in Section 6.3, and alternative-splicing results in Table 8, plus a comparison in Table 9 showing Dropout+Max-norm outperforming Max-norm and L2.

This part introduces overfitting and positions dropout as an alternative to traditional regularization and model averaging. It contrasts dropout with early stopping, L1/L2, and soft weight sharing. The paper’s core idea is to approximate Bayesian averaging over exponentially many subnetworks by sampling a different thinned network for each training case, with shared weights across subnetworks. At test time, a single network without dropout is used, with outgoing weights scaled by the retention probability p so that expected training-time output matches test-time output. A network with n units corresponds to 2^n thinned networks, but parameter count remains O(n^2) or less because of weight sharing. The intro says dropout reduces generalization error across many classification problems and can be applied beyond feed-forward nets, including Boltzmann machines; later sections will cover motivation, related work, model definition, training, experiments, network properties, Dropout RBMs, and marginalizing dropout.

This part contains a brief results-style summary: dropout with approximate test-time averaging is said to lower classification error across several tables/domains, including Reuters (Section 6.3, 31.05% versus 29.62%), and Dropout RBMs are said to show qualitative advantages in feature and sparsity comparisons, without a numerical performance comparison in those figures. Section 2 then motivates dropout with analogies to sexual reproduction and conspiracies: randomly combining parts discourages brittle co-adaptations and favors robust, mixable units/features. The key claim is that a unit trained with dropout must function with randomly sampled partners, so it learns useful features that do not depend on specific other units. This is contrasted with large, fragile coordinated schemes that may fit training conditions but fail on new data.

Section 3 positions dropout relative to prior work on noisy autoencoders and deterministic marginalization. It says dropout can be viewed as regularization via noise on hidden-unit states, extending denoising autoencoders from noisy inputs to hidden layers and from unsupervised feature learning to supervised learning. It also says dropout can be interpreted as model averaging and can be applied to neuron-based architectures including Boltzmann Machines. The section claims that while DAEs often use about 5% noise, dropout with test-time weight scaling can work with much higher noise, and reports that 20% input dropout and 50% hidden dropout were often optimal. It distinguishes dropout’s stochastic objective from adversarial feature-removal settings (Globerson & Roweis; Dekel et al.), which are described as choosing removed units adversarially and not examining hidden-unit models. The section notes that deterministic marginalization has been explored for blankout noise/dropout and denoising autoencoders.

Section 4 defines the network notation and the dropout mechanism. A feed-forward network has L hidden layers, with y^(0)=x, weights W^(l), biases b^(l), and standard activations z_i^(l+1)=w_i^(l+1) y^(l)+b_i^(l+1), y_i^(l+1)=f(z_i^(l+1)). Under dropout, each layer l draws an independent Bernoulli mask r^(l) with success probability p (i.e., retain probability p), forms thinned activations \tilde y^(l)=r^(l)*y^(l), and uses these as input to the next layer. This samples a sub-network; training backpropagates derivatives through the sampled sub-network. At test time, dropout is removed and the weights are scaled as W_test^(l)=p W^(l).

Section 5 covers training dropout networks. In backpropagation, SGD is used; for each mini-batch case a thinned subnetwork is sampled, forward and backward passes are done only through that network, and gradients are averaged across the mini-batch with unused parameters contributing zero gradient. Helpful SGD enhancements include momentum, learning-rate decay/annealing, and L2 weight decay. Max-norm regularization constrains each hidden unit’s incoming weight vector to have L2 norm at most c, projecting any vector that exceeds c back onto the sphere; a validation set chooses c. The text claims dropout alone improves performance and that combining dropout with max-norm, large decaying learning rates, and high momentum yields further gains. It gives a possible optimization explanation, but not a measured one.

For pretrained networks, pretraining can come from RBMs, autoencoders, or DBMs, using unlabeled data. Dropout may be applied during finetuning without altering pretraining, but pretrained weights should first be scaled by 1/p so that expected outputs under dropout match pretraining outputs. The paper says dropout finetuning can improve pretrained MNIST networks, and that too-large finetuning learning rates can erase pretrained information while smaller rates preserve it and improve generalization relative to finetuning without dropout.

Section 7 studies learned features, sparsity, and how dropout depends on retention probability and model size. 7.1 compares one-hidden-layer MNIST autoencoders with 256 ReLUs, with and without dropout at p=0.5 (Figure 7). Both have similar test reconstruction error, but the no-dropout features look co-adapted and less meaningful, while dropout features look like edges/strokes/spots; the paper argues dropout breaks co-adaptations.

7.2 uses the same 256-unit autoencoders to examine sparsity (Figure 8). Dropout produces sparser activations without an explicit sparsity regularizer: the no-dropout model has many activations away from zero and mean activation around 2.0, while the dropout model has a sharp peak at zero and mean activation around 0.7.

7.3 varies dropout rate on MNIST. Two settings are studied: (1) keep hidden-unit count fixed, using architecture 784-2048-2048-2048-10 without input dropout; (2) keep expected retained units pn fixed, so smaller p requires larger networks. For fixed size, small p underfits (high training error), error decreases as p increases, stays roughly flat for 0.4<=p<=0.8, then rises as p approaches 1. Figure 9 plots train and test classification error versus p for both settings.

Section 7.3 compares dropout rate on MNIST under two regimes: (1) fixed architecture 784-2048-2048-2048-10 with no input dropout, and (2) fixed expected retained units so smaller p uses larger networks. In the fixed-architecture case, low p underfits; error decreases as p rises, is roughly flat for 0.4<=p<=0.8, then worsens as p approaches 1. In the fixed-size case, low-p error is reduced; at p=0.1, error improves from 2.7% to 1.7%. Best performance is around p=0.6, and the usual default p=0.5 is close to optimal, with retained sizes pn=256,256,512 for the three hidden layers.

Section 7.4 varies MNIST training-set size (100, 500, 1K, 5K, 10K, 50K) using architecture 784-1024-1024-2048-10, with p=0.5 in hidden layers and p=0.8 at input. Dropout gives no improvement at 100 and 500 examples, but its benefit increases and then declines as data size grows, suggesting a sweet spot where the model is large enough to overfit yet not so data-rich that overfitting ceases to matter.

Section 7.5 compares Monte-Carlo model averaging to test-time weight scaling. Averaging k sampled dropout networks approaches the true model average as k increases; around k=50, Monte-Carlo averaging matches weight scaling, and further sampling is only slightly better and within one standard deviation. Weight scaling is presented as a good approximation to the true model average.

Section 8 defines Dropout RBMs as RBMs augmented with a binary mask r over hidden units, where each hidden unit is retained independently with probability p. The joint distribution factors as P(r)P(h,v|r), and conditioned on r the model is an RBM with the dropped hidden units removed; thus it is a mixture of exponentially many weight-sharing RBMs. Learning is done by sampling a new mask per training case/mini-batch and then applying standard RBM learning, using CD-1 in the experiments. On MNIST with 256 hidden units, dropout RBMs (p=0.5) are reported to learn qualitatively coarser features with fewer dead units than standard RBMs, and their hidden activations are described as much sparser even without extra sparsity regularization. Figures 12 and 13 provide qualitative evidence only; no numerical feature-quality or sparsity metric is reported.

Section 9 discusses marginalizing dropout noise to obtain deterministic models. It states that this removes the need for random bits and allows gradients of the marginalized loss to be computed. For linear regression, with input-dimension retention probability p, the expected loss under masking simplifies to ||y - pXw||^2 + p(1-p)||Γw||^2, where Γ = diag(XᵀX)^{1/2}. After rescaling ~tilde w = pw, the regularization constant becomes (1-p)/p, so stronger dropout means stronger regularization. For logistic regression and deep networks, exact marginalization is difficult; Wang and Manning (2013) provide an approximate marginalized logistic-regression method using Gaussian assumptions for inputs and gradients, reported here as faster and better than Monte-Carlo dropout, but the text says this approach does not directly extend to deep networks.

Section 10 generalizes dropout to multiplicative Gaussian noise. It considers hidden activations multiplied by either Bernoulli masks or Gaussian multipliers. The Gaussian formulation can be written as adding zero-mean noise proportional to the activation, or as multiplying by r' ~ N(1, σ^2). With the rescaled Bernoulli view, the multiplier is 1/p with probability p and 0 otherwise, giving mean 1 and variance (1-p)/p. Setting σ^2 = (1-p)/p matches the Gaussian multiplier’s first two moments to Bernoulli dropout. The paper notes that Gaussian multipliers have higher entropy than Bernoulli masks, and both extremes work well. Table 10 reports slightly better classification error for Gaussian dropout than Bernoulli dropout on MNIST (0.95 ± 0.04 vs 1.08 ± 0.04) and CIFAR-10 (12.5 ± 0.1 vs 12.6 ± 0.1), averaged over 10 random seeds. For MNIST, Bernoulli uses p=0.5 for hidden units and p=0.8 for input units; for CIFAR-10, p=(0.9, 0.75, 0.75, 0.5, 0.5, 0.5) from input to top layer.

Section 11 concludes that dropout reduces overfitting by breaking brittle co-adaptations. It claims broad benefits across object classification, digit recognition, speech recognition, document classification, and computational-biology analysis, and says dropout-based methods reach state-of-the-art on SVHN, ImageNet, CIFAR-100, and MNIST. The idea is said to extend to RBMs and other graphical models by repeatedly sampling/training smaller sub-models; Dropout RBMs are described as showing desirable properties. A drawback is longer training: about 2–3x slower than standard networks, due to noisy parameter updates and the fact that each case trains a different random architecture. It adds that more training time can allow more dropout and less overfitting. Marginalizing the noise can yield a modified L2 regularizer for linear regression, but an equivalent for more complex models is unclear. The section’s evidence bullets point to Tables 2–8, Section 6.3, qualitative RBM figures, and Section 9.1.

Appendix A gives practical heuristics: increase layer size to about n/p to compensate for dropout; use learning rates 10–100x the standard-network optimum; use momentum around 0.95–0.99 rather than 0.9; consider max-norm regularization with typical c around 3–4; and use hidden-unit retention p around 0.5–0.8 (0.8 for real-valued image patches or speech frames), with p chosen jointly with hidden size because smaller p requires larger n and can slow training or underfit.

Appendix B gives experiment details and implementation: GPU-based code using cudamat and cuda-convnet. MNIST: 60k train/10k test; 10k held out for validation, then train+validation reunited and trained for 1M updates. Figure 4 uses 2-, 3-, and 4-hidden-layer MLPs with 1024 or 2048 units per layer (6 architectures). For these and Table 2 models, hidden layers used p=0.5, input p=0.8, final momentum 0.95, and c=2. Larger 2-layer MNIST nets with 4096 and 8192 units were also tried; 2-layer models improved, deeper ones were slightly worse, and more dropout did not surpass them.

SVHN: about 600k train and 26k test images; validation set of 6000 formed from 400 standard + 200 extra examples per class. Inputs were RGB normalized to zero mean and unit variance; global/local contrast normalization and ZCA whitening gave no noticeable gain. Best model: 3 conv layers with 96/128/256 filters (5x5, stride 1), each followed by 3x3 max-pooling with stride 2, then two 2048-unit ReLU fully connected layers. Dropout retention p=(0.9,0.75,0.75,0.5,0.5,0.5), momentum 0.95, c=4. Test error reported from the best validation model; final training did not add back validation data. Result noted: 2.55% error.

CIFAR-10/100: 50k train/10k test, 5k validation, then validation merged back into training. Preprocessing: global contrast normalization per color channel and ZCA whitening. Architecture and dropout matched SVHN except input-layer learning rates were smaller.

TIMIT starts with Kaldi log-filterbanks, monophone forced alignment labels, 21-frame context to predict the central frame, no speaker-dependent operation, and mean-centered/unit-variance inputs.

The paper studies dropout as a method to prevent overfitting in large neural networks by randomly removing units/connections during training, effectively training many smaller shared-parameter networks and using a single scaled network at test time. It claims dropout improves generalization over non-dropout networks on every tested dataset, with experiments across images, speech, documents, and gene-splicing prediction. The paper says it reports state-of-the-art results on several benchmarks and also examines learned features, sparsity, retention rates, training-set size, RBMs, noise marginalization, and Gaussian corruption. Training is said to take about 2–3 times longer than a standard network of the same architecture.

The paper’s glossary defines the main dropout-related terms and abbreviations used later. Dropout is described as random removal of units and connections during training, with approximate averaging by one unthinned network at test time; thinned networks are subnetworks formed by removing units/connections. It defines core neural-network terms (units, hidden/visible layers, weights, biases, activations), regularizers (L1, L2/Tikhonov, max-norm, KL-sparsity, early stopping), and averaging concepts (model averaging, posterior-weighted averaging, geometric mean, weight scaling, Monte-Carlo averaging). It also names Bernoulli dropout, Gaussian dropout, and dropout-related noise/marginalization ideas. The glossary covers training procedures and settings such as backpropagation, SGD, mini-batches, momentum, learning rate/annealing, hyperparameters, validation, pretraining, finetuning, and CD-1. It also lists architectures and baselines used later: convolutional nets, pooling types, data augmentation, SVM, PCA, linear/ridge/logistic regression, Bayesian neural networks, bag-of-words, sparse representations, RBMs/DBMs/DBNs, dropout RBM, autoencoders, and some later comparison-specific notions like dead units, mix-ability, replica code, and non-stationarity.

This part is the title/front-matter page for the paper “Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting,” listing the five authors and their University of Toronto affiliations. It also gives an original-page map for the rest of the paper: pages 1930–1955 cover the introduction, figures, sections 2–11, table 1–10, acknowledgments, Appendix A (A.1–A.4), and Appendix B (B.1–B.6). No new technical notation or results appear in this part.

This part contains the abstract of the paper. It claims that dropout (referred to here as “QX2, or dropout”) temporarily removes randomly selected units and their connections during training, inhibits co-adaptation, samples exponentially many thinned networks sharing parameters, and that a single unthinned network with reduced weights approximates their averaged predictions. It also claims that dropout substantially reduces overfitting and improves results across vision, speech recognition, document classification, and computational biology, with evidence in Tables 2–8 and the unnumbered text-classification table in §6.3. No new notation or contradictions appear here.

This part is the Introduction. It says QX2/dropout trains many shared-parameter subnetworks and uses a single unthinned test-time network to approximate their combined predictions. It frames the method as approximating an equally weighted geometric mean of exponentially many learned models, with a network of n units corresponding to 2^n possible thinned networks but only O(n^2) or fewer parameters. It introduces standard regularizers/terms: early stopping, soft weight sharing, L1 (O3U), and L2 (Y5F). It also says model combination usually helps but is expensive, and that the practical inference rule T6R/weight scaling uses one unthinned network; X9M/Monte-Carlo model averaging samples members at test time. It claims T6R has lower generalization error than compared regularizers, citing Table 9 rows Y5F 1.62, V9C 1.35, QX2+Y5F 1.25, and QX2+V9C 1.05. It also introduces extension to graphical models via RBMs, with B8T/Dropout RBM. No contradictions found yet.

This part gives the paper’s motivation for dropout/QX2 using biological and game-theoretic analogies. It argues that breaking co-adapted gene sets via sexual reproduction can be advantageous because it favors ‘mix-ability’ and robustness, even if it seems worse for preserving successful combinations. It then maps this to QX2-trained hidden units: because hidden units face randomly selected partners, the method encourages independently useful, robust features rather than reliance on other units. The part also uses a conspiracy analogy to suggest that smaller interacting groups may be more robust under changing conditions than one large, fragile coordinated group. No direct contradictions with earlier sections are introduced here.

This part is the related-work section. It frames QX2 as connected to hidden-unit noise, model averaging, and earlier work on corruption, adversarial deletion, and marginalization. It says denoising autoencoders (S2H) corrupt inputs and reconstruct clean inputs, while QX2 extends this with effective hidden-layer corruption and a model-averaging interpretation. QX2 is claimed to apply to supervised and unsupervised learning and to other neuron-based architectures, including Boltzmann machines. It also contrasts QX2 with adversarial-removal models (Globerson and Roweis 2006; Dekel et al. 2010), which choose deletions under a fixed maximum rather than a probability distribution and are said to have no hidden units. Van der Maaten et al. (2013) are described as studying exponential-family input-noise regularizers, including QX2 under the name blankout noise, limited to models without hidden layers; Chen et al. (2012) studied marginalization for DAEs; Wang and Manning (2013) proposed marginalization to accelerate QX2. The table reports noise levels: S2H typical best 5%, QX2 often optimal input-unit removal 20%, and QX2 often optimal hidden-unit removal 50%.

steps.notes_before: Section 4 defines QX2/dropout-style corruption as independent Bernoulli gating of unit outputs during training: each entry \(r_j^{(l)}\sim Bernoulli(p)\), and \(	ilde y^{(l)} = r^{(l)} * y^{(l)}\). Ordinary feed-forward is \(z_i^{(l+1)}=w_i^{(l+1)} y^{(l)} + b_i^{(l+1)}\), \(y_i^{(l+1)}=f(z_i^{(l+1)})\); QX2 replaces \(y^{(l)}\) with \(	ilde y^{(l)}\). Any activation is allowed, including logistic. Applying the gating at every layer samples a subnetwork; backpropagation runs through that sampled subnetwork. Both hidden and visible units can be removed. At inference, no units are removed and weights are scaled as \(W^{(l)}_{test}=pW^{(l)}\).

Section 5 says QX2 training/backprop is ordinary backprop on a sampled thinned network: each mini-batch case uses its own sampled subnetwork, gradients are averaged, and unused parameters get zero gradient. The section argues that combining QX2 with high momentum, large decaying learning rates, and max-norm/V9C gives additional gains; V9C constrains each hidden unit’s incoming-weight vector to norm <= c, with projection back to the radius-c ball and c tuned on validation. It also offers a qualitative optimization story (weight ball allows large learning rates; QX2 noise explores weight space; decay shortens steps). For finetuning pretrained nets, smaller learning rates are important; too-large rates can erase pretrained information. Before QX2 finetuning, pretrained weights are multiplied by 1/p to preserve expected outputs under random removal. QX2 finetuning can be applied after pretraining from stacked U2L, autoencoders, or E5Q/DBMs. Reported evidence includes table values showing QX2 improving finetuning results (e.g., G6W: 1.18 to 0.92; E5Q: 0.96 to 0.79) and a best QX2 finetuning rate around 0.01 versus a higher listed rate of 0.1.

Learning uses standard RBM/CD methods: sample r for each training case and update only retained hidden units; experiments use CD-1.

With rescaled weights w~ = p w, the equivalent form is ||y-Xw~||^2 + ((1-p)/p)||Gamma w~||^2. The section’s main point is that dropout induces a data-dependent quadratic penalty whose strength grows as retention decreases and vanishes near p=1.

Section 9.2 says approximate marginalization helps logistic regression, citing Wang and Manning (2013) as improving both training time and generalization over Monte Carlo QX2. It also emphasizes that closed-form marginalized models are difficult for logistic regression and deep nets, and that the assumptions used weaken as layers are added, so the results do not directly apply to deep networks.

Noise marginalization can recover some benefits without stochasticity via an expectation-equivalent regularizer; for linear regression this yields modified Y5F, but analogous regularizers for more complex models are not obvious.

Appendix A gives practical heuristics for training QX2 networks while emphasizing they still require substantial hyperparameter tuning. Recommended widths are at least n/p for an n-unit standard-net layer; learning rates are often 10–100× the standard-net optimum, momentum around 0.95–0.99, and max-norm c about 3–4. Retention guidance: hidden units typically 0.5–0.8, real-valued inputs often 0.8, a broadly near-optimal simple default 0.5, and the input optimum is closer to 1 than to 0.5.

Appendix B gives reproduction code and experimental setup details. For H4Z, validation images were held out, hyperparameters were chosen by best validation error at a fixed 1M weight-update endpoint, then validation and training data were combined and rerun to the same endpoint for test evaluation. The H4Z sweep covered 2, 3, and 4 hidden layers with widths 1024 or 2048 (six architectures total). Hidden retention was p=0.5, input retention p=0.8, momentum 0.95, and max-norm c=2. Additional experiments used 2- and 3-layer nets with 4096 and 8192 units; the largest reported two-layer model had >65M parameters. A regularizer-comparison and data-size-comparison both used 784-1024-1024-2048-10; the data-size study used training sets of 100, 500, 1K, 5K, 10K, and 50K. A fixed-width rate comparison used 784-2048-2048-2048-10 with no input corruption. For fixed expected width, pn=256 in the first two hidden layers and pn=512 in the last. The appendix states larger two-layer models improve performance, while three-layer counterparts remain slightly worse even with stronger QX2.

For A2F, the validation set is mixed from standard and additional labeled portions using the Sermanet et al. procedure; the validation split is two-thirds/one-third, with 400 and 200 examples per class, totaling 6000. This is the paper’s summary. It claims dropout randomly removes units/connections during training to train many shared-parameter sub-networks, then uses a single reduced-weight network at test time to approximate the average prediction. It says dropout improves generalization on every tested data set, reports state-of-the-art results on several benchmarks, and studies learned features, sparsity, retention rates, training-set size, Restricted Boltzmann Machines, noise marginalization, and Gaussian corruption. This section is the Introduction. It says dropout/QX2 trains many shared-parameter subnetworks and approximates their combined predictions with one test-time network. The method approximates an equally weighted geometric mean of exponentially many learned models’ predictions. A network with n units represents 2^n possible thinned networks but keeps only O(n^2) or fewer parameters. Weight scaling (T6R) uses one unthinned network at test time; Monte-Carlo model averaging (X9M) averages sampled members and is more expensive. The paper claims T6R has lower generalization error than other regularizers, citing Table 9 rows Y5F 1.62, V9C 1.35, QX2+Y5F 1.25, and QX2+V9C 1.05. The paper map lists sections 2–9 and Appendix A. Earlier notes still hold: n is the network-unit count (or hidden-unit count in width comparisons); 2^n is the number of possible thinned networks; O(n^2) is the shared-parameter count; L is the number of hidden layers; l, i, j are local indices; x;y^(0) is the input; z^(l), y^(l), W^(l), b^(l), f, exp, p, r^(l), tilde y^(l), *, and W_test^(l)=pW^(l) are defined for the dropout model. Additional notation for RBMs, B8T, regression/dropout-noise, decay schedules, feature ordering, C4Y, and the X9M limit notation remains as noted.

Section 2 is the Motivation. It argues that dropout/QX2 reduces harmful co-adaptations by making hidden units learn to work with randomly selected partners, analogous to sexual reproduction favoring gene mix-ability over tightly co-adapted gene sets. It says this encourages independently useful, robust features rather than reliance on other hidden units to fix mistakes, and that units in the same layer still learn different functions. It also uses a conspiracy analogy: smaller conspiracies are likened to simpler co-adaptations that may be more robust under non-stationarity, while larger coordinated systems can work under stable conditions but may generalize worse.

Section 3 reviews related work. It says QX2 connects hidden-unit noise, model averaging, and prior work on corruption, adversarial deletion, and marginalization. Denoising autoencoders (Vincent et al. 2008, 2010) corrupt inputs and reconstruct clean inputs; QX2 extends this with effective hidden-layer corruption and a model-averaging interpretation, and it applies to supervised/unsupervised learning and neuron-based architectures such as Boltzmann machines. A table reports typical best noise levels: S2H 5%, QX2 input-unit removal 20%, QX2 hidden-unit removal 50%, supporting the claim that QX2 can use higher noise than S2H. Globerson & Roweis (2006) and Dekel et al. (2010) consider adversarial removals with a fixed budget, not a probability distribution, and their models have no hidden units. Van der Maaten et al. (2013) studied marginalization for exponential-family input-noise regularizers, including QX2 under the name blankout noise, but only for models without hidden layers. Chen et al. (2012) studied marginalization for denoising autoencoders, and Wang & Manning (2013) proposed marginalization to accelerate QX2.

steps.notes_before: Section 4 defines QX2 as independently masking unit outputs during training with Bernoulli(\(p\)) retention and scaling weights by \(p\) at test time. Hidden layers are indexed \(1,\dots,L\), with standard feed-forward computation \(z_i^{(l+1)}=\mathbf w_i^{(l+1)}\mathbf y^{(l)}+b_i^{(l+1)}\) and \(y_i^{(l+1)}=f(z_i^{(l+1)})\). Under QX2, a mask \(r_j^{(l)}\sim\mathrm{Bernoulli}(p)\) produces thinned activations \(\widetilde{\mathbf y}^{(l)}=\mathbf r^{(l)}*\mathbf y^{(l)}\), which are then fed forward. The operation is applied at every layer to sample a subnetwork; backpropagation occurs through that subnetwork. Both hidden and visible units can be removed. At inference no units are removed and weights are scaled as \(\mathbf W_{\mathrm{test}}^{(l)}=p\mathbf W^{(l)}\). The section also states that the retention probability can be tuned by validation, that the usual default is close to optimal, and that input retention is generally closer to full retention than hidden-unit retention.

Section 5 says QX2 training is ordinary backpropagation on a sampled thinned network: each mini-batch case uses its own subnetwork, gradients are averaged, and unused parameters get zero gradient. Optimization is helped by high momentum, decaying/annealed learning rates, and a max-norm constraint on incoming hidden-unit weight vectors, written as ||w||_2 <= c with projection back onto the radius-c ball; c is tuned on validation. The section claims QX2 plus V9C (max-norm regularization) gives further gains, and presents a weight-space explanation (fixed-radius ball, exploratory noise, then decaying steps). For finetuning pretrained nets, the paper says smaller learning rates are important, and that before QX2 finetuning pretrained weights are multiplied by 1/p so expected outputs match pretraining. QX2 finetuning is said to work after stacked U2L, autoencoders, or DBM pretraining, and then uses backpropagation. Section 7 discusses salient features of QX2: learned features, sparsity, retention, data size, and prediction averaging. 7.1 claims QX2 autoencoders learn localized visual features despite similar reconstruction errors; without QX2, first-layer units look nonmeaningful, while with QX2 they detect edges, strokes, and spots. Figure 7 compares identical single-hidden-layer H4Z/F3N autoencoders with 256 hidden units, using p=0.5 for QX2. The explanation offered is reduced co-adaptation, not a separate quantitative test. 7.2 claims QX2 produces sparse hidden activations without a sparsity regularizer. In the sparsity comparison, mean hidden-unit activation is about/close to 2.0 without QX2 versus about/around 0.7 with QX2; the no-QX2 histogram has a large off-zero mode, while QX2 has a sharp zero peak and few highly active units. Figure 8 uses the F3N autoencoders with p=0.5. 7.3 studies retention: with fixed architecture, low retention underfits and errors fall over an intermediate interval then rise near p=1; the flat-error interval is 0.4<=p<=0.8. When expected retained width pn is held fixed, low-retention errors decrease substantially, from 2.7% to 1.7% at p=0.1; lower-retention inference networks are larger in this setup. The apparently best retention for the chosen expected widths is close to 0.6, with 0.5 close to optimal. 7.4 begins a data-set-size section, stating that the QX2 gain is absent for the smallest sets, grows with more data, then declines.

Section 7.4 (data-set size) says QX2 gives no improvement on the two smallest training sets because the network can memorize them even with removal noise; as data increases, the gain first grows and then shrinks. It frames a “sweet spot” where there is enough data to resist noisy memorization but not so much that overfitting is irrelevant. Figure 10 is H4Z error vs randomly selected training-set size, with curves for With QX2 and Without QX2; Appendix B.1 lists training sizes 100, 500, 1K, 5K, 10K, 50K.

Section 7.5 compares X9M to T6R and says sampled averaging approaches weight scaling. With enough samples, X9M matches T6R and then becomes slightly better, within one standard deviation, so T6R is described as a fairly good approximation to the true model average. The H4Z comparison varies sample count k and uses a horizontal T6R reference. A quantity table says X9M becomes as good as T6R at about k=50; Figure 11 shows X9M and “Approximate averaging by T6R” over k from 0 to 120.

Section 8 introduces B8T, a dropout-style extension of shared-weight RBMs. It defines a retention vector r with Bernoulli(p) entries; conditional on r, hidden units with r_j=0 are forced to 0 while retained units follow the usual RBM conditionals. The visible conditional remains unchanged from U2L/RBM. Learning uses standard Contrastive Divergence: sample r for each training case and train only the retained hidden units; experiments use CD-1.

Section 8.3 says B8T features are coarser and have fewer dead units than ordinary U2L. Figure 12 compares 256-hidden-unit models, with B8T at p=0.5, ordered by L2 norm. Section 8.4 says B8T learns much sparser representations without an extra sparsity regularizer. Figure 13 contrasts histograms of hidden activations, showing many off-zero activations without QX2 and many near-zero / few high activations with p=0.5.

Section 9 discusses marginalizing QX2/dropout noise into deterministic objectives and regularizers. For linear regression, if each input dimension is retained independently with probability p, the expected squared error becomes ||y - pXw||^2 + p(1-p)||Gamma w||^2, where Gamma = (diag(X^T X))^{1/2}. After rescaling weights as w~ = p w, the objective becomes ||y - X w~||^2 + ((1-p)/p)||Gamma w~||^2, so the effective regularization grows as retention decreases. Section 9.2 says approximate marginalization (Wang and Manning 2013) improves logistic regression training time and generalization relative to Monte Carlo QX2. It also states that closed-form marginalized models are difficult for logistic regression and deep nets; under assumptions, Gaussian approximations yield computable means/variances, but the assumptions weaken with depth, so the results do not directly apply to deep networks.

Section 10 introduces multiplicative Gaussian noise as an alternative to Bernoulli dropout. It states that the binary variant is P7V (Bernoulli dropout) and the Gaussian variant is D4K (Gaussian dropout). The two can be matched in first and second moments by choosing the Gaussian multiplier variance to equal the Bernoulli variance under retention p: for the Bernoulli multiplier r_b, E[r_b]=1 and Var[r_b]=(1-p)/p; choosing sigma^2=(1-p)/p for the Gaussian multiplier r_g gives E[r_g]=1 and Var[r_g]=(1-p)/p. The paper says Gaussian noise has higher entropy than Bernoulli for these moments. Table 10 reports preliminary classification errors showing D4K slightly better than P7V on both H4Z (0.95±0.04 vs 1.08±0.04) and J3V (12.5±0.1 vs 12.6±0.1), averaged over 10 random seeds, with the listed layerwise retention settings. The text also says expected activations are unchanged, so no test-time scaling is needed, and it gives two equivalent training/test representations via rescaling weights or activations.

Appendix A gives practical heuristics for training QX2 networks, while emphasizing that extensive hyperparameter tuning is still needed. Recommended heuristics: widen layers to about n/p if a standard net uses n hidden units; use larger learning rates (typically 10–100 times the optimal standard-net rate) and momentum around 0.95–0.99; use max-norm V9C with c around 3–4; and choose retention jointly with width and input type. Hidden-unit retention is typically 0.5–0.8, real-valued inputs often 0.8, and a broadly near-optimal default is 0.5, while input-unit optimum is closer to 1 than to 0.5. Low retention can underfit and slow training.

Appendix B provides reproduction resources and detailed experiment/data settings. Reproduction code is at the dropout website, and GPU implementations use cudamat and cuda-convnet.

B.1 H4Z: validation-selected endpoints were used for architecture, regularizer, rate, and data-size comparisons. 10,000 training images were held out for validation; the final combined-data training run used the same 1-million-update endpoint. Architecture sweep considered 2, 3, and 4 hidden layers with widths 1024 or 2048 (six architectures). Reported QX2 settings used hidden-layer retention p=0.5, input retention p=0.8, momentum 0.95, and V9C bound c=2. Additional regularization-limit experiments used 2- and 3-layer nets with 4096 and 8192 units; the largest two-layer model exceeded 65 million parameters. Regularizer and data-size comparisons used architecture 784-1024-1024-2048-10; data-size runs used training sets of 100, 500, 1K, 5K, 10K, 50K with p=0.5 and input p=0.8. Fixed-width rate comparison used 784-2048-2048-2048-10 with no input corruption. Fixed-expected-width comparison set first two hidden layers to pn=256 and the last to pn=512. The text says larger two-layer nets improve performance, three-layer counterparts are slightly worse, and stronger QX2 improves but does not reverse that gap. X9M samples k thinned networks per test case; as k→∞ it approaches the true model average.

B.2 A2F: validation used a mixed-source split (two-thirds from the standard portion, one-third from the additional portion), totaling 6000 samples. Inputs were RGB pixels normalized to zero mean/unit variance; contrast normalization and ZCA whitening gave no noticeable improvement. Architecture: three conv layers (96, 128, 256 filters, 5×5, stride 1) each followed by 3×3 max-pooling with stride 2, then two 2048-unit fully connected hidden layers. Retentions were p=(0.9, 0.75, 0.75, 0.5, 0.5, 0.5), with c=4 and momentum 0.95.

B.3 J3V/W6R use held-out validation, contrast normalization and ZCA whitening with the A2F architecture. Each collection has 50,000 training and 10,000 test images; validation used 5,000 training images, then validation and training data were combined for final optimization. Preprocessing applies global contrast normalization per image/channel by subtracting the channel mean, then ZCA whitening. Architecture and retention rates match A2F; input-layer learning rates need smaller values.

B.4 N8Q speech data: 680 speakers, eight American-English dialects, ten phonetically rich sentences each, controlled/noise-free. Kaldi generated log-filter-bank features; a monophone system supplied forced alignments and frame labels. Consecutive-frame windows of 21 frames predict the central frame. No speaker-dependent operations. Inputs are mean-centered and scaled to unit variance. Settings: input retention 0.8, hidden retention 0.5, V9C c=4, momentum 0.95, high learning rate 0.1, decay epsilon0(1+t/T)^-1, Gaussian-U2L variance fixed to 1, best QX2 G6W-finetuning rate about 0.01. V9C during G6W finetuning gave no improvement.

B.5 M5X: Reuters subset for single-label document classification. Full corpus >800,000 docs in 103 tree-arranged classes; used subset has 402,738 articles, 2000-word vocabulary, 50 disjoint categories, each document in exactly one category. Equal train/test splits yield >200,000 training examples.

B.6 Z7P: genetics experiment on 3665 cassette exons, 1014 RNA features, four tissue types derived from 27 mouse tissues. Each input has four softmax outputs, one per tissue type, each over states {inc, exc, nc}. C4Y score is a summed log score comparing predicted probabilities to baseline state frequencies. Settings include QX2 hidden-unit scale 1000s, Bayesian-network scale a few tens, trained QX2 network with two 1024-unit layers, hidden retention 0.5, input retention 0.7, V9C with high decaying learning rates, and averaging over 5 folds as in Xiong et al. (2011).

final_notes:
The current part begins with a dataset whose network architecture and dropout rates were the same as SVHN’s, except the input-layer learning rates had to be smaller. TIMIT: Kaldi was used to make log-filter bank features; a monophone system provided forced alignment labels. Dropout NNs used 21-frame windows to predict the central frame, with no speaker-dependent operations. Inputs were mean-centered and unit-variance normalized. Retention probabilities were p=0.8 for input layers and p=0.5 for hidden layers; max-norm c=4 and momentum 0.95 were used, with learning-rate decay ε0(1+t/T)^−1. Reuters RCV1: >800k documents, 103 classes in a hierarchy. The paper used a subset of 402,738 articles, 2000-word vocabulary, and 50 single-label categories; data were split equally into training and test sets. Dropout improved accuracy across architectures, though less dramatically than for image/speech data, likely because the data set is large and overfitting is less severe.

Alternative Splicing: 3665 cassette exons, 1014 RNA features, 4 tissue types from 27 mouse tissues. Each input has four softmax outputs (one per tissue), each with states inc/exc/nc. The evaluation metric is the stated code-quality criterion. A two-layer dropout net with 1024 units per layer used p=0.5 hidden and p=0.7 input retention, max-norm regularization, and high decaying learning rates. Results were averaged over the same 5 folds as Xiong et al. (2011).

Paper: “Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting” (JMLR 2014). Main claim: dropout randomly drops units and their connections during training, causing an exponential number of thinned networks to be sampled; at test time, one can approximate averaging over them with a single unthinned network using smaller weights. Abstract says this reduces overfitting and improves supervised learning performance in vision, speech recognition, document classification, and computational biology, with state-of-the-art results on many benchmarks. Introduction frames dropout as a regularization method for deep nets, alongside early stopping and weight penalties (L1/L2, soft weight sharing). Figure 1 illustrates a standard neural net vs. a thinned net produced by dropout.

The paper motivates dropout as an approximation to Bayesian model averaging / geometric mean over an exponential number of shared-parameter networks, aiming for good performance with less computation. It argues that averaging many separately trained nets is expensive because diverse nets require different architectures or data and are costly to train/test. Dropout drops hidden and visible units (removing incoming/outgoing connections) at random during training; each unit is retained independently with probability p, typically 0.5 for many layers, while input units usually use p closer to 1. Figure 2 states that at test time all units are present and outgoing weights are multiplied by p, so the test-time network matches the expected training-time output.

During training, units are independently retained with probability p; hidden units often use p=0.5, while input units usually use p closer to 1. At test time, all units are present and outgoing weights are multiplied by p so the test-time network matches the expected training-time output. This part adds intuition for dropout via analogies to sexual reproduction and conspiracies: training each hidden unit to work with random subsets of others should make features more robust and less dependent on co-adaptations. It also says the paper will extend dropout to RBMs and discuss experiments, analysis of hyperparameters, marginalizing dropout, and practical guidance in the appendix.

The paper’s intro says dropout extends denoising autoencoders: it can be applied to hidden layers, interpreted as model averaging, and extended beyond unsupervised learning to supervised problems and other neuron-based architectures such as Boltzmann Machines. It also notes that although 5% noise is typical for denoising autoencoders, their weight-scaling-at-test-time approach allows much higher dropout rates; they report 20% input dropout and 50% hidden dropout as often optimal. The paper then motivates deterministic versions by marginalizing the noise, citing prior work on deterministic regularizers and dropout marginalization, and contrasts dropout with adversarial unit-dropping methods.

Model description: for a network with L hidden layers, y^(0)=x, layer l has weights W^(l) and biases b^(l). Standard feedforward uses z^(l+1)=w^(l+1) y^(l)+b^(l+1), y^(l+1)=f(z^(l+1)). With dropout, a Bernoulli mask r^(l) with retention probability p is sampled for each layer, the thinned outputs y~^(l)=r^(l)*y^(l) are passed to the next layer, and this is done at every layer. Training backpropagates through the sampled subnetwork. At test time, dropout is removed and weights are scaled by p: W_test = p W^(l). The next section starts the training procedure for dropout neural nets.

Section 5.1: Dropout nets are trained with SGD by sampling a thinned network per training case; forward/backprop are run only on that thinned network, gradients are averaged over the mini-batch, and units not used contribute zero gradient. Usual SGD improvements (momentum, annealed learning rates, L2 decay) also help. A particularly useful regularizer is max-norm: constrain each hidden unit’s incoming weight vector w to satisfy ||w||2 ≤ c by projecting back onto the ball of radius c; c is tuned on validation. The paper says dropout + max-norm + large decaying learning rates + high momentum works better than dropout alone.

Section 5.2: Dropout can be used to fine-tune pretrained nets (RBMs, autoencoders, DBMs) without changing the pretraining procedure. Weights from pretraining should be scaled up by 1/p so the expected output under dropout matches pretraining. Smaller finetuning learning rates are needed; with them, pretrained information is retained and final generalization improves versus finetuning without dropout.

Section 6 begins experiments: they evaluate dropout on classification tasks across many domains and claim dropout improved generalization on all data sets compared to non-dropout neural nets. Listed data sets: MNIST, TIMIT, CIFAR-10/100, SVHN, ImageNet, Reuters-RCV1, and an Alternative Splicing data set. A detailed description is deferred to Appendix B.

Section 8 introduces Dropout Restricted Boltzmann Machines (RBMs). An RBM with visible units v and hidden units h defines P(h,v;θ) ∝ exp(v^TWh + a^Th + b^Tv). Dropout RBMs add binary masks r over hidden units, with each r_j=1 retained with probability p. The joint distribution is P(r,h,v;p,θ)=P(r;p)P(h,v|r;θ), with a constraint g(h_j,r_j) that forces h_j=0 when r_j=0. Conditioned on r, h is factorial with P(h_j=1|r_j,v)=1(r_j=1)σ(b_j+∑_i W_{ij}v_i), and v conditioned on h has the usual RBM form P(v_i=1|h)=σ(a_i+∑_j W_{ij}h_j). The model can be viewed as a mixture of exponentially many RBMs sharing weights. Training uses standard RBM methods such as CD-1, with a fresh r sampled for each training case in each minibatch. The section begins to discuss feature quality; Figure 12 compares features from a 256-hidden-unit RBM with and without dropout (p=0.5), ordered by L2 norm.

The figure caption says one set of activations is mostly away from zero while the other is mostly near zero, consistent with dropout increasing sparsity. Section 9 introduces marginalizing dropout as a deterministic alternative to Monte-Carlo dropout. For linear regression with input dropout (retain probability p), the expected objective becomes ||y - pXw||^2 + p(1-p)||Γw||^2, equivalent to ridge regression with feature-scaled penalty; rewriting with w̃ = pw makes the regularization constant (1-p)/p explicit. For logistic regression, Wang and Manning’s approximate marginalization uses Gaussian approximations for inputs/gradients and is said to be faster and to generalize better than Monte-Carlo dropout, but the assumptions weaken in deeper networks. A table lists Bernoulli vs Gaussian dropout results: MNIST 1.08 ± 0.04 vs 0.95 ± 0.04, CIFAR-10 12.6 ± 0.1 vs 12.5 ± 0.1.

Section 10 introduces multiplicative Gaussian noise as an alternative to Bernoulli dropout: activations are multiplied by a random variable with mean 1, so no test-time weight scaling is needed. The paper notes that Bernoulli dropout can be viewed as multiplying by a variable with mean 1 and variance (1-p)/p, and Gaussian dropout matches these first two moments by choosing sigma^2=(1-p)/p. It argues the Gaussian version has higher entropy, and says Table 10 suggests it may work slightly better. Table 10 reports Bernoulli vs Gaussian classification error on MNIST and CIFAR-10: 1.08 ± 0.04 vs 0.95 ± 0.04 on MNIST, and 12.6 ± 0.1 vs 12.5 ± 0.1 on CIFAR-10, so Gaussian is slightly better in both cases.

A drawback is increased training time: about 2–3x slower than a standard network, due to noisy parameter updates and the fact that each case trains a different random architecture. The section suggests that marginalizing the noise can recover an equivalent regularizer in expectation, but only linear regression has a worked-out form; for more complex models, this remains open.

Appendix A gives practical heuristics: if a standard layer needs n hidden units and retain probability is p, a dropout net should have at least n/p units. Dropout nets typically need 10–100x the learning rate of standard nets and momentum around 0.95–0.99. Max-norm regularization with c around 3–4 can prevent weights from growing too large. Typical hidden-unit retain probabilities are 0.5–0.8; input layers often use p≈0.8 for real-valued inputs. Smaller p needs larger n and may slow training or underfit; larger p may not regularize enough.

Appendix B gives experimental details. The code is GPU-based using cudamat and cuda-convnet. MNIST: 60k train/10k test, with 10k held out for validation; hyperparameters were tuned so the best validation error occurred after 1M weight updates, then validation was merged back into training and the model was trained for another 1M updates. MNIST architectures in Figure 4 cover all 2-, 3-, and 4-layer nets with 1024 or 2048 units per layer (six architectures total). For these, p=0.5 in hidden layers, p=0.8 in the input layer, momentum 0.95, and max-norm c=2. Larger MNIST nets (4096/8192 units) improved for 2-layer nets; 3-layer nets were slightly worse unless dropout was increased, but still not better than the 2-layer nets.
