errors.claim: “A neural net with n units, can be seen as a collection of 2n possible thinned neural networks.”
errors.evidence: The same paragraph says dropout combines “2n networks with shared weights,” but the paper’s earlier summary in my notes describes dropout as averaging over an “exponential number of shared-parameter networks.”
errors.explanation: If n is the number of units, the number of possible thinned networks is exponential in n, not linear in n. The claim as written conflicts with the paper’s own description of dropout as involving exponentially many subnetworks.

errors.claim: “The weights obtained from pretraining should be scaled up by a factor of 1/(1-p).”
errors.evidence: Earlier notes from the paper define p as the retention probability in dropout, and say that at test time weights are scaled by p.
errors.explanation: If p is the retention probability, then the expected output under dropout is multiplied by p, so matching pretraining would require scaling by 1/p, not 1/(1-p). This conflicts with the earlier definition recorded in the notes.

errors.claim: “As expected, we found that Bayesian neural nets perform better than dropout.”

errors.claim: “P(h_j = 1|r_j, v) = 1(r_j = 1)σ(b_j + \sum_i W_{ij} v_i).”
errors.evidence: Earlier in the same section the RBM is defined as P(h, v; θ) = exp(v^T W h + a^T h + b^T v)/Z(θ), so a is the hidden bias vector and b is the visible bias vector. The conditional for a hidden unit given v should therefore use a_j, not b_j.

final_notes:
Appendix B continues with experimental details. A preceding fragment says another model used the same architecture and dropout rates as SVHN, but with smaller learning rates for the input layer.

TIMIT: data were preprocessed with Kaldi into log-filter banks; a monophone system provided forced alignments/labels. Dropout networks trained on 21-frame windows predicted the center-frame label, with no speaker-dependent operations. Inputs were mean-centered and normalized to unit variance. Reuters: the RCV1 corpus has 800k+ documents in 103 hierarchical classes. The paper used a subset of 402,738 articles, vocabulary size 2000, and 50 categories with exactly one class per document. The data were split into equal-sized training and test sets. Dropout improved classification accuracy across tried architectures, though less than on image/speech data, likely because the dataset is large (200k+ training examples).

Alternative Splicing: dataset has 3665 cassette exons, 1014 RNA features, and 4 tissue types from 27 mouse tissues. Targets are 4 softmax units (one per tissue), each with 3 states (inc, exc, nc). Evaluation is Code Quality, defined by a log-likelihood-style metric comparing predicted vs observed state distributions. A two-layer dropout network with 1024 units per layer was trained with p=0.5 hidden retention and p=0.7 input retention, max-norm regularization, and decaying learning rates. Results were averaged over the same 5 folds used by Xiong et al. (2011).

Paper: “Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting” (JMLR 2014). Main claim: dropout randomly drops units and their connections during training, causing an exponential number of thinned networks to be sampled; at test time, one can approximate averaging over them with a single unthinned network using smaller weights. Abstract says this reduces overfitting and improves supervised learning performance in vision, speech recognition, document classification, and computational biology, with state-of-the-art results on many benchmarks. Introduction frames dropout as a regularization method for deep nets, alongside early stopping and weight penalties (L1/L2, soft weight sharing). Figure 1 illustrates a standard neural net vs. a thinned net produced by dropout.

The paper motivates dropout as an approximation to Bayesian model averaging / geometric mean over an exponential number of shared-parameter networks, aiming for good performance with less computation. It argues that averaging many separately trained nets is expensive because diverse nets require different architectures or data and are costly to train/test. Dropout drops hidden and visible units (removing incoming/outgoing connections) at random during training; each unit is retained independently with probability p, typically 0.5 for many layers, while input units usually use p closer to 1. Figure 2 states that at test time all units are present and outgoing weights are multiplied by p, so the test-time network matches the expected training-time output.

Section 7.5 compares Monte-Carlo model averaging with the test-time weight-scaling approximation on MNIST. As the number of sampled networks k increases, the finite-sample average approaches the true model average; around k = 50 it matches the approximate method, and for larger k it is slightly better but within one standard deviation. Section 8 introduces Dropout Restricted Boltzmann Machines (RBMs). An RBM is defined over visible units v∈{0,1}^D and hidden units h∈{0,1}^F with parameters θ={W,a,b}. Dropout RBMs add binary mask variables r∈{0,1}^F with retention probability p, and if r_j=0 then h_j must be 0. The model can be viewed as a mixture of exponentially many RBMs sharing weights. Learning uses standard RBM methods such as CD-1, with a fresh mask r sampled per training case in each minibatch. The section then begins discussing whether dropout improves RBM features, comparing 256-hidden-unit RBMs with and without dropout (Figure 12).

Section 8.4 evaluates sparsity in RBM hidden activations. Figure 13 compares standard RBMs and dropout RBMs on a test minibatch; dropout RBMs are described as learning coarser features and having much sparser hidden-unit activations than standard RBMs, with very few dead units.

Section 9 introduces marginalizing dropout to obtain deterministic models that do not require random bits and allow gradients of marginalized losses. For linear regression, with Bernoulli input retention probability p, the marginalized objective becomes ||y - pXw||^2 + p(1-p)||Γw||^2, where Γ = (diag(X^T X))^{1/2}. After rescaling w̃ = pw, this is ||y - Xw̃||^2 + ((1-p)/p)||Γw̃||^2, i.e. ridge-like regularization whose strength increases as p decreases.

For logistic regression and deep networks, closed-form marginalization is unavailable. Wang and Manning (2013) approximate the marginalized model by assuming Gaussian distributions for preactivations and gradients; the paper says this improves training time and generalization over Monte-Carlo dropout, but is not directly applicable to deep nets. The table reports Bernoulli vs Gaussian dropout results: MNIST 1.08 ± 0.04 vs 0.95 ± 0.04, CIFAR-10 12.6 ± 0.1 vs 12.5 ± 0.1.

Section 10 introduces multiplicative Gaussian noise as a dropout variant. A unit activation hi can be perturbed as hi + hi r with r ~ N(0,1), equivalently hi r0 with r0 ~ N(1,1), or more generally r0 ~ N(1, σ^2). The expected activation stays the same, so no test-time weight scaling is needed. Standard Bernoulli dropout can be written as multiplying by rb with value 1/p with probability p and 0 otherwise, giving E[rb]=1 and Var[rb]=(1-p)/p. Choosing σ^2=(1-p)/p matches the Bernoulli mean/variance; Gaussian noise has the highest entropy among such distributions, Bernoulli the lowest. The text says both work well, with Gaussian perhaps slightly better. Table 10 compares Bernoulli vs Gaussian dropout on MNIST and CIFAR-10, averaged over 10 random seeds; Bernoulli uses p=0.5 hidden and 0.8 input for MNIST, and p=(0.9, 0.75, 0.75, 0.5, 0.5, 0.5) for CIFAR-10. Section 11 begins the conclusion and restates dropout as a regularizer against co-adaptation.

Section 11 concludes that dropout is a general technique: it improved performance across many domains and methods using dropout achieved state-of-the-art results on SVHN, ImageNet, CIFAR-100, and MNIST. It also says dropout can be extended to RBMs and other graphical models; the paper developed Dropout RBMs with desirable properties. A drawback is training time: dropout networks typically take 2-3 times longer than standard nets because updates are noisy and each case trains a different random architecture. The authors frame this as a trade-off between overfitting and training time, and note that marginalizing the noise can yield an equivalent regularizer; for linear regression this becomes a modified L2 regularizer.

Appendix A gives practical heuristics: because retaining probability p leaves pn units in expectation, a dropout net should often have at least n/p hidden units if a standard net needs n. Dropout training often benefits from learning rates 10-100x larger than standard, momentum around 0.95-0.99, and max-norm regularization with c about 3-4. Typical retention probabilities are 0.5-0.8 for hidden units and about 0.8 for real-valued inputs.

Appendix B gives experimental details. MNIST: 60k train/10k test, with 10k held out for validation; hyperparameters were tuned so best validation error occurred after 1M weight updates, then validation was merged back into training and the net was trained for another 1M updates. MNIST architectures included 2-, 3-, and 4-layer nets with 1024 or 2048 units per layer (6 total); all used hidden-layer retention p=0.5, input p=0.8, momentum 0.95, and max-norm c=2. Larger 4096/8192-unit nets were also tried; 3-layer nets were slightly worse than 2-layer nets, though higher dropout helped somewhat.

SVHN: about 600k train and 26k test images; validation set of 6000 samples drawn from both the standard and extra labeled sets (400/class from standard, 200/class from extra). Best model used 3 conv layers with 96, 128, 256 filters, each 5x5 stride 1, each followed by 3x3 max-pooling stride 2, then two 2048-unit fully connected layers; all ReLU. Dropout retention probabilities were (0.9, 0.75, 0.75, 0.5, 0.5, 0.5) from input through conv/FC layers; max-norm c=4, momentum 0.95. Because training data were large, validation was not merged back into training; final test error used the lowest-validation model.

CIFAR-10/100: 50k train/10k test each, with 5000 training images used for validation; then validation was merged back into training for final training. Preprocessing was global contrast normalization per color channel followed by ZCA whitening.

Authors: Nitish Srivastava, Geoffrey Hinton, Alex Krizhevsky, Ilya Sutskever, and Ruslan Salakhutdinov (University of Toronto); editor Yoshua Bengio. The paper map on the first pages lays out the structure across sections 2–11 plus appendices A and B. Abstract/intro claims: dropout randomly removes units and their connections during training, reducing co-adaptation and implicitly sampling exponentially many thinned networks; a single unthinned network with reduced weights approximates the averaged predictions. It claims dropout reduces overfitting and improves results across vision, speech recognition, document classification, and computational biology, often state of the art. Section 1 also says posterior-weighted averaging is the best regularization given unlimited computation, while dropout approximates an equally weighted geometric mean over exponentially many shared-parameter models. A network with n units corresponds to 2^n thinned networks and reuses O(n^2) or fewer parameters. The introduction contrasts dropout with stopping early, soft weight sharing, and L1/L2 penalties, and says model combination is powerful but expensive. It introduces the practical inference rule (weight scaling) versus Monte Carlo model averaging, and notes dropout extends to graphical models such as Boltzmann machines, including Restricted Boltzmann Machines and dropout RBMs. Figure 1 shows a standard two-hidden-layer net and a thinned version with crossed units removed.

Section 2 motivates dropout using analogies from evolution and robustness. It contrasts sexual vs asexual reproduction: recombination breaks co-adapted gene sets, suggesting a tension between individual-fitness optimization and the value of mixable, robust genes. The Livnat et al. view is that selection may favor gene sets that work with many partners; the paper maps this to hidden units trained with dropout, which must be useful with randomly selected partners and thus learn independently useful, robust features rather than depend on other units. It also uses a conspiracy analogy: smaller conspiracies are more robust to changing conditions than a larger one needing many correct participants. These examples support the claim that complex co-adaptations can fit training data yet generalize poorly, whereas simpler robust components may generalize better.

Section 3 surveys related work on noise-based regularization. It frames hidden-unit noise as a regularizer for QX2, connecting it to denoising autoencoders (Vincent et al. 2008, 2010): input corruption plus reconstruction, effective hidden-layer corruption, model averaging, supervised and unsupervised use, and applicability to other neuron-based architectures such as Boltzmann machines. A comparison table says typical best noise is 5% for S2H, while QX2 often works best at 20% input-unit removal or 50% hidden-unit removal. It contrasts stochastic noise training with adversarial removal methods (Globerson and Roweis 2006; Dekel et al. 2010), noting those have no hidden units. It also says analytically marginalizing QX2 yields deterministic regularizers in simple cases; related exponential-family input-noise regularizers (“blankout noise”) were studied by van der Maaten et al. (2013) for models without hidden layers. Chen et al. (2012) examined marginalization for denoising autoencoders, and Wang and Manning (2013) proposed marginalization to accelerate QX2.

steps.notes_before: Section 4 defines QX2 as stochastic deletion (“dropout”) applied to every layer: each layer output vector is multiplied elementwise by an independent Bernoulli mask with retention probability \(p\). Training samples a subnetwork and backpropagates through it; both hidden and visible units can be removed. At test time, no units are removed and the outgoing weights are scaled by \(p\): \(\mathbf W^{(l)}_{	ext{test}}=p\mathbf W^{(l)}\). The section states that validation can choose \(p\), but the default is usually near optimal and input retention is often closer to 1. It also claims that the expected output under deletion matches test-time output, though the formulas only directly show this for the preactivation, not necessarily after a nonlinear activation.

errors.claim: “Before QX2 finetuning, pretrained weights are multiplied by 1/(1-p), matching each unit’s expected random-removal output to its pretraining output.”
errors.evidence: Earlier notes from Section 4 define \(p\) as the retention probability for dropout, and say that at test time the outgoing weights are scaled by \(p\): “\(\mathbf W^{(l)}_{test}=p\mathbf W^{(l)}\).” With retention probability \(p\), the expected output after random removal is \(p\) times the original, so matching that expectation to the pretraining output would require scaling by \(1/p\), not \(1/(1-p)\).
errors.explanation: This scaling factor is inconsistent with the paper’s own definition of \(p\) as retention probability. The stated factor \(1/(1-p)\) would correspond to using the dropout probability instead.

steps.notes_before: Section 5 says QX2 training uses SGD on a per-case thinned network: each mini-batch case samples its own subnet, gradients are averaged, and unused parameters get zero gradient. Momentum, annealed learning rates, and Y5F remain useful. It also introduces V9C max-norm regularization: incoming hidden-unit weight vectors are constrained by \(\|\mathbf w\|_2\le c\), with projection back to the radius-\(c\) ball when exceeded. The section claims QX2 plus high momentum, large decaying learning rates, and V9C gives further gains, and that the max-norm constraint can help even without QX2. In the unsupervised-pretraining subsection, it says smaller finetuning learning rates preserve pretrained information better than no-QX2 finetuning, and that pretraining is otherwise unchanged. However, it states pretrained weights are multiplied by \(1/(1-p)\) before QX2 finetuning, which conflicts with the earlier definition of \(p\) as dropout retention probability and the test-time scaling rule \(\mathbf W_{test}=p\mathbf W\); this would suggest a factor of \(1/p\), not \(1/(1-p)\).

Section 11: Conclusion. The large-model construction repeatedly samples and trains smaller submodels from an easily overfitted model; U2L fits this construction, and B8T exhibits desirable empirical properties. QX2 methods achieve state of the art on A2F, K9D, W6R, and H4Z, with improvement over standard neural nets on other collections. Training is typically 2–3 times slower than standard networks, partly because each case trains a different random architecture and gradients are not those of the final inference architecture. Noise marginalization gives some benefits without stochasticity via an expectation-equivalent regularizer; the linear-regression case is explicit, but extensions to more complex models are not obvious.

Appendix B.4 continues with speech/DBN details: input retention p=0.8, hidden retention p=0.5, max-norm c=4, momentum 0.95, and a high learning rate of 0.1. The learning-rate decay is ε0(1+t/T)^−1. DBN pretraining used CD-1, with Gaussian RBM input-unit variance fixed at 1. For dropout finetuning, the best learning rate was about 0.01, and adding max-norm constraints gave no improvement. Reported speech performance appears in Table 7, with dropout rows 21.8%, 19.7%, and 19.7%.

B.5 Reuters: RCV1 has more than 800,000 documents in 103 tree-structured classes. The paper uses a 402,738-article subset with a 2000-word vocabulary and 50 categories; each document has exactly one class, and the subset is split equally into train and test. Dropout improved all tried architectures, but less than on image/speech tasks. The best-network comparison is 31.05% without dropout vs 29.62% with dropout. The suggested reason is the large training set (>200,000 training cases).

B.6 Alternative Splicing: 3665 cassette exons, 1014 RNA features, 4 tissue types from 27 mouse tissues. Targets have 4 softmax units, one per tissue type, each with states inc/exc/nc. Code Quality is defined by the given triple sum over data points, tissue types, and states. The model is a two-layer dropout network with 1024 units per layer, p=0.5 hidden retention and p=0.7 input retention, max-norm regularization, and decaying learning rates. Results were averaged over the same 5 folds used by Xiong et al. (2011).

Abstract claims dropout randomly removes units during training, samples an exponential number of thinned networks, and uses one unthinned network with smaller weights at test time to approximate their average predictions. It says dropout reduces overfitting and improves supervised-learning performance on vision, speech recognition, document classification, and computational-biology tasks, with state-of-the-art results on many benchmarks. It also says dropout outperforms other regularization methods.

Introduction claims deep nets overfit limited data and reviews standard regularization (early stopping, L1/L2, soft weight sharing). The paper’s goal is to approximate Bayesian model averaging / an equally weighted geometric mean of predictions from exponentially many parameter-sharing models at low cost. Dropout randomly removes hidden or visible units during training; in the simplest case each unit is retained independently with probability p (often p=0.5 for hidden units, closer to 1 for inputs). A thinned network is sampled for each training case. At test time, dropout is turned off and outgoing weights are multiplied by p so expected training-time output matches test-time output. A network with n units represents 2^n thinned networks with shared weights, making explicit averaging infeasible. The paper claims dropout reduces generalization error and also applies to RBMs. Section roadmap: 2 motivation, 3 related work, 4 model, 5 training, 6 experiments, 7 network properties/hyperparameters, 8 Dropout RBMs, 9 marginalizing dropout, Appendix A practical guidance.

Prior notes still hold: the paper frames dropout as approximate Bayesian model averaging / equally weighted geometric mean over exponentially many thinned networks; each unit is kept independently with probability p during training, and at test time weights are multiplied by p. The paper’s goal is to reduce generalization error at low cost; it also extends dropout to RBMs. 

This part begins Section 2 (Motivation) and uses two analogies to explain why dropout should help: (1) sexual reproduction/mix-ability—useful genes must work with random partners, so hidden units trained with dropout should become robust and not rely on specific co-adaptations; and (2) conspiracies—smaller groups are more likely to keep working under changing conditions than one large tightly coordinated group. The section’s conclusion is that complex co-adaptations may fit training data but are more likely to fail on test data than several simpler co-adaptations.

Section 4 defines standard feed-forward computation and dropout masks. Each layer’s inputs/outputs are denoted z^(l) and y^(l), with y^(0)=x. Under dropout, each layer output is multiplied elementwise by an independent Bernoulli(p) mask r^(l) before being fed to the next layer, producing a sampled sub-network. Training backpropagates through the sampled sub-network. At test time, the weights are scaled as W_test^(l)=p W^(l) and the network is used without dropout.

Section 5 covers dropout training. In backprop, each mini-batch case samples a thinned network; forward and backward passes use only that sampled network, gradients are averaged across the batch, and unused parameters contribute zero gradient. SGD refinements such as momentum, annealed learning rates, and L2 decay help. Max-norm regularization is especially useful: incoming weight vectors are constrained by ||w||2 <= c and projected back if they exceed c. The paper claims dropout + max-norm improves MNIST over dropout + L2 (Table 9: 1.05% vs 1.25%) and max-norm alone beats L2 (1.35% vs 1.62%).

For unsupervised pretraining, networks may start from RBMs, autoencoders, or DBMs, then be finetuned with dropout. The text says pretrained weights should be rescaled before dropout finetuning (but this scaling statement conflicts with the earlier keep-probability notation for p). Small finetuning learning rates preserve pretrained information better than larger ones. Dropout finetuning is reported to improve pretrained MNIST models (Table 2: DBN 1.18% vs 0.92%; DBM 0.96% vs 0.79%).

Section 6 presents experimental results across multiple domains and claims dropout improves generalization on every listed data set. Table 1 summarizes the data sets: MNIST, SVHN, CIFAR-10/100, ImageNet, TIMIT, Reuters-RCV1, and Alternative Splicing, with their dimensionalities and train/test sizes. The section emphasizes broad applicability of dropout.

In the image-data subsection, the paper studies MNIST, SVHN, CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and ImageNet, claiming state-of-the-art results on these with dropout-based models. For MNIST (Table 2), the key results are: standard NN 1.60%, dropout NN 1.35% (logistic), dropout NN 1.25% (ReLU), dropout + max-norm 1.06% to 0.95% depending on size, maxout 0.94%, DBN finetuning 1.18%, DBM finetuning 0.96%, DBN + dropout finetuning 0.92%, and DBM + dropout finetuning 0.79%. The text summarizes that dropout improves from 1.60% to 1.35%, ReLU to 1.25%, and max-norm to 1.06%.

Section 6.1.1 ends by reiterating that larger dropout networks perform better: a 2-hidden-layer network with 8192 units each reaches 0.95% test error, with more than 65 million parameters and 60,000 training cases. Goodfellow et al. (2013) gets 0.94% using maxout units. All dropout networks use p=0.5 for hidden units and p=0.8 for input units. DBM-pretrained dropout networks reach 0.79%, the best reported performance for the permutation-invariant setting. Figure 4 compares test-error trajectories for networks with 2–4 hidden layers and 1024–2048 units, showing dropout helps across fixed-hyperparameter architectures.

Section 6.1.2 (SVHN) studies 32x32 centered digit images with a Conv Net architecture of three convolutional layers plus two fully connected hidden layers, all ReLU units, each conv layer followed by max-pooling. Table 3 reports: Binary Features 36.7, HOG 15.0, Stacked Sparse Autoencoders 10.3, KMeans 9.4, multi-stage Conv Net average pooling 9.06, L2 pooling 5.36, L4 pooling + padding 4.90, Conv Net + max-pooling 3.95, max-pooling + dropout in fully connected layers 3.02, stochastic pooling 2.80, max-pooling + dropout in all layers 2.55, maxout 2.47, human performance 2.0. Section 7 studies learned features, sparsity, and how dropout depends on model/data choices. 7.1 compares 256-unit one-hidden-layer MNIST autoencoders with and without hidden dropout (p=0.5). The authors argue dropout reduces co-adaptation: without dropout the learned features look less meaningful, while with dropout they resemble edges, strokes, and spots. Both models have similar test reconstruction error. 7.2 examines sparsity using the same autoencoders: dropout yields fewer highly active units, a sharp peak at zero in the activation histogram, and lower mean activations (about 2.0 without dropout vs about 0.7 with dropout). 7.3 studies varying dropout rate on MNIST with a 784-2048-2048-2048-10 network. With hidden size fixed, error is high at small p (underfitting), then flattens for roughly 0.4<=p<=0.8, and rises as p approaches 1. A second setting keeps expected retained unit count pn fixed, so smaller p requires larger networks.

Section 7.3’s second dropout-rate experiment keeps expected retained unit counts fixed: pn=256 for the first two hidden layers and pn=512 for the last. This reduces the low-p error seen with fixed architecture; at p=0.1, error improves from 2.7% to 1.7% (Figure 9b vs. 9a). In this fixed-retained-size setting, p around 0.6 is best, and the usual default p=0.5 is close to optimal.

7.4 varies MNIST training-set size using architecture 784-1024-1024-2048-10 with p=0.5 in hidden layers and p=0.8 at the input. Dropout gives no improvement for 100 and 500 training cases, but its benefit grows with data size and then declines, suggesting a “sweet spot” of data/model/dropout settings.

7.5 compares Monte-Carlo model averaging with test-time weight scaling. Weight scaling is the efficient approximation; averaging k sampled dropout networks approaches it as k increases. On MNIST, around k=50 samples matches weight scaling, and beyond that Monte-Carlo averaging is slightly better but within one standard deviation.

Section 8 defines Dropout RBMs. An RBM has visible v∈{0,1}^D and hidden h∈{0,1}^F with P(h,v;θ)∝exp(v^TWh+a^Th+b^Tv). Dropout introduces a binary mask r∈{0,1}^F with independent retention probability p, giving P(r,h,v)=P(r;p)P(h,v|r;θ). The conditional enforces h_j=0 whenever r_j=0 via g(h_j,r_j)=1(r_j=1)+1(r_j=0)1(h_j=0). Given r, the model is an RBM with the dropped hidden units removed; thus dropout RBM is a mixture of exponentially many shared-weight RBMs. Learning is done by sampling a new mask each mini-batch and then applying standard RBM/CD-1 training to the retained units.

On MNIST with 256 hidden units, Figure 12 qualitatively shows dropout features (p=0.5) are coarser and have fewer dead units than standard RBM features. Figure 13 shows dropout yields much sparser hidden activations than standard RBM, even without explicit sparsity regularization.

Section 9 discusses deterministic models obtained by marginalizing dropout noise. It cites related prior work on robust feature deletion, denoising autoencoders, and dropout marginalization/regularization. For linear regression, with Bernoulli(p) masking of input dimensions, the expected objective becomes ||y - pXw||^2 + p(1-p)||Γw||^2, where Γ = diag(X^T X)^(1/2). After rescaling w̃ = pw, this is ||y - Xw̃||^2 + ((1-p)/p)||Γw̃||^2, so the regularization strength increases as p decreases. For logistic regression and deep networks, closed-form marginalization is difficult; Wang and Manning (2013) provide an approximate marginalized logistic-regression method using Gaussian means/variances, which the paper says is faster and better than Monte-Carlo dropout for logistic regression, but not directly applicable to deep networks because the assumptions weaken with depth.

Section 10 generalizes dropout to multiplicative Gaussian noise. A unit activation h_i is multiplied either by r~N(1,1), equivalently h_i + h_i r' with r'~N(0,1), or more generally r'~N(1,σ^2), where σ is a tunable hyperparameter. Because the expected activation is unchanged, no test-time weight scaling is needed. The section also describes the standard rescaled Bernoulli form where retained activations are multiplied by 1/p during training and test weights are left unchanged; under that form the Bernoulli multiplier has mean 1 and variance (1-p)/p. Choosing σ^2=(1-p)/p makes the Gaussian and Bernoulli multipliers match in first two moments. Table 10 reports preliminary classification errors showing Gaussian dropout slightly better than Bernoulli dropout on MNIST (0.95±0.04 vs 1.08±0.04) and CIFAR-10 (12.5±0.1 vs 12.6±0.1), averaged over 10 random seeds. MNIST uses p=0.5 for hidden units and p=0.8 for input units; CIFAR-10 uses p=(0.9, 0.75, 0.75, 0.5, 0.5, 0.5) from input to top.

Section 11 concludes that dropout reduces overfitting by breaking brittle co-adaptations. It claims dropout improves performance across object classification, digit recognition, speech recognition, document classification, and computational biology, and that methods using dropout reach state-of-the-art results on SVHN, ImageNet, CIFAR-100, and MNIST. The section also summarizes the RBM extension: the principle is to train large models by repeatedly sampling smaller sub-models, and RBMs fit this framework; the paper says its Dropout RBMs show desirable qualitative properties. A drawback is training time: dropout typically takes 2-3 times longer than a standard network, mainly because gradients are noisy and correspond to random sub-networks rather than the final test architecture. The section notes that marginalizing noise can yield regularization benefits, with linear regression giving an equivalent modified L2 penalty, while more complex models lack an obvious equivalent regularizer. The final bullet list points to evidence tables/figures for the application results, RBM sparsity/feature changes, the longer training claim, and the linear-regression regularization result.

Section 11 concludes dropout reduces overfitting by breaking brittle co-adaptations and claims improvements across object classification, digit recognition, speech recognition, document classification, and computational biology. It says dropout-based methods reach state-of-the-art on SVHN, ImageNet, CIFAR-100, and MNIST. It also summarizes the RBM extension: large models can be trained by repeatedly sampling smaller sub-models, and RBMs fit this framework; the paper reports Dropout RBMs show desirable qualitative properties. A drawback is training time: dropout typically takes 2-3 times longer than a standard network because gradients are noisy and correspond to random sub-networks rather than the final test architecture. The section notes that marginalizing noise can yield regularization benefits; for linear regression this is equivalent to a modified L2 penalty, but more complex models lack an obvious equivalent regularizer. The final bullet list points to evidence tables/figures for application results, RBM sparsity/feature changes, the longer-training claim, and the linear-regression regularization result. Appendix A then gives practical heuristics: use larger layers because a dropout layer with n units and retention p has pn active units in expectation, so a good size is at least n/p; dropout networks may need 10-100x the standard-network learning rate and momentum around 0.95-0.99; max-norm regularization with c about 3-4 helps control weight growth; typical hidden-unit retention is 0.5-0.8, with 0.8 common for real-valued image patches or speech frames.

Appendix B gives experimental details. MNIST: 60k train/10k test, with 10k held out for validation; hyperparameters were chosen so best validation error occurred after 1M updates, then training+validation were reunited and trained for 1M more updates. Figure 4 covers 6 architectures: 2/3/4 hidden layers with 1024 or 2048 units each; hidden layers used p=0.5, input p=0.8, momentum 0.95, max-norm c=2. Larger 2-layer MNIST models (4096, 8192 units) improved results; 3-layer versions were slightly worse and more dropout did not beat the 2-layer models. SVHN: ~600k train and 26k test images; validation set of 6000 made from 400/class standard + 200/class extra. Inputs are RGB normalized to zero mean/unit variance; contrast normalization/ZCA gave no noticeable improvement. Best SVHN architecture: 3 conv layers (96,128,256 filters), each with 5x5 receptive fields and 3x3 pooling with stride 2, followed by two 2048-unit fully connected layers, all ReLU. Retention probabilities across layers are (0.9,0.75,0.75,0.5,0.5,0.5), with max-norm c=4 and momentum 0.95; final model chosen by validation error, no retraining on combined data. CIFAR-10/100: 50k train/10k test, 5k validation, global contrast normalization per color channel and ZCA whitening; architecture and dropout rates match SVHN except smaller input-layer learning rates. TIMIT begins: Kaldi used to create log-filter banks, monophone forced alignment gives frame labels, inputs are 21-frame windows predicting the central frame, no speaker-dependent operation.

The paper studies dropout as a method to prevent overfitting in large neural networks by randomly removing units/connections during training, effectively training many smaller shared-parameter networks and using a single scaled network at test time. It claims dropout improves generalization over non-dropout networks on every tested dataset, with experiments across images, speech, documents, and gene-splicing prediction. The paper says it reports state-of-the-art results on several benchmarks and also examines learned features, sparsity, retention rates, training-set size, RBMs, noise marginalization, and Gaussian corruption. Training is said to take about 2–3 times longer than a standard network of the same architecture.

The paper’s glossary defines the main dropout-related terms and abbreviations used later. Dropout is described as random removal of units and connections during training, with approximate averaging by one unthinned network at test time; thinned networks are subnetworks formed by removing units/connections. It defines core neural-network terms (units, hidden/visible layers, weights, biases, activations), regularizers (L1, L2/Tikhonov, max-norm, KL-sparsity, early stopping), and averaging concepts (model averaging, posterior-weighted averaging, geometric mean, weight scaling, Monte-Carlo averaging). It also names Bernoulli dropout, Gaussian dropout, and dropout-related noise/marginalization ideas. The glossary covers training procedures and settings such as backpropagation, SGD, mini-batches, momentum, learning rate/annealing, hyperparameters, validation, pretraining, finetuning, and CD-1. The paper’s glossary now adds the main notation used in the dropout sections. Network notation: n is unit count / hidden width, 2^n possible thinned networks, O(n^2) shared-parameter count, L hidden layers, l layer index, i/j local indices, x;y^(0) input, z^(l) preactivations, y^(l) outputs, W^(l), b^(l), and activation f. Dropout notation: p is retention probability, r^(l) are Bernoulli retention vectors, ~tilde y^(l) are thinned outputs, * is elementwise product, W_test^(l)=pW^(l), and pn / n/p are expected retained width and the practical width heuristic. k is the number of independently sampled networks used for X9M, with k→∞ approximating the true model average. RBM/B8T notation: v/h are visible/hidden vectors, θ={W,a,b}, P is a model or conditional distribution, Z(θ) and Z'(θ,r) are normalizers, g(h_j,r_j) enforces h_j=0 when r_j=0, and σ is the activation in RBM conditionals. Regression/noise notation: X, y, R, Γ=(diag(X^TX))^(1/2), ~tilde w=pw, and the marginalized regression penalty coefficient is (1-p)/p; Gaussian noise/multipliers use r,r′ with N(0,1), N(1,1), or N(1,σ^2). N8Q decay schedule uses ε0(1+t/T)^−1. C4Y notation: s,t,i are state/tissue/input indices, p^s_{i,t} target probabilities, q^s_t(r_i) predictions, and the score is based on log probabilities averaged over data points.

This part is the title/front-matter page for the paper “Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting,” listing the five authors and their University of Toronto affiliations. It also gives an original-page map for the rest of the paper: pages 1930–1955 cover the introduction, figures, sections 2–11, table 1–10, acknowledgments, Appendix A (A.1–A.4), and Appendix B (B.1–B.6). No new technical notation or results appear in this part.

This part contains the abstract of the paper. It claims that dropout (referred to here as “QX2, or dropout”) temporarily removes randomly selected units and their connections during training, inhibits co-adaptation, samples exponentially many thinned networks sharing parameters, and that a single unthinned network with reduced weights approximates their averaged predictions. It also claims that dropout substantially reduces overfitting and improves results across vision, speech recognition, document classification, and computational biology, with evidence in Tables 2–8 and the unnumbered text-classification table in §6.3. No new notation or contradictions appear here.

This part is the Introduction. It says QX2/dropout trains many shared-parameter subnetworks and uses a single unthinned test-time network to approximate their combined predictions. It frames the method as approximating an equally weighted geometric mean of exponentially many learned models, with a network of n units corresponding to 2^n possible thinned networks but only O(n^2) or fewer parameters. It introduces standard regularizers/terms: early stopping, soft weight sharing, L1 (O3U), and L2 (Y5F). It also says model combination usually helps but is expensive, and that the practical inference rule T6R/weight scaling uses one unthinned network; X9M/Monte-Carlo model averaging samples members at test time. It claims T6R has lower generalization error than compared regularizers, citing Table 9 rows Y5F 1.62, V9C 1.35, QX2+Y5F 1.25, and QX2+V9C 1.05. It also introduces extension to graphical models via RBMs, with B8T/Dropout RBM. No contradictions found yet.

This part gives the paper’s motivation for dropout/QX2 using biological and game-theoretic analogies. It argues that breaking co-adapted gene sets via sexual reproduction can be advantageous because it favors ‘mix-ability’ and robustness, even if it seems worse for preserving successful combinations. It then maps this to QX2-trained hidden units: because hidden units face randomly selected partners, the method encourages independently useful, robust features rather than reliance on other units. The part also uses a conspiracy analogy to suggest that smaller interacting groups may be more robust under changing conditions than one large, fragile coordinated group. No direct contradictions with earlier sections are introduced here.

This part is the related-work section. It frames QX2 as connected to hidden-unit noise, model averaging, and earlier work on corruption, adversarial deletion, and marginalization. It says denoising autoencoders (S2H) corrupt inputs and reconstruct clean inputs, while QX2 extends this with effective hidden-layer corruption and a model-averaging interpretation. QX2 is claimed to apply to supervised and unsupervised learning and to other neuron-based architectures, including Boltzmann machines. It also contrasts QX2 with adversarial-removal models (Globerson and Roweis 2006; Dekel et al. 2010), which choose deletions under a fixed maximum rather than a probability distribution and are said to have no hidden units. Van der Maaten et al. (2013) are described as studying exponential-family input-noise regularizers, including QX2 under the name blankout noise, limited to models without hidden layers; Chen et al. (2012) studied marginalization for DAEs; Wang and Manning (2013) proposed marginalization to accelerate QX2. The table reports noise levels: S2H typical best 5%, QX2 often optimal input-unit removal 20%, and QX2 often optimal hidden-unit removal 50%.

final_notes:
CIFAR-10/100 subsection continues from prior text: images are rotated back after augmentation; the network architecture and dropout rates are the same as for SVHN, except the input-layer learning rates had to be smaller. 

TIMIT: Kaldi was used to preprocess into log-filterbanks; a monophone system provided forced alignments and frame labels. Networks used 21-frame windows to predict the central frame, with no speaker-dependent operations. Inputs were mean-centered and unit-variance normalized. Dropout used retention p=0.8 on inputs and p=0.5 on hidden layers, with max-norm c=4, momentum 0.95, and learning rate 0.1 decayed as ε0(1+t/T)^{-1}. For DBN pretraining, RBMs were trained with CD-1 and Gaussian-RBM input variance fixed to 1. Finetuning with dropout worked best with a smaller learning rate (~0.01); max-norm constraints did not improve results.

Reuters: RCV1 has >800k documents and 103 classes; they built a subset of 402,738 articles, 2000-word vocabulary, and 50 categories with exactly one class per document. The data was split equally into train and test sets; dropout improved accuracy across architectures, though less dramatically than on image/speech data.

Alternative Splicing: dataset has 3665 cassette exons, 1014 RNA features, and 4 tissue types from 27 mouse tissues. Targets are 4 softmax units (one per tissue type), each with 3 states (inc, exc, nc). The metric called Code Quality compares predicted and target distributions relative to class priors. A two-layer dropout net with 1024 units per layer used p=0.7 on input, p=0.5 hidden, max-norm regularization, and decaying learning rates; results were averaged over the same 5 folds as Xiong et al. (2011).

Paper: “Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting” (JMLR 2014). Main claim: dropout randomly drops units and their connections during training, causing an exponential number of thinned networks to be sampled; at test time, one can approximate averaging over them with a single unthinned network using smaller weights. Abstract says this reduces overfitting and improves supervised learning performance in vision, speech recognition, document classification, and computational biology, with state-of-the-art results on many benchmarks. Introduction frames dropout as a regularization method for deep nets, alongside early stopping and weight penalties (L1/L2, soft weight sharing). Figure 1 illustrates a standard neural net vs. a thinned net produced by dropout.

The paper motivates dropout as an approximation to Bayesian model averaging / geometric mean over an exponential number of shared-parameter networks, aiming for good performance with less computation. It argues that averaging many separately trained nets is expensive because diverse nets require different architectures or data and are costly to train/test. Dropout drops hidden and visible units (removing incoming/outgoing connections) at random during training; each unit is retained independently with probability p, typically 0.5 for many layers, while input units usually use p closer to 1. Figure 2 states that at test time all units are present and outgoing weights are multiplied by p, so the test-time network matches the expected training-time output.

At test time, all units are present and outgoing weights are multiplied by p so the test-time network matches the expected training-time output. This part adds that dropout can be viewed as sampling a thinned network for each training case, with heavy weight sharing, and that the paper will also extend dropout to RBMs and discuss experiments, analysis of hyperparameters, marginalizing dropout, and practical guidance in the appendix.

Dropout is presented as approximating Bayesian model averaging / geometric mean over an exponential number of shared-parameter subnetworks, reducing computation versus training many separate networks. During training, units are independently retained with probability p; hidden units often use p=0.5, while input units usually use p closer to 1. At test time, all units are present and outgoing weights are multiplied by p so the test-time network matches the expected training-time output. This part adds intuition for dropout via analogies to sexual reproduction and conspiracies: training each hidden unit to work with random subsets of others should make features more robust and less dependent on co-adaptations. It also says the paper will extend dropout to RBMs and discuss experiments, analysis of hyperparameters, marginalizing dropout, and practical guidance in the appendix.

The paper’s intro says dropout extends denoising autoencoders: it can be applied to hidden layers, interpreted as model averaging, and extended beyond unsupervised learning to supervised problems and other neuron-based architectures such as Boltzmann Machines. It also notes that although 5% noise is typical for denoising autoencoders, their weight-scaling-at-test-time approach allows much higher dropout rates; they report 20% input dropout and 50% hidden dropout as often optimal. The paper then motivates deterministic versions by marginalizing the noise, citing prior work on deterministic regularizers and dropout marginalization, and contrasts dropout with adversarial unit-dropping methods.

Model description: for a network with L hidden layers, y^(0)=x, layer l has weights W^(l) and biases b^(l). Standard feedforward uses z^(l+1)=w^(l+1) y^(l)+b^(l+1), y^(l+1)=f(z^(l+1)). With dropout, a Bernoulli mask r^(l) with retention probability p is sampled for each layer, the thinned outputs y~^(l)=r^(l)*y^(l) are passed to the next layer, and this is done at every layer. Training backpropagates through the sampled subnetwork. At test time, dropout is removed and weights are scaled by p: W_test = p W^(l). The next section starts the training procedure for dropout neural nets.

Section 5.1: Dropout nets are trained with SGD by sampling a thinned network per training case; forward/backprop are run only on that thinned network, gradients are averaged over the mini-batch, and units not used contribute zero gradient. Usual SGD improvements (momentum, annealed learning rates, L2 decay) also help. A particularly useful regularizer is max-norm: constrain each hidden unit’s incoming weight vector w to satisfy ||w||2 ≤ c by projecting back onto the ball of radius c; c is tuned on validation. The paper says dropout + max-norm + large decaying learning rates + high momentum works better than dropout alone.

Section 5.2: Dropout can be used to fine-tune pretrained nets (RBMs, autoencoders, DBMs) without changing the pretraining procedure. Weights from pretraining should be scaled up by 1/p so the expected output under dropout matches pretraining. Smaller finetuning learning rates are needed; with them, pretrained information is retained and final generalization improves versus finetuning without dropout.

Section 6 begins experiments: they evaluate dropout on classification tasks across many domains and claim dropout improved generalization on all data sets compared to non-dropout neural nets. Listed data sets: MNIST, TIMIT, CIFAR-10/100, SVHN, ImageNet, Reuters-RCV1, and an Alternative Splicing data set. A detailed description is deferred to Appendix B.

Section 7.3 compares two ways of varying dropout on MNIST. In the first, the architecture is fixed at 784-2048-2048-2048-10 and p is the retention probability; small p causes underfitting and high training/test error, error decreases as p increases, is fairly flat for 0.4 ≤ p ≤ 0.8, then rises as p approaches 1. Section 7.4 studies data-set size on MNIST with architecture 784-1024-1024-2048-10, dropout p=0.5 in hidden layers and p=0.8 at input. Dropout does not help much for very small sets (100, 500), but its benefit increases with data size up to a point and then declines, suggesting a “sweet spot” for dataset size.

Section 7.5 (Monte-Carlo model averaging) says that sampling k dropout networks and averaging predictions approaches the true model average as k grows; empirically on MNIST, around k=50 the Monte-Carlo method matches the approximate weight-scaling method, and for larger k it is slightly better but within one standard deviation. Section 8 introduces Dropout RBMs: binary visible units v∈{0,1}^D and hidden units h∈{0,1}^F with standard RBM energy. Dropout adds binary mask variables r∈{0,1}^F with retention probability p, independently per hidden unit; if r_j=0 then h_j must be 0. Conditioned on r, the model is an RBM using only the retained hidden units, so the dropout RBM is a mixture of exponentially many RBMs with shared weights. Learning can use standard RBM training such as CD-1, sampling a fresh r for each training case in each minibatch. Section 8.3 begins an empirical comparison of features learned by ordinary vs dropout RBMs with 256 hidden units on MNIST.

Paper: "Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting" (JMLR 15, 2014, pp. 1929–1958). Authors: Nitish Srivastava, Geoffrey Hinton, Alex Krizhevsky, Ilya Sutskever, and Ruslan Salakhutdinov (University of Toronto); editor Yoshua Bengio. The paper map on the first pages lays out the structure across sections 2–11 plus appendices A and B. Abstract/intro claims: dropout randomly removes units and their connections during training, reducing co-adaptation and implicitly sampling exponentially many thinned networks; a single unthinned network with reduced weights approximates the averaged predictions. It claims dropout reduces overfitting and improves results across vision, speech recognition, document classification, and computational biology, often state of the art. Section 1 also says posterior-weighted averaging is the best regularization given unlimited computation, while dropout approximates an equally weighted geometric mean over exponentially many shared-parameter models. A network with n units corresponds to 2^n thinned networks and reuses O(n^2) or fewer parameters. The introduction contrasts dropout with stopping early, soft weight sharing, and L1/L2 penalties, and says model combination is powerful but expensive. It introduces the practical inference rule (weight scaling) versus Monte Carlo model averaging, and notes dropout extends to graphical models such as Boltzmann machines, including Restricted Boltzmann Machines and dropout RBMs. Figure 1 shows a standard two-hidden-layer net and a thinned version with crossed units removed.

Section 2 motivates dropout using analogies from evolution and robustness. It contrasts sexual vs asexual reproduction: recombination breaks co-adapted gene sets, suggesting a tension between individual-fitness optimization and the value of mixable, robust genes. The Livnat et al. view is that selection may favor gene sets that work with many partners; the paper maps this to hidden units trained with dropout, which must be useful with randomly selected partners and thus learn independently useful, robust features rather than depend on other units. It also uses a conspiracy analogy: smaller conspiracies are more robust to changing conditions than a larger one needing many correct participants. These examples support the claim that complex co-adaptations can fit training data yet generalize poorly, whereas simpler robust components may generalize better.

Section 3 surveys related work on noise-based regularization. It frames hidden-unit noise as a regularizer for QX2, connecting it to denoising autoencoders (Vincent et al. 2008, 2010): input corruption plus reconstruction, effective hidden-layer corruption, model averaging, supervised and unsupervised use, and applicability to other neuron-based architectures such as Boltzmann machines. A comparison table says typical best noise is 5% for S2H, while QX2 often works best at 20% input-unit removal or 50% hidden-unit removal. It contrasts stochastic noise training with adversarial removal methods (Globerson and Roweis 2006; Dekel et al. 2010), noting those have no hidden units. It also says analytically marginalizing QX2 yields deterministic regularizers in simple cases; related exponential-family input-noise regularizers (“blankout noise”) were studied by van der Maaten et al. (2013) for models without hidden layers. Chen et al. (2012) examined marginalization for denoising autoencoders, and Wang and Manning (2013) proposed marginalization to accelerate QX2.

It also claims that the expected output under deletion matches test-time output, though the formulas only directly show this for the preactivation, not necessarily after a nonlinear activation.

Section 5 says QX2 training uses standard SGD on a per-case sampled thinned network: each case is forwarded/backpropagated through its own sampled subnetwork, gradients are averaged, and absent parameters contribute zero. It highlights that QX2 works well with high momentum, large decaying learning rates, and V9C max-norm regularization, where each incoming hidden-unit weight vector is constrained by ||w||_2 <= c and projected back onto the radius-c ball if it exceeds it. The section also notes that this constraint is a validation-tuned hyperparameter and can help deep-net training even without QX2. For unsupervised pretraining, the procedure is unchanged, but before QX2 finetuning pretrained weights are multiplied by 1/p so that expected random-removal output matches the pretrained output. Abstract claims dropout randomly removes units during training, samples an exponential number of thinned networks, and uses one unthinned network with smaller weights at test time to approximate their average predictions. It says dropout reduces overfitting and improves supervised-learning performance on vision, speech recognition, document classification, and computational-biology tasks, with state-of-the-art results on many benchmarks. It also says dropout outperforms other regularization methods.

Introduction claims deep nets overfit limited data and reviews standard regularization (early stopping, L1/L2, soft weight sharing). The paper’s goal is to approximate Bayesian model averaging / an equally weighted geometric mean of predictions from exponentially many parameter-sharing models at low cost. Dropout randomly removes hidden or visible units during training; in the simplest case each unit is retained independently with probability p (often p=0.5 for hidden units, closer to 1 for inputs). A thinned network is sampled for each training case. At test time, dropout is turned off and outgoing weights are multiplied by p so expected training-time output matches test-time output. A network with n units represents 2^n thinned networks with shared weights, making explicit averaging infeasible. The paper claims dropout reduces generalization error and also applies to RBMs. Section roadmap: 2 motivation, 3 related work, 4 model, 5 training, 6 experiments, 7 network properties/hyperparameters, 8 Dropout RBMs, 9 marginalizing dropout, Appendix A practical guidance.

Section 5 covers learning dropout nets. Training uses SGD on a sampled thinned network per mini-batch case; gradients are averaged and inactive parameters contribute zero gradient. Helpful SGD tricks include momentum, learning-rate decay, and L2 weight decay. Max-norm regularization constrains each hidden unit’s incoming weight vector to norm <= c and is especially useful with dropout; the paper claims dropout + max-norm beats dropout + L2 (Table 9: 1.05% vs 1.25%), and max-norm alone beats L2 (1.35% vs 1.62%).

For unsupervised pretraining, the paper says pretrained weights should be multiplied by 1/p before dropout finetuning so expected outputs match pretraining. Dropout finetuning is said to preserve pretrained information only with smaller learning rates; with larger finetuning rates it can erase pretrained information. The section claims improved pretrained MNIST results using dropout finetuning, citing Table 2 DBN and DBM rows with error pairs 1.18% vs 0.92% and 0.96% vs 0.79%.

Section 6 reports experimental results across multiple domains and claims dropout improves generalization on every data set versus networks without dropout. Section 7 on salient features: dropout is argued to improve generalization by reducing co-adaptation and increasing sparsity. Figure 7 compares 256-unit MNIST autoencoders with and without dropout (p=0.5): both have similar test reconstruction error, but the no-dropout features look less meaningful, while dropout yields edge/stroke-like features. Figure 8 shows that dropout makes activations sparser: the no-dropout model has mean activations around 2.0 and substantial activation mass away from zero, while the dropout model has mean activations around 0.7 and a sharp peak at zero. Section 7.3 varies retention probability p on MNIST using a 784-2048-2048-2048-10 network without input dropout. With hidden size fixed, small p underfits, error decreases as p rises, is fairly flat for p≈0.4 to 0.8, and increases again near p=1. The second setting keeps expected retained units pn fixed, so smaller p requires larger networks; test networks then differ in size even though expected retained count is held constant.

Section 7.3 continues the retention-probability study. In the fixed-expected-size setting, the first two hidden layers use pn=256 and the last uses pn=512. Figure 9b has much lower errors at low p than Figure 9a; at p=0.1, error drops from 2.7% to 1.7%. For these retained sizes, p≈0.6 is best, and the usual default p=0.5 is close to optimal. 

Section 7.4 varies MNIST training-set size using architecture 784-1024-1024-2048-10 with p=0.5 in hidden layers and p=0.8 at the input. Training-set sizes are 100, 500, 1K, 5K, 10K, and 50K. Dropout gives no improvement at 100 and 500 cases; its gain then increases with data size and later declines, suggesting a sweet spot.

Section 7.5 compares Monte-Carlo model averaging with weight scaling at test time. Weight scaling is the efficient approximation; averaging k sampled dropout networks converges to the true model average. Around k=50, Monte-Carlo averaging matches weight scaling, and with larger k it is slightly better but within one standard deviation.

Section 8 defines Dropout RBMs: an RBM with a binary mask r over hidden units, where each r_j=1 with probability p. Conditioned on r, the model is an RBM with the dropped hidden units removed, so a Dropout RBM is a mixture of exponentially many weight-sharing RBMs. Training samples a fresh mask for each mini-batch and uses CD-1. On MNIST with 256 hidden units and p=0.5, dropout RBM features look coarser and have fewer dead units than standard RBM features, and their hidden activations are sparser even without an added sparsity regularizer.

Section 9 introduces marginalizing dropout noise to obtain deterministic models with no random bits, and cites related prior work (feature deletion, denoising autoencoders, linear regression, input-noise regularization, adaptive regularization). Section 9.1 derives marginalized dropout for linear regression: with input masking R~Bernoulli(p), the expected loss becomes ||y-pXw||^2 + p(1-p)||Γw||^2, where Γ = diag(X^T X)^{1/2}. This is equivalent in expectation to ridge regression with feature-specific penalties; after reparameterizing ~w = pw, the regularization constant is (1-p)/p and increases as p decreases. Section 9.2 says closed-form marginalization is hard for logistic regression and deep networks; Wang and Manning (2013) provide an approximate marginalized logistic-regression method with efficient mean/variance computations, better training time and generalization than Monte-Carlo dropout, but the assumptions weaken with depth so the result does not directly extend to deep networks.

Section 10 generalizes dropout to multiplicative Gaussian noise. Hidden activations can be multiplied by r' ~ N(1,σ^2), equivalently h_i + h_i r with r ~ N(0,1) when σ=1. More generally σ is a tunable hyperparameter, and because the expected activation is unchanged, no test-time weight scaling is needed. The section also restates the standard Bernoulli-dropout scaling trick: either drop units with probability 1-p and scale weights by p at test time, or equivalently multiply retained activations by 1/p during training and leave test weights unchanged (with suitable learning-rate/init scaling). Under this second form, the Bernoulli multiplier has mean 1 and variance (1-p)/p; Gaussian dropout matches these moments by setting σ^2=(1-p)/p, i.e. σ=sqrt((1-p)/p). The paper notes Gaussian has the highest entropy among distributions with those moments, Bernoulli the lowest. Table 10 reports slightly better Gaussian results: MNIST 0.95±0.04 vs Bernoulli 1.08±0.04, and CIFAR-10 12.5±0.1 vs 12.6±0.1, averaged over 10 random seeds. For MNIST Bernoulli p values are 0.5 for hidden units and 0.8 for inputs; for CIFAR-10 p=(0.9,0.75,0.75,0.5,0.5,0.5) from input to top.

Section 11 concludes that dropout reduces overfitting by breaking co-adaptations, improves several application domains, and is claimed to achieve state-of-the-art on SVHN, ImageNet, CIFAR-100, and MNIST. It extends to RBMs/graphical models by training sampled sub-models. A drawback is training time: dropout typically takes 2–3× longer than standard training because each case trains a different random architecture, so gradients are noisy. The section also notes that marginalizing the noise can yield regularization; for linear regression this gives a modified L2 penalty.

Appendix A gives practical heuristics: use at least n/p units in a dropout layer if n units are optimal without dropout; use learning rates about 10–100× the standard optimum; momentum around 0.95–0.99; max-norm c typically 3–4; hidden-unit retention p typically 0.5–0.8, with input retention around 0.8 for real-valued image patches or speech frames.

Appendix B gives detailed experiment and data-set settings. MNIST: 60k train/10k test; 10k of the training set were held out for validation, then combined back for final 1M-update training. Figure 4 covers all 2-, 3-, and 4-hidden-layer networks with 1024 or 2048 units; hidden-layer retention p=0.5, input p=0.8, momentum 0.95, max-norm c=2. Larger 2-layer networks (4096, 8192) improved results; 3-layer versions were slightly worse and more dropout did not surpass 2-layer nets. SVHN: about 600k train and 26k test images; validation set of 6000 made from 400 standard + 200 extra examples per class. Preprocessing used normalized RGB pixels; contrast normalization and ZCA whitening did not help. Best model: 3 conv layers (96, 128, 256 filters, 5x5, stride 1), each with max-pooling (3x3, stride 2), followed by two 2048-unit ReLU layers; dropout p=(0.9,0.75,0.75,0.5,0.5,0.5), max-norm c=4, momentum 0.95, and no retraining on validation set. CIFAR-10/100: 50k train/10k test, 5k validation; global contrast normalization and ZCA whitening; architecture/dropout matched SVHN except smaller input-layer learning rates. TIMIT begins by using Kaldi to extract log-filter banks from 21-frame windows with central-frame labels and no speaker-dependent operation.

grade.reason: The reviewer flagged an inconsistency about dropout finetuning and DBN/DBM error rates, which does not identify the planted false claim about ReLU vs maxout MNIST error.

errors.claim: “For every hidden unit, expected output under training-time deletion equals actual test-time output under the prescribed reduced weights.”
errors.evidence: The same section says “Any activation is admissible, including the logistic function” and defines \(y_i^{(l+1)}=f(z_i^{(l+1)})\) after the random gating step.
errors.explanation: With arbitrary nonlinear activations allowed, the section’s blanket equality between the stochastic training-time output and the deterministic test-time output is not supported by the equations as stated. The later allowance of nonlinear \(f\) conflicts with an exact equivalence claim.

errors.claim: “L8J, or maxout, worsens results (Goodfellow et al., 2013).”
errors.evidence: The same table reports “QX2 NN + V9C (Goodfellow et al., 2013) | L8J | 2 layers, (5 × 240) units | 0.94,” which is better than the preceding non-maxout QX2 NN + V9C F3N result of 0.95 and the other non-finetuned results in the table.

errors.claim: “QX2 nevertheless substantially improves standard neural nets and exceeds every other method.”
errors.evidence: Earlier in the same subsection it says, “On the small Z7P data set, QX2 beats the non-Bayesian comparisons but remains below Bayesian neural networks,” and Table 8 lists Bayesian Neural Network at 623 versus Neural Network with QX2 at 567.

errors.claim:
The ordinary U2L defines
\(P(\mathbf h,\mathbf v;\theta)=\frac{1}{Z(\theta)}\exp(\mathbf v^\top\mathbf W\mathbf h+\mathbf a^\top\mathbf h+\mathbf b^\top\mathbf v)\).
errors.evidence: A few lines later the paper says \(P(h_j=1\mid r_j,\mathbf v)=\mathbf1(r_j=1)\,\sigma\!\left(b_j+\sum_iW_{ij}v_i\right)\), and \(P(v_i=1\mid\mathbf h)=\sigma\!\left(a_i+\sum_jW_{ij}h_j\right)\).
errors.explanation: The joint distribution assigns \(\mathbf a\) to hidden units and \(\mathbf b\) to visible units, but the conditional equations use \(b_j\) as the hidden bias and \(a_i\) as the visible bias. Those roles conflict within the same section.

B.3 J3V and W6R: held-out validation; 50,000 training and 10,000 test images each; J3V has 10 classes, W6R 100. Validation used 5,000 training images. After hyperparameter selection, training and validation data were combined for final optimization. They use the A2F architecture plus contrast normalization and ZCA whitening. Preprocessing: global contrast normalization per image/channel subtracts that channel’s mean pixel intensity; ZCA whitening mean-centers, rotates to PCs, normalizes each component, then rotates back. Input learning rates need to be smaller.

B.4 N8Q: 680 speakers, eight American-English dialects, each reading 10 phonetically rich sentences. Kaldi produced log-filter-bank features. A monophone system supplied forced alignments and frame labels; 21 consecutive frames predict the central frame’s label. No speaker-dependent operations. Inputs are mean-centered and unit-variance scaled. Settings: input retention 0.8, hidden retention 0.5, V9C c=4, momentum 0.95, high lr 0.1, decay eps0(1+t/T)^-1, Gaussian-U2L variance fixed to 1, best G6W finetuning lr about 0.01. V9C during finetuning gave no improvement.

B.5 M5X: Reuters subset with 402,738 articles, 2000-word vocabulary, 50 disjoint categories; each doc has exactly one category. Equal-sized train/test splits give more than 200,000 training examples.

B.6 Z7P: 3665 cassette exons, 1014 RNA features, four tissue types derived from 27 mouse tissues. Each input has four target softmax units, one per tissue type; each softmax has states {inc, exc, nc}. Score C4Y sums over data points, tissue types, and states: p log(q/pbar), with p target probs, q predicted probs, and pbar the average of p over i,t. Settings: QX2 hidden scale in the 1000s, Bayesian-network hidden scale in the tens, trained QX2 has two 1024-unit layers, hidden retention 0.5, input retention 0.7, V9C with high decaying learning rates, and results averaged over the same 5 folds as Xiong et al. (2011). Table 8 reports Z7P results: QX2 567 bits, early-stopped neural net 440, Bayesian neural net 623.

The paper studies dropout as a method to prevent overfitting in large neural networks by randomly removing units/connections during training, effectively training many smaller shared-parameter networks and using a single scaled network at test time. It claims dropout improves generalization over non-dropout networks on every tested dataset, with experiments across images, speech, documents, and gene-splicing prediction. The paper says it reports state-of-the-art results on several benchmarks and also examines learned features, sparsity, retention rates, training-set size, RBMs, noise marginalization, and Gaussian corruption. Training is said to take about 2–3 times longer than a standard network of the same architecture.

The paper’s glossary defines the main dropout-related terms and abbreviations used later. Dropout is described as random removal of units and connections during training, with approximate averaging by one unthinned network at test time; thinned networks are subnetworks formed by removing units/connections. It defines core neural-network terms (units, hidden/visible layers, weights, biases, activations), regularizers (L1, L2/Tikhonov, max-norm, KL-sparsity, early stopping), and averaging concepts (model averaging, posterior-weighted averaging, geometric mean, weight scaling, Monte-Carlo averaging). It also names Bernoulli dropout, Gaussian dropout, and dropout-related noise/marginalization ideas. The glossary covers training procedures and settings such as backpropagation, SGD, mini-batches, momentum, learning rate/annealing, hyperparameters, validation, pretraining, finetuning, and CD-1. It also lists architectures and baselines used later: convolutional nets, pooling types, data augmentation, SVM, PCA, linear/ridge/logistic regression, Bayesian neural networks, bag-of-words, sparse representations, RBMs/DBMs/DBNs, dropout RBM, autoencoders, and some later comparison-specific notions like dead units, mix-ability, replica code, and non-stationarity.

It also defines evaluation terms such as phone error rate, top-1 error, top-5 error, validation/test labels, and a C4Y code-quality score based on negative KL divergence. The glossary includes many baselines and features used in comparisons: WDCH, HOG, KMeans, SIFT variants, LBP, GIST, Fisher Vectors, Sparse Coding, RGB, global/local contrast normalization, ZCA whitening, log-filter banks, monophone system, forced alignment, and Kaldi. It also lists implementation/support terms (GPU, CUDA, cudamat, cuda-convnet, OGS, NSERC, Early Researcher Award) and table abbreviations such as NA, K, M, dim, conv, Avg, NN, %, and bits.

The paper’s glossary now adds the main notation used in the dropout sections. Network notation: n is unit count / hidden width, 2^n possible thinned networks, O(n^2) shared-parameter count, L hidden layers, l layer index, i/j local indices, x;y^(0) input, z^(l) preactivations, y^(l) outputs, W^(l), b^(l), and activation f. Dropout notation: p is retention probability, r^(l) are Bernoulli retention vectors, ~tilde y^(l) are thinned outputs, * is elementwise product, W_test^(l)=pW^(l), and pn / n/p are expected retained width and the practical width heuristic. k is the number of independently sampled networks used for X9M, with k→∞ approximating the true model average. RBM/B8T notation: v/h are visible/hidden vectors, θ={W,a,b}, P is a model or conditional distribution, Z(θ) and Z'(θ,r) are normalizers, g(h_j,r_j) enforces h_j=0 when r_j=0, and σ is the activation in RBM conditionals. Regression/noise notation: X, y, R, Γ=(diag(X^TX))^(1/2), ~tilde w=pw, and the marginalized regression penalty coefficient is (1-p)/p; Gaussian noise/multipliers use r,r′ with N(0,1), N(1,1), or N(1,σ^2). N8Q decay schedule uses ε0(1+t/T)^−1. C4Y notation: s,t,i are state/tissue/input indices, p^s_{i,t} target probabilities, q^s_t(r_i) predictions, and the score is based on log probabilities averaged over data points.

This part is the title/front-matter page for the paper “Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting,” listing the five authors and their University of Toronto affiliations. It also gives an original-page map for the rest of the paper: pages 1930–1955 cover the introduction, figures, sections 2–11, table 1–10, acknowledgments, Appendix A (A.1–A.4), and Appendix B (B.1–B.6). No new technical notation or results appear in this part.

This part contains the abstract of the paper. It claims that dropout (referred to here as “QX2, or dropout”) temporarily removes randomly selected units and their connections during training, inhibits co-adaptation, samples exponentially many thinned networks sharing parameters, and that a single unthinned network with reduced weights approximates their averaged predictions. It also claims that dropout substantially reduces overfitting and improves results across vision, speech recognition, document classification, and computational biology, with evidence in Tables 2–8 and the unnumbered text-classification table in §6.3. No new notation or contradictions appear here.

This part is the Introduction. It says QX2/dropout trains many shared-parameter subnetworks and uses a single unthinned test-time network to approximate their combined predictions. It frames the method as approximating an equally weighted geometric mean of exponentially many learned models, with a network of n units corresponding to 2^n possible thinned networks but only O(n^2) or fewer parameters. It introduces standard regularizers/terms: early stopping, soft weight sharing, L1 (O3U), and L2 (Y5F). It also says model combination usually helps but is expensive, and that the practical inference rule T6R/weight scaling uses one unthinned network; X9M/Monte-Carlo model averaging samples members at test time. It claims T6R has lower generalization error than compared regularizers, citing Table 9 rows Y5F 1.62, V9C 1.35, QX2+Y5F 1.25, and QX2+V9C 1.05. It also introduces extension to graphical models via RBMs, with B8T/Dropout RBM. No contradictions found yet.

This part gives the paper’s motivation for dropout/QX2 using biological and game-theoretic analogies. It argues that breaking co-adapted gene sets via sexual reproduction can be advantageous because it favors ‘mix-ability’ and robustness, even if it seems worse for preserving successful combinations. It then maps this to QX2-trained hidden units: because hidden units face randomly selected partners, the method encourages independently useful, robust features rather than reliance on other units. The part also uses a conspiracy analogy to suggest that smaller interacting groups may be more robust under changing conditions than one large, fragile coordinated group. No direct contradictions with earlier sections are introduced here.

This part is the related-work section. It frames QX2 as connected to hidden-unit noise, model averaging, and earlier work on corruption, adversarial deletion, and marginalization. It says denoising autoencoders (S2H) corrupt inputs and reconstruct clean inputs, while QX2 extends this with effective hidden-layer corruption and a model-averaging interpretation. QX2 is claimed to apply to supervised and unsupervised learning and to other neuron-based architectures, including Boltzmann machines. It also contrasts QX2 with adversarial-removal models (Globerson and Roweis 2006; Dekel et al. 2010), which choose deletions under a fixed maximum rather than a probability distribution and are said to have no hidden units. Van der Maaten et al. (2013) are described as studying exponential-family input-noise regularizers, including QX2 under the name blankout noise, limited to models without hidden layers; Chen et al. (2012) studied marginalization for DAEs; Wang and Manning (2013) proposed marginalization to accelerate QX2. The table reports noise levels: S2H typical best 5%, QX2 often optimal input-unit removal 20%, and QX2 often optimal hidden-unit removal 50%.

Appendix A gives practical heuristics: QX2 layers should be wider, with a good hidden-layer width at least n/p for an n-unit standard layer, because only pn units survive in expectation; this is said to help for both convolutional and fully connected layers. Recommended learning rates are typically 10–100 times the optimal standard-net rate, with momentum around 0.95–0.99 rather than the common 0.9. Max-norm bound c is typically 3–4. Retention should be chosen jointly with width and input type: hidden-unit retention is typically 0.5–0.8, real-valued inputs often use 0.8, a broadly near-optimal default is 0.5, and the input-unit optimum is closer to 1 than to 0.5. Low retention can underfit, while high retention may not remove enough units to prevent overfitting.

Appendix B gives reproduction resources and experiment settings. H4Z uses validation-selected endpoints and then retrains on combined validation+training data to the same 1M-update endpoint, with no early stopping needed. H4Z settings: 10,000 held-out validation images; architecture sweep over 2, 3, 4 hidden layers with widths 1024 and 2048 (six architectures); hidden retention p=0.5, input retention p=0.8; momentum 0.95; max-norm c=2; extra regularization-limit runs with 2 or 3 layers and 4096/8192 units. Appendix B continues with dataset-specific training details. One preceding section says the network architecture and dropout rates were the same as SVHN, except the input-layer learning rates had to be smaller.

TIMIT: Kaldi was used to preprocess speech into log-filterbanks; a monophone system produced forced alignments and frame labels. Networks were trained on 21-frame windows to predict the central frame. Inputs were mean-centered and normalized to unit variance. Dropout retention was p=0.8 on the input layer and p=0.5 on hidden layers; max-norm c=4 and momentum 0.95 were used. Learning rate started at 0.1 and decayed as ε0(1+t/T)^−1. Reuters: RCV1 has 800,000+ docs and 103 classes. They used a subset of 402,738 articles, 2000-word vocabulary, 50 categories, single-label classification, split equally into train/test. Dropout improved accuracy for all tried architectures, but less dramatically than on image/speech tasks.

Alternative Splicing: dataset has 3665 cassette exons, 1014 RNA features, and 4 tissue types from 27 mouse tissues. Each input predicts four softmax units, one per tissue type, each over 3 states (inc, exc, nc). Evaluation is a Code Quality metric based on predicted vs observed state distributions. They trained a two-layer dropout net with 1024 units per layer, p=0.7 input and p=0.5 hidden, with max-norm and high decaying learning rates, averaged over the same 5 folds as Xiong et al. (2011).
