Paper: “Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting” (JMLR 2014). Main claim: dropout randomly drops units and their connections during training, causing an exponential number of thinned networks to be sampled; at test time, one can approximate averaging over them with a single unthinned network using smaller weights. Abstract says this reduces overfitting and improves supervised learning performance in vision, speech recognition, document classification, and computational biology, with state-of-the-art results on many benchmarks. Introduction frames dropout as a regularization method for deep nets, alongside early stopping and weight penalties (L1/L2, soft weight sharing). Figure 1 illustrates a standard neural net vs. a thinned net produced by dropout.

The paper motivates dropout as an approximation to Bayesian model averaging / geometric mean over an exponential number of shared-parameter networks, aiming for good performance with less computation. It argues that averaging many separately trained nets is expensive because diverse nets require different architectures or data and are costly to train/test. Dropout drops hidden and visible units (removing incoming/outgoing connections) at random during training; each unit is retained independently with probability p, typically 0.5 for many layers, while input units usually use p closer to 1. Figure 2 states that at test time all units are present and outgoing weights are multiplied by p, so the test-time network matches the expected training-time output.

Dropout is presented as approximating Bayesian model averaging / geometric mean over an exponential number of shared-parameter subnetworks, reducing computation versus training many separate networks. During training, units are independently retained with probability p; hidden units often use p=0.5, while input units usually use p closer to 1. At test time, all units are present and outgoing weights are multiplied by p so the test-time network matches the expected training-time output. This part adds intuition for dropout via analogies to sexual reproduction and conspiracies: training each hidden unit to work with random subsets of others should make features more robust and less dependent on co-adaptations. It also says the paper will extend dropout to RBMs and discuss experiments, analysis of hyperparameters, marginalizing dropout, and practical guidance in the appendix.

The paper’s intro says dropout extends denoising autoencoders: it can be applied to hidden layers, interpreted as model averaging, and extended beyond unsupervised learning to supervised problems and other neuron-based architectures such as Boltzmann Machines. It also notes that although 5% noise is typical for denoising autoencoders, their weight-scaling-at-test-time approach allows much higher dropout rates; they report 20% input dropout and 50% hidden dropout as often optimal. The paper then motivates deterministic versions by marginalizing the noise, citing prior work on deterministic regularizers and dropout marginalization, and contrasts dropout with adversarial unit-dropping methods.

Model description: for a network with L hidden layers, y^(0)=x, layer l has weights W^(l) and biases b^(l). Standard feedforward uses z^(l+1)=w^(l+1) y^(l)+b^(l+1), y^(l+1)=f(z^(l+1)). With dropout, a Bernoulli mask r^(l) with retention probability p is sampled for each layer, the thinned outputs y~^(l)=r^(l)*y^(l) are passed to the next layer, and this is done at every layer. Training backpropagates through the sampled subnetwork. At test time, dropout is removed and weights are scaled by p: W_test = p W^(l). The next section starts the training procedure for dropout neural nets.

Section 5.1: Dropout nets are trained with SGD by sampling a thinned network per training case; forward/backprop are run only on that thinned network, gradients are averaged over the mini-batch, and units not used contribute zero gradient. Usual SGD improvements (momentum, annealed learning rates, L2 decay) also help. A particularly useful regularizer is max-norm: constrain each hidden unit’s incoming weight vector w to satisfy ||w||2 ≤ c by projecting back onto the ball of radius c; c is tuned on validation. The paper says dropout + max-norm + large decaying learning rates + high momentum works better than dropout alone.

Section 5.2: Dropout can be used to fine-tune pretrained nets (RBMs, autoencoders, DBMs) without changing the pretraining procedure. Weights from pretraining should be scaled up by 1/p so the expected output under dropout matches pretraining. Smaller finetuning learning rates are needed; with them, pretrained information is retained and final generalization improves versus finetuning without dropout.

Section 6 begins experiments: they evaluate dropout on classification tasks across many domains and claim dropout improved generalization on all data sets compared to non-dropout neural nets. Listed data sets: MNIST, TIMIT, CIFAR-10/100, SVHN, ImageNet, Reuters-RCV1, and an Alternative Splicing data set. A detailed description is deferred to Appendix B.

Section 7.1 argues dropout reduces co-adaptation. It compares MNIST autoencoders with one hidden layer of 256 ReLU units trained with and without dropout (p=0.5). Both had similar test reconstruction errors, but without dropout the learned features appear co-adapted and not individually meaningful, while with dropout they look like edges, strokes, and spots. The text concludes dropout breaks up co-adaptations and likely lowers generalization error. Section 7.2 claims dropout also induces sparse hidden activations even without explicit sparsity regularization. Using the same autoencoders, it compares histograms of mean activations and activation distributions on a test minibatch: without dropout the average hidden activation is around 2.0 and many units have high activation; with dropout the average is around 0.7 and activations have a sharper peak at zero. Section 7.3 begins an exploration of the dropout rate p, defined as the probability of retaining a unit, in two settings: holding the number of hidden units fixed, and adjusting hidden units so the expected number retained after dropout stays constant.

Section 7.3 compares two ways of varying dropout rate p, where p is the probability of retaining a unit. In the first setting, the network architecture is fixed (784-2048-2048-2048-10) with no input dropout. Small p causes underfitting and high training error; test error falls as p increases, is fairly flat for 0.4–0.8, and rises again as p approaches 1. In the second setting, pn is held constant so smaller p implies more hidden units; the expected number of active units after dropout is matched across architectures. They use pn=256 for the first two hidden layers and pn=512 for the last hidden layer. Under this setup, small-p cases improve substantially relative to fixed architecture, and p around 0.6 performs best, with 0.5 close to optimal.

Section 7.4 studies dataset size on MNIST with dropout. The same 784-1024-1024-2048-10 network is trained on random subsets of size 100, 500, 1K, 5K, 10K, and 50K. Dropout uses p=0.5 on hidden layers and p=0.8 on the input layer. Dropout does not help on the smallest datasets (100 and 500), but its benefit grows with dataset size up to a point and then declines, suggesting a sweet spot between too little data (memorization despite dropout noise) and too much data (where overfitting is less of a problem).

Section 7.5 begins a comparison of test-time inference methods: Monte Carlo model averaging by sampling multiple dropout networks versus the proposed weight-scaling approximation.

Section 7.5 compares test-time inference by Monte Carlo averaging over k sampled dropout networks versus the weight-scaling approximation. On MNIST, the finite-sample Monte Carlo average approaches the approximate method quickly; around k = 50 it matches it, and for larger k it is slightly better but within one standard deviation. The authors conclude weight scaling is a good approximation of the true model average.

Section 8 introduces dropout for Restricted Boltzmann Machines. An RBM with visible units v and hidden units h has energy-based distribution P(h,v;θ) ∝ exp(v^TWh + a^Th + b^Tv). Dropout RBMs add binary mask variables r_j ~ Bernoulli(p) over hidden units, with g(h_j,r_j) enforcing h_j=0 whenever r_j=0. The conditional P(h|r,v) factorizes, with P(h_j=1|r_j,v)=1(r_j=1)σ(b_j + Σ_i W_ij v_i), and P(v|h) remains the standard RBM conditional. Thus a dropout RBM is a mixture of many RBMs sharing weights but using different hidden subsets. Training uses standard CD-1, sampling a fresh r for each training case in each minibatch. Section 8.3 begins showing features learned by ordinary versus dropout RBMs with 256 hidden units on MNIST.

Section 8.4 says dropout RBMs learn much sparser hidden representations than standard RBMs even without an explicit sparsity regularizer. Figure 13 compares hidden-unit activation histograms and means for a standard RBM (13a) and a dropout RBM (13b) on a test mini-batch. The text says the dropout RBM features are qualitatively coarser than the standard RBM’s stroke-like features and that there seem to be very few dead units in the dropout RBM relative to the standard RBM.

Section 9 reframes dropout as marginalizing noise to obtain deterministic models. In linear regression, with dropout mask R_{ij} ~ Bernoulli(p), the expected squared-loss objective becomes a ridge-like objective: ||y - pXw||^2 + p(1-p)||Γw||^2, equivalently with regularization strength (1-p)/p after rescaling w. For logistic regression and deep nets, exact marginalization is intractable; Wang and Manning’s approximation is described as faster and better than Monte Carlo dropout for logistic regression, but not directly applicable to deep networks. A table reports Bernoulli vs Gaussian dropout results: MNIST 1.08 ± 0.04 vs 0.95 ± 0.04, and CIFAR-10 12.6 ± 0.1 vs 12.5 ± 0.1.

steps.notes_before: Section 10 introduces multiplicative Gaussian noise as a dropout variant: hidden activations are perturbed by hi + hi r with r ~ N(0,1), equivalently hi r0 with r0 ~ N(1,1), and more generally r0 ~ N(1, σ^2). The text says the activation mean is unchanged, so no test-time weight scaling is needed. It then contrasts the standard Bernoulli-rescaling view (multiply by 1/p with probability p, else 0) with Gaussian multiplicative noise, noting that matching mean and variance gives σ^2 = (1-p)/p. The section claims the Gaussian version has higher entropy than Bernoulli and that both work well, with Table 10 suggesting Gaussian may be slightly better. Table 10 compares classification errors for Bernoulli vs Gaussian dropout on MNIST and CIFAR-10, using p = 0.5 hidden / 0.8 input for MNIST and p = (0.9, 0.75, 0.75, 0.5, 0.5, 0.5) for CIFAR-10, averaged over 10 seeds. The conclusion begins by restating dropout as a way to reduce brittle co-adaptations and improve generalization.

The conclusion reiterates dropout as a general method for reducing co-adaptations and improving generalization, and says it has been successful across many domains. It also states dropout can be extended to RBMs and that dropout RBMs were developed with desirable properties. A drawback is training time: dropout networks typically take 2-3× longer to train because gradients are noisy and each case trains a different random architecture; this stochasticity may help prevent overfitting. The appendix gives practical heuristics: if a standard network uses n hidden units and retention probability is p, a dropout net may need at least n/p units. Dropout usually needs much higher learning rates (10-100× standard) and momentum around 0.95-0.99; max-norm regularization with typical c≈3-4 can help. Typical dropout retention rates are 0.5-0.8 for hidden units and about 0.8 for real-valued inputs. Smaller p requires larger n and can slow training/underfit; larger p may not regularize enough.

Appendix B gives experimental details. For MNIST, 10,000 training images were held out for validation; hyperparameters were tuned to the best validation error after 1 million weight updates, then the validation set was merged back into training for another 1 million updates before test evaluation. MNIST architectures in Fig. 4 include all 2-, 3-, and 4-layer networks with 1024 or 2048 units per layer (six architectures total). For these models, hidden-layer dropout retention was p=0.5, input retention p=0.8, momentum 0.95, and max-norm c=2. Larger MNIST nets with 4096 and 8192 units were also tried; 2-layer nets improved, while 3-layer nets were slightly worse than 2-layer nets at the same dropout level.

For SVHN, the data set has about 600,000 training images and 26,000 test images. The validation set was 6,000 examples drawn from both standard and extra labeled training sets (400/class from standard, 200/class from extra), following Sermanet et al. The best SVHN model has three conv layers (96, 128, 256 filters), each with 5x5 filters and stride 1, each followed by 3x3 max pooling with stride 2, then two fully connected layers of 2048 units. All units use ReLU; dropout retain probabilities are (0.9, 0.75, 0.75, 0.5, 0.5, 0.5) from input through the network, with max-norm c=4 and momentum 0.95. Because the training set was large, validation was not merged into training for final fitting.

For CIFAR-10/100, there are 50,000 training and 10,000 test images, with 5,000 training images used for validation; after tuning, validation was merged with training. Preprocessing uses global contrast normalization per color channel and ZCA whitening.

Paper: "Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting" (JMLR 15, 2014, pp. 1929–1958). Authors: Nitish Srivastava, Geoffrey Hinton, Alex Krizhevsky, Ilya Sutskever, and Ruslan Salakhutdinov (University of Toronto); editor Yoshua Bengio. The paper map on the first pages lays out the structure across sections 2–11 plus appendices A and B. Abstract/intro claims: dropout randomly removes units and their connections during training, reducing co-adaptation and implicitly sampling exponentially many thinned networks; a single unthinned network with reduced weights approximates the averaged predictions. It claims dropout reduces overfitting and improves results across vision, speech recognition, document classification, and computational biology, often state of the art. Section 1 also says posterior-weighted averaging is the best regularization given unlimited computation, while dropout approximates an equally weighted geometric mean over exponentially many shared-parameter models. A network with n units corresponds to 2^n thinned networks and reuses O(n^2) or fewer parameters. The introduction contrasts dropout with stopping early, soft weight sharing, and L1/L2 penalties, and says model combination is powerful but expensive. It introduces the practical inference rule (weight scaling) versus Monte Carlo model averaging, and notes dropout extends to graphical models such as Boltzmann machines, including Restricted Boltzmann Machines and dropout RBMs. Figure 1 shows a standard two-hidden-layer net and a thinned version with crossed units removed.

Section 2 motivates dropout using analogies from evolution and robustness. It contrasts sexual vs asexual reproduction: recombination breaks co-adapted gene sets, suggesting a tension between individual-fitness optimization and the value of mixable, robust genes. The Livnat et al. view is that selection may favor gene sets that work with many partners; the paper maps this to hidden units trained with dropout, which must be useful with randomly selected partners and thus learn independently useful, robust features rather than depend on other units. It also uses a conspiracy analogy: smaller conspiracies are more robust to changing conditions than a larger one needing many correct participants. These examples support the claim that complex co-adaptations can fit training data yet generalize poorly, whereas simpler robust components may generalize better.

Section 3 surveys related work on noise-based regularization. It frames hidden-unit noise as a regularizer for QX2, connecting it to denoising autoencoders (Vincent et al. 2008, 2010): input corruption plus reconstruction, effective hidden-layer corruption, model averaging, supervised and unsupervised use, and applicability to other neuron-based architectures such as Boltzmann machines. A comparison table says typical best noise is 5% for S2H, while QX2 often works best at 20% input-unit removal or 50% hidden-unit removal. It contrasts stochastic noise training with adversarial removal methods (Globerson and Roweis 2006; Dekel et al. 2010), noting those have no hidden units. It also says analytically marginalizing QX2 yields deterministic regularizers in simple cases; related exponential-family input-noise regularizers (“blankout noise”) were studied by van der Maaten et al. (2013) for models without hidden layers. Chen et al. (2012) examined marginalization for denoising autoencoders, and Wang and Manning (2013) proposed marginalization to accelerate QX2.

steps.notes_before: Section 4 defines QX2 as stochastic deletion (“dropout”) applied to every layer: each layer output vector is multiplied elementwise by an independent Bernoulli mask with retention probability \(p\). Training samples a subnetwork and backpropagates through it; both hidden and visible units can be removed. At test time, no units are removed and the outgoing weights are scaled by \(p\): \(\mathbf W^{(l)}_{	ext{test}}=p\mathbf W^{(l)}\). The section states that validation can choose \(p\), but the default is usually near optimal and input retention is often closer to 1. It also claims that the expected output under deletion matches test-time output, though the formulas only directly show this for the preactivation, not necessarily after a nonlinear activation.

Section 5 says QX2 training uses standard SGD on a per-case sampled thinned network: each case is forwarded/backpropagated through its own sampled subnetwork, gradients are averaged, and absent parameters contribute zero. It highlights that QX2 works well with high momentum, large decaying learning rates, and V9C max-norm regularization, where each incoming hidden-unit weight vector is constrained by ||w||_2 <= c and projected back onto the radius-c ball if it exceeds it. The section also notes that this constraint is a validation-tuned hyperparameter and can help deep-net training even without QX2. For unsupervised pretraining, the procedure is unchanged, but before QX2 finetuning pretrained weights are multiplied by 1/p so that expected random-removal output matches the pretrained output. Smaller finetuning learning rates are said to preserve pretrained information better than rates comparable to best randomly initialized-net rates.

Section 6 reports experimental results. It claims QX2 improved generalization over non-QX2 neural nets on every tested data set and that models attaining state of the art on all five vision collections use QX2. Table 1 lists datasets: H4Z/MNIST (784, 60K/10K), A2F/SVHN (3072, 600K/26K), J3V/W6R/CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 (3072, 60K/10K), K9D/ImageNet ILSVRC-2012 (65536, 1.2M/150K), N8Q/TIMIT (2520, 1.1M frames/58K frames), M5X/Reuters-RCV1 (2000, 200K/200K), and Z7P/Alternative Splicing (1014, 2932/733). In H4Z, QX2 improves over standard neural nets; ReLUs, max-norm regularization (V9C), larger architectures, and maxout (L8J) each improve further. Best H4Z listed result is E5Q + QX2 finetuning at 0.79% error; G6W + QX2 finetuning gets 0.92%, while E5Q + finetuning without QX2 is 0.96%. Figure 4 compares training trajectories with and without QX2 under fixed hyperparameters, yielding two separated error clusters. The A2F section says convolutional nets outperform other methods; adding QX2 to fully connected layers helps, adding it to convolutional layers helps more, and maxout helps further.

Table 1 lists datasets: H4Z/MNIST (784, 60K/10K), A2F/SVHN (3072, 600K/26K), J3V/W6R/CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 (3072, 60K/10K), K9D/ImageNet ILSVRC-2012 (65536, 1.2M/150K), N8Q/TIMIT (2520, 1.1M frames/58K frames), M5X/Reuters-RCV1 (2000, 200K/200K), and Z7P/Alternative Splicing (1014, 2932/733). In H4Z, QX2 improves over standard neural nets; ReLUs, max-norm regularization (V9C), larger architectures, and maxout (L8J) each improve further. Best H4Z listed result is E5Q + QX2 finetuning at 0.79% error; G6W + QX2 finetuning gets 0.92%, while E5Q + finetuning without QX2 is 0.96%. Figure 4 compares training trajectories with and without QX2 under fixed hyperparameters, yielding two separated error clusters. A2F tables show QX2 helps, but maxout is slightly better than the best QX2 model. J3V/W6R: QX2 improves over max pooling, and L8J is best on both. K9D: Conv Net + QX2 beats prior vision-feature methods on ILSVRC-2010 and achieves the strong 2012 validation/test numbers reported in Tables 5–6.

Section 7 summarizes qualitative effects of QX2. In autoencoders, first-layer features without QX2 are described as co-adapted and not meaningful, while QX2 units detect edges, strokes, and spots in localized image regions. QX2 is also said to produce sparse hidden activations without an explicit sparsity regularizer; in the shown histograms, no-QX2 units have mean activation around 2.0 with a large off-zero mode, while QX2 units average around 0.7 with a sharp zero peak. For retention rate, fixed-architecture models underfit at low p; error is flat for roughly 0.4<=p<=0.8, the low-retention comparison uses p=0.1, and error is 2.7% with fixed architecture versus 1.7% when expected retained width is held fixed. The paper says the best retention for the chosen expected widths is near 0.6, with 0.5 as the usual near-optimal default. For dataset size, the two smallest training sets show no QX2 gain; improvement rises with data size and then falls, suggesting a sweet spot where overfitting is reduced but not eliminated. Finally, in the X9M vs. T6R comparison, X9M becomes as good as T6R at about k=50 and then slightly outperforms it within one standard deviation.

steps.notes_before: Section 8 introduces B8T as a mixture of exponentially many shared-weight U2L models, each defined by a retention vector r that independently keeps each hidden unit with probability p. Conditional on r, dropped hidden units are forced to 0, and the visible conditionals remain the same as in U2L; the hidden conditionals factorize and are zero when a unit is dropped. Learning uses ordinary U2L algorithms by first sampling r for each training case; experiments use CD-1. The section claims B8T features are coarser than ordinary U2L stroke-like features and that B8T has very few dead units relative to U2L. It also claims B8T learns much sparser hidden representations than U2L without an extra sparsity regularizer. Figure 12 compares ordinary U2L to B8T with p=0.5.

Section 9 discusses QX2 marginalization. It states that deterministic noise-marginalized models need no random bits and allow gradients of marginalized losses, unlike standard Monte-Carlo QX2. It references prior work on test-time feature deletion, linear-regression marginalization, and adaptive-regularizer views of QX2.

For linear regression, if each input dimension is retained independently with probability p, then the expected objective – minimizing E||y - (R*X)w||^2 – reduces to ||y - pXw||^2 + p(1-p)||Γw||^2, where Γ = diag(X^T X)^{1/2}. Reparameterizing with w~ = pw yields ||y - Xw~||^2 + ((1-p)/p)||Γw~||^2.

For logistic regression and deep networks, exact marginalized models are said to be difficult. Under reasonable assumptions, logistic-unit inputs and marginalized gradients are approximately Gaussian with computable means and variances, but the assumptions become progressively weaker as layers are added, so the results are not directly applicable to deep networks. The section also claims approximate marginalization beats Monte-Carlo QX2 in training time and generalization for logistic regression.

Section 10 says multiplicative Gaussian corruption is comparable to, and maybe slightly better than, Bernoulli dropout in preliminary experiments. Table 10 reports classification error rates: H4Z 1.08±0.04 for P7V vs 0.95±0.04 for D4K, and J3V 12.6±0.1 vs 12.5±0.1, so Gaussian is slightly better in both cases. The section argues that Bernoulli and Gaussian multipliers can be matched by first and second moments; for Bernoulli retention p, the equivalent multiplier has mean 1 and variance (1-p)/p, and choosing Gaussian variance σ²=(1-p)/p matches these moments. It also states that using Gaussian multipliers can remove test-time scaling, analogous to the Bernoulli case.

The conclusion says the paper’s QX2 methods get state of the art on A2F, K9D, W6R, and H4Z, with strong gains on other collections; training is typically 2–3× slower than a standard network because each run uses a different random architecture and gradients do not match the final inference architecture; stochasticity may reduce overfitting; and an expectation-equivalent regularizer can recover some noise-marginalization benefits, though only linear regression has an explicit form so far.

Appendix A gives practical heuristics for training QX2 networks. It says QX2 still requires extensive hyperparameter tuning. For a standard net layer with n hidden units, a QX2 layer should have at least n/p units because only pn units remain in expectation and identities change each sample. QX2 usually needs much higher learning rates (about 10–100× the standard-net rate) and higher momentum (roughly 0.95–0.99 vs. 0.9). V9C constrains each hidden unit’s incoming-weight vector norm, with c typically 3–4. Retention p controls intensity: lower p means stronger QX2, more width needed, slower training, and more risk of underfitting; higher p may under-regularize. Typical hidden-unit retention is 0.5–0.8; real-valued inputs such as image patches and speech frames often use p≈0.8; a broadly near-optimal simple default is 0.5, while input-unit optimum is usually closer to 1 than to 0.5.

Appendix B lists experimental details. Reproduction code is at the Toronto dropout page; GPU code used cudamat and cuda-convnet. B.1 (H4Z): digit classification with 10,000 held-out training images for validation; both validation tuning and final combined-data training used 1M update steps. Architecture sweep covered 2, 3, and 4 hidden layers with widths 1024 or 2048 (six combinations). Reported/sweep QX2 settings used hidden-layer retention p=0.5, input retention p=0.8, momentum 0.95, and V9C bound c=2. Additional regularization-limit experiments used 2- and 3-layer nets with 4096/8192 units; largest reported two-hidden-layer model had >65M parameters. Regularizer/data-size comparisons used 784-1024-1024-2048-10; fixed-width rate comparison used 784-2048-2048-2048-10. X9M samples many thinned networks and averages predictions. B.2 (A2F): validation split from standard and extra labeled data; 6000 validation samples total. Network has 3 conv layers (96,128,256 filters, 5x5, stride 1) each followed by 3x3 max-pooling stride 2, then two 2048-unit FC layers; activations F3N; retention p=(0.9,0.75,0.75,0.5,0.5,0.5); V9C c=4; momentum 0.95. Final training kept the large training set separate and used best validation checkpoint. B.3 (J3V/W6R): 50k train/10k test, 10 and 100 classes; validation used 5k training images, then combined validation/training optimization. Preprocessing: global contrast normalization per channel and ZCA whitening; architecture and retention match A2F, but input-layer learning rates must be smaller. B.4 (N8Q): 680 speakers, 8 dialects, 10 sentences each; Kaldi log-filter banks; monophone forced alignment; consecutive-frame windows predict central-frame labels; no speaker-dependent operations; inputs mean-centered and unit-variance.

final_notes:
Appendix B.4 (DBN/speech): dropout finetuning used input retention p=0.8, hidden retention p=0.5, max-norm c=4, momentum 0.95, and a high learning rate of 0.1. The learning-rate schedule was epsilon_0(1+t/T)^-1. For DBN pretraining, RBMs used CD-1 and Gaussian RBM input variance was fixed at 1. Best dropout finetuning results needed a smaller learning rate, about 0.01; adding max-norm gave no improvement. Reported speech performance in Table 7 had dropout error rates 21.8%, 19.7%, and 19.7%.

Appendix B.5 (Reuters): RCV1 has >800k documents in 103 hierarchical classes. They created a 402,738-article subset with a 2000-word vocabulary and 50 categories; each document has exactly one class and the split was equally sized train/test. Dropout improved all tried architectures, but less than on image/speech tasks. Best-network comparison: 31.05% without dropout vs 29.62% with dropout. Large-data explanation: >200k training cases, so overfitting less serious.

Appendix B.6 (Alternative splicing): 3665 cassette exons, 1014 RNA features, 4 tissue types from 27 mouse tissues. Each input has 4 softmax outputs (one per tissue), each with states inc/exc/nc. Code Quality objective is a summed log ratio using p_i,t^s, q_t^s(r_i), and average state frequency \bar p^s. They trained a two-layer dropout net with 1024 units per layer, hidden p=0.5, input p=0.7, max-norm regularization, and high decaying learning rates. Results were averaged over the same 5 folds used by Xiong et al. (2011).

Abstract claims dropout randomly removes units during training, samples an exponential number of thinned networks, and uses one unthinned network with smaller weights at test time to approximate their average predictions. It says dropout reduces overfitting and improves supervised-learning performance on vision, speech recognition, document classification, and computational-biology tasks, with state-of-the-art results on many benchmarks. It also says dropout outperforms other regularization methods.

Introduction claims deep nets overfit limited data and reviews standard regularization (early stopping, L1/L2, soft weight sharing). The paper’s goal is to approximate Bayesian model averaging / an equally weighted geometric mean of predictions from exponentially many parameter-sharing models at low cost. Dropout randomly removes hidden or visible units during training; in the simplest case each unit is retained independently with probability p (often p=0.5 for hidden units, closer to 1 for inputs). A thinned network is sampled for each training case. At test time, dropout is turned off and outgoing weights are multiplied by p so expected training-time output matches test-time output. A network with n units represents 2^n thinned networks with shared weights, making explicit averaging infeasible. The paper claims dropout reduces generalization error and also applies to RBMs. Section roadmap: 2 motivation, 3 related work, 4 model, 5 training, 6 experiments, 7 network properties/hyperparameters, 8 Dropout RBMs, 9 marginalizing dropout, Appendix A practical guidance.

Prior notes still hold: the paper frames dropout as approximate Bayesian model averaging / equally weighted geometric mean over exponentially many thinned networks; each unit is kept independently with probability p during training, and at test time weights are multiplied by p. This part begins Section 2 (Motivation) and uses two analogies to explain why dropout should help: (1) sexual reproduction/mix-ability—useful genes must work with random partners, so hidden units trained with dropout should become robust and not rely on specific co-adaptations; and (2) conspiracies—smaller groups are more likely to keep working under changing conditions than one large tightly coordinated group. The section’s conclusion is that complex co-adaptations may fit training data but are more likely to fail on test data than several simpler co-adaptations.

It says dropout can be seen as regularization via noise in hidden states; Denoising Autoencoders add noise to unit states / inputs and reconstruct clean input. Section 4 defines standard feed-forward computation and dropout masks. Each layer’s inputs/outputs are denoted z^(l) and y^(l), with y^(0)=x. Under dropout, each layer output is multiplied elementwise by an independent Bernoulli(p) mask r^(l) before being fed to the next layer, producing a sampled sub-network. Training backpropagates through the sampled sub-network. At test time, the weights are scaled as W_test^(l)=p W^(l) and the network is used without dropout.

steps.notes_before:
Section 5 covers learning dropout nets. Training uses SGD on a sampled thinned network per mini-batch case; gradients are averaged and inactive parameters contribute zero gradient. Helpful SGD tricks include momentum, learning-rate decay, and L2 weight decay. Max-norm regularization constrains each hidden unit’s incoming weight vector to norm <= c and is especially useful with dropout; the paper claims dropout + max-norm beats dropout + L2 (Table 9: 1.05% vs 1.25%), and max-norm alone beats L2 (1.35% vs 1.62%).

For unsupervised pretraining, the paper says pretrained weights should be multiplied by 1/p before dropout finetuning so expected outputs match pretraining. Dropout finetuning is said to preserve pretrained information only with smaller learning rates; with larger finetuning rates it can erase pretrained information. The section claims improved pretrained MNIST results using dropout finetuning, citing Table 2 DBN and DBM rows with error pairs 1.18% vs 0.92% and 0.96% vs 0.79%.

Section 6 reports experimental results across multiple domains and claims dropout improves generalization on every data set versus networks without dropout. Table 1 lists data sets and sizes: MNIST 60K/10K, SVHN 600K/26K, CIFAR-10/100 60K/10K, ImageNet 1.2M/150K, TIMIT 1.1M frames/58K, Reuters-RCV1 200K/200K, Alternative Splicing 2932/733.

Image results: Section 6.1 says the five image data sets are MNIST, SVHN, CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, ImageNet. It claims state-of-the-art results on these use dropout.

MNIST Table 2: standard NN 1.60%; SVM Gaussian kernel 1.40%; dropout NN logistic 1.35%; dropout NN ReLU 1.25%; dropout NN + max-norm ReLU 1.06%, 1.04% (larger nets), 1.01%, 0.95%; maxout dropout 0.94%; DBN finetuning 1.18%; DBM finetuning 0.96%; DBN + dropout finetuning 0.92%; DBM + dropout finetuning 0.79%. The text says permutation-invariant best no-dropout/no-pretraining is about 1.60%; dropout reduces to 1.35%; ReLUs to 1.25%; max-norm to 1.06%.

Section 6.1 continues MNIST results and then starts SVHN. For MNIST, the paper reports that larger dropout networks improve performance: 2 hidden layers of 8192 units each reach 0.95% error with >65M parameters on 60k training cases. Maxout reaches 0.94%. Pretraining with RBMs/DBMs further improves dropout networks: DBN-pretrained dropout gets 0.92% and DBM-pretrained dropout gets 0.79%, the best reported permutation-invariant result. The paper also says dropout generalizes across architectures without tuning hyperparameters: Figure 4 compares 2–4 hidden-layer networks with 1024–2048 units and shows distinct error trajectories with and without dropout.

For SVHN, the task is 32x32 color house-number classification using a Conv Net with 3 convolutional layers and 2 fully connected hidden layers, all ReLUs, with max-pooling after each conv layer. Table 3 lists results: best non-dropout Conv Net 3.95%; dropout only in fully connected layers 3.02%; dropout in all layers 2.55%; maxout 2.47%; human performance 2.0%. The paper says dropout was applied throughout the network with retention probabilities p=(0.9,0.75,0.75,0.5,0.5,0.5) from input through conv and fully connected layers, and max-norm regularization was used.

Section 6.1.3 covers CIFAR-10/100. Table 4 reports CIFAR-10 error rates: max-pooling 14.98, dropout in fully connected layers 14.32, dropout in all layers 12.61, and maxout 11.68. For CIFAR-100, the corresponding errors are 43.48 (max-pooling), 41.26 (FC dropout), 37.20 (all-layer dropout), and 38.57 (maxout). The text says no data augmentation was used beyond input dropout.

Section 7.5 compares Monte-Carlo model averaging with test-time weight scaling. It says that averaging predictions from about k=50 sampled networks matches weight scaling, and that beyond this point Monte-Carlo averaging is slightly better but within one standard deviation. The conclusion is that weight scaling is a fairly good approximation to the true model average.

Section 8 introduces Dropout RBMs. The model adds a binary mask r over hidden units, with each r_j=1 independently with probability p. Conditioned on r, the model is an RBM with the r_j=0 hidden units effectively removed, so a Dropout RBM is a mixture of exponentially many RBMs sharing weights. Learning is done by sampling a new mask for each training case/mini-batch and then applying standard RBM learning, using CD-1 in the experiments.

The paper compares standard and dropout RBMs on MNIST with 256 hidden units and p=0.5. Qualitatively, dropout RBM features look coarser and there appear to be fewer dead units than in the standard RBM. It also reports that dropout leads to much sparser hidden activations, even without an additional sparsity regularizer.

Section 9 discusses deterministic models obtained by marginalizing dropout noise. It notes prior related work on robustness to feature deletion, denoising autoencoders, and dropout marginalization/adaptive regularization.

For linear regression, with input-dimension dropout \(R_{ij}\sim\mathrm{Bernoulli}(p)\), the marginalized objective is \(\mathbb E_R[\|y-(R*X)w\|^2]\), which simplifies to \(\|y-pXw\|^2 + p(1-p)\|\Gamma w\|^2\) where \(\Gamma=(\mathrm{diag}(X^\top X))^{1/2}\). After rescaling \(\tilde w=pw\), this becomes \(\|y-X\tilde w\|^2 + \frac{1-p}{p}\|\Gamma\tilde w\|^2\). Thus the effective regularization grows as \(p\) decreases.

For logistic regression and deep networks, closed-form marginalization is hard. Wang and Manning (2013) provide an approximate marginalized logistic-regression method by approximating inputs and gradients as Gaussian; the text says this improves training time and generalization over Monte-Carlo dropout, but the approximation does not directly extend to deep networks because the assumptions weaken with added layers.

Section 10 generalizes dropout to multiplicative Gaussian noise and compares it with Bernoulli dropout. A hidden activation can be written as \(h_i+h_i r\) with \(r\sim N(0,1)\), equivalently as \(h_i r'\) with \(r'\sim N(1,1)\); more generally \(r'\sim N(1,\sigma^2)\), with \(\sigma\) a tunable hyperparameter. Under the alternate dropout scaling convention (retain with probability \(p\), scale retained activations by \(1/p\) at train time), the Bernoulli multiplier has mean 1 and variance \((1-p)/p\). Setting Gaussian variance to the same value matches first and second moments. The text claims the Gaussian multiplier then has highest entropy and the Bernoulli multiplier lowest. Table 10 reports Gaussian dropout slightly outperforming Bernoulli on MNIST (0.95 ± 0.04 vs 1.08 ± 0.04) and CIFAR-10 (12.5 ± 0.1 vs 12.6 ± 0.1). For MNIST, Bernoulli p-values are 0.5 for hidden units and 0.8 for input units; for CIFAR-10, p=(0.9, 0.75, 0.75, 0.5, 0.5, 0.5) from input to top. Gaussian \(\sigma\) is set per layer as \(\sqrt{(1-p)/p}\).

Section 11 concludes that dropout reduces overfitting by breaking co-adaptations via random omission of hidden units. It claims dropout improves many tasks (object classification, digit recognition, speech recognition, document classification, computational biology) and that dropout methods achieve state-of-the-art results on SVHN, ImageNet, CIFAR-100, and MNIST. It says the idea extends to RBMs and other graphical models by training an overcomplete model via sampled smaller sub-models; the paper’s Dropout RBMs show different features and greater sparsity. A drawback is training time: a dropout network typically takes 2–3x longer to train than a standard network, due to noisy updates and each case training a different random architecture. Marginalizing the noise can replace stochastic dropout in some settings; for linear regression this gives a modified L2 regularizer, but no obvious equivalent regularizer is known for more complex models.

Appendix A gives practical heuristics: because dropout with retention probability p leaves pn units expected, layers should often be widened to at least n/p units. It recommends learning rates 10–100x higher than standard-network optima and momentum around 0.95–0.99 (vs. common 0.9). Max-norm regularization with hidden-unit incoming weight norm bound c around 3–4 helps prevent weights from growing too large. Typical hidden-unit retention probabilities are 0.5–0.8; for real-valued image patches or speech frames, input retention around 0.8 is typical. Smaller p requires larger n, which can slow training and underfit; larger p may not regularize enough.

Appendix B gives experimental details. MNIST: 60k train/10k test; 10k train images held out for validation. Hyperparameters were chosen so best validation error occurred after 1M updates, then training and validation were reunited and the model trained for another 1M updates. The paper studies dropout as a method to prevent overfitting in large neural networks by randomly removing units/connections during training, effectively training many smaller shared-parameter networks and using a single scaled network at test time. It claims dropout improves generalization over non-dropout networks on every tested dataset, with experiments across images, speech, documents, and gene-splicing prediction. The paper says it reports state-of-the-art results on several benchmarks and also examines learned features, sparsity, retention rates, training-set size, RBMs, noise marginalization, and Gaussian corruption. Training is said to take about 2–3 times longer than a standard network of the same architecture.

The paper’s glossary defines the main dropout-related terms and abbreviations used later. Dropout is described as random removal of units and connections during training, with approximate averaging by one unthinned network at test time; thinned networks are subnetworks formed by removing units/connections. It defines core neural-network terms (units, hidden/visible layers, weights, biases, activations), regularizers (L1, L2/Tikhonov, max-norm, KL-sparsity, early stopping), and averaging concepts (model averaging, posterior-weighted averaging, geometric mean, weight scaling, Monte-Carlo averaging). It also names Bernoulli dropout, Gaussian dropout, and dropout-related noise/marginalization ideas. This part is the title/front-matter page for the paper “Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting,” listing the five authors and their University of Toronto affiliations. It also gives an original-page map for the rest of the paper: pages 1930–1955 cover the introduction, figures, sections 2–11, table 1–10, acknowledgments, Appendix A (A.1–A.4), and Appendix B (B.1–B.6). No new technical notation or results appear in this part.

This part contains the abstract of the paper. It claims that dropout (referred to here as “QX2, or dropout”) temporarily removes randomly selected units and their connections during training, inhibits co-adaptation, samples exponentially many thinned networks sharing parameters, and that a single unthinned network with reduced weights approximates their averaged predictions. It also claims that dropout substantially reduces overfitting and improves results across vision, speech recognition, document classification, and computational biology, with evidence in Tables 2–8 and the unnumbered text-classification table in §6.3. No new notation or contradictions appear here.

This part is the Introduction. It says QX2/dropout trains many shared-parameter subnetworks and uses a single unthinned test-time network to approximate their combined predictions. It frames the method as approximating an equally weighted geometric mean of exponentially many learned models, with a network of n units corresponding to 2^n possible thinned networks but only O(n^2) or fewer parameters. It introduces standard regularizers/terms: early stopping, soft weight sharing, L1 (O3U), and L2 (Y5F). It also says model combination usually helps but is expensive, and that the practical inference rule T6R/weight scaling uses one unthinned network; X9M/Monte-Carlo model averaging samples members at test time. It claims T6R has lower generalization error than compared regularizers, citing Table 9 rows Y5F 1.62, V9C 1.35, QX2+Y5F 1.25, and QX2+V9C 1.05. It also introduces extension to graphical models via RBMs, with B8T/Dropout RBM. No contradictions found yet.

This part gives the paper’s motivation for dropout/QX2 using biological and game-theoretic analogies. It argues that breaking co-adapted gene sets via sexual reproduction can be advantageous because it favors ‘mix-ability’ and robustness, even if it seems worse for preserving successful combinations. It then maps this to QX2-trained hidden units: because hidden units face randomly selected partners, the method encourages independently useful, robust features rather than reliance on other units. The part also uses a conspiracy analogy to suggest that smaller interacting groups may be more robust under changing conditions than one large, fragile coordinated group. No direct contradictions with earlier sections are introduced here.

This part is the related-work section. It frames QX2 as connected to hidden-unit noise, model averaging, and earlier work on corruption, adversarial deletion, and marginalization. It says denoising autoencoders (S2H) corrupt inputs and reconstruct clean inputs, while QX2 extends this with effective hidden-layer corruption and a model-averaging interpretation. QX2 is claimed to apply to supervised and unsupervised learning and to other neuron-based architectures, including Boltzmann machines. It also contrasts QX2 with adversarial-removal models (Globerson and Roweis 2006; Dekel et al. 2010), which choose deletions under a fixed maximum rather than a probability distribution and are said to have no hidden units. Van der Maaten et al. (2013) are described as studying exponential-family input-noise regularizers, including QX2 under the name blankout noise, limited to models without hidden layers; Chen et al. (2012) studied marginalization for DAEs; Wang and Manning (2013) proposed marginalization to accelerate QX2. The table reports noise levels: S2H typical best 5%, QX2 often optimal input-unit removal 20%, and QX2 often optimal hidden-unit removal 50%.

steps.notes_before: Section 4 defines QX2/dropout-style corruption as independent Bernoulli gating of unit outputs during training: each entry \(r_j^{(l)}\sim Bernoulli(p)\), and \(	ilde y^{(l)} = r^{(l)} * y^{(l)}\). Ordinary feed-forward is \(z_i^{(l+1)}=w_i^{(l+1)} y^{(l)} + b_i^{(l+1)}\), \(y_i^{(l+1)}=f(z_i^{(l+1)})\); QX2 replaces \(y^{(l)}\) with \(	ilde y^{(l)}\). Any activation is allowed, including logistic. Applying the gating at every layer samples a subnetwork; backpropagation runs through that sampled subnetwork. Both hidden and visible units can be removed. At inference, no units are removed and weights are scaled as \(W^{(l)}_{test}=pW^{(l)}\).

Section 5 says QX2 training/backprop is ordinary backprop on a sampled thinned network: each mini-batch case uses its own sampled subnetwork, gradients are averaged, and unused parameters get zero gradient. The section argues that combining QX2 with high momentum, large decaying learning rates, and max-norm/V9C gives additional gains; V9C constrains each hidden unit’s incoming-weight vector to norm <= c, with projection back to the radius-c ball and c tuned on validation. It also offers a qualitative optimization story (weight ball allows large learning rates; QX2 noise explores weight space; decay shortens steps). For finetuning pretrained nets, smaller learning rates are important; too-large rates can erase pretrained information. Before QX2 finetuning, pretrained weights are multiplied by 1/p to preserve expected outputs under random removal. QX2 finetuning can be applied after pretraining from stacked U2L, autoencoders, or E5Q/DBMs. Reported evidence includes table values showing QX2 improving finetuning results (e.g., G6W: 1.18 to 0.92; E5Q: 0.96 to 0.79) and a best QX2 finetuning rate around 0.01 versus a higher listed rate of 0.1.

Section 9 explains dropout/QX2 marginalization. It says deterministic noise-marginalized models need no random bits and allow gradients of marginalized losses, unlike standard Monte Carlo QX2. In linear regression, the expected dropout squared error equals ridge regression with a data-dependent quadratic penalty: 
E[||y-(R*X)w||^2] = ||y-pXw||^2 + p(1-p)||Γw||^2, where Γ = (diag(X^T X))^{1/2}. After rescaling weights ~w = p w, the penalty coefficient becomes (1-p)/p. The section claims this means features with higher variance are penalized more strongly. For logistic regression, it cites Wang and Manning (2013) as showing approximate marginalization improves training time and generalization versus Monte Carlo QX2. It also says closed-form marginalization is harder for logistic regression and deep nets, and that the stated Gaussian assumptions weaken with depth so the results do not directly apply to deep networks.

Appendix A gives practical heuristics for training QX2 networks and emphasizes that they still need extensive hyperparameter tuning. A.1 recommends making QX2 layers at least n/p wide if the standard net optimum is n hidden units, since only pn units survive in expectation; this was useful for both convolutional and fully connected layers. A.2 says QX2 often needs much larger learning rates than standard nets—typically 10–100x the standard-net optimum—and momentum around 0.95 to 0.99, compared with common standard momentum 0.9. A.3 recommends max-norm constraint c in the range 3 to 4 to control very large weights from high learning rates/momentum. A.4 says retention must be chosen jointly with width and input type: lower p requires wider layers, slows training, and can underfit; too high p may not regularize enough. Hidden-layer p is typically 0.5 to 0.8; real-valued inputs such as image patches and speech frames are typically around 0.8; a broadly near-optimal simple default is 0.5; input-unit optimum is closer to 1 than to 0.5.

Appendix B gives reproduction resources and detailed experimental settings. Code is available online; GPU implementations use cudamat and cuda-convnet. B.1 (H4Z): validation-selected endpoints were used for architecture, regularizer, rate, and data-size comparisons. 10,000 training images were held out for validation; hyperparameters were tuned at 1 million weight updates, then training and validation data were combined and the final run was repeated to the same endpoint. Architecture sweep covered 2, 3, and 4 hidden layers with widths 1024 or 2048 (six architectures total). Reported QX2 models used hidden-layer retention p=0.5, input retention p=0.8, momentum 0.95, and V9C bound c=2. Additional regularization-limit experiments used 2- and 3-layer nets with 4096 and 8192 units. The largest reported two-layer model had more than 65 million parameters. The regularizer-comparison and data-size-comparison architecture was 784-1024-1024-2048-10; data-size runs used training sets of 100, 500, 1K, 5K, 10K, and 50K. Fixed-width rate comparison used 784-2048-2048-2048-10 with no input corruption. Fixed-expected-width comparisons used pn=256 in the first two hidden layers and pn=512 in the last. B.2 (A2F): training data include a standard labeled portion plus extra easy examples; validation is drawn from both per Sermanet et al. (2012). Inputs are RGB pixels normalized to zero mean and unit variance; contrast normalization and ZCA whitening did not help. The architecture has 3 conv layers (96, 128, 256 filters, 5x5, stride 1), each followed by 3x3 max-pooling with stride 2, then two 2048-unit fully connected layers. All hidden activations are F3N; retention is p=(0.9,0.75,0.75,0.5,0.5,0.5); V9C uses c=4; momentum is 0.95.

B.2 A2F: validation tuned hyperparameters; the large training set stayed separate from validation during final training, and the model with the smallest validation error gave the reported test error. The table says A2F used 6000 validation samples, 96/128/256 conv filters, and two 2048-unit fully connected layers. Alternative normalization/whitening methods gave no noticeable improvement.

B.3 J3V and W6R: both image collections use held-out validation, contrast normalization, ZCA whitening, and the A2F architecture. Each has 50,000 training and 10,000 test images; J3V has 10 classes, W6R has 100. Validation used 5,000 training images, then training and validation were combined for final optimization. B.4 N8Q: speech data are 680 speakers, eight American-English dialects, each reading ten sentences. Features are Kaldi-generated log-filter banks; forced alignment comes from a monophone system. Inputs are mean-centered and unit-scaled; consecutive 21-frame windows predict the central frame label. B.5 M5X: Reuters subset has 402,738 articles, 2000-word vocabulary, 50 disjoint categories, one label per document; equal train/test splits give over 200,000 training examples.

B.4 TIMIT: Kaldi was used to preprocess into log-filter banks; a monophone system provided forced alignments/labels. Dropout nets were trained on 21-frame windows to predict the central frame. No speaker-dependent operations; inputs were mean-centered and unit-variance normalized. Retention probabilities were p=0.8 for input layers and p=0.5 for hidden layers. Paper: “Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting” (JMLR 2014). Main claim: dropout randomly drops units and their connections during training, causing an exponential number of thinned networks to be sampled; at test time, one can approximate averaging over them with a single unthinned network using smaller weights. Abstract says this reduces overfitting and improves supervised learning performance in vision, speech recognition, document classification, and computational biology, with state-of-the-art results on many benchmarks. Introduction frames dropout as a regularization method for deep nets, alongside early stopping and weight penalties (L1/L2, soft weight sharing). Figure 1 illustrates a standard neural net vs. a thinned net produced by dropout.

The paper motivates dropout as an approximation to Bayesian model averaging / geometric mean over an exponential number of shared-parameter networks, aiming for good performance with less computation. It argues that averaging many separately trained nets is expensive because diverse nets require different architectures or data and are costly to train/test. Dropout drops hidden and visible units (removing incoming/outgoing connections) at random during training; each unit is retained independently with probability p, typically 0.5 for many layers, while input units usually use p closer to 1. Figure 2 states that at test time all units are present and outgoing weights are multiplied by p, so the test-time network matches the expected training-time output.

Dropout is presented as approximating Bayesian model averaging / geometric mean over an exponential number of shared-parameter subnetworks, reducing computation versus training many separate networks. During training, units are independently retained with probability p; hidden units often use p=0.5, while input units usually use p closer to 1. At test time, all units are present and outgoing weights are multiplied by p so the test-time network matches the expected training-time output. This part adds intuition for dropout via analogies to sexual reproduction and conspiracies: training each hidden unit to work with random subsets of others should make features more robust and less dependent on co-adaptations. It also says the paper will extend dropout to RBMs and discuss experiments, analysis of hyperparameters, marginalizing dropout, and practical guidance in the appendix.

The paper’s intro says dropout extends denoising autoencoders: it can be applied to hidden layers, interpreted as model averaging, and extended beyond unsupervised learning to supervised problems and other neuron-based architectures such as Boltzmann Machines. It also notes that although 5% noise is typical for denoising autoencoders, their weight-scaling-at-test-time approach allows much higher dropout rates; they report 20% input dropout and 50% hidden dropout as often optimal. The paper then motivates deterministic versions by marginalizing the noise, citing prior work on deterministic regularizers and dropout marginalization, and contrasts dropout with adversarial unit-dropping methods.

Model description: for a network with L hidden layers, y^(0)=x, layer l has weights W^(l) and biases b^(l). Standard feedforward uses z^(l+1)=w^(l+1) y^(l)+b^(l+1), y^(l+1)=f(z^(l+1)). With dropout, a Bernoulli mask r^(l) with retention probability p is sampled for each layer, the thinned outputs y~^(l)=r^(l)*y^(l) are passed to the next layer, and this is done at every layer. Training backpropagates through the sampled subnetwork. At test time, dropout is removed and weights are scaled by p: W_test = p W^(l). The next section starts the training procedure for dropout neural nets.

Section 5.1: Dropout nets are trained with SGD by sampling a thinned network per training case; forward/backprop are run only on that thinned network, gradients are averaged over the mini-batch, and units not used contribute zero gradient. Usual SGD improvements (momentum, annealed learning rates, L2 decay) also help. A particularly useful regularizer is max-norm: constrain each hidden unit’s incoming weight vector w to satisfy ||w||2 ≤ c by projecting back onto the ball of radius c; c is tuned on validation. The paper says dropout + max-norm + large decaying learning rates + high momentum works better than dropout alone.

Section 5.2: Dropout can be used to fine-tune pretrained nets (RBMs, autoencoders, DBMs) without changing the pretraining procedure. Weights from pretraining should be scaled up by 1/p so the expected output under dropout matches pretraining. Smaller finetuning learning rates are needed; with them, pretrained information is retained and final generalization improves versus finetuning without dropout.

Section 6 begins experiments: they evaluate dropout on classification tasks across many domains and claim dropout improved generalization on all data sets compared to non-dropout neural nets. Listed data sets: MNIST, TIMIT, CIFAR-10/100, SVHN, ImageNet, Reuters-RCV1, and an Alternative Splicing data set. A detailed description is deferred to Appendix B.

Section 7.3 begins an experiment on the effect of dropout rate p, considering two settings: (1) fixed number of hidden units, and (2) adjusting hidden units so the expected number retained after dropout stays constant.

Section 7.3 studies dropout rate p on MNIST with a 784-2048-2048-2048-10 network. In the first setting, architecture is fixed and no input dropout is used. Small p causes very few active units, leading to underfitting and high training error; test error decreases as p increases, is roughly flat for 0.4 ≤ p ≤ 0.8, then rises as p approaches 1. In the second setting, pn is held constant so smaller p uses more hidden units; the expected number of retained units stays the same across architectures, but test networks differ in size. They set pn = 256 for the first two hidden layers and 512 for the last. Under this setup, small-p errors improve a lot (e.g., p=0.1 drops from 2.7% to 1.7%), and p near 0.6 performs best, with 0.5 close to optimal. Section 7.4 studies dataset size effects on MNIST using a 784-1024-1024-2048-10 network, with dropout p=0.5 in hidden layers and p=0.8 at the input. Data sizes are 100, 500, 1K, 5K, 10K, and 50K. Dropout does not help much for the smallest datasets, but as dataset size increases the benefit grows and then declines, suggesting a sweet spot. Section 7.5 begins a comparison of Monte-Carlo model averaging with the faster weight-scaling approximation at test time.

Section 7.5 compares Monte-Carlo model averaging with the faster weight-scaling approximation on MNIST. They average predictions from k randomly sampled neural networks and compare test error to the weight-scaling horizontal line. Around k = 50, Monte-Carlo averaging becomes as good as the approximate method; for larger k it is slightly better but within one standard deviation, suggesting weight scaling is a fairly good approximation to the true model average. Section 8 introduces Dropout Restricted Boltzmann Machines (RBMs). An RBM has visible units v in {0,1}^D and hidden units h in {0,1}^F with P(h,v;θ) ∝ exp(v^TWh + a^Th + b^Tv). A dropout RBM adds binary mask variables r_j ~ Bernoulli(p) over hidden units; if r_j=0 then h_j must be 0. The joint is P(r,h,v;p,θ)=P(r;p)P(h,v|r;θ), with a constraint factor g(h_j,r_j)=1(r_j=1)+1(r_j=0)1(h_j=0). Conditioned on r, the model is like an RBM with some hidden units removed, so it can be viewed as a mixture of exponentially many RBMs sharing weights. Learning uses standard RBM methods such as CD-1, sampling a fresh r for each training case in each minibatch. Section 8.3 begins examining features learned by binary RBMs vs dropout RBMs, both with 256 hidden units.

Section 8.3 says dropout RBM features are qualitatively different from standard RBM features: coarser, less stroke-like, with very few dead units. Section 8.4 studies sparsity using histograms of hidden activations on a test minibatch after training a standard RBM vs a dropout RBM; the dropout RBM is reported to learn much sparser representations even without an explicit sparsity regularizer. Section 9 introduces marginalized/“deterministic” dropout models, contrasting them with Monte-Carlo dropout. In linear regression, marginalizing Bernoulli dropout noise yields an objective equivalent to ridge regression with a data-dependent penalty: ||y - pXw||^2 + p(1-p)||Γw||^2, or after rescaling weights, a regularization constant (1-p)/p. For logistic regression and deep nets, exact marginalization is intractable; Wang and Manning’s approximate Gaussian method is said to be faster and to generalize better than Monte-Carlo dropout, but the assumptions weaken in deeper models. A small table reports Bernoulli vs Gaussian dropout results: Gaussian is slightly better on MNIST (0.95±0.04 vs 1.08±0.04) and CIFAR-10 (12.5±0.1 vs 12.6±0.1).

Section 10 generalizes dropout to multiplicative Gaussian noise: hidden activations can be multiplied by r0 ~ N(1,σ²), which is equivalent to adding Gaussian noise with zero mean and standard deviation proportional to the activation. The paper notes that if σ² = (1-p)/p, the Gaussian multiplier and the Bernoulli multiplier have the same mean (1) and variance ((1-p)/p). It also reframes Bernoulli dropout as multiplying by 1/p with probability p and 0 otherwise. The section argues that, among distributions with the same first two moments, the Gaussian has higher entropy than the Bernoulli. Table 10 compares Bernoulli vs Gaussian dropout on MNIST and CIFAR-10 (averaged over 10 random seeds) and suggests the Gaussian/high-entropy version performs slightly better.

The paper concludes that dropout is a broadly useful technique, not specific to any domain, with reported state-of-the-art results on SVHN, ImageNet, CIFAR-100, and MNIST. It also extends dropout to RBMs and says Dropout RBMs have desirable properties. A drawback is longer training: dropout networks typically take 2–3x longer than standard nets because the gradients are noisy and each case trains a different random sub-model. The paper notes that marginalizing the noise can yield an equivalent regularizer in expectation; for linear regression this becomes a modified L2 regularization.

Appendix A gives practical heuristics. Because dropout leaves only pn units active in expectation, a good dropout net should often have at least n/p hidden units if n is optimal without dropout. Dropout introduces extra gradient noise, so the recommended learning rate is about 10–100x that used for standard nets, with momentum around 0.95–0.99 rather than 0.9. Max-norm regularization is suggested to prevent weights from growing too large, with typical max-norm c around 3–4. Typical hidden-unit retention probabilities p are 0.5–0.8; p=1 means no dropout. For real-valued inputs such as image patches or speech frames, a typical input-layer retention probability is 0.8.

Appendix B gives detailed experimental setups. MNIST: 60,000 training and 10,000 test images; 10,000 training images were held out for validation. Hyperparameters were tuned to best validation error after 1 million updates, then validation was merged back into training and the model trained for another 1 million updates. The MNIST architectures in Figure 4 cover all 2-, 3-, and 4-layer nets with 1024 or 2048 units (six architectures total). For these, hidden-layer retention was p=0.5, input retention p=0.8, final momentum 0.95, and max-norm c=2. Larger 4096/8192-unit 2- and 3-layer nets were also tested; 2-layer nets improved, 3-layer nets were slightly worse, though more dropout helped somewhat.

SVHN: about 600,000 training and 26,000 test images. The validation set had 6000 examples, with 400 per class from the standard set and 200 per class from the extra set. Inputs were RGB pixels normalized to zero mean and unit variance; contrast normalization and ZCA whitening did not help. Best SVHN model: 3 conv layers (96, 128, 256 filters), each 5x5 stride 1 followed by 3x3 max-pooling stride 2, then two fully connected ReLU layers of 2048 units. Dropout retention probabilities from input through layers were (0.9, 0.75, 0.75, 0.5, 0.5, 0.5), with max-norm c=4 and momentum 0.95. Validation was kept separate because the training set was large, and test error was reported for the model with smallest validation error.

Paper: "Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting" (JMLR 15, 2014, pp. 1929–1958). Authors: Nitish Srivastava, Geoffrey Hinton, Alex Krizhevsky, Ilya Sutskever, and Ruslan Salakhutdinov (University of Toronto); editor Yoshua Bengio. The paper map on the first pages lays out the structure across sections 2–11 plus appendices A and B. Abstract/intro claims: dropout randomly removes units and their connections during training, reducing co-adaptation and implicitly sampling exponentially many thinned networks; a single unthinned network with reduced weights approximates the averaged predictions. It claims dropout reduces overfitting and improves results across vision, speech recognition, document classification, and computational biology, often state of the art. Section 1 also says posterior-weighted averaging is the best regularization given unlimited computation, while dropout approximates an equally weighted geometric mean over exponentially many shared-parameter models. A network with n units corresponds to 2^n thinned networks and reuses O(n^2) or fewer parameters. The introduction contrasts dropout with stopping early, soft weight sharing, and L1/L2 penalties, and says model combination is powerful but expensive. It introduces the practical inference rule (weight scaling) versus Monte Carlo model averaging, and notes dropout extends to graphical models such as Boltzmann machines, including Restricted Boltzmann Machines and dropout RBMs. Figure 1 shows a standard two-hidden-layer net and a thinned version with crossed units removed.

Section 2 motivates dropout using analogies from evolution and robustness. It contrasts sexual vs asexual reproduction: recombination breaks co-adapted gene sets, suggesting a tension between individual-fitness optimization and the value of mixable, robust genes. The Livnat et al. view is that selection may favor gene sets that work with many partners; the paper maps this to hidden units trained with dropout, which must be useful with randomly selected partners and thus learn independently useful, robust features rather than depend on other units. It also uses a conspiracy analogy: smaller conspiracies are more robust to changing conditions than a larger one needing many correct participants. These examples support the claim that complex co-adaptations can fit training data yet generalize poorly, whereas simpler robust components may generalize better.

Section 3 surveys related work on noise-based regularization. It frames hidden-unit noise as a regularizer for QX2, connecting it to denoising autoencoders (Vincent et al. 2008, 2010): input corruption plus reconstruction, effective hidden-layer corruption, model averaging, supervised and unsupervised use, and applicability to other neuron-based architectures such as Boltzmann machines. A comparison table says typical best noise is 5% for S2H, while QX2 often works best at 20% input-unit removal or 50% hidden-unit removal. It contrasts stochastic noise training with adversarial removal methods (Globerson and Roweis 2006; Dekel et al. 2010), noting those have no hidden units. It also says analytically marginalizing QX2 yields deterministic regularizers in simple cases; related exponential-family input-noise regularizers (“blankout noise”) were studied by van der Maaten et al. (2013) for models without hidden layers. Chen et al. (2012) examined marginalization for denoising autoencoders, and Wang and Manning (2013) proposed marginalization to accelerate QX2.

steps.notes_before: Section 4 defines QX2 as stochastic deletion (“dropout”) applied to every layer: each layer output vector is multiplied elementwise by an independent Bernoulli mask with retention probability \(p\). Training samples a subnetwork and backpropagates through it; both hidden and visible units can be removed. At test time, no units are removed and the outgoing weights are scaled by \(p\): \(\mathbf W^{(l)}_{	ext{test}}=p\mathbf W^{(l)}\). The section states that validation can choose \(p\), but the default is usually near optimal and input retention is often closer to 1. It also claims that the expected output under deletion matches test-time output, though the formulas only directly show this for the preactivation, not necessarily after a nonlinear activation.

Section 5 says QX2 training uses standard SGD on a per-case sampled thinned network: each case is forwarded/backpropagated through its own sampled subnetwork, gradients are averaged, and absent parameters contribute zero. It highlights that QX2 works well with high momentum, large decaying learning rates, and V9C max-norm regularization, where each incoming hidden-unit weight vector is constrained by ||w||_2 <= c and projected back onto the radius-c ball if it exceeds it. The section also notes that this constraint is a validation-tuned hyperparameter and can help deep-net training even without QX2. For unsupervised pretraining, the procedure is unchanged, but before QX2 finetuning pretrained weights are multiplied by 1/p so that expected random-removal output matches the pretrained output. Smaller finetuning learning rates are said to preserve pretrained information better than rates comparable to best randomly initialized-net rates.

Section 6 reports experimental results across seven data sets: H4Z/MNIST, A2F/SVHN, J3V/CIFAR-10, W6R/CIFAR-100, K9D/ImageNet (ILSVRC-2012), N8Q/TIMIT, M5X/Reuters-RCV1, and Z7P/Alternative Splicing. For H4Z, Table 2 shows errors decreasing from a standard NN (1.60) to QX2 logistic (1.35), QX2 ReLU (1.25), QX2+V9C (1.06 to 0.95 as size increases), and maxout (0.94). Abstract claims dropout randomly removes units during training, samples an exponential number of thinned networks, and uses one unthinned network with smaller weights at test time to approximate their average predictions. It says dropout reduces overfitting and improves supervised-learning performance on vision, speech recognition, document classification, and computational-biology tasks, with state-of-the-art results on many benchmarks. It also says dropout outperforms other regularization methods.

Introduction claims deep nets overfit limited data and reviews standard regularization (early stopping, L1/L2, soft weight sharing). The paper’s goal is to approximate Bayesian model averaging / an equally weighted geometric mean of predictions from exponentially many parameter-sharing models at low cost. Dropout randomly removes hidden or visible units during training; in the simplest case each unit is retained independently with probability p (often p=0.5 for hidden units, closer to 1 for inputs). A thinned network is sampled for each training case. At test time, dropout is turned off and outgoing weights are multiplied by p so expected training-time output matches test-time output. A network with n units represents 2^n thinned networks with shared weights, making explicit averaging infeasible. The paper claims dropout reduces generalization error and also applies to RBMs. Section roadmap: 2 motivation, 3 related work, 4 model, 5 training, 6 experiments, 7 network properties/hyperparameters, 8 Dropout RBMs, 9 marginalizing dropout, Appendix A practical guidance.

This part begins Section 2 (Motivation) and uses two analogies to explain why dropout should help: (1) sexual reproduction/mix-ability—useful genes must work with random partners, so hidden units trained with dropout should become robust and not rely on specific co-adaptations; and (2) conspiracies—smaller groups are more likely to keep working under changing conditions than one large tightly coordinated group. The section’s conclusion is that complex co-adaptations may fit training data but are more likely to fail on test data than several simpler co-adaptations.

Section 7 examines why dropout helps. In 7.1, it compares 256-ReLU MNIST autoencoders with and without hidden-layer dropout p=0.5; both have similar test reconstruction error, but the dropout model’s learned features look more like edges/strokes/spots, while the no-dropout model appears co-adapted and less meaningful. In 7.2, the same autoencoders are evaluated on a random test mini-batch: dropout yields sparser hidden activations, with mean activation dropping from about 2.0 to about 0.7 and a sharp peak at zero. In 7.3, dropout rate p is varied on MNIST. With fixed network size 784-2048-2048-2048-10, low p underfits, error decreases as p increases, is flat for roughly 0.4 to 0.8, then rises as p approaches 1. The section also studies a setting where expected retained units pn is held fixed, implying smaller p requires larger networks.

Section 7.3: With fixed architecture 784-2048-2048-2048-10, dropout error is flat for roughly 0.4<=p<=0.8, low p underfits, and error rises as p approaches 1. In the variant that keeps expected retained units fixed (pn=256 for the first two hidden layers and pn=512 for the last), low-p performance improves substantially; at p=0.1 error drops from 2.7% to 1.7%. In that setting, p near 0.6 is best and 0.5 is close to optimal. Section 7.4 varies MNIST training-set size (100, 500, 1K, 5K, 10K, 50K) with architecture 784-1024-1024-2048-10, hidden-layer retention 0.5 and input retention 0.8; dropout gives no improvement at 100 and 500 cases, and its benefit first increases then declines as data size grows. Section 7.5 compares Monte-Carlo model averaging with weight scaling on MNIST: averaging about k=50 sampled networks matches weight scaling, and further sampling is only slightly better, within one standard deviation.

Section 8 defines Dropout RBMs as RBMs augmented with a binary mask r over hidden units, where each r_j is 1 with probability p. Conditioned on r, the model is an RBM with the dropped hidden units removed; the hidden conditional factorizes with P(h_j=1|r_j,v)=1(r_j=1)σ(b_j+Σ_i W_ij v_i), and visible conditionals are unchanged from a standard RBM. Learning uses standard RBM methods such as CD-1 after sampling a new dropout mask for each training case in each mini-batch. Qualitatively, on MNIST with 256 hidden units and p=0.5, dropout RBM features appear coarser and have fewer dead units than standard RBM features. Dropout also yields sparser hidden activations than a standard RBM, even without an explicit sparsity regularizer, as shown by the activation histograms in Figure 13.

Section 9 discusses marginalizing dropout noise to obtain deterministic models. It cites related work by Globerson and Roweis, Chen et al., Srivastava, Wang and Manning, van der Maaten et al., and Wager et al. For linear regression, with input mask R_{ij}~Bernoulli(p), the marginalized objective is E||y-(R*X)w||^2, which reduces to ||y-pXw||^2 + p(1-p)||Γw||^2 where Γ = diag(X^T X)^{1/2}. After rescaling w~ = p w, this becomes ||y-X w~||^2 + ((1-p)/p)||Γ w~||^2, so the regularization strength increases as p decreases. For logistic regression and deep networks, closed-form marginalization is said to be difficult; Wang and Manning’s approximation uses Gaussian means/variances for inputs and gradients, improves training time and generalization for logistic regression, but does not directly extend to deep networks.

Section 10 introduces multiplicative Gaussian noise as an alternative to Bernoulli dropout. A hidden activation can be written as h_i + h_i r with r ~ N(0,1), equivalently h_i r' with r' ~ N(1,1). More generally, r' ~ N(1, σ^2) with σ as a tunable hyperparameter. The section also describes the rescaled Bernoulli formulation: retained activations are multiplied by 1/p at training, with test weights unchanged, giving multiplier r_b = 1/p with probability p and 0 otherwise; then E[r_b]=1 and Var[r_b]=(1-p)/p. Matching moments sets Gaussian variance σ^2=(1-p)/p, so r_g has the same mean/variance. The paper claims Gaussian has higher entropy than Bernoulli and both work well. Table 10 reports slightly better Gaussian results on MNIST (0.95 ± 0.04 vs 1.08 ± 0.04) and CIFAR-10 (12.5 ± 0.1 vs 12.6 ± 0.1), averaged over 10 random seeds. For MNIST, Bernoulli p values are 0.5 for hidden units and 0.8 for inputs; for CIFAR-10, p = (0.9, 0.75, 0.75, 0.5, 0.5, 0.5) from input to top.

Section 11 concludes that dropout reduces overfitting by breaking co-adaptations, and summarizes its broad empirical success across object classification, digit recognition, speech recognition, document classification, and computational-biology tasks. It claims dropout-based methods achieve state-of-the-art results on SVHN, ImageNet, CIFAR-100, and MNIST. The conclusion also says the idea extends to RBMs and other graphical models via training on sampled smaller sub-models, with RBMs fitting this framework and showing desirable properties. A major drawback is that dropout training typically takes 2–3 times longer than standard training because updates are noisy and optimize random architectures rather than the final test network. The section notes marginalizing the noise can yield a modified L2 regularizer for linear regression, but a general equivalent regularizer is unclear.
