Appendix A gives practical dropout heuristics: use larger layers, about n/p units if n is optimal without dropout; learning rates about 10–100 times standard; momentum around 0.95–0.99 instead of 0.9; max-norm c typically 3–4; hidden retention probabilities typically 0.5–0.8, with 0.8 typical for real-valued image patches or speech frames. Smaller p requires larger n and can slow training/underfit; too large p may under-regularize.

Appendix B gives experiment/data details. MNIST: 60k train/10k test, with 10k held out for validation; after hyperparameter selection, training and validation were reunited and the model was trained for 1M updates. Figure 4 uses all 2-, 3-, and 4-hidden-layer combinations with 1024 or 2048 units; these and Table 2 use hidden p=0.5, input p=0.8, momentum 0.95, c=2. Larger 2-layer networks (4096, 8192) improved results; 3-layer networks were slightly worse. SVHN: ~600k train and 26k test images, with a 6000-case validation set made from 400 standard + 200 extra per class; no data was added back for final training. Best model: 3 conv layers (96/128/256 filters, 5x5, stride 1), each with 3x3 max-pooling stride 2, then two 2048-unit ReLU layers; dropout p=(0.9,0.75,0.75,0.5,0.5,0.5), c=4, momentum 0.95. CIFAR-10/100: 50k train/10k test, 5000 validation images, then validation merged back; preprocessing used per-channel global contrast normalization and ZCA whitening; architecture and dropout matched SVHN except smaller input-layer learning rates. The paper studies dropout as a method to prevent overfitting in large neural networks by randomly removing units/connections during training, effectively training many smaller shared-parameter networks and using a single scaled network at test time. It claims dropout improves generalization over non-dropout networks on every tested dataset, with experiments across images, speech, documents, and gene-splicing prediction. The paper says it reports state-of-the-art results on several benchmarks and also examines learned features, sparsity, retention rates, training-set size, RBMs, noise marginalization, and Gaussian corruption. Training is said to take about 2–3 times longer than a standard network of the same architecture.

The paper’s glossary defines the main dropout-related terms and abbreviations used later. Dropout is described as random removal of units and connections during training, with approximate averaging by one unthinned network at test time; thinned networks are subnetworks formed by removing units/connections. It defines core neural-network terms (units, hidden/visible layers, weights, biases, activations), regularizers (L1, L2/Tikhonov, max-norm, KL-sparsity, early stopping), and averaging concepts (model averaging, posterior-weighted averaging, geometric mean, weight scaling, Monte-Carlo averaging). It also names Bernoulli dropout, Gaussian dropout, and dropout-related noise/marginalization ideas. The glossary covers training procedures and settings such as backpropagation, SGD, mini-batches, momentum, learning rate/annealing, hyperparameters, validation, pretraining, finetuning, and CD-1. It also lists architectures and baselines used later: convolutional nets, pooling types, data augmentation, SVM, PCA, linear/ridge/logistic regression, Bayesian neural networks, bag-of-words, sparse representations, RBMs/DBMs/DBNs, dropout RBM, autoencoders, and some later comparison-specific notions like dead units, mix-ability, replica code, and non-stationarity.

This part is the title/front-matter page for the paper “Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting,” listing the five authors and their University of Toronto affiliations. It also gives an original-page map for the rest of the paper: pages 1930–1955 cover the introduction, figures, sections 2–11, table 1–10, acknowledgments, Appendix A (A.1–A.4), and Appendix B (B.1–B.6). No new technical notation or results appear in this part.

This part contains the abstract of the paper. It claims that dropout (referred to here as “QX2, or dropout”) temporarily removes randomly selected units and their connections during training, inhibits co-adaptation, samples exponentially many thinned networks sharing parameters, and that a single unthinned network with reduced weights approximates their averaged predictions. It also claims that dropout substantially reduces overfitting and improves results across vision, speech recognition, document classification, and computational biology, with evidence in Tables 2–8 and the unnumbered text-classification table in §6.3. No new notation or contradictions appear here.

This part is the Introduction. It says QX2/dropout trains many shared-parameter subnetworks and uses a single unthinned test-time network to approximate their combined predictions. It frames the method as approximating an equally weighted geometric mean of exponentially many learned models, with a network of n units corresponding to 2^n possible thinned networks but only O(n^2) or fewer parameters. It introduces standard regularizers/terms: early stopping, soft weight sharing, L1 (O3U), and L2 (Y5F). It also says model combination usually helps but is expensive, and that the practical inference rule T6R/weight scaling uses one unthinned network; X9M/Monte-Carlo model averaging samples members at test time. It claims T6R has lower generalization error than compared regularizers, citing Table 9 rows Y5F 1.62, V9C 1.35, QX2+Y5F 1.25, and QX2+V9C 1.05. It also introduces extension to graphical models via RBMs, with B8T/Dropout RBM. No contradictions found yet.

This part gives the paper’s motivation for dropout/QX2 using biological and game-theoretic analogies. It argues that breaking co-adapted gene sets via sexual reproduction can be advantageous because it favors ‘mix-ability’ and robustness, even if it seems worse for preserving successful combinations. It then maps this to QX2-trained hidden units: because hidden units face randomly selected partners, the method encourages independently useful, robust features rather than reliance on other units. The part also uses a conspiracy analogy to suggest that smaller interacting groups may be more robust under changing conditions than one large, fragile coordinated group. No direct contradictions with earlier sections are introduced here.

This part is the related-work section. It frames QX2 as connected to hidden-unit noise, model averaging, and earlier work on corruption, adversarial deletion, and marginalization. It says denoising autoencoders (S2H) corrupt inputs and reconstruct clean inputs, while QX2 extends this with effective hidden-layer corruption and a model-averaging interpretation. QX2 is claimed to apply to supervised and unsupervised learning and to other neuron-based architectures, including Boltzmann machines. It also contrasts QX2 with adversarial-removal models (Globerson and Roweis 2006; Dekel et al. 2010), which choose deletions under a fixed maximum rather than a probability distribution and are said to have no hidden units. Van der Maaten et al. (2013) are described as studying exponential-family input-noise regularizers, including QX2 under the name blankout noise, limited to models without hidden layers; Chen et al. (2012) studied marginalization for DAEs; Wang and Manning (2013) proposed marginalization to accelerate QX2. The table reports noise levels: S2H typical best 5%, QX2 often optimal input-unit removal 20%, and QX2 often optimal hidden-unit removal 50%.

steps.notes_before: Section 4 defines QX2/dropout-style corruption as independent Bernoulli gating of unit outputs during training: each entry \(r_j^{(l)}\sim Bernoulli(p)\), and \(	ilde y^{(l)} = r^{(l)} * y^{(l)}\). Ordinary feed-forward is \(z_i^{(l+1)}=w_i^{(l+1)} y^{(l)} + b_i^{(l+1)}\), \(y_i^{(l+1)}=f(z_i^{(l+1)})\); QX2 replaces \(y^{(l)}\) with \(	ilde y^{(l)}\). Any activation is allowed, including logistic. Applying the gating at every layer samples a subnetwork; backpropagation runs through that sampled subnetwork. Both hidden and visible units can be removed. At inference, no units are removed and weights are scaled as \(W^{(l)}_{test}=pW^{(l)}\).

Section 5 says QX2 training/backprop is ordinary backprop on a sampled thinned network: each mini-batch case uses its own sampled subnetwork, gradients are averaged, and unused parameters get zero gradient. The section argues that combining QX2 with high momentum, large decaying learning rates, and max-norm/V9C gives additional gains; V9C constrains each hidden unit’s incoming-weight vector to norm <= c, with projection back to the radius-c ball and c tuned on validation. It also offers a qualitative optimization story (weight ball allows large learning rates; QX2 noise explores weight space; decay shortens steps). For finetuning pretrained nets, smaller learning rates are important; too-large rates can erase pretrained information. Before QX2 finetuning, pretrained weights are multiplied by 1/p to preserve expected outputs under random removal. QX2 finetuning can be applied after pretraining from stacked U2L, autoencoders, or E5Q/DBMs. Reported evidence includes table values showing QX2 improving finetuning results (e.g., G6W: 1.18 to 0.92; E5Q: 0.96 to 0.79) and a best QX2 finetuning rate around 0.01 versus a higher listed rate of 0.1.

Section 6.5 compares regularizers on H4Z and reports QX2+V9C as the best listed result (1.05), ahead of QX2+Y5F (1.25) and non-QX2 baselines (1.62, 1.60, 1.55, 1.35).

Section 7 discusses qualitative effects of QX2. Section 7.1 says QX2 autoencoders learn more localized visual features (edges, strokes, spots) than identical non-QX2 autoencoders, even though reconstruction errors are described as similar; the explanation offered is reduced co-adaptation, not a separate numerical test. Section 7.2 says QX2 produces sparser hidden activations without a sparsity regularizer; the comparison table reports mean activation about 2.0 without QX2 vs about 0.7 with QX2, with a sharp zero peak under QX2 and substantial off-zero mass without it. Section 7.3 says with fixed architecture, retention shows a U-shaped error pattern: an intermediate flat interval \(0.4\le p\le 0.8\), with \(p=0.1\) giving high error; when expected retained width is held fixed, low-retention error drops from 2.7% to 1.7%, and the best retention for the chosen widths is close to 0.6, with 0.5 near optimal. Lower-retention networks are larger under fixed expected width. Section 7.4 begins a data-set-size discussion and states that the QX2 gain is absent for the smallest sets, grows with more data, and then declines.

Section 7.4 says the QX2 benefit depends on training-set size: the two smallest sets show no improvement, then the gain increases and later decreases. The paper frames this as a “sweet spot” where there is enough data to resist noisy memorization but not so much that overfitting stops mattering. It says standard training of huge nets on small collections massively overfits, and no separate numerical test is given for the memorization explanation. Figure 10 compares H4Z error for With QX2 vs Without QX2 across dataset sizes; Appendix B.1 lists sizes 100, 500, 1K, 5K, 10K, 50K.

Section 7.5 compares X9M to T6R. With enough samples, X9M matches T6R and then becomes slightly better, within one standard deviation, so T6R is described as a fairly good approximation to the true model average. The comparison varies sample count k and uses a horizontal T6R reference; the table says X9M becomes as good as T6R at around k=50. Figure 11 plots X9M vs an approximate averaging baseline by T6R over k=0 to 120.

Section 8 introduces B8T, a dropout-style extension of shared-weight RBMs/U2L models. It defines a retention vector r over hidden units and gives the joint P(r,h,v)=P(r)P(h,v|r), with each hidden unit independently retained with probability p. Conditional hidden activations factorize, and dropped hidden units are forced to 0; the visible conditional remains the standard U2L form. Learning uses ordinary Contrastive Divergence (CD-1): sample r for each training case and train only the retained hidden units, with a different r per case per mini-batch.

The section claims B8T features are coarser and have fewer dead units than ordinary U2L features. Figure 12 shows 256-hidden-unit models ordered by L2 norm, comparing ordinary U2L to B8T with p=0.5. No numerical feature-quality or dead-unit counts are reported.

It also claims B8T learns much sparser representations without an additional sparsity regularizer. Figure 13 is described as contrasting many off-zero activations without QX2 against many near-zero and very few high activations with p=0.5. No numerical sparsity measure is provided.

Section 9 discusses marginalizing QX2/dropout noise to obtain deterministic objectives and regularizers. It cites prior work: Globerson and Roweis on robustness to feature deletion, Srivastava on QX2 marginalization for linear regression, and Wager et al. on QX2 as an adaptive regularizer.

For linear regression, with input matrix X, targets y, weights w, and Bernoulli retention matrix R (entries iid with probability p), the expected dropout objective is claimed to reduce to ||y - pXw||^2 + p(1-p)||Gamma w||^2, where Gamma = (diag(X^T X))^{1/2}. After rescaling w~ = p w, this becomes ||y - X w~||^2 + ((1-p)/p)||Gamma w~||^2. The section emphasizes that weights on high-variance dimensions are penalized more strongly and that the regularization coefficient grows as p decreases.

For logistic regression, the section says approximate marginalization (Wang and Manning 2013) improves training time and generalization over Monte Carlo QX2. It also states that closed-form marginalization is difficult for logistic regression and deep nets; under reasonable assumptions, logistic-unit inputs and marginalized gradients are Gaussian, but these assumptions weaken with depth, so the results do not directly apply to deep networks.

Section 10 introduces multiplicative Gaussian noise as an alternative to Bernoulli (binary) dropout. It claims preliminary experiments suggest Gaussian multiplicative corruption performs as well as, or slightly better than, Bernoulli dropout, and Table 10 reports classification error (%) on H4Z and J3V: H4Z 1.08±0.04 (Bernoulli) vs 0.95±0.04 (Gaussian); J3V 12.6±0.1 vs 12.5±0.1. The comparison uses 10 random seeds. The paper says the two variants can be matched by first and second moments. For Bernoulli retention p, the corresponding Gaussian multiplier is N(1,σ^2) with σ^2=(1-p)/p, giving mean 1 and variance (1-p)/p for both. It also states Gaussian has the highest entropy among distributions with those moments. For multiplicative Gaussian noise, expected activations are unchanged, so test-time scaling is unnecessary. The section presents two equivalent training/test representations, one keeping activations unchanged and scaling test weights by p, the other scaling retained activations by 1/p and leaving test weights unchanged.

Section 11 concludes that QX2 improves generalization by training sampled submodels, but this comes with a training-time cost. It reiterates that QX2/U2L/B8T methods achieve state of the art on A2F, K9D, W6R, and H4Z, and improve standard neural nets on other datasets. Specific cited results are A2F error 2.47 (Table 3), K9D top-5 test error 16.4 (Table 6), W6R error 37.20 (Table 4), H4Z error 0.79 (Table 2), plus other improvements from Table 7 (23.4 vs 21.8), a §6.3 table (31.05% vs 29.62%), and Table 8 (440 vs 567). The section claims training typically takes 2–3 times as long as a standard network because noisy parameter updates are a major cause and each case trains a different random architecture, so the gradients are not those of the final inference architecture. It argues stochasticity likely helps prevent overfitting, creating a trade-off between training time and overfitting. Noise marginalization is presented as a way to capture some benefits without stochasticity via an expectation-equivalent regularizer; for linear regression this yields modified Y5F, while analogous regularizers for more complex models are not obvious. No timing table is given, and the causal/trade-off language is framed as likely rather than definitive.

Appendix A gives practical heuristics for QX2 training and reiterates that extensive hyperparameter tuning is still needed. It recommends wider QX2 layers: if a standard layer’s optimum is n units, QX2 should use at least n/p units, since only pn units survive in expectation. It reports this heuristic as useful for both convolutional and fully connected layers. For optimization, it says higher learning rates and momentum help because QX2 introduces more gradient noise; a table lists learning rates typically 10–100 times the optimal standard-net rate and momentum around 0.95–0.99 (vs common standard-net 0.9). It also recommends max-norm bounds c≈3–4. For retention, hidden-layer p is coupled to width, with typical hidden ranges 0.5–0.8, real-valued inputs typically 0.8, a broadly near-optimal default 0.5, and input-unit optimum in general closer to 1 than to 0.5.

Appendix B provides reproduction code and detailed experimental settings. B.1 (H4Z) says validation images were held out, hyperparameters were selected by best validation error at a fixed endpoint, then training and validation data were combined for a final run to the same endpoint before test evaluation. The H4Z settings table lists 10,000 held-out validation images, a 1,000,000-update endpoint, architecture sweeps over 2/3/4 hidden layers with widths 1024 or 2048, hidden retention p=0.5, input retention p=0.8, momentum 0.95, max-norm c=2, and several comparison setups including a 784-1024-1024-2048-10 architecture, data-size comparisons, fixed-width comparisons, and fixed-expected-width comparisons (pn=256 for the first two hidden layers and pn=512 for the last). It states larger two-layer networks improve performance, three-layer counterparts are slightly worse at the same QX2 level, and stronger QX2 improves three-layer nets without surpassing the two-layer nets. X9M is described as test-time averaging over k sampled thinned networks, approaching the true model average as k→∞.

B.2 (A2F) says the training set includes a standard labeled portion plus extra easy examples, and validation is drawn from both. RGB inputs are normalized to zero mean/unit variance; contrast normalization and ZCA whitening did not help. The A2F architecture uses three convolutional layers with 96, 128, 256 filters, 5x5 receptive fields, stride 1, max-pooling 3x3 with stride 2 after each conv layer, then two fully connected hidden layers of 2048 units. All hidden activations are F3N. Retention is p=(0.9,0.75,0.75,0.5,0.5,0.5), V9C uses c=4, and momentum is 0.95.

Appendix B continues with experiment details. B.2 (A2F) says validation tuned hyperparameters; the large training set stayed separate from validation during final training, and the model with the smallest validation error gave the reported test error. The section notes that alternative normalization/whitening methods gave no noticeable improvement. The A2F setup in the table includes 6000 validation samples, 96/128/256 conv filters, two 2048-unit fully connected layers, and the same retention/momentum/V9C settings recorded earlier (F3N activations; p=(0.9,0.75,0.75,0.5,0.5,0.5); c=4; momentum 0.95).

B.3 (J3V/W6R) says these image sets use held-out validation, contrast normalization, ZCA whitening, and the A2F architecture. Each has 50,000 training and 10,000 test images; J3V has 10 classes and W6R has 100. Validation uses 5,000 training images, and after hyperparameter selection, training and validation are combined for optimization, as in H4Z. Preprocessing applies global contrast normalization per image/color channel (subtracting that channel’s mean pixel intensity) and then ZCA whitening. Architecture and retention match A2F, but input-layer learning rates need to be smaller.

B.4 (N8Q) uses 680 speakers, 8 dialects, 10 sentences each, Kaldi log-filter-bank features, forced alignments from a monophone system, 21-frame windows, mean-centered/unit-variance inputs, p=0.8 input retention, p=0.5 hidden retention, c=4, momentum 0.95, learning-rate schedule \(\epsilon_0(1+t/T)^{-1}\), CD-1 pretraining, and best QX2 finetuning learning rate about 0.01; V9C did not help.

B.5 (M5X) uses a 402,738-document Reuters subset with 50 disjoint categories, 2000-word vocabulary, and equal-size train/test splits.

final_notes:
B.4 TIMIT: Used Kaldi to preprocess into log-filter banks; forced alignment from a monophone system produced frame labels. Trained dropout nets on 21-frame windows to predict the central frame. No speaker-dependent operations. Inputs were mean-centered and unit-variance normalized. Retention probabilities were p=0.8 input, p=0.5 hidden; max-norm c=4; momentum 0.95; learning rate 0.1 with decay ε0(1+t/T)^{-1}. For DBN pretraining, used CD-1 RBMs with Gaussian RBM input variance fixed to 1. For dropout finetuning, a smaller learning rate (~0.01) was important; max-norm gave no improvement.

B.5 Reuters: RCV1 has >800k documents and 103 hierarchical classes. They built a subset with 402,738 articles, 2000-word vocabulary, 50 flat categories (each doc in exactly one class). Data split equally into train/test. Dropout improved accuracy across tried architectures, but less than on image/speech data, likely because the dataset is large and overfitting is less severe.

B.6 Alternative Splicing: Dataset has 3665 cassette exons, 1014 RNA features, and 4 tissue types from 27 mouse tissues. Each input has 4 softmax units (one per tissue type), each with 3 states: inc, exc, nc. Metric is a custom “Code Quality” based on predicted vs target state distributions normalized by average target probabilities. They used a 2-layer dropout net with 1024 units per layer; p=0.7 input and p=0.5 hidden; max-norm regularization and high decaying learning rates; results averaged over the same 5 folds as Xiong et al. (2011).

Paper: “Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting” (JMLR 2014). Main claim: dropout randomly drops units and their connections during training, causing an exponential number of thinned networks to be sampled; at test time, one can approximate averaging over them with a single unthinned network using smaller weights. Abstract says this reduces overfitting and improves supervised learning performance in vision, speech recognition, document classification, and computational biology, with state-of-the-art results on many benchmarks. Introduction frames dropout as a regularization method for deep nets, alongside early stopping and weight penalties (L1/L2, soft weight sharing). Figure 1 illustrates a standard neural net vs. a thinned net produced by dropout.

The paper motivates dropout as an approximation to Bayesian model averaging / geometric mean over an exponential number of shared-parameter networks, aiming for good performance with less computation. It argues that averaging many separately trained nets is expensive because diverse nets require different architectures or data and are costly to train/test. Dropout drops hidden and visible units (removing incoming/outgoing connections) at random during training; each unit is retained independently with probability p, typically 0.5 for many layers, while input units usually use p closer to 1. Figure 2 states that at test time all units are present and outgoing weights are multiplied by p, so the test-time network matches the expected training-time output.

Dropout is presented as approximating Bayesian model averaging / geometric mean over an exponential number of shared-parameter subnetworks, reducing computation versus training many separate networks. During training, units are independently retained with probability p; hidden units often use p=0.5, while input units usually use p closer to 1. At test time, all units are present and outgoing weights are multiplied by p so the test-time network matches the expected training-time output. This part adds intuition for dropout via analogies to sexual reproduction and conspiracies: training each hidden unit to work with random subsets of others should make features more robust and less dependent on co-adaptations. It also says the paper will extend dropout to RBMs and discuss experiments, analysis of hyperparameters, marginalizing dropout, and practical guidance in the appendix.

The paper’s intro says dropout extends denoising autoencoders: it can be applied to hidden layers, interpreted as model averaging, and extended beyond unsupervised learning to supervised problems and other neuron-based architectures such as Boltzmann Machines. It also notes that although 5% noise is typical for denoising autoencoders, their weight-scaling-at-test-time approach allows much higher dropout rates; they report 20% input dropout and 50% hidden dropout as often optimal. The paper then motivates deterministic versions by marginalizing the noise, citing prior work on deterministic regularizers and dropout marginalization, and contrasts dropout with adversarial unit-dropping methods.

Model description: for a network with L hidden layers, y^(0)=x, layer l has weights W^(l) and biases b^(l). Standard feedforward uses z^(l+1)=w^(l+1) y^(l)+b^(l+1), y^(l+1)=f(z^(l+1)). With dropout, a Bernoulli mask r^(l) with retention probability p is sampled for each layer, the thinned outputs y~^(l)=r^(l)*y^(l) are passed to the next layer, and this is done at every layer. Training backpropagates through the sampled subnetwork. At test time, dropout is removed and weights are scaled by p: W_test = p W^(l). The next section starts the training procedure for dropout neural nets.

Section 5.1: Dropout nets are trained with SGD by sampling a thinned network per training case; forward/backprop are run only on that thinned network, gradients are averaged over the mini-batch, and units not used contribute zero gradient. Usual SGD improvements (momentum, annealed learning rates, L2 decay) also help. A particularly useful regularizer is max-norm: constrain each hidden unit’s incoming weight vector w to satisfy ||w||2 ≤ c by projecting back onto the ball of radius c; c is tuned on validation. The paper says dropout + max-norm + large decaying learning rates + high momentum works better than dropout alone.

Section 5.2: Dropout can be used to fine-tune pretrained nets (RBMs, autoencoders, DBMs) without changing the pretraining procedure. Weights from pretraining should be scaled up by 1/p so the expected output under dropout matches pretraining. Smaller finetuning learning rates are needed; with them, pretrained information is retained and final generalization improves versus finetuning without dropout.

Section 6 begins experiments: they evaluate dropout on classification tasks across many domains and claim dropout improved generalization on all data sets compared to non-dropout neural nets. Listed data sets: MNIST, TIMIT, CIFAR-10/100, SVHN, ImageNet, Reuters-RCV1, and an Alternative Splicing data set. A detailed description is deferred to Appendix B.

Section 7.3 starts an analysis of varying dropout rate p, comparing cases where hidden units are held constant vs where expected retained units are held constant.

Section 7.3 studies varying dropout rate on MNIST. Two settings: (1) keep architecture fixed using a 784-2048-2048-2048-10 network with no input dropout; small p causes underfitting, test and training error are high; error decreases as p increases, is flat for 0.4 <= p <= 0.8, then rises as p approaches 1. (2) keep pn fixed so expected retained units are constant across architectures; use pn=256 for first two hidden layers and pn=512 for last hidden layer. In this setting small-p performance improves substantially versus fixed architecture (example: p=0.1 test error drops from 2.7% to 1.7%), best p is around 0.6, and default p=0.5 is close to optimal. Section 7.4 varies MNIST dataset size (100, 500, 1K, 5K, 10K, 50K) with the 784-1024-1024-2048-10 network; dropout uses p=0.5 on hidden layers and p=0.8 on input. Dropout gives no benefit for very small datasets (100, 500), improvement grows with data size up to a point, then declines; this is described as a 'sweet spot.' Section 7.5 begins comparing Monte Carlo model averaging to approximate averaging by weight scaling at test time.

Section 7.5 compares Monte Carlo model averaging with approximate averaging by weight scaling on MNIST. Sampling k networks and averaging predictions, the test error approaches the weight-scaling error; around k = 50 the Monte Carlo method becomes as good as the approximate method, and for larger k it is slightly better but within one standard deviation, suggesting weight scaling is a good approximation to the true model average.

Section 8 introduces Dropout Restricted Boltzmann Machines (RBMs). An RBM has visible v in {0,1}^D and hidden h in {0,1}^F with energy-based distribution P(h,v;θ) ∝ exp(v^TWh + a^Th + b^Tv). Dropout RBMs add binary mask variables r_j ~ Bernoulli(p); if r_j=0, hidden unit h_j is forced to 0 via g(h_j,r_j). Conditioned on r, the model is an RBM over the retained hidden units, so a Dropout RBM is a mixture of exponentially many RBMs sharing weights. Training uses standard RBM learning (CD-1), sampling a new r for each training case in each minibatch. Section 8.3 begins comparing learned features: features from a 256-hidden-unit binary RBM vs a dropout RBM with the same size, ordered by L2 norm.

Section 8.4 studies sparsity of hidden activations in RBMs. Figure 13 compares standard RBMs and dropout RBMs on test mini-batches; the dropout RBMs are described as learning much sparser representations than standard RBMs, even without an explicit sparsity regularizer. The text also says the dropout RBM features look coarser than the standard RBM’s sharper stroke-like features, and there are very few dead units in the dropout RBM relative to the standard RBM.

Section 9 introduces marginalizing dropout noise to obtain deterministic models. These models do not require random bits and allow gradients of marginalized loss functions. For linear regression with dropout on inputs, marginalizing the Bernoulli mask yields an objective equivalent to ridge regression: ||y − pXw||^2 + p(1−p)||Γw||^2, where Γ = (diag(X^T X))^{1/2}. Reparameterizing with w̃ = pw makes the regularization strength proportional to (1−p)/p, so more dropout means stronger regularization.

For logistic regression and deep nets, no closed form is available, but Wang and Manning’s approximate marginalization applies to logistic regression; it is said to outperform Monte-Carlo dropout in training time and generalization. The paper notes this approximation becomes less directly applicable as networks get deeper. A table reports Bernoulli vs Gaussian dropout test errors: MNIST 1.08 ± 0.04 vs 0.95 ± 0.04, CIFAR-10 12.6 ± 0.1 vs 12.5 ± 0.1.

steps.notes_before: Section 10 introduces multiplicative Gaussian noise as an alternative to Bernoulli dropout: activations are multiplied by a random variable drawn from N(1,σ²), which can also be written hi + hi r with r ~ N(0,1). The text says the expected activation is unchanged, so no test-time weight scaling is needed. It then explains that standard dropout can be viewed as multiplying hi by a Bernoulli variable taking 1/p with probability p and 0 otherwise, giving mean 1 and variance (1−p)/p. Choosing Gaussian noise with σ² = (1−p)/p matches these first two moments; Bernoulli has the lowest entropy and Gaussian the highest. Table 10 compares Bernoulli and Gaussian dropout on MNIST and CIFAR-10 using layer-specific p values (MNIST: p=0.5 hidden, p=0.8 input; CIFAR-10: p=(0.9,0.75,0.75,0.5,0.5,0.5)).

Section 11 concludes that dropout is broadly effective across domains and has achieved state-of-the-art results on several benchmarks. It reiterates that dropout usually increases training time by about 2-3x because each case trains a different random submodel, but suggests marginalizing the noise can yield an equivalent regularizer in expectation; for linear regression this becomes a modified L2 regularizer. Appendix A gives practical heuristics: because only pn hidden units are present in expectation when retaining units with probability p, a dropout network should often use at least n/p units if n works well without dropout. Recommended optimization settings are learning rates 10-100x higher than standard nets, momentum around 0.95-0.99, and max-norm regularization with c around 3-4. Typical dropout retain probabilities are 0.5-0.8 for hidden units and about 0.8 for real-valued input layers; p=1 means no dropout.

Paper: "Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting" (JMLR 15, 2014, pp. 1929–1958). Authors: Nitish Srivastava, Geoffrey Hinton, Alex Krizhevsky, Ilya Sutskever, and Ruslan Salakhutdinov (University of Toronto); editor Yoshua Bengio. The paper map on the first pages lays out the structure across sections 2–11 plus appendices A and B. Abstract/intro claims: dropout randomly removes units and their connections during training, reducing co-adaptation and implicitly sampling exponentially many thinned networks; a single unthinned network with reduced weights approximates the averaged predictions. It claims dropout reduces overfitting and improves results across vision, speech recognition, document classification, and computational biology, often state of the art. Section 1 also says posterior-weighted averaging is the best regularization given unlimited computation, while dropout approximates an equally weighted geometric mean over exponentially many shared-parameter models. A network with n units corresponds to 2^n thinned networks and reuses O(n^2) or fewer parameters. The introduction contrasts dropout with stopping early, soft weight sharing, and L1/L2 penalties, and says model combination is powerful but expensive. It introduces the practical inference rule (weight scaling) versus Monte Carlo model averaging, and notes dropout extends to graphical models such as Boltzmann machines, including Restricted Boltzmann Machines and dropout RBMs. Figure 1 shows a standard two-hidden-layer net and a thinned version with crossed units removed.

Section 2 motivates dropout using analogies from evolution and robustness. It contrasts sexual vs asexual reproduction: recombination breaks co-adapted gene sets, suggesting a tension between individual-fitness optimization and the value of mixable, robust genes. The Livnat et al. view is that selection may favor gene sets that work with many partners; the paper maps this to hidden units trained with dropout, which must be useful with randomly selected partners and thus learn independently useful, robust features rather than depend on other units. It also uses a conspiracy analogy: smaller conspiracies are more robust to changing conditions than a larger one needing many correct participants. These examples support the claim that complex co-adaptations can fit training data yet generalize poorly, whereas simpler robust components may generalize better.

Section 3 surveys related work on noise-based regularization. It frames hidden-unit noise as a regularizer for QX2, connecting it to denoising autoencoders (Vincent et al. 2008, 2010): input corruption plus reconstruction, effective hidden-layer corruption, model averaging, supervised and unsupervised use, and applicability to other neuron-based architectures such as Boltzmann machines. A comparison table says typical best noise is 5% for S2H, while QX2 often works best at 20% input-unit removal or 50% hidden-unit removal. It contrasts stochastic noise training with adversarial removal methods (Globerson and Roweis 2006; Dekel et al. 2010), noting those have no hidden units. It also says analytically marginalizing QX2 yields deterministic regularizers in simple cases; related exponential-family input-noise regularizers (“blankout noise”) were studied by van der Maaten et al. (2013) for models without hidden layers. Chen et al. (2012) examined marginalization for denoising autoencoders, and Wang and Manning (2013) proposed marginalization to accelerate QX2.

steps.notes_before: Section 4 defines QX2 as stochastic deletion (“dropout”) applied to every layer: each layer output vector is multiplied elementwise by an independent Bernoulli mask with retention probability \(p\). Training samples a subnetwork and backpropagates through it; both hidden and visible units can be removed. At test time, no units are removed and the outgoing weights are scaled by \(p\): \(\mathbf W^{(l)}_{	ext{test}}=p\mathbf W^{(l)}\). The section states that validation can choose \(p\), but the default is usually near optimal and input retention is often closer to 1. It also claims that the expected output under deletion matches test-time output, though the formulas only directly show this for the preactivation, not necessarily after a nonlinear activation.

Section 5 says QX2 training uses standard SGD on a per-case sampled thinned network: each case is forwarded/backpropagated through its own sampled subnetwork, gradients are averaged, and absent parameters contribute zero. It highlights that QX2 works well with high momentum, large decaying learning rates, and V9C max-norm regularization, where each incoming hidden-unit weight vector is constrained by ||w||_2 <= c and projected back onto the radius-c ball if it exceeds it. The section also notes that this constraint is a validation-tuned hyperparameter and can help deep-net training even without QX2. For unsupervised pretraining, the procedure is unchanged, but before QX2 finetuning pretrained weights are multiplied by 1/p so that expected random-removal output matches the pretrained output. Smaller finetuning learning rates are said to preserve pretrained information better than rates comparable to best randomly initialized-net rates.

final_notes:
Appendix B.4 (DBN finetuning): input retention p=0.8, hidden p=0.5, max-norm c=4, momentum 0.95, and an initial learning rate of 0.1 with decay schedule ε0(1+t/T)^-1. RBM pretraining used CD-1 with Gaussian RBM input variance fixed at 1. For dropout finetuning, the best results used a smaller learning rate of about 0.01, and adding max-norm gave no improvement.

Appendix B.5 (Reuters): Reuters RCV1 has >800,000 documents in 103 tree-structured classes. They created a subset of 402,738 articles using a 2000-word vocabulary and 50 categories; each document has exactly one class. The subset was split equally into training and test sets, so training is >200,000 cases. Dropout improved accuracy on all tried architectures, but less than on image/speech data.

Appendix B.6 (Alternative Splicing): Data has 3665 cassette exons, 1014 RNA features, and 4 tissue types derived from 27 mouse tissues. Targets use 4 softmax outputs (one per tissue), each with 3 states: inc, exc, nc. Code Quality is defined as a triple sum over data points, tissue types, and states using target probabilities p, predicted probabilities q, and average state frequencies p̄. The reported model is a two-layer dropout net with 1024 units per layer, hidden retention 0.5, input retention 0.7, plus max-norm and decaying high learning rates; results were averaged over the same 5 folds as Xiong et al. (2011).

The paper studies dropout as a way to reduce overfitting in large neural networks without training many separate models. Abstract claims dropout randomly removes units during training, samples an exponential number of thinned networks, and uses one unthinned network with smaller weights at test time to approximate their average predictions. It says dropout reduces overfitting and improves supervised-learning performance on vision, speech recognition, document classification, and computational-biology tasks, with state-of-the-art results on many benchmarks. It also says dropout outperforms other regularization methods.

Introduction claims deep nets overfit limited data and reviews standard regularization (early stopping, L1/L2, soft weight sharing). The paper’s goal is to approximate Bayesian model averaging / an equally weighted geometric mean of predictions from exponentially many parameter-sharing models at low cost. Dropout randomly removes hidden or visible units during training; in the simplest case each unit is retained independently with probability p (often p=0.5 for hidden units, closer to 1 for inputs). A thinned network is sampled for each training case. At test time, dropout is turned off and outgoing weights are multiplied by p so expected training-time output matches test-time output. A network with n units represents 2^n thinned networks with shared weights, making explicit averaging infeasible. The paper claims dropout reduces generalization error and also applies to RBMs. Section roadmap: 2 motivation, 3 related work, 4 model, 5 training, 6 experiments, 7 network properties/hyperparameters, 8 Dropout RBMs, 9 marginalizing dropout, Appendix A practical guidance.

Prior notes still hold: the paper frames dropout as approximate Bayesian model averaging / equally weighted geometric mean over exponentially many thinned networks; each unit is kept independently with probability p during training, and at test time weights are multiplied by p. This part begins Section 2 (Motivation) and uses two analogies to explain why dropout should help: (1) sexual reproduction/mix-ability—useful genes must work with random partners, so hidden units trained with dropout should become robust and not rely on specific co-adaptations; and (2) conspiracies—smaller groups are more likely to keep working under changing conditions than one large tightly coordinated group. The section’s conclusion is that complex co-adaptations may fit training data but are more likely to fail on test data than several simpler co-adaptations.

Section 3 relates dropout to noisy autoencoders and robustness. It says dropout can be seen as regularization via noise in hidden states; Denoising Autoencoders add noise to unit states / inputs and reconstruct clean input. Dropout extends this idea to hidden layers and to supervised learning, and to other neuron-based architectures including Boltzmann Machines. It claims that although 5% noise is typical for DAEs, test-time weight scaling allows much higher noise, with 20% input dropout and 50% hidden dropout often optimal. Section 5 covers learning dropout nets. Training uses SGD on a sampled thinned network per mini-batch case; gradients are averaged and inactive parameters contribute zero gradient. Helpful SGD tricks include momentum, learning-rate decay, and L2 weight decay. Max-norm regularization constrains each hidden unit’s incoming weight vector to norm <= c and is especially useful with dropout; the paper claims dropout + max-norm beats dropout + L2 (Table 9: 1.05% vs 1.25%), and max-norm alone beats L2 (1.35% vs 1.62%).

For unsupervised pretraining, the paper says pretrained weights should be multiplied by 1/p before dropout finetuning so expected outputs match pretraining. Dropout finetuning is said to preserve pretrained information only with smaller learning rates; with larger finetuning rates it can erase pretrained information. The section claims improved pretrained MNIST results using dropout finetuning, citing Table 2 DBN and DBM rows with error pairs 1.18% vs 0.92% and 0.96% vs 0.79%.

Table 1 gives dataset sizes: MNIST 60K/10K; SVHN 600K/26K; CIFAR-10/100 60K/10K; ImageNet (ILSVRC-2012) 1.2M/150K; TIMIT 1.1M frames/58K frames; Reuters-RCV1 200K/200K; Alternative Splicing 2932/733. The paper claims dropout improved generalization on every dataset versus neural nets without dropout. Section 6.1 says the image datasets include MNIST, SVHN, CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and ImageNet. For MNIST, Table 2 reports: standard neural net 1.60%; SVM Gaussian kernel 1.40%; dropout NN logistic 1.35%; dropout NN ReLU 1.25%; dropout NN + max-norm ReLU 1.06%, 1.04%, 1.01%, 0.95% as size increases; maxout dropout model 0.94%; DBN finetuning 1.18%; DBM finetuning 0.96%; DBN + dropout finetuning 0.92%; DBM + dropout finetuning 0.79%. Section 6.1 incorrectly says SVHN is smaller than MNIST; Table 1 shows the opposite.

Section 6.1.1 (MNIST) reports that larger dropout networks perform better: 2 hidden layers of 8192 units each reach 0.95% error with >65M parameters. Goodfellow et al. (2013) get 0.94% with maxout units. All dropout networks use p=0.5 for hidden units and p=0.8 for input units. DBM-pretrained dropout networks reach 0.79%, the best reported performance for the permutation invariant setting. Figure 4 shows that with fixed hyperparameters, architectures with and without dropout form distinct test-error trajectories; the networks have 2–4 hidden layers with 1024–2048 units.

Section 6.1.2 (SVHN) uses 32x32 color images and a Conv Net with 3 convolutional layers plus 2 fully connected hidden layers, all ReLU units. Table 3 reports: Binary Features 36.7; HOG 15.0; Stacked Sparse Autoencoders 10.3; KMeans 9.4; multi-stage Conv Net average pooling 9.06; L2 pooling 5.36; L4 pooling + padding 4.90; Conv Net + max-pooling 3.95; dropout only in fully connected layers 3.02; stochastic pooling 2.80; dropout in all layers 2.55; maxout 2.47; human performance 2.0. Dropout was applied throughout with retention probabilities p=(0.9,0.75,0.75,0.5,0.5,0.5), and max-norm regularization was used. Section 7 studies features, sparsity, and how dropout depends on retention probability and network size. In 7.1, a one-hidden-layer MNIST autoencoder with 256 ReLUs is compared with and without dropout \(p=0.5\); both have similar test reconstruction error, but dropout features look more like meaningful edges/strokes and less co-adapted. In 7.2, the same autoencoders show that dropout yields sparser activations: mean activation drops from about 2.0 without dropout to about 0.7 with dropout, with a sharper peak at zero. In 7.3, dropout rate is varied on MNIST for architecture 784-2048-2048-2048-10. With fixed network size, error is high at small \(p\), decreases, is roughly flat for \(0.4\le p\le 0.8\), and rises as \(p\to 1\). The second setting keeps expected retained units \(pn\) fixed, so smaller \(p\) means larger networks; this setup is introduced but its detailed results are not yet in these notes.

Section 7.3’s second setting fixes expected retained sizes rather than network architecture: pn=256 for the first two hidden layers and pn=512 for the last. Under this setup, Figure 9b shows much lower error at small p than the fixed-architecture case in Figure 9a; at p=0.1, error drops from 2.7% to 1.7%. The best p is around 0.6, and the usual default p=0.5 is close to optimal.

Section 7.4 varies MNIST training-set size with architecture 784-1024-1024-2048-10 and dropout p=0.5 in hidden layers, p=0.8 at input. For 100 and 500 training cases, dropout gives no improvement. Section 7.5 compares Monte-Carlo model averaging to weight scaling at test time. Weight scaling is the efficient approximation; Monte-Carlo averaging samples k dropout networks and averages predictions. Around k=50, Monte-Carlo averaging matches weight scaling; beyond that it is slightly better but within one standard deviation, supporting weight scaling as a good approximation.

Section 8 introduces Dropout RBMs: an RBM over visible units v and hidden units h augmented with a binary mask r, where each hidden unit is independently retained with probability p. Conditioned on r, the model is an RBM with the dropped hidden units forced to zero, so the overall model is a mixture of exponentially many weight-sharing RBMs. Learning follows standard RBM methods: sample a fresh mask for each training case/minibatch and use CD-1.

The empirical results are qualitative. With 256 hidden units on MNIST, the dropout RBM (p=0.5) learns coarser-looking features than a standard RBM and appears to have fewer dead units. It also produces sparser hidden activations without an extra sparsity regularizer, as shown by activation histograms comparing standard vs dropout RBMs.

Section 9 discusses deterministic models from marginalizing dropout noise. It cites related work: Globerson & Roweis on robust deterministic algorithms, Chen et al. on denoising autoencoders, Srivastava on linear regression dropout, Wang & Manning on accelerated dropout marginalization, van der Maaten et al. on input-noise regularizers, and Wager et al. on adaptive regularization.

For linear regression, with inputs X, targets y, and independent Bernoulli(p) masks on input dimensions, minimizing the expected squared error over masks yields an objective equivalent to ridge regression in expectation: ||y - pXw||^2 + p(1-p)||Γw||^2, where Γ = diag(X^T X)^{1/2}. After rescaling by \tilde w = pw, the objective becomes ||y - X\tilde w||^2 + ((1-p)/p)||Γ\tilde w||^2. Thus the regularization strength increases as p decreases.

For logistic regression and deep networks, closed-form marginalization is difficult. Wang and Manning (2013) provide an approximate marginalized logistic-regression dropout method by assuming Gaussian distributions for unit inputs and marginalized gradients. The approximation is said to improve training time and generalization over Monte-Carlo dropout, but the assumptions weaken as layers are added, so the result does not directly extend to deep networks.

Section 10 generalizes dropout to multiplicative Gaussian noise. It says hidden activations can be multiplied either by Bernoulli masks or by Gaussian multipliers. A unit activation \(h_i\) with Gaussian noise can be written as \(h_i+h_i r\) with \(r\sim N(0,1)\), equivalently \(h_i r'\) with \(r'\sim N(1,1)\). More generally, \(r'\sim N(1,\sigma^2)\), where \(\sigma\) is a tunable hyperparameter analogous to dropout probability \(p\). Because the mean multiplier is 1, no test-time weight scaling is needed.

The section then matches Bernoulli and Gaussian dropout by using the rescaled Bernoulli multiplier \(r_b\in\{0,1/p\}\), which has mean 1 and variance \((1-p)/p\). Setting Gaussian variance to \(\sigma^2=(1-p)/p\) gives the same first two moments for the Gaussian multiplier \(r_g\). The text claims that, given these moments, the Gaussian has the highest entropy and Bernoulli the lowest, and that both work well.

Table 10 compares classification error under Bernoulli vs Gaussian dropout. For MNIST, Bernoulli gives 1.08 ± 0.04% and Gaussian 0.95 ± 0.04%; for CIFAR-10, Bernoulli gives 12.6 ± 0.1% and Gaussian 12.5 ± 0.1%. The caption says MNIST uses p=0.5 for hidden units and p=0.8 for inputs, while CIFAR-10 uses p=(0.9, 0.75, 0.75, 0.5, 0.5, 0.5) from input to top. Results are averaged over 10 random seeds.

Section 11 concludes that dropout reduces overfitting by preventing brittle co-adaptations: each hidden unit becomes unreliable during training. It claims dropout improves object classification, digit recognition, speech recognition, document classification, and computational-biology analysis, and that dropout methods achieve state-of-the-art results on SVHN, ImageNet, CIFAR-100, and MNIST. The conclusion also says dropout extends to RBMs and other graphical models, using a large-overfitting-model / sampled-smaller-submodels principle; the paper’s Dropout RBMs reportedly show desirable properties. A stated drawback is that dropout training typically takes 2–3 times longer than standard training because updates are noisy and each case trains a different random architecture. The section says marginalizing the noise can help, and for linear regression this yields an equivalent modified L2 regularizer, while analogous regularizers for more complex models are not obvious.

Appendix A gives practical heuristics: because dropout reduces expected active units to pn, a layer that is optimal with n units should often be widened to at least n/p units. Recommended learning rates are 10–100× the standard-network optimum, with momentum around 0.95–0.99 instead of 0.9. Max-norm regularization is suggested to prevent large weights, with typical c values 3–4. Typical hidden-unit retention probabilities are 0.5–0.8; for real-valued image patches or speech frames, input retention around 0.8 is typical. Smaller p requires larger n and can slow training and underfit; larger p may be too weak to prevent overfitting.

Appendix B gives experimental details. MNIST: 60k train/10k test, with 10k held out for validation; hyperparameters were chosen so best validation error occurred after 1M updates, then training+validation were reunited and trained for another 1M updates. Figure 4 covers 2-, 3-, and 4-hidden-layer nets with 1024 or 2048 units; hidden layers used p=0.5, input p=0.8, final momentum 0.95, and max-norm c=2. They also tried 2- and 3-layer 4096/8192-unit nets; larger 2-layer nets improved results, 3-layer nets were slightly worse, and stronger dropout still did not beat the 2-layer nets. SVHN: about 600k train and 26k test images; validation set of 6000 cases made from 400/class from the standard set and 200/class from the extra set. Inputs were RGB normalized to zero mean/unit variance; contrast normalization and ZCA whitening did not help. Best architecture: 3 conv layers (96, 128, 256 filters), each with 5x5 receptive fields and stride 1, each followed by 3x3 max-pooling with stride 2, then two 2048-unit ReLU hidden layers. Retention probabilities were (0.9, 0.75, 0.75, 0.5, 0.5, 0.5), with c=4 and momentum 0.95; validation selected these settings and the final reported test error used the best validation model. CIFAR-10/100: 50k train/10k test each; 5k training images used for validation, then merged back after selection. Preprocessing used global contrast normalization per color channel and ZCA whitening; architecture and dropout matched SVHN except smaller input-layer learning rates. TIMIT: Kaldi was used to produce log-filter banks; monophone forced alignment provided frame labels; networks used 21 consecutive frames, predicted the central frame, performed no speaker-dependent operation, and inputs were mean-centered and variance-normalized.

The paper studies dropout as a method to prevent overfitting in large neural networks by randomly removing units/connections during training, effectively training many smaller shared-parameter networks and using a single scaled network at test time. The paper says it reports state-of-the-art results on several benchmarks and also examines learned features, sparsity, retention rates, training-set size, RBMs, noise marginalization, and Gaussian corruption. Training is said to take about 2–3 times longer than a standard network of the same architecture.

It defines core neural-network terms (units, hidden/visible layers, weights, biases, activations), regularizers (L1, L2/Tikhonov, max-norm, KL-sparsity, early stopping), and averaging concepts (model averaging, posterior-weighted averaging, geometric mean, weight scaling, Monte-Carlo averaging). It also gives an original-page map for the rest of the paper: pages 1930–1955 cover the introduction, figures, sections 2–11, table 1–10, acknowledgments, Appendix A (A.1–A.4), and Appendix B (B.1–B.6). No new technical notation or results appear in this part.

This part contains the abstract of the paper. It claims that dropout (referred to here as “QX2, or dropout”) temporarily removes randomly selected units and their connections during training, inhibits co-adaptation, samples exponentially many thinned networks sharing parameters, and that a single unthinned network with reduced weights approximates their averaged predictions. It also claims that dropout substantially reduces overfitting and improves results across vision, speech recognition, document classification, and computational biology, with evidence in Tables 2–8 and the unnumbered text-classification table in §6.3. No new notation or contradictions appear here.

This part is the Introduction. It says QX2/dropout trains many shared-parameter subnetworks and uses a single unthinned test-time network to approximate their combined predictions. It frames the method as approximating an equally weighted geometric mean of exponentially many learned models, with a network of n units corresponding to 2^n possible thinned networks but only O(n^2) or fewer parameters. It introduces standard regularizers/terms: early stopping, soft weight sharing, L1 (O3U), and L2 (Y5F). It also says model combination usually helps but is expensive, and that the practical inference rule T6R/weight scaling uses one unthinned network; X9M/Monte-Carlo model averaging samples members at test time. It claims T6R has lower generalization error than compared regularizers, citing Table 9 rows Y5F 1.62, V9C 1.35, QX2+Y5F 1.25, and QX2+V9C 1.05. It also introduces extension to graphical models via RBMs, with B8T/Dropout RBM. No contradictions found yet.

This part gives the paper’s motivation for dropout/QX2 using biological and game-theoretic analogies. It argues that breaking co-adapted gene sets via sexual reproduction can be advantageous because it favors ‘mix-ability’ and robustness, even if it seems worse for preserving successful combinations. It then maps this to QX2-trained hidden units: because hidden units face randomly selected partners, the method encourages independently useful, robust features rather than reliance on other units. The part also uses a conspiracy analogy to suggest that smaller interacting groups may be more robust under changing conditions than one large, fragile coordinated group. No direct contradictions with earlier sections are introduced here.

This part is the related-work section. It frames QX2 as connected to hidden-unit noise, model averaging, and earlier work on corruption, adversarial deletion, and marginalization. It says denoising autoencoders (S2H) corrupt inputs and reconstruct clean inputs, while QX2 extends this with effective hidden-layer corruption and a model-averaging interpretation. QX2 is claimed to apply to supervised and unsupervised learning and to other neuron-based architectures, including Boltzmann machines. It also contrasts QX2 with adversarial-removal models (Globerson and Roweis 2006; Dekel et al. 2010), which choose deletions under a fixed maximum rather than a probability distribution and are said to have no hidden units. Van der Maaten et al. (2013) are described as studying exponential-family input-noise regularizers, including QX2 under the name blankout noise, limited to models without hidden layers; Chen et al. (2012) studied marginalization for DAEs; Wang and Manning (2013) proposed marginalization to accelerate QX2. The table reports noise levels: S2H typical best 5%, QX2 often optimal input-unit removal 20%, and QX2 often optimal hidden-unit removal 50%.

steps.notes_before: Section 4 defines QX2/dropout-style corruption as independent Bernoulli gating of unit outputs during training: each entry \(r_j^{(l)}\sim Bernoulli(p)\), and \(	ilde y^{(l)} = r^{(l)} * y^{(l)}\). Ordinary feed-forward is \(z_i^{(l+1)}=w_i^{(l+1)} y^{(l)} + b_i^{(l+1)}\), \(y_i^{(l+1)}=f(z_i^{(l+1)})\); QX2 replaces \(y^{(l)}\) with \(	ilde y^{(l)}\). Any activation is allowed, including logistic. Applying the gating at every layer samples a subnetwork; backpropagation runs through that sampled subnetwork. Both hidden and visible units can be removed. At inference, no units are removed and weights are scaled as \(W^{(l)}_{test}=pW^{(l)}\).

Section 5 says QX2 training/backprop is ordinary backprop on a sampled thinned network: each mini-batch case uses its own sampled subnetwork, gradients are averaged, and unused parameters get zero gradient. The section argues that combining QX2 with high momentum, large decaying learning rates, and max-norm/V9C gives additional gains; V9C constrains each hidden unit’s incoming-weight vector to norm <= c, with projection back to the radius-c ball and c tuned on validation. It also offers a qualitative optimization story (weight ball allows large learning rates; QX2 noise explores weight space; decay shortens steps). For finetuning pretrained nets, smaller learning rates are important; too-large rates can erase pretrained information. Before QX2 finetuning, pretrained weights are multiplied by 1/p to preserve expected outputs under random removal. QX2 finetuning can be applied after pretraining from stacked U2L, autoencoders, or E5Q/DBMs. Reported evidence includes table values showing QX2 improving finetuning results (e.g., G6W: 1.18 to 0.92; E5Q: 0.96 to 0.79) and a best QX2 finetuning rate around 0.01 versus a higher listed rate of 0.1.

Appendix A gives practical heuristics for QX2 while emphasizing that extensive hyperparameter tuning is still needed. Recommended widths are at least n/p for a standard layer of n hidden units, since only pn units survive in expectation. Learning rates are typically 10–100× standard-net rates, with momentum around 0.95–0.99; max-norm constraint c is typically 3–4. Retention should be chosen jointly with width and input type: hidden units typically use p=0.5–0.8, real-valued inputs around 0.8, a broadly near-optimal default is 0.5, and input-unit optima are closer to 1 than 0.5. Lower retention increases underfitting and slows training.

Paper: “Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting” (JMLR 2014). Main claim: dropout randomly drops units and their connections during training, causing an exponential number of thinned networks to be sampled; at test time, one can approximate averaging over them with a single unthinned network using smaller weights. Abstract says this reduces overfitting and improves supervised learning performance in vision, speech recognition, document classification, and computational biology, with state-of-the-art results on many benchmarks. Introduction frames dropout as a regularization method for deep nets, alongside early stopping and weight penalties (L1/L2, soft weight sharing). Figure 1 illustrates a standard neural net vs. a thinned net produced by dropout.

The paper motivates dropout as an approximation to Bayesian model averaging / geometric mean over an exponential number of shared-parameter networks, aiming for good performance with less computation. It argues that averaging many separately trained nets is expensive because diverse nets require different architectures or data and are costly to train/test. Dropout drops hidden and visible units (removing incoming/outgoing connections) at random during training; each unit is retained independently with probability p, typically 0.5 for many layers, while input units usually use p closer to 1. Figure 2 states that at test time all units are present and outgoing weights are multiplied by p, so the test-time network matches the expected training-time output.

During training, units are independently retained with probability p; hidden units often use p=0.5, while input units usually use p closer to 1. At test time, all units are present and outgoing weights are multiplied by p so the test-time network matches the expected training-time output. This part adds intuition for dropout via analogies to sexual reproduction and conspiracies: training each hidden unit to work with random subsets of others should make features more robust and less dependent on co-adaptations. It also says the paper will extend dropout to RBMs and discuss experiments, analysis of hyperparameters, marginalizing dropout, and practical guidance in the appendix.

The paper’s intro says dropout extends denoising autoencoders: it can be applied to hidden layers, interpreted as model averaging, and extended beyond unsupervised learning to supervised problems and other neuron-based architectures such as Boltzmann Machines. It also notes that although 5% noise is typical for denoising autoencoders, their weight-scaling-at-test-time approach allows much higher dropout rates; they report 20% input dropout and 50% hidden dropout as often optimal. The paper then motivates deterministic versions by marginalizing the noise, citing prior work on deterministic regularizers and dropout marginalization, and contrasts dropout with adversarial unit-dropping methods.

Model description: for a network with L hidden layers, y^(0)=x, layer l has weights W^(l) and biases b^(l). Standard feedforward uses z^(l+1)=w^(l+1) y^(l)+b^(l+1), y^(l+1)=f(z^(l+1)). With dropout, a Bernoulli mask r^(l) with retention probability p is sampled for each layer, the thinned outputs y~^(l)=r^(l)*y^(l) are passed to the next layer, and this is done at every layer. Training backpropagates through the sampled subnetwork. At test time, dropout is removed and weights are scaled by p: W_test = p W^(l). The next section starts the training procedure for dropout neural nets.

Section 5.1: Dropout nets are trained with SGD by sampling a thinned network per training case; forward/backprop are run only on that thinned network, gradients are averaged over the mini-batch, and units not used contribute zero gradient. Usual SGD improvements (momentum, annealed learning rates, L2 decay) also help. A particularly useful regularizer is max-norm: constrain each hidden unit’s incoming weight vector w to satisfy ||w||2 ≤ c by projecting back onto the ball of radius c; c is tuned on validation. The paper says dropout + max-norm + large decaying learning rates + high momentum works better than dropout alone.

Section 5.2: Dropout can be used to fine-tune pretrained nets (RBMs, autoencoders, DBMs) without changing the pretraining procedure. Weights from pretraining should be scaled up by 1/p so the expected output under dropout matches pretraining. Smaller finetuning learning rates are needed; with them, pretrained information is retained and final generalization improves versus finetuning without dropout.

Section 6 begins experiments: they evaluate dropout on classification tasks across many domains and claim dropout improved generalization on all data sets compared to non-dropout neural nets. Listed data sets: MNIST, TIMIT, CIFAR-10/100, SVHN, ImageNet, Reuters-RCV1, and an Alternative Splicing data set. A detailed description is deferred to Appendix B.

Section 7.1-7.2 argues dropout breaks co-adaptations and induces sparsity: Figure 7 compares MNIST autoencoder features learned with one hidden layer of 256 ReLUs without dropout vs. with dropout p=0.5; the paper says both autoencoders had similar test reconstruction errors, but the dropout model’s features are more meaningful. Figure 8 shows that dropout also lowers hidden-unit activations, with mean activation about 2.0 without dropout and about 0.7 with dropout.

Section 7.3 studies sensitivity to dropout rate on MNIST. Two regimes are compared using Figure 9. (1) Fixed architecture 784-2048-2048-2048-10, no input dropout: small p causes underfitting (high training error); test error decreases as p increases, is roughly flat for 0.4 ≤ p ≤ 0.8, then rises again as p→1. (2) Holding pn constant across architectures: pn=256 for the first two hidden layers and pn=512 for the last hidden layer. With this setup, small-p errors are much lower than in (1) (e.g., p=0.1 improves from 2.7% to 1.7%), and p around 0.6 performs best; the usual default p=0.5 is close to optimal. Section 7.4 varies MNIST training set size with network 784-1024-1024-2048-10, using dropout p=0.5 on hidden layers and p=0.8 on the input layer. Data sizes are 100, 500, 1K, 5K, 10K, and 50K; dropout does not help for the smallest sets, but its benefit grows with data size up to a point and then declines, implying a sweet spot. Section 7.5 begins comparing Monte-Carlo model averaging to the paper’s test-time weight scaling approximation.

Section 7.5 compares Monte-Carlo model averaging with the paper’s test-time weight scaling approximation on MNIST. The test error for finite-sample averaging approaches the true model average as k increases; around k=50, Monte-Carlo averaging becomes about as good as weight scaling, and beyond that it is slightly better but within one standard deviation. 

Section 8 introduces Dropout Restricted Boltzmann Machines. Visible units v and hidden units h are binary; the joint RBM distribution is proportional to exp(v^T W h + a^T h + b^T v). Dropout RBMs add binary mask variables r_j with retention probability p. If r_j=0, hidden unit h_j is forced to 0; the joint distribution factorizes as P(r)P(h,v|r), and conditioned on r the model is an RBM with some hidden units removed. Learning can use standard RBM algorithms such as CD-1, with a fresh r sampled for each training case in each minibatch. Figure 12 compares features learned by a 256-hidden-unit binary RBM without dropout versus with dropout p=0.5.

Section 8.4 studies sparsity in hidden activations for RBMs trained with and without dropout. Figure 13 compares histograms of hidden unit activations on a test minibatch: standard RBMs have many activations away from zero, while dropout RBMs have many near zero, indicating sparser representations. The text also says dropout RBMs appear to learn coarser features and have very few dead units relative to standard RBMs.

Section 9 introduces marginalizing dropout noise to obtain deterministic models. It frames dropout as noise on hidden states and notes that these marginalized models do not need random bits and allow gradients of marginalized losses. For linear regression, if inputs are dropped independently with retention probability p, minimizing the expected squared error is equivalent to ridge regression with objective ||y - pXw||^2 + p(1-p)||Γw||^2, where Γ = (diag(X^T X))^{1/2}. Reparameterizing with w̃ = pw makes the dependence on p explicit: smaller p means stronger regularization.

For logistic regression, Wang and Manning (2013) provide an approximate marginalized model using Gaussian approximations to input and gradient distributions; this can outperform Monte-Carlo dropout in training time and generalization, but the assumptions weaken for deeper networks, so the result is not directly applicable to deep nets. A table reports Bernoulli vs Gaussian dropout performance on MNIST and CIFAR-10.

Section 10 introduces multiplicative Gaussian noise as an alternative to Bernoulli dropout: hidden activations can be perturbed as hi + hi r with r ~ N(0,1), equivalently hi r0 with r0 ~ N(1,1). More generally, r0 ~ N(1, σ^2), and choosing σ^2 = (1-p)/p matches the Bernoulli dropout factor’s mean and variance. The text argues that this Gaussian noise has higher entropy than Bernoulli noise, and that both forms work well, with Table 10 suggesting the Gaussian/high-entropy case may be slightly better. The Gaussian formulation preserves the expected activation, so no test-time weight scaling is needed. Table 10 compares Bernoulli and Gaussian dropout classification error on MNIST and CIFAR-10, using p = 0.5 (hidden) and 0.8 (input) for MNIST, and p = (0.9, 0.75, 0.75, 0.5, 0.5, 0.5) across CIFAR-10 layers; results are averaged over 10 random seeds. The conclusion starts by summarizing dropout as reducing overfitting by breaking up co-adaptations.

The conclusion says dropout broadly improves performance by breaking co-adaptations, with state-of-the-art results reported on SVHN, ImageNet, CIFAR-100, and MNIST, but Reuters is an exception where standard nets do better without dropout. It frames dropout as repeatedly sampling and training smaller sub-models from an overfitting large model, and notes that RBMs fit this framework; the authors developed Dropout RBMs with desirable properties. A drawback is training time: dropout nets typically take 2-3x longer than standard nets because gradients are noisy and each case trains a different random architecture. Marginalizing the noise can recover an expectation-equivalent regularizer; for linear regression this becomes a modified L2 penalty. Appendix heuristics: if a layer has n units and retention probability p, dropout leaves pn units in expectation, so a dropout net may need at least n/p units. Recommended learning rates are 10-100x those of standard nets, with momentum around 0.95-0.99. Max-norm regularization with c about 3-4 can control weight growth. Typical dropout rates are p=0.5-0.8 for hidden units and about 0.8 for real-valued inputs; p=1 means no dropout.

Appendix B gives experiment/data details and says the code is GPU-based using cudamat and cuda-convnet. MNIST: 60k train/10k test, 10k train held out for validation; hyperparameters tuned so best validation error occurred after 1M updates, then validation was merged back into training and the model was trained for another 1M updates. MNIST architectures in Figure 4 cover all 2-, 3-, and 4-layer nets with 1024 or 2048 units per layer (6 total). For all MNIST architectures, hidden-layer retention p=0.5, input p=0.8, final momentum 0.95, and max-norm c=2. Larger 2/3-layer MNIST nets with 4096/8192 units were also tried; 2-layer nets improved, 3-layer nets were slightly worse, and higher dropout helped but not enough. SVHN: ~600k train and 26k test images, with a validation set built from both standard and extra labeled sets (400/class from standard, 200/class from extra; 6000 total). Inputs are RGB normalized to zero mean/unit variance; no gain from contrast normalization or ZCA. Best SVHN model: 3 conv layers (96, 128, 256 filters), each 5x5 stride 1, each followed by 3x3 max-pooling stride 2, then two 2048-unit fully connected hidden layers, ReLU throughout. Dropout retention probabilities were (0.9, 0.75, 0.75, 0.5, 0.5, 0.5) from input through layers, with max-norm c=4 and momentum 0.95; validation error selected the test model, and validation was not merged into training because the training set was large. CIFAR-10/100 begin here: 50k train/10k test each, 5k validation, global contrast normalization per color channel and ZCA whitening.

Authors: Nitish Srivastava, Geoffrey Hinton, Alex Krizhevsky, Ilya Sutskever, and Ruslan Salakhutdinov, all at University of Toronto. Editor: Yoshua Bengio. Paper: "Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting" (JMLR 15, 2014, pp. 1929–1958). Authors: Nitish Srivastava, Geoffrey Hinton, Alex Krizhevsky, Ilya Sutskever, and Ruslan Salakhutdinov (University of Toronto); editor Yoshua Bengio. The paper map on the first pages lays out the structure across sections 2–11 plus appendices A and B. Abstract/intro claims: dropout randomly removes units and their connections during training, reducing co-adaptation and implicitly sampling exponentially many thinned networks; a single unthinned network with reduced weights approximates the averaged predictions. It claims dropout reduces overfitting and improves results across vision, speech recognition, document classification, and computational biology, often state of the art. Section 1 also says posterior-weighted averaging is the best regularization given unlimited computation, while dropout approximates an equally weighted geometric mean over exponentially many shared-parameter models. A network with n units corresponds to 2^n thinned networks and reuses O(n^2) or fewer parameters. The introduction contrasts dropout with stopping early, soft weight sharing, and L1/L2 penalties, and says model combination is powerful but expensive. It introduces the practical inference rule (weight scaling) versus Monte Carlo model averaging, and notes dropout extends to graphical models such as Boltzmann machines, including Restricted Boltzmann Machines and dropout RBMs. Figure 1 shows a standard two-hidden-layer net and a thinned version with crossed units removed.

Section 2 motivates dropout using analogies from evolution and robustness. It contrasts sexual vs asexual reproduction: recombination breaks co-adapted gene sets, suggesting a tension between individual-fitness optimization and the value of mixable, robust genes. The Livnat et al. view is that selection may favor gene sets that work with many partners; the paper maps this to hidden units trained with dropout, which must be useful with randomly selected partners and thus learn independently useful, robust features rather than depend on other units. It also uses a conspiracy analogy: smaller conspiracies are more robust to changing conditions than a larger one needing many correct participants. These examples support the claim that complex co-adaptations can fit training data yet generalize poorly, whereas simpler robust components may generalize better.

Section 3 surveys related work on noise-based regularization. It frames hidden-unit noise as a regularizer for QX2, connecting it to denoising autoencoders (Vincent et al. 2008, 2010): input corruption plus reconstruction, effective hidden-layer corruption, model averaging, supervised and unsupervised use, and applicability to other neuron-based architectures such as Boltzmann machines. A comparison table says typical best noise is 5% for S2H, while QX2 often works best at 20% input-unit removal or 50% hidden-unit removal. It contrasts stochastic noise training with adversarial removal methods (Globerson and Roweis 2006; Dekel et al. 2010), noting those have no hidden units. It also says analytically marginalizing QX2 yields deterministic regularizers in simple cases; related exponential-family input-noise regularizers (“blankout noise”) were studied by van der Maaten et al. (2013) for models without hidden layers. Chen et al. (2012) examined marginalization for denoising autoencoders, and Wang and Manning (2013) proposed marginalization to accelerate QX2.
