steps.notes_before: Section 4 defines QX2 as stochastic deletion (“dropout”) applied to every layer: each layer output vector is multiplied elementwise by an independent Bernoulli mask with retention probability \(p\). Training samples a subnetwork and backpropagates through it; both hidden and visible units can be removed. At test time, no units are removed and the outgoing weights are scaled by \(p\): \(\mathbf W^{(l)}_{	ext{test}}=p\mathbf W^{(l)}\). The section states that validation can choose \(p\), but the default is usually near optimal and input retention is often closer to 1. It also claims that the expected output under deletion matches test-time output, though the formulas only directly show this for the preactivation, not necessarily after a nonlinear activation.

Section 5 says QX2 training uses standard SGD on a per-case sampled thinned network: each case is forwarded/backpropagated through its own sampled subnetwork, gradients are averaged, and absent parameters contribute zero. It highlights that QX2 works well with high momentum, large decaying learning rates, and V9C max-norm regularization, where each incoming hidden-unit weight vector is constrained by ||w||_2 <= c and projected back onto the radius-c ball if it exceeds it. The section also notes that this constraint is a validation-tuned hyperparameter and can help deep-net training even without QX2. For unsupervised pretraining, the procedure is unchanged, but before QX2 finetuning pretrained weights are multiplied by 1/p so that expected random-removal output matches the pretrained output. Smaller finetuning learning rates are said to preserve pretrained information better than rates comparable to best randomly initialized-net rates.

Section 6 reports experimental results. It claims QX2 improved generalization over non-QX2 neural nets on every tested data set and that models attaining state of the art on all five vision collections use QX2. Table 1 lists datasets: H4Z/MNIST (784, 60K/10K), A2F/SVHN (3072, 600K/26K), J3V/W6R/CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 (3072, 60K/10K), K9D/ImageNet ILSVRC-2012 (65536, 1.2M/150K), N8Q/TIMIT (2520, 1.1M frames/58K frames), M5X/Reuters-RCV1 (2000, 200K/200K), and Z7P/Alternative Splicing (1014, 2932/733). In H4Z, QX2 improves over standard neural nets; ReLUs, max-norm regularization (V9C), larger architectures, and maxout (L8J) each improve further. Best H4Z listed result is E5Q + QX2 finetuning at 0.79% error; G6W + QX2 finetuning gets 0.92%, while E5Q + finetuning without QX2 is 0.96%. Figure 4 compares training trajectories with and without QX2 under fixed hyperparameters, yielding two separated error clusters. The A2F section says convolutional nets outperform other methods; adding QX2 to fully connected layers helps, adding it to convolutional layers helps more, and maxout helps further.

Section 7 discusses qualitative effects of QX2. 7.1 says QX2 yields more meaningful first-layer features (edges/strokes/spots) than no QX2, and attributes lower generalization error to breaking co-adaptations. 7.2 says QX2 produces sparse hidden activations without explicit sparsity regularizers; in the autoencoder comparison, mean unit activity is about 2.0 without QX2 vs about 0.7 with QX2, with a sharp zero peak under QX2. 7.3 says fixed architecture has underfitting at low retention; test error is flat for p≈0.4–0.8, with low-retention comparison at p=0.1 showing 2.7% error fixed architecture vs 1.7% when expected retained width is fixed; best retention for chosen widths is near 0.6, default 0.5. 7.4 says the two smallest training sets show no QX2 improvement, then gain rises and later falls as data grows. 7.5 says X9M catches T6R around k=50 and then is slightly better, within one standard deviation.

Section 8 introduces B8T as a mixture of exponentially many shared-weight U2L models, each corresponding to a different hidden-unit subset selected by a binary retention vector r with independent retention probability p. Conditioned on r, the model is just an ordinary U2L with the dropped hidden units forced to zero; the visible conditional remains standard U2L, and hidden units are factorial with P(h_j=1|r_j,v)=1(r_j=1)σ(b_j+Σ_i W_ij v_i). Learning uses standard CD-style U2L training after sampling r, with each mini-batch case getting a different r. Qualitatively, B8T features are described as coarser than U2L features but with very few dead units. It also learns much sparser hidden activations than U2L even without an added sparsity regularizer; Figure 13 shows many activations near zero and very few high activations for p=0.5.

Section 9 discusses marginalizing QX2 noise models. Deterministic noise-marginalized models need no random bits and allow gradients of the marginalized loss, unlike standard Monte-Carlo QX2. The section cites prior work on test-time feature deletion, linear-regression marginalization, and QX2 as an adaptive regularizer.

For linear regression, if each input dimension is retained independently with probability p, the expected objective becomes ridge-like: ||y - pXw||^2 + p(1-p)||Γw||^2, where Γ = (diag(X^T X))^(1/2). With w~ = p w, this can be rewritten as ||y - X w~||^2 + ((1-p)/p)||Γ w~||^2. The text emphasizes that dimensions with larger variance get penalized more strongly.

For logistic regression and deep networks, exact marginalization is difficult. The paper says approximate marginalization outperforms Monte-Carlo QX2 for logistic regression, and that under reasonable assumptions logistic-unit inputs and marginalized gradients are Gaussian with computable means/variances, but these assumptions become weaker with depth, so the results are not directly applicable to deep networks.

It reports preliminary classification errors showing D4K (Gaussian dropout) slightly better than P7V (Bernoulli dropout) on H4Z (0.95 vs 1.08) and essentially tied on J3V (12.5 vs 12.6), and states that Gaussian multipliers have higher entropy while Bernoulli multipliers have lower entropy, with slight evidence favoring the high-entropy case.

The section defines Bernoulli dropout as multiplying hidden activations by 1 with probability p and 0 otherwise, and notes that this generalizes to other multiplier distributions. A Gaussian multiplier r'~N(1,1) is equivalent to adding zero-mean Gaussian noise with standard deviation equal to the unit activation; more generally r'~N(1,σ^2) makes σ a tunable hyperparameter analogous to p. Unchanged expected activations eliminate test-time scaling.

It also states the standard equivalence between training-time retention with test-time weight scaling and training-time scaling by 1/p with unchanged test weights. Abstract claims dropout randomly removes units during training, samples an exponential number of thinned networks, and uses one unthinned network with smaller weights at test time to approximate their average predictions. It says dropout reduces overfitting and improves supervised-learning performance on vision, speech recognition, document classification, and computational-biology tasks, with state-of-the-art results on many benchmarks. It also says dropout outperforms other regularization methods.

Introduction claims deep nets overfit limited data and reviews standard regularization (early stopping, L1/L2, soft weight sharing). The paper’s goal is to approximate Bayesian model averaging / an equally weighted geometric mean of predictions from exponentially many parameter-sharing models at low cost. Dropout randomly removes hidden or visible units during training; in the simplest case each unit is retained independently with probability p (often p=0.5 for hidden units, closer to 1 for inputs). A thinned network is sampled for each training case. At test time, dropout is turned off and outgoing weights are multiplied by p so expected training-time output matches test-time output. A network with n units represents 2^n thinned networks with shared weights, making explicit averaging infeasible. The paper claims dropout reduces generalization error and also applies to RBMs. Section roadmap: 2 motivation, 3 related work, 4 model, 5 training, 6 experiments, 7 network properties/hyperparameters, 8 Dropout RBMs, 9 marginalizing dropout, Appendix A practical guidance.

Prior notes still hold: the paper frames dropout as approximate Bayesian model averaging / equally weighted geometric mean over exponentially many thinned networks; each unit is kept independently with probability p during training, and at test time weights are multiplied by p. The paper’s goal is to reduce generalization error at low cost; it also extends dropout to RBMs. 

This part begins Section 2 (Motivation) and uses two analogies to explain why dropout should help: (1) sexual reproduction/mix-ability—useful genes must work with random partners, so hidden units trained with dropout should become robust and not rely on specific co-adaptations; and (2) conspiracies—smaller groups are more likely to keep working under changing conditions than one large tightly coordinated group. The section’s conclusion is that complex co-adaptations may fit training data but are more likely to fail on test data than several simpler co-adaptations.

Section 3 relates dropout to noisy autoencoders and robustness. It says dropout can be seen as regularization via noise in hidden states; Denoising Autoencoders add noise to unit states / inputs and reconstruct clean input. Dropout extends this idea to hidden layers and to supervised learning, and to other neuron-based architectures including Boltzmann Machines. It claims that although 5% noise is typical for DAEs, test-time weight scaling allows much higher noise, with 20% input dropout and 50% hidden dropout often optimal. Section 5 covers learning dropout nets. Training uses SGD on a sampled thinned network per mini-batch case; gradients are averaged and inactive parameters contribute zero gradient. Helpful SGD tricks include momentum, learning-rate decay, and L2 weight decay. Max-norm regularization constrains each hidden unit’s incoming weight vector to norm <= c and is especially useful with dropout; the paper claims dropout + max-norm beats dropout + L2 (Table 9: 1.05% vs 1.25%), and max-norm alone beats L2 (1.35% vs 1.62%).

For unsupervised pretraining, the paper says pretrained weights should be multiplied by 1/p before dropout finetuning so expected outputs match pretraining. Dropout finetuning is said to preserve pretrained information only with smaller learning rates; with larger finetuning rates it can erase pretrained information. The section claims improved pretrained MNIST results using dropout finetuning, citing Table 2 DBN and DBM rows with error pairs 1.18% vs 0.92% and 0.96% vs 0.79%.

Section 6 reports experimental results across multiple domains and claims dropout improves generalization on every data set versus networks without dropout. Table 1 lists data sets and sizes: MNIST 60K/10K, SVHN 600K/26K, CIFAR-10/100 60K/10K, ImageNet 1.2M/150K, TIMIT 1.1M frames/58K, Reuters-RCV1 200K/200K, Alternative Splicing 2932/733.

Table 9 test errors: L2 1.62, L2+L1 late 1.60, L2+KL-sparsity 1.55, Max-norm 1.35, Dropout+L2 1.25, Dropout+Max-norm 1.05. The best result in this comparison is dropout combined with max-norm.

Section 7 studies how dropout affects learned features, sparsity, and sensitivity to retention probability. In 7.1, the paper compares two otherwise identical MNIST autoencoders with 256 ReLU hidden units, one without dropout and one with hidden-layer dropout at p=0.5. It claims both have similar test reconstruction error, but dropout yields more interpretable features (edges, strokes, spots) and reduces co-adaptation. In 7.2, the same autoencoders are evaluated on a random test mini-batch: without dropout, mean activation is about 2.0 and activations have a large mass away from zero; with dropout, mean activation is about 0.7 and activations are sharply peaked at zero. Thus dropout makes activations sparser without an explicit sparsity penalty. In 7.3, the paper varies dropout rate on MNIST using architecture 784-2048-2048-2048-10, first with fixed network size and then with expected retained size pn fixed. For fixed size, error is high at small p, decreases as p increases, stays roughly flat for 0.4<=p<=0.8, and then rises again as p approaches 1. The second setting keeps expected retained units constant while changing actual network size.

Section 7.3 varies dropout rate on MNIST autoencoders. For fixed architecture 784-2048-2048-2048-10, error is high at small p, falls as p increases, is roughly flat for 0.4<=p<=0.8, and rises again near p=1. A second experiment keeps expected retained units constant while changing actual network size; with retained sizes pn=256 for the first two hidden layers and pn=512 for the last, Figure 9b has much lower error at low p than Figure 9a (at p=0.1, 2.7% vs 1.7%). For these retained sizes, p around 0.6 is best and p=0.5 is close to optimal.

Section 7.4 varies MNIST training-set size using architecture 784-1024-1024-2048-10 with p=0.5 in all hidden layers and p=0.8 at the input. Training-set sizes are 100, 500, 1K, 5K, 10K, and 50K. Dropout gives no improvement at 100 and 500 cases, but its gain first increases and then declines as data size grows, suggesting an architecture- and dropout-dependent sweet spot.

Section 7.5 compares Monte-Carlo model averaging with weight scaling. Test-time averaging over k sampled dropout networks approaches the true model average as k increases. On MNIST, about k=50 samples match the weight-scaling approximation; beyond that, Monte-Carlo averaging is slightly better but within one standard deviation, so weight scaling is a good approximation.

Section 8 defines Dropout RBMs as a mixture over hidden-unit subsets. An RBM over v,h has standard energy-based joint P(h,v;θ). A dropout mask r∈{0,1}^F is sampled with independent retention probability p per hidden unit; if r_j=0 then h_j is constrained to 0 via a factor g(h_j,r_j). Conditioned on r, the model is just an RBM with the dropped hidden units removed, so the full model is a mixture of exponentially many RBMs sharing weights. Learning uses standard RBM methods (e.g., CD-1) after sampling a new mask for each training case in each mini-batch.

The section qualitatively compares standard and dropout RBMs on MNIST with 256 hidden units. Figure 12 shows dropout (p=0.5) learns coarser-looking features and appears to have fewer dead units than the standard RBM. Figure 13 suggests dropout also yields sparser hidden activations: many units near zero and few high-activation units, even without any explicit sparsity regularizer.

Section 9 studies deterministic models formed by marginalizing dropout noise. It notes prior related work on feature deletion, denoising autoencoders, linear regression, and adaptive regularization. For linear regression, with inputs X, targets y, and Bernoulli(p) masking of each input entry, the expected squared-loss objective becomes ||y-pXw||^2 + p(1-p)||Γw||^2, where Γ = diag(X^T X)^(1/2). After rescaling w via \tilde w = p w, the objective is ||y-X\tilde w||^2 + ((1-p)/p)||Γ\tilde w||^2, so the regularization strength increases as p decreases. The text interprets this as ridge regression with feature-dependent penalties proportional to input standard deviations. For logistic regression, exact marginalization is said to be difficult; Wang and Manning (2013) provide an approximation using Gaussian means/variances of unit inputs and gradients, which is claimed to improve training time and generalization over Monte-Carlo dropout. The paper also states that the approximation assumptions become weaker in deeper networks, so the result does not directly extend to deep models.

Section 10 generalizes dropout to multiplicative Gaussian noise. A unit activation h_i can be perturbed as h_i+h_i r with r~N(0,1), equivalently h_i r' with r'~N(1,1); more generally r'~N(1,σ^2). Because the mean is 1, no test-time weight scaling is needed. The section also describes the standard dropout rescaling equivalence: retaining units with probability p and scaling weights at test time is equivalent to scaling retained training activations by 1/p and leaving test weights unchanged. Under this rescaled view, the Bernoulli multiplier r_b is 1/p with probability p and 0 otherwise, with mean 1 and variance (1-p)/p. Matching Gaussian variance to σ^2=(1-p)/p makes Bernoulli and Gaussian multipliers share first two moments; Gaussian has higher entropy and Bernoulli lower entropy. Table 10 reports preliminary classification errors showing Gaussian dropout slightly better than Bernoulli on MNIST (0.95±0.04 vs 1.08±0.04) and CIFAR-10 (12.5±0.1 vs 12.6±0.1), using p values specified per layer and 10 random seeds.

Section 11 concludes that dropout reduces overfitting by breaking co-adaptations. It claims dropout methods achieved state-of-the-art results on SVHN, ImageNet, CIFAR-100, and MNIST, while Reuters is an exception where standard networks performed better without dropout (Reuters error 31.05% vs 29.62%). The conclusion also says dropout extends to RBMs and other graphical models, with Dropout RBMs showing desirable qualitative properties. A key drawback is longer training: dropout networks typically take 2–3 times as long to train as standard networks, because each case trains a different random architecture and the updates are noisy. It reiterates that marginalizing dropout noise can yield a modified L2 regularizer for linear regression, but an equivalent regularizer for more complex models is not obvious.

Section 11 is the conclusion: dropout reduces overfitting by breaking co-adaptations and achieved state-of-the-art on SVHN, ImageNet, CIFAR-100, and MNIST; Reuters is an exception where standard networks were better (Reuters error 31.05% vs 29.62%). Dropout extends to RBMs and other graphical models, with Dropout RBMs showing desirable qualitative properties. A drawback is longer training: dropout networks typically take 2–3 times as long to train as standard networks, because each case trains a different random architecture and updates are noisy. Marginalizing dropout noise can yield a modified L2 regularizer for linear regression, but not an obvious equivalent regularizer for more complex models.

Appendix A gives practical dropout heuristics. A.1: dropping units reduces capacity; if a standard network needs n units, a dropout layer should have at least n/p units, where p is retention probability. This heuristic is said to be useful for both convolutional and fully connected networks. A.2: dropout introduces substantial gradient noise; recommended learning rates are 10–100 times the standard-network optimum, and momentum values around 0.95–0.99 work better than 0.9. A.3: max-norm regularization bounds each hidden unit’s incoming weight-vector norm by c, with typical c in the 3–4 range. A.4: typical hidden-layer retention probabilities are 0.5–0.8; for real-valued image patches or speech frames, input retention around 0.8 is typical. Smaller p requires larger n and can slow training or cause underfitting.

Appendix B gives experiment details and implementation: GPU-based code using cudamat and cuda-convnet. MNIST: 60k train/10k test, with 10k held out for validation; hyperparameters chosen so best validation error occurred after 1M updates, then train+val were reunited and trained for another 1M updates. Figure 4 covers all 2-, 3-, and 4-hidden-layer networks with 1024 or 2048 units per layer (six architectures). For Figure 4 and Table 2 MNIST models, hidden layers used p=0.5, input p=0.8, final momentum 0.95, and max-norm c=2. Larger 2-layer nets with 4096 and 8192 units improved results; 3-layer versions were slightly worse.

SVHN: about 600k train and 26k test images, with a 6000-case validation set (400 per class from standard labels and 200 per class from extra data). Inputs were RGB normalized to zero mean/unit variance; global/local contrast normalization and ZCA whitening helped little. Best model: 3 conv layers (96/128/256 filters, 5x5, stride 1), each followed by 3x3 max-pooling with stride 2, then two 2048-unit ReLU hidden layers. Dropout retention probabilities from input through layers: (0.9, 0.75, 0.75, 0.5, 0.5, 0.5). All weights used c=4 and momentum 0.95. Validation selected settings; because training set was large, validation data was not added back for final training.

CIFAR-10/100: 50k train/10k test each, 5k validation, then train+val combined. Preprocessing used global contrast normalization per color channel and ZCA whitening. Architecture and dropout rates matched SVHN, except input-layer learning rates had to be smaller.

TIMIT begins: Kaldi produced log-filter banks, a monophone system provided forced alignment and speech-frame labels, and networks used 21 consecutive frames to predict the center frame; inputs were mean-centered and normalized to unit variance.

This part is the title/front-matter page for the paper “Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting,” listing the five authors and their University of Toronto affiliations. It also gives an original-page map for the rest of the paper: pages 1930–1955 cover the introduction, figures, sections 2–11, table 1–10, acknowledgments, Appendix A (A.1–A.4), and Appendix B (B.1–B.6). No new technical notation or results appear in this part.

This part contains the abstract of the paper. It claims that dropout (referred to here as “QX2, or dropout”) temporarily removes randomly selected units and their connections during training, inhibits co-adaptation, samples exponentially many thinned networks sharing parameters, and that a single unthinned network with reduced weights approximates their averaged predictions. It also claims that dropout substantially reduces overfitting and improves results across vision, speech recognition, document classification, and computational biology, with evidence in Tables 2–8 and the unnumbered text-classification table in §6.3. No new notation or contradictions appear here.

This part is the Introduction. It says QX2/dropout trains many shared-parameter subnetworks and uses a single unthinned test-time network to approximate their combined predictions. It frames the method as approximating an equally weighted geometric mean of exponentially many learned models, with a network of n units corresponding to 2^n possible thinned networks but only O(n^2) or fewer parameters. It introduces standard regularizers/terms: early stopping, soft weight sharing, L1 (O3U), and L2 (Y5F). It also says model combination usually helps but is expensive, and that the practical inference rule T6R/weight scaling uses one unthinned network; X9M/Monte-Carlo model averaging samples members at test time. It claims T6R has lower generalization error than compared regularizers, citing Table 9 rows Y5F 1.62, V9C 1.35, QX2+Y5F 1.25, and QX2+V9C 1.05. It also introduces extension to graphical models via RBMs, with B8T/Dropout RBM. No contradictions found yet.

This part gives the paper’s motivation for dropout/QX2 using biological and game-theoretic analogies. It argues that breaking co-adapted gene sets via sexual reproduction can be advantageous because it favors ‘mix-ability’ and robustness, even if it seems worse for preserving successful combinations. It then maps this to QX2-trained hidden units: because hidden units face randomly selected partners, the method encourages independently useful, robust features rather than reliance on other units. The part also uses a conspiracy analogy to suggest that smaller interacting groups may be more robust under changing conditions than one large, fragile coordinated group. No direct contradictions with earlier sections are introduced here.

This part is the related-work section. It frames QX2 as connected to hidden-unit noise, model averaging, and earlier work on corruption, adversarial deletion, and marginalization. It says denoising autoencoders (S2H) corrupt inputs and reconstruct clean inputs, while QX2 extends this with effective hidden-layer corruption and a model-averaging interpretation. QX2 is claimed to apply to supervised and unsupervised learning and to other neuron-based architectures, including Boltzmann machines. It also contrasts QX2 with adversarial-removal models (Globerson and Roweis 2006; Dekel et al. 2010), which choose deletions under a fixed maximum rather than a probability distribution and are said to have no hidden units. Van der Maaten et al. (2013) are described as studying exponential-family input-noise regularizers, including QX2 under the name blankout noise, limited to models without hidden layers; Chen et al. (2012) studied marginalization for DAEs; Wang and Manning (2013) proposed marginalization to accelerate QX2. The table reports noise levels: S2H typical best 5%, QX2 often optimal input-unit removal 20%, and QX2 often optimal hidden-unit removal 50%.

steps.notes_before: Section 4 defines QX2/dropout-style corruption as independent Bernoulli gating of unit outputs during training: each entry \(r_j^{(l)}\sim Bernoulli(p)\), and \(	ilde y^{(l)} = r^{(l)} * y^{(l)}\). Ordinary feed-forward is \(z_i^{(l+1)}=w_i^{(l+1)} y^{(l)} + b_i^{(l+1)}\), \(y_i^{(l+1)}=f(z_i^{(l+1)})\); QX2 replaces \(y^{(l)}\) with \(	ilde y^{(l)}\). Any activation is allowed, including logistic. Applying the gating at every layer samples a subnetwork; backpropagation runs through that sampled subnetwork. Both hidden and visible units can be removed. At inference, no units are removed and weights are scaled as \(W^{(l)}_{test}=pW^{(l)}\).

Section 5 says QX2 training/backprop is ordinary backprop on a sampled thinned network: each mini-batch case uses its own sampled subnetwork, gradients are averaged, and unused parameters get zero gradient. The section argues that combining QX2 with high momentum, large decaying learning rates, and max-norm/V9C gives additional gains; V9C constrains each hidden unit’s incoming-weight vector to norm <= c, with projection back to the radius-c ball and c tuned on validation. For finetuning pretrained nets, smaller learning rates are important; too-large rates can erase pretrained information. Before QX2 finetuning, pretrained weights are multiplied by 1/p to preserve expected outputs under random removal. Retention experiments report that with fixed architecture test error is flat for roughly p in [0.4, 0.8], while with fixed expected retained width low-retention error improves from 2.7% to 1.7% at p=0.1; best retention for the chosen expected widths is around 0.6 and the default 0.5 is close to optimal. Section 7.4 begins a data-set-size discussion, stating the QX2 gain is absent for the smallest sets, grows with more data, then declines.

Section 7.4’s data-size discussion says QX2 gives no improvement on the two smallest training sets, then gains increase as data grows and later decrease; the authors interpret this as a sweet spot where there is enough data to resist noisy memorization but not so much that overfitting matters. The section notes Figure 10 and Appendix B.1’s dataset sizes (100, 500, 1K, 5K, 10K, 50K), but no exact curve values are given. Section 7.5 compares X9M to T6R: with enough samples, X9M matches T6R around k=50 and then becomes slightly better, within one standard deviation. T6R is presented as a good approximation to the true model average based on this comparison.

Section 8 introduces B8T, a dropout-style extension for shared-weight RBMs. It defines a retention vector r over hidden units: if r_j=1, h_j behaves normally; if r_j=0, h_j is forced to 0. The joint model factors as P(r;p)P(h,v|r;θ), with independent Bernoulli retention probability p. The hidden conditional factorizes and the visible conditional remains the standard RBM form. Learning uses standard RBM/CD methods: sample r for each training case and update only retained hidden units; experiments use CD-1.

Section 8.3 says B8T features are coarser and have fewer dead units than ordinary U2L features. Figure 12 compares 256-hidden-unit models, with B8T using p=0.5. Section 8.4 says B8T learns sparser representations without an extra sparsity regularizer; Figure 13 shows many off-zero activations without the method and many near-zero activations with p=0.5. No numerical feature-quality or sparsity metrics are given.

Section 9 discusses marginalizing QX2 dropout noise to get deterministic objectives/regularizers. It cites prior work on test-time feature deletion, linear regression marginalization, and adaptive regularization. Section 9.1 derives the expected squared-error objective for linear regression with Bernoulli retention on inputs: minimizing E||y-(R*X)w||^2 reduces to ||y-pXw||^2 + p(1-p)||Gamma w||^2, where Gamma=(diag(X^T X))^{1/2}. With rescaled weights w~ = p w, the equivalent form is ||y-Xw~||^2 + ((1-p)/p)||Gamma w~||^2. The section’s main point is that dropout induces a data-dependent quadratic penalty whose strength grows as retention decreases and vanishes near p=1.

Section 9.2 says approximate marginalization helps logistic regression, citing Wang and Manning (2013) as improving both training time and generalization over Monte Carlo QX2. It also emphasizes that closed-form marginalized models are difficult for logistic regression and deep nets, and that the assumptions used weaken as layers are added, so the results do not directly apply to deep networks.

Section 10 introduces multiplicative Gaussian noise as an alternative to Bernoulli dropout. It calls the binary variant P7V / Bernoulli dropout and the Gaussian variant D4K / Gaussian dropout. The paper claims preliminary experiments slightly favor Gaussian corruption, with Table 10 reporting lower classification error for D4K on both H4Z (0.95±0.04 vs 1.08±0.04) and J3V (12.5±0.1 vs 12.6±0.1). The comparison uses 10 random seeds and specific retention settings (H4Z hidden p=0.5, input p=0.8; J3V input-to-top p=(0.9,0.75,0.75,0.5,0.5,0.5)).

The section shows that a Gaussian multiplier r'~N(1,σ^2) can be viewed as multiplicative noise on activations, equivalent to additive Gaussian noise h_i -> h_i + h_i r. It states that expected activations are unchanged under mean-1 Gaussian noise, so no test-time scaling is needed for that variant. For Bernoulli dropout, it presents two equivalent parameterizations: either keep retained activations unchanged and scale outgoing test weights by p, or scale retained activations by 1/p and leave test weights unchanged. In this latter view, the Bernoulli multiplier has mean 1 and variance (1-p)/p, and choosing σ^2=(1-p)/p matches the Gaussian multiplier’s first two moments.

Section 11 concludes that QX2 improves generalization by training sampled submodels, but at a training-time cost. It summarizes the main empirical claims: QX2 reaches state of the art on A2F, K9D, W6R, and H4Z, while on M5X ordinary neural nets do better without QX2. Training is said to take about 2–3× longer than a standard network with the same architecture, mainly because of noisy parameter updates and because each case trains a different random architecture, so the gradients are not those of the final inference architecture. The section frames the method as a trade-off between overfitting and training time and says accelerating QX2 is future work. It also notes that noise marginalization can recover some benefits without stochasticity via expectation-equivalent regularizers; for linear regression this gives the modified Y5F objective, but analogous regularizers for more complex models are not obvious.

Appendix A gives practical heuristics for training QX2 while emphasizing that hyperparameter tuning is still extensive. It recommends widening QX2 layers to at least n/p units when a standard net uses n hidden units, since only pn units survive in expectation; this was useful for both convolutional and fully connected layers. It also says high learning rates and momentum help counter gradient noise, with learning rates typically 10–100× the standard-net optimum and momentum around 0.95–0.99 versus 0.9. V9C max-norm bounds hidden-unit incoming weights, with c typically 3–4. Retention p should be chosen jointly with width and input type: lower p needs wider layers and can underfit, while high p may not regularize enough. Typical hidden retention is 0.5–0.8, real-valued inputs typically use 0.8, 0.5 is a broadly near-optimal default, and input-unit retention in general should be closer to 1 than to 0.5.

Appendix B gives reproduction resources and detailed experiment settings. H4Z uses a 10,000-image validation holdout and a 1-million-update endpoint; validation-selected hyperparameters were then rerun on combined train+validation data with no early stopping. The architecture sweep covered 2, 3, and 4 hidden layers with widths 1024 or 2048, using hidden retention p=0.5 and input retention p=0.8, momentum 0.95, and max-norm c=2. Additional experiments used 2- and 3-layer models with 4096 or 8192 units; the largest reported 2-layer model has over 65 million parameters. Regularizer and data-size comparisons use architecture 784-1024-1024-2048-10, F3N, SGD, and training sets of 100 to 50K examples; a fixed-width rate comparison uses 784-2048-2048-2048-10 with no input corruption. Fixed expected-width comparisons set pn=256 in the first two hidden layers and pn=512 in the last. X9M is described as sampling k thinned networks per test case and averaging, converging to the true model average as k→∞. A2F uses mixed-source validation, normalized RGB inputs, and found no benefit from contrast normalization or ZCA whitening. Its network has three convolutional layers with 96, 128, and 256 filters of size 5x5, stride 1, max-pooling 3x3 with stride 2, then two 2048-unit fully connected layers; all hidden activations are F3N, with retention p=(0.9,0.75,0.75,0.5,0.5,0.5), c=4, and momentum 0.95.

B.3 J3V/W6R: image collections use held-out validation, contrast normalization, ZCA whitening, and the A2F architecture. Each has 50,000 training and 10,000 test images; J3V has 10 classes and W6R 100. Validation used 5,000 training images, then training and validation were combined for final optimization. Preprocessing: per-image/per-channel global contrast normalization, then ZCA whitening. Architecture and retention rates match A2F; input-layer learning rates are smaller.

B.4 N8Q: speech recordings from 680 speakers in eight American-English dialects, 10 sentences each. Kaldi generates log-filter banks; monophone forced alignment provides frame labels. Inputs are 21-frame windows, mean-centered and unit-variance scaled, with no speaker-dependent operations. B.5 M5X: Reuters subset for single-label 50-category document classification. Paper: “Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting” (JMLR 2014). Main claim: dropout randomly drops units and their connections during training, causing an exponential number of thinned networks to be sampled; at test time, one can approximate averaging over them with a single unthinned network using smaller weights. Abstract says this reduces overfitting and improves supervised learning performance in vision, speech recognition, document classification, and computational biology, with state-of-the-art results on many benchmarks. Introduction frames dropout as a regularization method for deep nets, alongside early stopping and weight penalties (L1/L2, soft weight sharing). Figure 1 illustrates a standard neural net vs. a thinned net produced by dropout.

The paper motivates dropout as an approximation to Bayesian model averaging / geometric mean over an exponential number of shared-parameter networks, aiming for good performance with less computation. It argues that averaging many separately trained nets is expensive because diverse nets require different architectures or data and are costly to train/test. Dropout drops hidden and visible units (removing incoming/outgoing connections) at random during training; each unit is retained independently with probability p, typically 0.5 for many layers, while input units usually use p closer to 1. Figure 2 states that at test time all units are present and outgoing weights are multiplied by p, so the test-time network matches the expected training-time output.

During training, units are independently retained with probability p; hidden units often use p=0.5, while input units usually use p closer to 1. At test time, all units are present and outgoing weights are multiplied by p so the test-time network matches the expected training-time output. This part adds intuition for dropout via analogies to sexual reproduction and conspiracies: training each hidden unit to work with random subsets of others should make features more robust and less dependent on co-adaptations. It also says the paper will extend dropout to RBMs and discuss experiments, analysis of hyperparameters, marginalizing dropout, and practical guidance in the appendix.

The paper’s intro says dropout extends denoising autoencoders: it can be applied to hidden layers, interpreted as model averaging, and extended beyond unsupervised learning to supervised problems and other neuron-based architectures such as Boltzmann Machines. It also notes that although 5% noise is typical for denoising autoencoders, their weight-scaling-at-test-time approach allows much higher dropout rates; they report 20% input dropout and 50% hidden dropout as often optimal. The paper then motivates deterministic versions by marginalizing the noise, citing prior work on deterministic regularizers and dropout marginalization, and contrasts dropout with adversarial unit-dropping methods.

Model description: for a network with L hidden layers, y^(0)=x, layer l has weights W^(l) and biases b^(l). Standard feedforward uses z^(l+1)=w^(l+1) y^(l)+b^(l+1), y^(l+1)=f(z^(l+1)). With dropout, a Bernoulli mask r^(l) with retention probability p is sampled for each layer, the thinned outputs y~^(l)=r^(l)*y^(l) are passed to the next layer, and this is done at every layer. Training backpropagates through the sampled subnetwork. At test time, dropout is removed and weights are scaled by p: W_test = p W^(l). The next section starts the training procedure for dropout neural nets.

Section 5.1: Dropout nets are trained with SGD by sampling a thinned network per training case; forward/backprop are run only on that thinned network, gradients are averaged over the mini-batch, and units not used contribute zero gradient. Usual SGD improvements (momentum, annealed learning rates, L2 decay) also help. A particularly useful regularizer is max-norm: constrain each hidden unit’s incoming weight vector w to satisfy ||w||2 ≤ c by projecting back onto the ball of radius c; c is tuned on validation. The paper says dropout + max-norm + large decaying learning rates + high momentum works better than dropout alone.

Section 5.2: Dropout can be used to fine-tune pretrained nets (RBMs, autoencoders, DBMs) without changing the pretraining procedure. Weights from pretraining should be scaled up by 1/p so the expected output under dropout matches pretraining. Smaller finetuning learning rates are needed; with them, pretrained information is retained and final generalization improves versus finetuning without dropout.

Section 6 begins experiments: they evaluate dropout on classification tasks across many domains and claim dropout improved generalization on all data sets compared to non-dropout neural nets. Listed data sets: MNIST, TIMIT, CIFAR-10/100, SVHN, ImageNet, Reuters-RCV1, and an Alternative Splicing data set. A detailed description is deferred to Appendix B.

Hidden activations hi are perturbed as hi + hi r with r ~ N(0,1), equivalently hi r' with r' ~ N(1,1), and more generally r' ~ N(1,σ^2). Because the mean activation is unchanged, no test-time weight scaling is needed for this Gaussian-noise variant. The paper contrasts this with Bernoulli dropout viewed as multiplying by rb that equals 1/p with probability p and 0 otherwise; rb has mean 1 and variance (1-p)/p. Matching moments gives σ^2=(1-p)/p for the Gaussian case. The text claims both Bernoulli and Gaussian forms work well, with preliminary Table 10 results suggesting the high-entropy Gaussian case may work slightly better. Table 10 compares Bernoulli vs Gaussian dropout on MNIST and CIFAR-10; for MNIST the Bernoulli dropout rates are p=0.5 for hidden units and p=0.8 for input units, and for CIFAR-10 a layerwise p vector is used, with Gaussian σ set from the corresponding Bernoulli p.

The paper also concludes dropout is broad/general, with reported state-of-the-art results on SVHN, ImageNet, CIFAR-100, and MNIST, and notes an extension to RBMs and other graphical models via training an ensemble of sub-models.

Appendix A gives practical heuristics: because dropout leaves about pn units active in expectation, a dropout net should often use at least n/p units if n was optimal without dropout. Dropout training is typically 2-3x slower than standard nets, so it often uses 10-100x the usual learning rate and momentum around 0.95-0.99; max-norm regularization with c around 3-4 can help control weight growth. Typical dropout keep-probabilities are 0.5-0.8 for hidden units and about 0.8 for real-valued inputs.

Paper: "Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting" (JMLR 15, 2014, pp. 1929–1958). Authors: Nitish Srivastava, Geoffrey Hinton, Alex Krizhevsky, Ilya Sutskever, and Ruslan Salakhutdinov (University of Toronto); editor Yoshua Bengio. The paper map on the first pages lays out the structure across sections 2–11 plus appendices A and B. Abstract/intro claims: dropout randomly removes units and their connections during training, reducing co-adaptation and implicitly sampling exponentially many thinned networks; a single unthinned network with reduced weights approximates the averaged predictions. It claims dropout reduces overfitting and improves results across vision, speech recognition, document classification, and computational biology, often state of the art. Section 1 also says posterior-weighted averaging is the best regularization given unlimited computation, while dropout approximates an equally weighted geometric mean over exponentially many shared-parameter models. A network with n units corresponds to 2^n thinned networks and reuses O(n^2) or fewer parameters. The introduction contrasts dropout with stopping early, soft weight sharing, and L1/L2 penalties, and says model combination is powerful but expensive. It introduces the practical inference rule (weight scaling) versus Monte Carlo model averaging, and notes dropout extends to graphical models such as Boltzmann machines, including Restricted Boltzmann Machines and dropout RBMs. Figure 1 shows a standard two-hidden-layer net and a thinned version with crossed units removed.

Section 2 motivates dropout using analogies from evolution and robustness. It contrasts sexual vs asexual reproduction: recombination breaks co-adapted gene sets, suggesting a tension between individual-fitness optimization and the value of mixable, robust genes. The Livnat et al. view is that selection may favor gene sets that work with many partners; the paper maps this to hidden units trained with dropout, which must be useful with randomly selected partners and thus learn independently useful, robust features rather than depend on other units. It also uses a conspiracy analogy: smaller conspiracies are more robust to changing conditions than a larger one needing many correct participants. These examples support the claim that complex co-adaptations can fit training data yet generalize poorly, whereas simpler robust components may generalize better.

Section 3 surveys related work on noise-based regularization. It frames hidden-unit noise as a regularizer for QX2, connecting it to denoising autoencoders (Vincent et al. 2008, 2010): input corruption plus reconstruction, effective hidden-layer corruption, model averaging, supervised and unsupervised use, and applicability to other neuron-based architectures such as Boltzmann machines. A comparison table says typical best noise is 5% for S2H, while QX2 often works best at 20% input-unit removal or 50% hidden-unit removal. It contrasts stochastic noise training with adversarial removal methods (Globerson and Roweis 2006; Dekel et al. 2010), noting those have no hidden units. It also says analytically marginalizing QX2 yields deterministic regularizers in simple cases; related exponential-family input-noise regularizers (“blankout noise”) were studied by van der Maaten et al. (2013) for models without hidden layers. Chen et al. (2012) examined marginalization for denoising autoencoders, and Wang and Manning (2013) proposed marginalization to accelerate QX2.

steps.notes_before: Section 4 defines QX2 as stochastic deletion (“dropout”) applied to every layer: each layer output vector is multiplied elementwise by an independent Bernoulli mask with retention probability \(p\). Training samples a subnetwork and backpropagates through it; both hidden and visible units can be removed. At test time, no units are removed and the outgoing weights are scaled by \(p\): \(\mathbf W^{(l)}_{	ext{test}}=p\mathbf W^{(l)}\). The section states that validation can choose \(p\), but the default is usually near optimal and input retention is often closer to 1. It also claims that the expected output under deletion matches test-time output, though the formulas only directly show this for the preactivation, not necessarily after a nonlinear activation.

Section 5 says QX2 training uses standard SGD on a per-case sampled thinned network: each case is forwarded/backpropagated through its own sampled subnetwork, gradients are averaged, and absent parameters contribute zero. It highlights that QX2 works well with high momentum, large decaying learning rates, and V9C max-norm regularization, where each incoming hidden-unit weight vector is constrained by ||w||_2 <= c and projected back onto the radius-c ball if it exceeds it. The section also notes that this constraint is a validation-tuned hyperparameter and can help deep-net training even without QX2. For unsupervised pretraining, the procedure is unchanged, but before QX2 finetuning pretrained weights are multiplied by 1/p so that expected random-removal output matches the pretrained output. Smaller finetuning learning rates are said to preserve pretrained information better than rates comparable to best randomly initialized-net rates.

The conclusion says the large-model construction repeatedly samples and trains smaller submodels from an easily overfitted model; U2L fits this construction and B8T has desirable empirical properties. It claims QX2 methods achieve state of the art on A2F, K9D, W6R, and H4Z, with considerable improvement over standard neural nets on other collections. It also says training typically takes 2–3 times as long as a standard network of the same architecture, attributes this largely to noisy parameter updates and the mismatch between sampled architectures and the final inference architecture, and notes that stochasticity may help prevent overfitting. Finally, it says noise marginalization can recover some benefits without stochasticity via an expectation-equivalent regularizer, with linear regression yielding modified Y5F, but that analogous regularizers for more complex models are not obvious.

Appendix A gives practical heuristics for training QX2 networks and emphasizes that they still require extensive hyperparameter tuning. For a standard-net layer with optimal size n, a QX2 layer should have at least n/p units because sampling leaves only pn units in expectation and prevents unrestricted co-adaptation. QX2 often needs a much higher learning rate than a standard net of the same architecture, typically 10–100x the optimal standard-net rate, and momentum around 0.95–0.99 (vs common standard 0.9) helps offset gradient noise. V9C is recommended to bound hidden-unit incoming-weight norms, with c typically 3–4. The paper studies dropout as a way to reduce overfitting in large neural networks without training many separate models. Dropout randomly removes units and their connections during training, implicitly sampling many smaller networks that share weights; at test time, a single full network with appropriately scaled weights approximates their combined predictions. The paper claims improvements on image, speech, text, and alternative-splicing tasks, and compares dropout with other regularizers and Bayesian neural networks. Section 7.5 compares Monte-Carlo model averaging with weight scaling. Test-time averaging over k sampled dropout networks approaches the true model average as k increases. On MNIST, about k=50 samples match the weight-scaling approximation; beyond that, Monte-Carlo averaging is slightly better but within one standard deviation, so weight scaling is a good approximation.

Section 8 defines Dropout RBMs as a mixture over hidden-unit subsets. An RBM over v,h has standard energy-based joint P(h,v;θ). A dropout mask r∈{0,1}^F is sampled with independent retention probability p per hidden unit; if r_j=0 then h_j is constrained to 0 via a factor g(h_j,r_j). Conditioned on r, the model is just an RBM with the dropped hidden units removed, so the full model is a mixture of exponentially many RBMs sharing weights. Learning uses standard RBM methods (e.g., CD-1) after sampling a new mask for each training case in each mini-batch.

The section qualitatively compares standard and dropout RBMs on MNIST with 256 hidden units. steps.notes_before:
Section 9 discusses marginalizing dropout noise to get deterministic models. It cites prior work on marginalization/robustness (Globerson and Roweis; Chen et al.; Srivastava; Wang and Manning; van der Maaten et al.; Wager et al.).

For linear regression, with input masking \(R_{ij}\sim\text{Bernoulli}(p)\), the marginalized objective becomes
\(\|y-pXw\|^2 + p(1-p)\|\Gamma w\|^2\), where \(\Gamma = (\operatorname{diag}(X^\top X))^{1/2}\). After rescaling \(\tilde w=pw\), this is
\(\|y-X\tilde w\|^2 + \frac{1-p}{p}\|\Gamma\tilde w\|^2\). So dropout is equivalent in expectation to a ridge-like penalty whose strength increases as \(p\) decreases.

For logistic regression, exact marginalization is difficult; Wang and Manning (2013) use Gaussian approximations for unit inputs and gradients, giving a training-time/generalization improvement over Monte-Carlo dropout. The section is presented as limited for deep networks, though it contains a conflicting sentence claiming the results apply directly to arbitrary-depth networks.

Section 10 introduces multiplicative Gaussian noise as an alternative to Bernoulli dropout. A hidden activation \(h_i\) can be perturbed as \(h_i+h_ir\) with \(r\sim\mathcal N(0,1)\), equivalently \(h_ir'\) with \(r'\sim\mathcal N(1,1)\). More generally, \(r'\sim\mathcal N(1,\sigma^2)\), where σ is a tunable noise standard deviation.

The section distinguishes two equivalent dropout parameterizations: (1) retain units with probability \(p\) during training and scale weights by \(p\) at test time; or (2) multiply retained training activations by \(1/p\) and leave test weights unchanged. Under the second form, the Bernoulli multiplier \(r_b\) equals \(1/p\) with probability \(p\) and 0 otherwise, giving \(\mathbb E[r_b]=1\) and \(\mathrm{Var}[r_b]=(1-p)/p\). Matching first and second moments gives Gaussian variance \(\sigma^2=(1-p)/p\), so \(r_g\sim\mathcal N(1,(1-p)/p)\) has the same mean and variance.

The paper argues that Gaussian noise has higher entropy than Bernoulli for these matched moments, and Table 10 reports slightly better classification errors for Gaussian dropout than Bernoulli on MNIST (0.95 vs 1.08) and CIFAR-10 (12.5 vs 12.6), averaged over 10 random seeds. For MNIST, Bernoulli uses \(p=0.5\) for hidden units and \(p=0.8\) for input units; for CIFAR-10, \(p=(0.9,0.75,0.75,0.5,0.5,0.5)\) from input to top.

Section 11 concludes that dropout reduces overfitting by breaking co-adaptations, and says it improves performance across several domains: object classification, digit recognition, speech recognition, document classification, and computational biology. It claims methods using dropout achieve state-of-the-art results on SVHN, ImageNet, CIFAR-100, and MNIST, and that dropout also improves standard networks on other datasets. The conclusion extends the idea to RBMs and other graphical models, describing dropout RBMs as fitting the general strategy of training large overfitting models via repeated sampling of smaller sub-models. It also emphasizes a drawback: training typically takes 2–3 times longer than standard networks because each case effectively trains a different random architecture, so gradients are noisy and not those of the final test architecture. The section notes that marginalizing noise can yield an equivalent regularizer for linear regression but that this is not obvious for more complex models, and frames faster dropout training as future work.

It claims state-of-the-art results with dropout on SVHN, ImageNet, CIFAR-100, and MNIST, and notes dropout also improves standard networks on other datasets. A drawback is that training typically takes 2–3 times longer than standard networks because each case effectively trains a different random architecture, making gradients noisy and not those of the final test architecture. It notes that marginalizing noise yields an equivalent regularizer for linear regression, but this is not obvious for more complex models, and faster dropout training is future work.

Appendix A gives practical dropout heuristics: increase hidden-layer size to about n/p if n units work for a standard network; use learning rates 10–100× the standard optimum; use momentum around 0.95–0.99; apply max-norm regularization with typical c values 3–4; and choose hidden-unit retention probabilities typically 0.5–0.8, with input retention around 0.8 for real-valued image patches or speech frames. Smaller p requires larger n and can slow training and cause underfitting.

Appendix B gives experimental details and implementation: GPU-based code using cudamat and cuda-convnet, with reproduction code online. MNIST: 60k train/10k test; 10k training images held out for validation, then training+validation were reunited for a final 1M updates. Figure 4 covers all 2-, 3-, and 4-hidden-layer MNIST nets with 1024 or 2048 units; all hidden layers used p=0.5, input p=0.8, final momentum 0.95, and max-norm c=2. Larger 2-layer MNIST nets (4096, 8192 units) improved results; 3-layer nets were slightly worse, and more dropout did not beat 2-layer nets. SVHN: about 600k train and 26k test images; validation set of 6000 built from 400/class standard and 200/class extra examples. Inputs were RGB normalized to zero mean/unit variance; contrast normalization and ZCA whitening did not help. Best SVHN model: 3 conv layers (96, 128, 256 filters, 5x5, stride 1), each followed by 3x3 max-pooling with stride 2, then two 2048-unit ReLU fully connected layers. Dropout retention probabilities were (0.9, 0.75, 0.75, 0.5, 0.5, 0.5), with c=4 and momentum 0.95; validation chose settings and the validation set was not merged back for final training. CIFAR-10/100: 50k train/10k test, 5k validation; preprocessing used per-channel global contrast normalization and ZCA whitening, and architecture/dropout matched SVHN except for smaller input-layer learning rates. TIMIT begins with Kaldi log-filter banks, forced alignment from a monophone system, 21-frame contexts predicting the central frame, and mean-centered/unit-variance inputs.

The paper studies dropout as a method to prevent overfitting in large neural networks by randomly removing units/connections during training, effectively training many smaller shared-parameter networks and using a single scaled network at test time. It claims dropout improves generalization over non-dropout networks on every tested dataset, with experiments across images, speech, documents, and gene-splicing prediction. The paper says it reports state-of-the-art results on several benchmarks and also examines learned features, sparsity, retention rates, training-set size, RBMs, noise marginalization, and Gaussian corruption. Training is said to take about 2–3 times longer than a standard network of the same architecture.

The paper’s glossary defines the main dropout-related terms and abbreviations used later. Dropout is described as random removal of units and connections during training, with approximate averaging by one unthinned network at test time; thinned networks are subnetworks formed by removing units/connections. It defines core neural-network terms (units, hidden/visible layers, weights, biases, activations), regularizers (L1, L2/Tikhonov, max-norm, KL-sparsity, early stopping), and averaging concepts (model averaging, posterior-weighted averaging, geometric mean, weight scaling, Monte-Carlo averaging). It also names Bernoulli dropout, Gaussian dropout, and dropout-related noise/marginalization ideas. The glossary covers training procedures and settings such as backpropagation, SGD, mini-batches, momentum, learning rate/annealing, hyperparameters, validation, pretraining, finetuning, and CD-1. It also lists architectures and baselines used later: convolutional nets, pooling types, data augmentation, SVM, PCA, linear/ridge/logistic regression, Bayesian neural networks, bag-of-words, sparse representations, RBMs/DBMs/DBNs, dropout RBM, autoencoders, and some later comparison-specific notions like dead units, mix-ability, replica code, and non-stationarity.

Dropout notation: p is retention probability, r^(l) are Bernoulli retention vectors, ~tilde y^(l) are thinned outputs, * is elementwise product, W_test^(l)=pW^(l), and pn / n/p are expected retained width and the practical width heuristic. k is the number of independently sampled networks used for X9M, with k→∞ approximating the true model average. This part is the title/front-matter page for the paper “Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting,” listing the five authors and their University of Toronto affiliations. It also gives an original-page map for the rest of the paper: pages 1930–1955 cover the introduction, figures, sections 2–11, table 1–10, acknowledgments, Appendix A (A.1–A.4), and Appendix B (B.1–B.6). No new technical notation or results appear in this part.

This part contains the abstract of the paper. It claims that dropout (referred to here as “QX2, or dropout”) temporarily removes randomly selected units and their connections during training, inhibits co-adaptation, samples exponentially many thinned networks sharing parameters, and that a single unthinned network with reduced weights approximates their averaged predictions. It also claims that dropout substantially reduces overfitting and improves results across vision, speech recognition, document classification, and computational biology, with evidence in Tables 2–8 and the unnumbered text-classification table in §6.3. No new notation or contradictions appear here.

This part is the Introduction. It says QX2/dropout trains many shared-parameter subnetworks and uses a single unthinned test-time network to approximate their combined predictions. It frames the method as approximating an equally weighted geometric mean of exponentially many learned models, with a network of n units corresponding to 2^n possible thinned networks but only O(n^2) or fewer parameters. It introduces standard regularizers/terms: early stopping, soft weight sharing, L1 (O3U), and L2 (Y5F). It also says model combination usually helps but is expensive, and that the practical inference rule T6R/weight scaling uses one unthinned network; X9M/Monte-Carlo model averaging samples members at test time. It claims T6R has lower generalization error than compared regularizers, citing Table 9 rows Y5F 1.62, V9C 1.35, QX2+Y5F 1.25, and QX2+V9C 1.05. It also introduces extension to graphical models via RBMs, with B8T/Dropout RBM. No contradictions found yet.

This part gives the paper’s motivation for dropout/QX2 using biological and game-theoretic analogies. It argues that breaking co-adapted gene sets via sexual reproduction can be advantageous because it favors ‘mix-ability’ and robustness, even if it seems worse for preserving successful combinations. It then maps this to QX2-trained hidden units: because hidden units face randomly selected partners, the method encourages independently useful, robust features rather than reliance on other units. The part also uses a conspiracy analogy to suggest that smaller interacting groups may be more robust under changing conditions than one large, fragile coordinated group. No direct contradictions with earlier sections are introduced here.

This part is the related-work section. It frames QX2 as connected to hidden-unit noise, model averaging, and earlier work on corruption, adversarial deletion, and marginalization. It says denoising autoencoders (S2H) corrupt inputs and reconstruct clean inputs, while QX2 extends this with effective hidden-layer corruption and a model-averaging interpretation. QX2 is claimed to apply to supervised and unsupervised learning and to other neuron-based architectures, including Boltzmann machines. It also contrasts QX2 with adversarial-removal models (Globerson and Roweis 2006; Dekel et al. 2010), which choose deletions under a fixed maximum rather than a probability distribution and are said to have no hidden units. Van der Maaten et al. (2013) are described as studying exponential-family input-noise regularizers, including QX2 under the name blankout noise, limited to models without hidden layers; Chen et al. (2012) studied marginalization for DAEs; Wang and Manning (2013) proposed marginalization to accelerate QX2. The table reports noise levels: S2H typical best 5%, QX2 often optimal input-unit removal 20%, and QX2 often optimal hidden-unit removal 50%.

steps.notes_before: Section 4 defines QX2/dropout-style corruption as independent Bernoulli gating of unit outputs during training: each entry \(r_j^{(l)}\sim Bernoulli(p)\), and \(	ilde y^{(l)} = r^{(l)} * y^{(l)}\). Ordinary feed-forward is \(z_i^{(l+1)}=w_i^{(l+1)} y^{(l)} + b_i^{(l+1)}\), \(y_i^{(l+1)}=f(z_i^{(l+1)})\); QX2 replaces \(y^{(l)}\) with \(	ilde y^{(l)}\). Any activation is allowed, including logistic. Applying the gating at every layer samples a subnetwork; backpropagation runs through that sampled subnetwork. Both hidden and visible units can be removed. At inference, no units are removed and weights are scaled as \(W^{(l)}_{test}=pW^{(l)}\).

Section 5 says QX2 training/backprop is ordinary backprop on a sampled thinned network: each mini-batch case uses its own sampled subnetwork, gradients are averaged, and unused parameters get zero gradient. The section argues that combining QX2 with high momentum, large decaying learning rates, and max-norm/V9C gives additional gains; V9C constrains each hidden unit’s incoming-weight vector to norm <= c, with projection back to the radius-c ball and c tuned on validation. It also offers a qualitative optimization story (weight ball allows large learning rates; QX2 noise explores weight space; decay shortens steps). For finetuning pretrained nets, smaller learning rates are important; too-large rates can erase pretrained information. Before QX2 finetuning, pretrained weights are multiplied by 1/p to preserve expected outputs under random removal. QX2 finetuning can be applied after pretraining from stacked U2L, autoencoders, or E5Q/DBMs. Reported evidence includes table values showing QX2 improving finetuning results (e.g., G6W: 1.18 to 0.92; E5Q: 0.96 to 0.79) and a best QX2 finetuning rate around 0.01 versus a higher listed rate of 0.1.

Section 8 introduces B8T, a dropout-style extension for shared-weight RBMs. It defines a retention vector r over hidden units: if r_j=1, h_j behaves normally; if r_j=0, h_j is forced to 0. The joint model factors as P(r;p)P(h,v|r;θ), with independent Bernoulli retention probability p. The hidden conditional factorizes and the visible conditional remains the standard RBM form. Learning uses standard RBM/CD methods: sample r for each training case and update only retained hidden units; experiments use CD-1.

Section 11 concludes that QX2 improves generalization by repeatedly sampling and training smaller submodels from a large model, at the cost of slower training. It says training usually takes 2–3 times longer than a standard network of the same architecture because noisy parameter updates are a major cause and each case trains a different random architecture, so gradients are not those of the final inference model. The section states this stochasticity likely helps prevent overfitting, implying a trade-off between more training time and less overfitting. It also says noise marginalization can recover some benefits without stochasticity via an expectation-equivalent regularizer; for linear regression this yields the modified Y5F objective, but for more complex models equivalent regularizers are not obvious. Appendix A gives practical heuristics for QX2 training while still emphasizing extensive hyperparameter tuning. Wider layers are recommended: if an ordinary net uses n hidden units, a QX2 layer should have at least n/p units because only pn units survive in expectation. Larger learning rates and momentum are recommended; practical values are about 10–100× the standard-net learning rate and momentum around 0.95–0.99 versus 0.9. Max-norm constraint c is typically 3–4. Retention should be chosen jointly with width and input type: hidden-unit retention is typically 0.5–0.8, real-valued inputs about 0.8, a broad default is 0.5, and the input-unit optimum is closer to 1 than 0.5. Low retention can underfit, illustrated by the cited comparison for p=0.1.

Paper: “Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting” (JMLR 2014). Main claim: dropout randomly drops units and their connections during training, causing an exponential number of thinned networks to be sampled; at test time, one can approximate averaging over them with a single unthinned network using smaller weights. Abstract says this reduces overfitting and improves supervised learning performance in vision, speech recognition, document classification, and computational biology, with state-of-the-art results on many benchmarks. Introduction frames dropout as a regularization method for deep nets, alongside early stopping and weight penalties (L1/L2, soft weight sharing). Figure 1 illustrates a standard neural net vs. a thinned net produced by dropout.

The paper motivates dropout as an approximation to Bayesian model averaging / geometric mean over an exponential number of shared-parameter networks, aiming for good performance with less computation. It argues that averaging many separately trained nets is expensive because diverse nets require different architectures or data and are costly to train/test. Dropout drops hidden and visible units (removing incoming/outgoing connections) at random during training; each unit is retained independently with probability p, typically 0.5 for many layers, while input units usually use p closer to 1. Figure 2 states that at test time all units are present and outgoing weights are multiplied by p, so the test-time network matches the expected training-time output.

During training, units are independently retained with probability p; hidden units often use p=0.5, while input units usually use p closer to 1. At test time, all units are present and outgoing weights are multiplied by p so the test-time network matches the expected training-time output. This part adds intuition for dropout via analogies to sexual reproduction and conspiracies: training each hidden unit to work with random subsets of others should make features more robust and less dependent on co-adaptations. It also says the paper will extend dropout to RBMs and discuss experiments, analysis of hyperparameters, marginalizing dropout, and practical guidance in the appendix.

The paper’s intro says dropout extends denoising autoencoders: it can be applied to hidden layers, interpreted as model averaging, and extended beyond unsupervised learning to supervised problems and other neuron-based architectures such as Boltzmann Machines. It also notes that although 5% noise is typical for denoising autoencoders, their weight-scaling-at-test-time approach allows much higher dropout rates; they report 20% input dropout and 50% hidden dropout as often optimal. The paper then motivates deterministic versions by marginalizing the noise, citing prior work on deterministic regularizers and dropout marginalization, and contrasts dropout with adversarial unit-dropping methods.

Model description: for a network with L hidden layers, y^(0)=x, layer l has weights W^(l) and biases b^(l). Standard feedforward uses z^(l+1)=w^(l+1) y^(l)+b^(l+1), y^(l+1)=f(z^(l+1)). With dropout, a Bernoulli mask r^(l) with retention probability p is sampled for each layer, the thinned outputs y~^(l)=r^(l)*y^(l) are passed to the next layer, and this is done at every layer. Training backpropagates through the sampled subnetwork. At test time, dropout is removed and weights are scaled by p: W_test = p W^(l). The next section starts the training procedure for dropout neural nets.

Section 5.1: Dropout nets are trained with SGD by sampling a thinned network per training case; forward/backprop are run only on that thinned network, gradients are averaged over the mini-batch, and units not used contribute zero gradient. Usual SGD improvements (momentum, annealed learning rates, L2 decay) also help. A particularly useful regularizer is max-norm: constrain each hidden unit’s incoming weight vector w to satisfy ||w||2 ≤ c by projecting back onto the ball of radius c; c is tuned on validation. The paper says dropout + max-norm + large decaying learning rates + high momentum works better than dropout alone.

Section 5.2: Dropout can be used to fine-tune pretrained nets (RBMs, autoencoders, DBMs) without changing the pretraining procedure. Weights from pretraining should be scaled up by 1/p so the expected output under dropout matches pretraining. Smaller finetuning learning rates are needed; with them, pretrained information is retained and final generalization improves versus finetuning without dropout.

Section 6 begins experiments: they evaluate dropout on classification tasks across many domains and claim dropout improved generalization on all data sets compared to non-dropout neural nets. Listed data sets: MNIST, TIMIT, CIFAR-10/100, SVHN, ImageNet, Reuters-RCV1, and an Alternative Splicing data set. A detailed description is deferred to Appendix B.

Section 8 introduces Dropout RBMs: visible units v∈{0,1}^D, hidden units h∈{0,1}^F, and binary dropout mask r∈{0,1}^F with retention probability p. If r_j=0, hidden unit h_j is forced to 0. The model factorizes as P(r)P(h,v|r), conditioned on r the model is an RBM with dropped hidden units, and P(h|r,v) and P(v|h) remain factorial. Learning uses standard RBM methods such as CD-1, sampling a fresh r per training case/minibatch. Figure 12 compares learned features for a 256-hidden-unit RBM with and without dropout.

Section 8.4 studies sparsity in dropout RBMs. Figure 13 compares hidden-unit activation histograms for a standard RBM and a dropout RBM on a test minibatch; the paper claims the dropout RBM yields much sparser hidden representations, even without any explicit sparsity regularizer. Section 9 introduces marginalizing dropout noise to get deterministic models with gradients for marginalized losses. For linear regression, dropout on inputs with retention probability p is equivalent in expectation to ridge regression with an added penalty p(1-p)||Γw||^2, where Γ depends on feature variances; after absorbing p into w, the regularization strength scales as (1-p)/p. For logistic regression and deep nets, exact marginalization is not tractable, but Wang and Manning’s approximate marginalization is described as faster and better than Monte-Carlo dropout; a table reports MNIST error 1.08±0.04 for Bernoulli dropout vs 0.95±0.04 for Gaussian dropout, and CIFAR-10 error 12.6±0.1 vs 12.5±0.1 respectively.

Section 10 introduces multiplicative Gaussian noise as an alternative to Bernoulli dropout: activations are multiplied by r0 ~ N(1, 1) (or more generally N(1, σ^2)), with no test-time weight scaling needed because the mean multiplier is 1. The paper notes that standard Bernoulli dropout can also be viewed as multiplying by rb taking value 1/p with probability p and 0 otherwise, so E[rb]=1 and Var[rb]=(1-p)/p. Matching the first two moments gives σ^2=(1-p)/p for Gaussian dropout. Table 10 compares Bernoulli vs Gaussian dropout on MNIST and CIFAR-10; the text says the Gaussian/high-entropy case may work slightly better. Section 11 begins the conclusion, restating that dropout improves neural networks by reducing overfitting and breaking brittle co-adaptations.

Section 11 concludes that dropout is broadly useful across many domains and achieves state-of-the-art results on several benchmarks, including SVHN, ImageNet, CIFAR-100, and MNIST. It also says dropout extends to RBMs and other graphical models; the authors developed Dropout RBMs and found desirable properties. A drawback is slower training: dropout nets typically take 2-3 times longer than standard nets because each case trains a different random architecture and gradients are very noisy. One way to reduce stochasticity is to marginalize the noise, yielding a regularizer; for linear regression this becomes a modified L2 penalty. Appendix A gives practical heuristics: use larger networks (about n/p hidden units if p is the retention probability), increase learning rate by 10-100x relative to standard nets, use momentum around 0.95-0.99, and apply max-norm regularization (typical c=3-4). Typical hidden-unit retention rates are 0.5-0.8, with around 0.8 for real-valued inputs.

Appendix B summarizes datasets/experiments. H4Z: 10k validation images held out; final training ran to fixed 1M updates after validation tuning and recombining train/val. Architecture sweeps covered 2/3/4 hidden layers with widths 1024 or 2048 (6 architectures). Reported QX2 settings used input retention p=0.8, hidden retention p=0.5, momentum 0.95, V9C c=2. Other H4Z experiments used 2- and 3-layer nets with 4096/8192 units; largest reported 2-layer model had >65M parameters. A2F: training-image count is approximate; training data include a standard labeled portion plus an additional easy-example portion. Validation uses 6000 samples total: two-thirds from the standard portion (400/class) and one-third from the additional portion (200/class). Model: 3 conv layers (96, 128, 256 filters), 5x5 kernels, stride 1, max-pooling after each conv with 3x3 regions and stride 2, then two FC hidden layers of 2048 units. Retention p=(0.9,0.75,0.75,0.5,0.5,0.5), c=4, momentum 0.95.

J3V/W6R: each has 50k training and 10k test images, with 10 and 100 classes respectively. Validation used 5k training images; hyperparameters were retrained on combined validation/training data. Preprocessing: global contrast normalization per image/channel, then ZCA whitening. Architecture and retention rates match A2F; input-layer learning rates are smaller.

N8Q: 680 speakers, eight American-English dialects, 10 sentences each, controlled/noise-free recordings; Kaldi produced log-filter banks, monophone alignments/labels, and consecutive-frame windows predict the central frame with no speaker-dependent ops and mean-centered unit-variance inputs.

M5X uses 402,738 articles from a 50-category subset of an 800k+ document tree corpus. Z7P uses 3665 cassette exons, 1014 RNA features, and four tissue types from 27 mouse tissues; each tissue has states inc/exc/nc.
