Abstract/intro claims: dropout randomly removes units and their connections during training, reducing co-adaptation and implicitly sampling exponentially many thinned networks; a single unthinned network with reduced weights approximates the averaged predictions. It claims dropout reduces overfitting and improves results across vision, speech recognition, document classification, and computational biology, often state of the art. Section 1 also says posterior-weighted averaging is the best regularization given unlimited computation, while dropout approximates an equally weighted geometric mean over exponentially many shared-parameter models. A network with n units corresponds to 2^n thinned networks and reuses O(n^2) or fewer parameters. The introduction contrasts dropout with stopping early, soft weight sharing, and L1/L2 penalties, and says model combination is powerful but expensive. It introduces the practical inference rule (weight scaling) versus Monte Carlo model averaging, and notes dropout extends to graphical models such as Boltzmann machines, including Restricted Boltzmann Machines and dropout RBMs. Figure 1 shows a standard two-hidden-layer net and a thinned version with crossed units removed.

Section 2 motivates dropout using analogies from evolution and robustness. It contrasts sexual vs asexual reproduction: recombination breaks co-adapted gene sets, suggesting a tension between individual-fitness optimization and the value of mixable, robust genes. The Livnat et al. view is that selection may favor gene sets that work with many partners; the paper maps this to hidden units trained with dropout, which must be useful with randomly selected partners and thus learn independently useful, robust features rather than depend on other units. It also uses a conspiracy analogy: smaller conspiracies are more robust to changing conditions than a larger one needing many correct participants. These examples support the claim that complex co-adaptations can fit training data yet generalize poorly, whereas simpler robust components may generalize better.

Section 3 surveys related work on noise-based regularization. It frames hidden-unit noise as a regularizer for QX2, connecting it to denoising autoencoders (Vincent et al. 2008, 2010): input corruption plus reconstruction, effective hidden-layer corruption, model averaging, supervised and unsupervised use, and applicability to other neuron-based architectures such as Boltzmann machines. A comparison table says typical best noise is 5% for S2H, while QX2 often works best at 20% input-unit removal or 50% hidden-unit removal. It contrasts stochastic noise training with adversarial removal methods (Globerson and Roweis 2006; Dekel et al. 2010), noting those have no hidden units. It also says analytically marginalizing QX2 yields deterministic regularizers in simple cases; related exponential-family input-noise regularizers (“blankout noise”) were studied by van der Maaten et al. (2013) for models without hidden layers. Chen et al. (2012) examined marginalization for denoising autoencoders, and Wang and Manning (2013) proposed marginalization to accelerate QX2.

errors.claim: “For every hidden unit, expected output under the training deletion distribution equals actual test-time output under the prescribed reduced weights.”
errors.evidence: The same section defines a nonlinear activation after deletion, and says “Any activation \(f\) is admissible, including \(f(x)=1/(1+\exp(-x))\).” It also applies random gates before \(f\): \(z_i^{(l+1)}=\mathbf w_i^{(l+1)}\widetilde{\mathbf y}^{\,l}+b_i^{(l+1)},\; y_i^{(l+1)}=f(z_i^{(l+1)})\).
errors.explanation: The equations justify equality of the expected preactivation with the test-time preactivation after scaling, but not equality of the expected post-nonlinearity output for arbitrary \(f\). So the claim is too strong as written and conflicts with the model description in this section.

steps.notes_before: Section 4 defines QX2 as stochastic deletion (“dropout”) applied to every layer: each layer output vector is multiplied elementwise by an independent Bernoulli mask with retention probability \(p\). Training samples a subnetwork and backpropagates through it; both hidden and visible units can be removed. At test time, no units are removed and the outgoing weights are scaled by \(p\): \(\mathbf W^{(l)}_{	ext{test}}=p\mathbf W^{(l)}\). The section states that validation can choose \(p\), but the default is usually near optimal and input retention is often closer to 1. It also claims that the expected output under deletion matches test-time output, though the formulas only directly show this for the preactivation, not necessarily after a nonlinear activation.

Section 5 says QX2 training uses standard SGD on a per-case sampled thinned network: each case is forwarded/backpropagated through its own sampled subnetwork, gradients are averaged, and absent parameters contribute zero. It highlights that QX2 works well with high momentum, large decaying learning rates, and V9C max-norm regularization, where each incoming hidden-unit weight vector is constrained by ||w||_2 <= c and projected back onto the radius-c ball if it exceeds it. The section also notes that this constraint is a validation-tuned hyperparameter and can help deep-net training even without QX2. For unsupervised pretraining, the procedure is unchanged, but before QX2 finetuning pretrained weights are multiplied by 1/p so that expected random-removal output matches the pretrained output. Smaller finetuning learning rates are said to preserve pretrained information better than rates comparable to best randomly initialized-net rates.

Section 6 reports experimental results. It claims QX2 improved generalization over non-QX2 neural nets on every tested data set and that models attaining state of the art on all five vision collections use QX2. Table 1 lists datasets: H4Z/MNIST (784, 60K/10K), A2F/SVHN (3072, 600K/26K), J3V/W6R/CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 (3072, 60K/10K), K9D/ImageNet ILSVRC-2012 (65536, 1.2M/150K), N8Q/TIMIT (2520, 1.1M frames/58K frames), M5X/Reuters-RCV1 (2000, 200K/200K), and Z7P/Alternative Splicing (1014, 2932/733). In H4Z, QX2 improves over standard neural nets; ReLUs, max-norm regularization (V9C), larger architectures, and maxout (L8J) each improve further. Best H4Z listed result is E5Q + QX2 finetuning at 0.79% error; G6W + QX2 finetuning gets 0.92%, while E5Q + finetuning without QX2 is 0.96%. Figure 4 compares training trajectories with and without QX2 under fixed hyperparameters, yielding two separated error clusters. The A2F section says convolutional nets outperform other methods; adding QX2 to fully connected layers helps, adding it to convolutional layers helps more, and maxout helps further.

steps.notes_before: Section 7 argues that QX2 changes learned features and improves generalization by breaking co-adaptations. 7.1 says unregularized H4Z autoencoder features are not meaningful, while QX2 features show edges, strokes, and spots; Figure 7 compares identical single-hidden-layer autoencoders with 256 F3N units, no QX2 vs hidden-layer QX2 (p=0.5). 7.2 says QX2 yields sparse hidden activations without explicit sparsity regularizers; the table reports mean activation about 2.0 without QX2 vs about 0.7 with QX2, a large off-zero mode vs a sharp zero peak, and many vs very few highly active units. 7.3 says with fixed architecture low retention underfits; error is flat for p≈0.4–0.8, and low-retention fixed-architecture error is 2.7% vs 1.7% when expected retained width is fixed; best retention is around 0.6 and 0.5 is near-optimal. 7.4 says the two smallest training sets show no QX2 gain, then gain rises and later falls as data increases. 7.5 says X9M versus T6R depends on sample count, with a stated crossover around k=50, but the prose also contains a contradiction about whether X9M or T6R is better.

Section 8 introduces B8T, a mixture of exponentially many shared-weight U2Ls indexed by a binary retention vector r. Given r, the model is just a standard U2L with the dropped hidden units forced to 0. The hidden conditional is factorial and the visible conditional is unchanged from U2L. Learning uses standard CD-style training: sample a fresh r for each training case (each mini-batch case) and update only the retained hidden units; experiments use CD-1. B8T is reported to produce coarser features than ordinary U2L but with very few dead units, and without any extra sparsity regularizer it learns much sparser hidden representations than U2L. Figures 12 and 13 compare ordinary U2L with B8T at p=0.5.

Section 9 discusses marginalizing QX2 (noise/missing-feature models). It distinguishes deterministic marginalized models, which need no random bits and allow gradients of the marginalized loss, from standard Monte-Carlo QX2. It cites prior work on deterministic test-time feature deletion, linear-regression marginalization, and QX2 as an adaptive regularizer. In linear regression with input retention probability p, the marginalized objective equals ||y - pXw||^2 + p(1-p)||Γw||^2, where Γ = diag(X^T X)^(1/2); with w~ = p w, this becomes ||y - Xw~||^2 + ((1-p)/p)||Γw~||^2. The section then says approximate marginalization beats Monte-Carlo QX2 for logistic regression, but closed-form marginalization is difficult for logistic regression and deep nets; under assumptions, inputs/gradients are Gaussian with computable means and variances, though the assumptions become weaker with depth and are not directly applicable to deep networks.

Section 10 introduces multiplicative Gaussian noise as an alternative to Bernoulli dropout. It says preliminary experiments suggest Gaussian corruption can match or slightly outperform Bernoulli corruption, while allowing matched first and second moments despite opposite entropy extremes. Table 10 reports classification error (%) on H4Z and J3V: H4Z 1.08±0.04 for P7V vs 0.95±0.04 for D4K; J3V 12.6±0.1 vs 12.5±0.1. The comparison settings are p=0.5 for H4Z hidden units, p=0.8 for H4Z input units, and p=(0.9,0.75,0.75,0.5,0.5,0.5) for J3V input to top; Gaussian dropout uses σ=sqrt((1-p)/p), averaged over 10 seeds.

The section explains that multiplying hidden activations by Bernoulli variables generalizes to other multiplier distributions. A multiplier N(1,1) is equivalent to adding zero-mean Gaussian noise with standard deviation equal to the activation value; more generally r'~N(1,σ^2) makes σ a tunable hyperparameter analogous to p. Because expected activations stay unchanged, test-time scaling is unnecessary.

It also states an equivalence between the usual dropout implementation (keep activations at training, scale outgoing weights by p at test time) and a representation where retained training activations are multiplied by 1/p and test weights are unchanged, assuming suitable rescaling of learning rates and initializations. In this latter form, the Bernoulli multiplier has mean 1 and variance (1-p)/p, and choosing σ^2=(1-p)/p for the Gaussian multiplier matches those moments.

Conclusion: the large-model construction repeatedly samples and trains smaller submodels from an easily overfitted model; U2L fits this construction, and B8T has desirable empirical properties. QX2 methods achieve state of the art on A2F, K9D, W6R and H4Z, with considerable improvement over standard neural nets on other collections. Training typically takes 2–3 times as long as a standard network of the same architecture, largely due to stochastic updates and architecture sampling; more training time may yield stronger QX2 and less overfitting. Noise marginalization can recover some benefits without stochasticity via an expectation-equivalent regularizer, with a linear-regression example, but analogous regularizers for more complex models are unclear.

Appendix B details experiments/data sets. H4Z: 10k validation images held out; final training ran to a fixed 1M-update endpoint after validation tuning and recombining train/val. Architecture sweeps covered 2/3/4 hidden layers with widths 1024 or 2048 (6 architectures). Reported QX2 settings used p=0.5 hidden retention and p=0.8 input retention, momentum 0.95, V9C c=2. Additional experiments used 2- and 3-layer nets with 4096/8192 units; largest reported 2-layer model had >65M parameters. Other H4Z comparisons used 784-1024-1024-2048-10, 784-2048-2048-2048-10, and a fixed-expected-width setup with pn=256 for the first two hidden layers and pn=512 for the last.

A2F: training-image count is approximate; training data include a standard labeled portion plus an additional easy-example portion. Validation uses 6000 samples total: two-thirds from the standard portion (400/class) and one-third from the additional portion (200/class). Model: 3 conv layers (96, 128, 256 filters), 5x5 kernels, stride 1, max-pooling after each conv with 3x3 regions and stride 2, then two FC hidden layers of 2048 units. Retention p=(0.9,0.75,0.75,0.5,0.5,0.5), c=4, momentum 0.95.

J3V/W6R: each has 50k training and 10k test images, with 10 and 100 classes respectively. Validation used 5k training images; hyperparameters were then retrained on combined validation/training data. Preprocessing: global contrast normalization per image/channel, then ZCA whitening. Architecture and retention rates match A2F; input-layer learning rates are smaller.

N8Q: 680 speakers, eight American-English dialects, 10 sentences each, controlled/noise-free recordings; Kaldi produced log-filter banks, monophone alignments/labels, and consecutive-frame windows predict the central frame with no speaker-dependent ops and mean-centered unit-variance inputs.

final_notes: Appendix B gives experimental details. MNIST: 60k train/10k test; 10k held out for validation, then train+validation reused for 1M updates. Figure 4 uses six architectures: 2/3/4 hidden layers with 1024 or 2048 units; hidden p=0.5, input p=0.8, momentum 0.95, max-norm c=2. Larger 2-layer MNIST nets (4096, 8192) improved; 3-layer nets were slightly worse and more dropout did not beat them. SVHN: ~600k train, 26k test; validation set of 6000 made from 400/class standard + 200/class extra. Inputs are normalized RGB; contrast normalization/ZCA did not help. Best SVHN model has 3 conv layers (96, 128, 256 filters, 5x5, stride 1), each followed by 3x3 max-pooling with stride 2, then two 2048-unit ReLU layers. Dropout retention probs are (0.9, 0.75, 0.75, 0.5, 0.5, 0.5), max-norm c=4, momentum 0.95; test error 2.55%. CIFAR-10/100: 50k train/10k test, 5k validation, same architecture/dropout as SVHN but smaller input learning rates; preprocessing uses global contrast normalization per color channel and ZCA whitening. TIMIT/speech setup: Kaldi log-filterbanks, forced alignment labels, 21-frame context, central-frame prediction, no speaker-dependent processing, mean-centered/unit-variance inputs. Also, a DBN setup uses input retention 0.8, hidden retention 0.5, max-norm c=4, momentum 0.95, initial learning rate 0.1 with decay ε0(1+t/T)^-1; DBN pretraining uses CD-1 with Gaussian RBM input variance fixed at 1, and dropout finetuning works best around learning rate 0.01 with max-norm giving no improvement. Reuters RCV1: 402,738 articles, 2000-word vocabulary, 50 categories, equally split train/test; dropout helps but less than on image/speech tasks, best network 31.05% without dropout vs 29.62% with dropout. Alternative splicing: 3665 cassette exons, 1014 RNA features, 4 tissue types from 27 mouse tissues; code quality is defined over inc/exc/nc states, and a two-layer dropout net with 1024 units per layer uses hidden p=0.5, input p=0.7, max-norm, and decaying learning rates; results averaged over 5 folds.

Abstract claims dropout randomly removes units during training, samples an exponential number of thinned networks, and uses one unthinned network with smaller weights at test time to approximate their average predictions. It says dropout reduces overfitting and improves supervised-learning performance on vision, speech recognition, document classification, and computational-biology tasks, with state-of-the-art results on many benchmarks. It also says dropout outperforms other regularization methods.

Introduction claims deep nets overfit limited data and reviews standard regularization (early stopping, L1/L2, soft weight sharing). The paper’s goal is to approximate Bayesian model averaging / an equally weighted geometric mean of predictions from exponentially many parameter-sharing models at low cost. Dropout randomly removes hidden or visible units during training; in the simplest case each unit is retained independently with probability p (often p=0.5 for hidden units, closer to 1 for inputs). A thinned network is sampled for each training case. At test time, dropout is turned off and outgoing weights are multiplied by p so expected training-time output matches test-time output. A network with n units represents 2^n thinned networks with shared weights, making explicit averaging infeasible. The paper claims dropout reduces generalization error and also applies to RBMs. Section roadmap: 2 motivation, 3 related work, 4 model, 5 training, 6 experiments, 7 network properties/hyperparameters, 8 Dropout RBMs, 9 marginalizing dropout, Appendix A practical guidance.

This part begins Section 2 (Motivation) and uses two analogies to explain why dropout should help: (1) sexual reproduction/mix-ability—useful genes must work with random partners, so hidden units trained with dropout should become robust and not rely on specific co-adaptations; and (2) conspiracies—smaller groups are more likely to keep working under changing conditions than one large tightly coordinated group. The section’s conclusion is that complex co-adaptations may fit training data but are more likely to fail on test data than several simpler co-adaptations.

Section 4 defines standard feed-forward computation and dropout masks. Each layer’s inputs/outputs are denoted z^(l) and y^(l), with y^(0)=x. Under dropout, each layer output is multiplied elementwise by an independent Bernoulli(p) mask r^(l) before being fed to the next layer, producing a sampled sub-network. Training backpropagates through the sampled sub-network. At test time, the weights are scaled as W_test^(l)=p W^(l) and the network is used without dropout.

Section 5 covers learning dropout nets. Training uses SGD on a sampled thinned network per mini-batch case; gradients are averaged and inactive parameters contribute zero gradient. Helpful SGD tricks include momentum, learning-rate decay, and L2 weight decay. Max-norm regularization constrains each hidden unit’s incoming weight vector to norm <= c and is especially useful with dropout; the paper claims dropout + max-norm beats dropout + L2 (Table 9: 1.05% vs 1.25%), and max-norm alone beats L2 (1.35% vs 1.62%).

Section 7 studies how dropout affects learned features, sparsity, and sensitivity to retention probability. In 7.1, the paper compares two otherwise identical MNIST autoencoders with 256 ReLU hidden units, one without dropout and one with hidden-layer dropout at p=0.5. It claims both have similar test reconstruction error, but dropout yields more interpretable features (edges, strokes, spots) and reduces co-adaptation. In 7.2, the same autoencoders are evaluated on a random test mini-batch: without dropout, mean activation is about 2.0 and activations have a large mass away from zero; with dropout, mean activation is about 0.7 and activations are sharply peaked at zero. Thus dropout makes activations sparser without an explicit sparsity penalty. In 7.3, the paper varies dropout rate on MNIST using architecture 784-2048-2048-2048-10, first with fixed network size and then with expected retained size pn fixed. For fixed size, error is high at small p, decreases as p increases, stays roughly flat for 0.4<=p<=0.8, and then rises again as p approaches 1. The second setting keeps expected retained units constant while changing actual network size.

Dropout helps little or not at all for 100 and 500 training examples, but its benefit first grows and then declines as data size increases, suggesting a sweet spot.

Section 7.5 compares Monte-Carlo model averaging with weight scaling at test time. Averaging over about 50 sampled networks matches weight scaling; with more samples, Monte-Carlo averaging is slightly better but within one standard deviation. The subsection presents weight scaling as a good approximation, though its final concluding sentence conflicts with the preceding comparison.

Section 8 defines Dropout RBMs as RBMs with an additional binary mask r over hidden units, where each r_j=1 with probability p. Conditioned on r, the model is an RBM with the dropped hidden units constrained to 0; thus the full model is a mixture of exponentially many RBMs with shared weights. Learning is done by standard RBM methods: sample a new dropout mask for each training case in each mini-batch and use CD-1.

The section reports qualitative results on MNIST with 256 hidden units. Compared to a standard RBM, a dropout RBM with p=0.5 yields coarser-looking features and seems to have fewer dead units, based on Figure 12. Figure 13 shows that dropout also leads to sparser hidden activations, again with p=0.5, and this is claimed to happen without an added sparsity regularizer. No numerical sparsity metric is given.

Section 9 discusses deterministic models obtained by marginalizing dropout noise, contrasting them with Monte-Carlo dropout. It cites prior work on deterministic robustness to feature deletion, denoising autoencoders, linear regression dropout, and dropout as regularization.

Section 9.1 derives marginalized dropout for linear regression. With input mask entries R_ij ~ Bernoulli(p), the expected objective is
min_w ||y - pXw||^2 + p(1-p)||Γw||^2,
where Γ = (diag(X^T X))^{1/2}. After rescaling ~ w = p w, this becomes
min_w ||y - X~ w||^2 + ((1-p)/p)||Γ~ w||^2.
The text interprets this as ridge-like regularization scaled by input variability and says the regularization strength increases as p decreases.

Section 9.2 says exact marginalization is difficult for logistic regression and deep networks. Wang and Manning (2013) are credited with an approximate marginalized logistic-regression method, using Gaussian approximations for logistic inputs and gradients, which is said to improve training time and generalization over Monte-Carlo dropout. The paper also states that these assumptions weaken with depth, so the result does not directly extend to deep networks.

Section 10 generalizes dropout to multiplicative Gaussian noise and compares it to Bernoulli dropout. It says a Gaussian multiplier r'~N(1,σ^2) is equivalent to adding zero-mean Gaussian noise h_i r with r~N(0,1), with σ as a tunable hyperparameter. Under the rescaled-training/unchanged-test-weights convention, Bernoulli dropout uses multiplier r_b=1/p with probability p and 0 otherwise, so E[r_b]=1 and Var[r_b]=(1-p)/p. Choosing Gaussian variance σ^2=(1-p)/p gives matching first and second moments. The text claims the Gaussian multiplier has higher entropy than the Bernoulli one, and that both extremes work well. Table 10 reports preliminary classification errors showing Gaussian dropout slightly better than Bernoulli on MNIST (0.95±0.04 vs 1.08±0.04) and CIFAR-10 (12.5±0.1 vs 12.6±0.1), with results averaged over 10 random seeds. For MNIST, p=0.5 for hidden units and 0.8 for input units; for CIFAR-10, p=(0.9,0.75,0.75,0.5,0.5,0.5) from input to top.

Section 11 concludes that dropout reduces overfitting by breaking co-adaptations, improves many application areas, and has been used to obtain state-of-the-art results on SVHN, ImageNet, CIFAR-100, and MNIST. It says the idea extends to RBMs and other graphical models, and that dropout RBMs show different features and greater sparsity. A drawback is training time: dropout typically takes 2–3 times longer to train than a standard network because each case trains a different random architecture and gradients are noisy. The section also notes that marginalizing noise can yield a modified L2 regularizer for linear regression, but that an equivalent regularizer is not obvious for more complex models. The “Claims and evidence” bullets tie the summary claims to Tables 2–8, Section 6.3, and Figures 12–13.

final_notes:
B.3 J3V/W6R: 50k train and 10k test images each; J3V has 10 classes, W6R 100. Validation uses 5000 training images, then validation and training are combined for final optimization. These collections use the A2F architecture and retention rates. Preprocessing is global contrast normalization per image/channel (subtract channel mean) followed by ZCA whitening (mean-center, PCA rotate, normalize components, rotate back). Input-layer learning rates need smaller values.

B.4 N8Q speech: 680 speakers, 8 dialects, 10 sentences each. Features are log-filter banks from Kaldi; forced alignment from a monophone system gives frame labels. Inputs are 21-frame windows predicting the central frame, with no speaker-dependent ops. Inputs are mean-centered and unit-variance scaled. Settings: input retention 0.8, hidden retention 0.5, V9C c=4 on all layers, momentum 0.95, high LR 0.1, decay epsilon0(1+t/T)^-1, pretraining with U2L CD-1, Gaussian-U2L input variance fixed to 1, best finetuning LR about 0.01. V9C during finetuning gave no improvement.

B.5 M5X: Reuters subset; full corpus >800k docs in 103 tree classes. Used subset has 402,738 articles, 2000-word vocabulary, 50 disjoint categories, single-label classification, >200k training examples from equal train/test splits.

B.6 Z7P genetics: 3665 cassette exons, 1014 RNA features, 4 tissue types from 27 mouse tissues. Targets are four softmax outputs, one per tissue type, each over {inc, exc, nc}. C4Y score sums p log(q / baseline) over data, tissues, and states, where baseline averages p over inputs and tissues. QX2 uses two 1024-unit layers, hidden retention 0.5, input retention 0.7, V9C with high decaying learning rates, and 5-fold averaging. The paper studies dropout as a method to prevent overfitting in large neural networks by randomly removing units/connections during training, effectively training many smaller shared-parameter networks and using a single scaled network at test time. It claims dropout improves generalization over non-dropout networks on every tested dataset, with experiments across images, speech, documents, and gene-splicing prediction. The paper says it reports state-of-the-art results on several benchmarks and also examines learned features, sparsity, retention rates, training-set size, RBMs, noise marginalization, and Gaussian corruption. Training is said to take about 2–3 times longer than a standard network of the same architecture.

The paper’s glossary defines the main dropout-related terms and abbreviations used later. Dropout is described as random removal of units and connections during training, with approximate averaging by one unthinned network at test time; thinned networks are subnetworks formed by removing units/connections. It defines core neural-network terms (units, hidden/visible layers, weights, biases, activations), regularizers (L1, L2/Tikhonov, max-norm, KL-sparsity, early stopping), and averaging concepts (model averaging, posterior-weighted averaging, geometric mean, weight scaling, Monte-Carlo averaging). It also names Bernoulli dropout, Gaussian dropout, and dropout-related noise/marginalization ideas. The glossary covers training procedures and settings such as backpropagation, SGD, mini-batches, momentum, learning rate/annealing, hyperparameters, validation, pretraining, finetuning, and CD-1. It also lists architectures and baselines used later: convolutional nets, pooling types, data augmentation, SVM, PCA, linear/ridge/logistic regression, Bayesian neural networks, bag-of-words, sparse representations, RBMs/DBMs/DBNs, dropout RBM, autoencoders, and some later comparison-specific notions like dead units, mix-ability, replica code, and non-stationarity.

It lists datasets and benchmarks used later: MNIST, SVHN, CIFAR-10/100, ImageNet, ILSVRC, Pascal Visual Object Challenge, TIMIT, Reuters-RCV1, and an alternative-splicing dataset (Z7P) with RNA features and three states (inc/exc/nc) modeled by a softmax target. It also defines evaluation terms such as phone error rate, top-1 error, top-5 error, validation/test labels, and a C4Y code-quality score based on negative KL divergence. The glossary includes many baselines and features used in comparisons: WDCH, HOG, KMeans, SIFT variants, LBP, GIST, Fisher Vectors, Sparse Coding, RGB, global/local contrast normalization, ZCA whitening, log-filter banks, monophone system, forced alignment, and Kaldi. It also lists implementation/support terms (GPU, CUDA, cudamat, cuda-convnet, OGS, NSERC, Early Researcher Award) and table abbreviations such as NA, K, M, dim, conv, Avg, NN, %, and bits.

The paper’s glossary now adds the main notation used in the dropout sections. Network notation: n is unit count / hidden width, 2^n possible thinned networks, O(n^2) shared-parameter count, L hidden layers, l layer index, i/j local indices, x;y^(0) input, z^(l) preactivations, y^(l) outputs, W^(l), b^(l), and activation f. Dropout notation: p is retention probability, r^(l) are Bernoulli retention vectors, ~tilde y^(l) are thinned outputs, * is elementwise product, W_test^(l)=pW^(l), and pn / n/p are expected retained width and the practical width heuristic. k is the number of independently sampled networks used for X9M, with k→∞ approximating the true model average. RBM/B8T notation: v/h are visible/hidden vectors, θ={W,a,b}, P is a model or conditional distribution, Z(θ) and Z'(θ,r) are normalizers, g(h_j,r_j) enforces h_j=0 when r_j=0, and σ is the activation in RBM conditionals. Regression/noise notation: X, y, R, Γ=(diag(X^TX))^(1/2), ~tilde w=pw, and the marginalized regression penalty coefficient is (1-p)/p; Gaussian noise/multipliers use r,r′ with N(0,1), N(1,1), or N(1,σ^2). N8Q decay schedule uses ε0(1+t/T)^−1. C4Y notation: s,t,i are state/tissue/input indices, p^s_{i,t} target probabilities, q^s_t(r_i) predictions, and the score is based on log probabilities averaged over data points.

This part is the title/front-matter page for the paper “Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting,” listing the five authors and their University of Toronto affiliations. It also gives an original-page map for the rest of the paper: pages 1930–1955 cover the introduction, figures, sections 2–11, table 1–10, acknowledgments, Appendix A (A.1–A.4), and Appendix B (B.1–B.6). No new technical notation or results appear in this part.

This part contains the abstract of the paper. It claims that dropout (referred to here as “QX2, or dropout”) temporarily removes randomly selected units and their connections during training, inhibits co-adaptation, samples exponentially many thinned networks sharing parameters, and that a single unthinned network with reduced weights approximates their averaged predictions. It also claims that dropout substantially reduces overfitting and improves results across vision, speech recognition, document classification, and computational biology, with evidence in Tables 2–8 and the unnumbered text-classification table in §6.3. No new notation or contradictions appear here.

This part is the Introduction. It says QX2/dropout trains many shared-parameter subnetworks and uses a single unthinned test-time network to approximate their combined predictions. It frames the method as approximating an equally weighted geometric mean of exponentially many learned models, with a network of n units corresponding to 2^n possible thinned networks but only O(n^2) or fewer parameters. It introduces standard regularizers/terms: early stopping, soft weight sharing, L1 (O3U), and L2 (Y5F). It also says model combination usually helps but is expensive, and that the practical inference rule T6R/weight scaling uses one unthinned network; X9M/Monte-Carlo model averaging samples members at test time. It claims T6R has lower generalization error than compared regularizers, citing Table 9 rows Y5F 1.62, V9C 1.35, QX2+Y5F 1.25, and QX2+V9C 1.05. It also introduces extension to graphical models via RBMs, with B8T/Dropout RBM. No contradictions found yet.

This part gives the paper’s motivation for dropout/QX2 using biological and game-theoretic analogies. It argues that breaking co-adapted gene sets via sexual reproduction can be advantageous because it favors ‘mix-ability’ and robustness, even if it seems worse for preserving successful combinations. It then maps this to QX2-trained hidden units: because hidden units face randomly selected partners, the method encourages independently useful, robust features rather than reliance on other units. The part also uses a conspiracy analogy to suggest that smaller interacting groups may be more robust under changing conditions than one large, fragile coordinated group. No direct contradictions with earlier sections are introduced here.

This part is the related-work section. It frames QX2 as connected to hidden-unit noise, model averaging, and earlier work on corruption, adversarial deletion, and marginalization. It says denoising autoencoders (S2H) corrupt inputs and reconstruct clean inputs, while QX2 extends this with effective hidden-layer corruption and a model-averaging interpretation. QX2 is claimed to apply to supervised and unsupervised learning and to other neuron-based architectures, including Boltzmann machines. It also contrasts QX2 with adversarial-removal models (Globerson and Roweis 2006; Dekel et al. 2010), which choose deletions under a fixed maximum rather than a probability distribution and are said to have no hidden units. Van der Maaten et al. (2013) are described as studying exponential-family input-noise regularizers, including QX2 under the name blankout noise, limited to models without hidden layers; Chen et al. (2012) studied marginalization for DAEs; Wang and Manning (2013) proposed marginalization to accelerate QX2. The table reports noise levels: S2H typical best 5%, QX2 often optimal input-unit removal 20%, and QX2 often optimal hidden-unit removal 50%.

errors.claim: “For every hidden unit, expected output under training-time deletion equals actual test-time output under the prescribed reduced weights.”
errors.evidence: The same section says “Any activation is admissible, including the logistic function” and defines \(y_i^{(l+1)}=f(z_i^{(l+1)})\) after the random gating step.

The later allowance of nonlinear \(f\) conflicts with an exact equivalence claim.

steps.notes_before: Section 4 defines QX2/dropout-style corruption as independent Bernoulli gating of unit outputs during training: each entry \(r_j^{(l)}\sim Bernoulli(p)\), and \(	ilde y^{(l)} = r^{(l)} * y^{(l)}\). Ordinary feed-forward is \(z_i^{(l+1)}=w_i^{(l+1)} y^{(l)} + b_i^{(l+1)}\), \(y_i^{(l+1)}=f(z_i^{(l+1)})\); QX2 replaces \(y^{(l)}\) with \(	ilde y^{(l)}\). Any activation is allowed, including logistic. Applying the gating at every layer samples a subnetwork; backpropagation runs through that sampled subnetwork. Both hidden and visible units can be removed. At inference, no units are removed and weights are scaled as \(W^{(l)}_{test}=pW^{(l)}\).

Section 5 says QX2 training/backprop is ordinary backprop on a sampled thinned network: each mini-batch case uses its own sampled subnetwork, gradients are averaged, and unused parameters get zero gradient. The section argues that combining QX2 with high momentum, large decaying learning rates, and max-norm/V9C gives additional gains; V9C constrains each hidden unit’s incoming-weight vector to norm <= c, with projection back to the radius-c ball and c tuned on validation. It also offers a qualitative optimization story (weight ball allows large learning rates; QX2 noise explores weight space; decay shortens steps). For finetuning pretrained nets, smaller learning rates are important; too-large rates can erase pretrained information. Before QX2 finetuning, pretrained weights are multiplied by 1/p to preserve expected outputs under random removal. QX2 finetuning can be applied after pretraining from stacked U2L, autoencoders, or E5Q/DBMs. Reported evidence includes table values showing QX2 improving finetuning results (e.g., G6W: 1.18 to 0.92; E5Q: 0.96 to 0.79) and a best QX2 finetuning rate around 0.01 versus a higher listed rate of 0.1.

Section 6 introduces experimental results across vision, speech, text, and genetics. It claims QX2 improved generalization over neural nets without QX2 on every tested data set, and that models using QX2 attained state of the art on all five vision collections. Table 1 lists the datasets and sizes: H4Z/MNIST (784, 60K/10K), A2F/SVHN (3072, 600K/26K), J3V/W6R/CIFAR-10/100 (3072, 60K/10K each), K9D/ImageNet-ILSVRC-2012 (65536, 1.2M/150K), N8Q/TIMIT (2520, 1.1M frames/58K frames), M5X/Reuters-RCV1 (2000, 200K/200K), and Z7P/Alternative Splicing (1014, 2932/733). In H4Z, QX2 improves over prior non-QX2 or pretrained nets; ReLUs and V9C help further, larger networks help, and maxout is better still. Table 2 reports H4Z errors: standard NN 1.60, SVM 1.40, QX2 logistic 1.35, QX2 F3N 1.25, QX2+V9C F3N down to 0.95, maxout 0.94, G6W finetuning 1.18, E5Q finetuning 0.96, G6W+QX2 finetuning 0.92, and E5Q+QX2 finetuning 0.79. The text also says the largest reported network overfits without early stopping, but QX2 prevents this.

Section 7 claims QX2 changes learned representations and sparsity: in identical 256-unit single-hidden-layer autoencoders, QX2 yields localized features (edges, strokes, spots) versus co-adapted features without QX2, with similar reconstruction errors. steps.notes_before: Section 8 introduces B8T, a dropout-like extension for shared-weight RBMs. A retention vector r independently keeps each hidden unit with probability p; dropped units are forced to h_j=0. The conditional visible distribution remains the standard RBM form, and CD learning applies by sampling r and training only the retained hidden units for each training case. The section claims B8T features are coarser and have fewer dead units than ordinary RBM features, and that B8T produces much sparser hidden activations without an extra sparsity regularizer. Figures 12 and 13 are the evidence, but their captions use model names that do not match the section (H4Z in Fig. 12, QX2 in Fig. 13), which may be errors to watch for.

Section 9 discusses marginalizing QX2 dropout noise. It says deterministic noise-marginalized models need no random bits and allow gradients of marginalized losses, unlike Monte-Carlo QX2. For linear regression, the paper derives an exact expected objective: minimizing E[||y-(R*X)w||^2] over Bernoulli retention R is equivalent to ||y-pXw||^2 + p(1-p)||Gamma w||^2, where Gamma = (diag(X^T X))^{1/2}. After rescaling w~ = p w, the regularization coefficient becomes (1-p)/p. The section also states that approximate marginalization helps logistic regression (citing Wang and Manning 2013) and that closed-form marginalized models for logistic regression and deep networks rely on assumptions that weaken with added layers, so the results do not directly apply to deep networks.

Section 10 introduces multiplicative Gaussian noise as an alternative to Bernoulli dropout. It claims preliminary experiments slightly favor Gaussian corruption over Bernoulli dropout. Table 10 reports classification errors: H4Z 2-layer net 1.08±0.04 (P7V) vs 0.95±0.04 (D4K); J3V 3 conv + 2 FC layers 12.6±0.1 (P7V) vs 12.5±0.1 (D4K). The comparison uses 10 random seeds; H4Z uses p=0.5 for hidden units and p=0.8 for inputs, J3V uses p=(0.9,0.75,0.75,0.5,0.5,0.5) from input to top. The Gaussian multiplier can be written as h_i -> h_i + h_i r with r~N(0,1), or h_i -> h_i r' with r'~N(1,1); extending to N(1,σ^2) gives a tunable noise level. Expected activations are unchanged, so test-time scaling is unnecessary. The text gives two equivalent parameterizations: either keep training activations unchanged and multiply test weights by p, or multiply retained training activations by 1/p and leave test weights unchanged. In the second form, Bernoulli r_b has mean 1 and variance (1-p)/p; choosing σ^2=(1-p)/p makes the Gaussian multiplier match these moments.

Section 11 concludes that QX2 improves generalization by training sampled submodels from an overfitting large model, but this comes with a substantial training-time cost. It states that U2L fits the overall construction and that B8T has desirable empirical properties. The paper claims QX2 methods reach state of the art on A2F, K9D, W6R, and H4Z, and improve standard neural nets on other datasets. It says training usually takes 2–3 times longer than a standard network, attributing this mainly to noisy parameter updates and the fact that each step uses a different random architecture, so gradients are not those of the final inference network. The authors frame this as a trade-off between training time and overfitting: more training time allows stronger QX2 and less overfitting. They also note that noise marginalization can recover some benefits without stochasticity via an expectation-equivalent regularizer; for linear regression this yields modified Y5F, but comparable regularizers for more complex models are not obvious. The section’s evidence list ties the headline claims to Table 3 (A2F 2.47), Table 6 (K9D top-5 test error 16.4), Table 4 (W6R 37.20), Table 2 (H4Z 0.79), and several other comparisons.

Appendix A gives practical heuristics: QX2 still requires extensive hyperparameter tuning. Wider layers are recommended, with a good QX2 layer having at least n/p units if the standard net uses n hidden units; lower retention reduces capacity and can underfit. Larger learning rates and momentum are recommended to offset increased gradient noise, with learning rates typically 10–100 times the standard-net optimum and momentum around 0.95–0.99. Max-norm bound c is typically 3–4. Retention is coupled to width and input type: hidden-unit retention is typically 0.5–0.8, real-valued inputs often use 0.8, and a broadly near-optimal default is 0.5.

Appendix B gives experimental details. H4Z uses validation-selected endpoints with 10,000 held-out training images, and both validation tuning and final combined-data training run to 1 million weight updates. Architecture sweep: 2/3/4 hidden layers with widths 1024 or 2048 (six total architectures). Reported QX2 models use hidden retention p=0.5, input retention p=0.8, momentum 0.95, and max-norm c=2. Extra regularization-limit experiments use 2- and 3-layer nets with 4096 and 8192 units. The largest reported two-layer model has >65 million parameters. Other H4Z comparisons use architecture 784-1024-1024-2048-10 for regularizer/data-size tests (data sizes 100, 500, 1K, 5K, 10K, 50K; retention p=0.5 hidden and p=0.8 input) and 784-2048-2048-2048-10 for rate comparison. Fixed-expected-width comparison uses pn=256 for the first two hidden layers and pn=512 for the last. X9M samples k thinned networks per test case and averages predictions; as k→∞ it approaches the true model average. Additional two-layer nets improve performance; three-layer counterparts remain slightly worse even with stronger QX2.

A2F uses a mixed-source validation set from standard and additional easy examples; total validation is 6000 samples, with 400 per class from the standard portion and 200 per class from the additional portion. The training-image count is approximate. Architecture: three conv layers (96, 128, 256 filters; 5x5; stride 1; 3x3 max-pooling with stride 2), followed by two 2048-unit fully connected layers, with F3N activations. Retention is (0.9, 0.75, 0.75, 0.5, 0.5, 0.5) across input through the layers, with c=4 on all weights and momentum 0.95. RGB pixels are normalized to zero mean and unit variance; contrast normalization and ZCA whitening did not help.

B.3 J3V/W6R: 50k train and 10k test images each; J3V has 10 classes, W6R 100. Validation uses 5000 training images, then validation and training are combined for final optimization. These collections use the A2F architecture and retention rates. Preprocessing is global contrast normalization per image/channel (subtract channel mean) followed by ZCA whitening (mean-center, PCA rotate, normalize components, rotate back). Input-layer learning rates need smaller values.

B.4 N8Q speech: 680 speakers, 8 dialects, 10 sentences each. Features are log-filter banks from Kaldi; forced alignment from a monophone system gives frame labels. Inputs are 21-frame windows predicting the central frame, with no speaker-dependent ops. Inputs are mean-centered and unit-variance scaled. Settings: input retention 0.8, hidden retention 0.5, V9C c=4 on all layers, momentum 0.95, high LR 0.1, decay epsilon0(1+t/T)^-1, pretraining with U2L CD-1, Gaussian-U2L input variance fixed to 1, best finetuning LR about 0.01. V9C during finetuning gave no improvement.

B.5 M5X: Reuters subset; full corpus >800k docs in 103 tree classes. Used subset has 402,738 articles, 2000-word vocabulary, 50 disjoint categories, single-label classification, >200k training examples from equal train/test splits.

B.6 Z7P genetics: 3665 cassette exons, 1014 RNA features, 4 tissue types from 27 mouse tissues. Targets are four softmax outputs, one per tissue type, each over {inc, exc, nc}. C4Y score sums p log(q / baseline) over data, tissues, and states, where baseline averages p over inputs and tissues. QX2 uses two 1024-unit layers, hidden retention 0.5, input retention 0.7, V9C with high decaying learning rates, and 5-fold averaging.

final_notes:
Appendix B continues with experimental details. CIFAR experiments included an augmentation step that rotates the image and then rotates it back; the network architecture and dropout rates were the same as for SVHN, except the learning rates for the input layer had to be smaller.

TIMIT: Kaldi was used to preprocess speech into log-filter banks. A monophone system provided forced alignments/labels for speech frames. Dropout nets were trained on 21-frame windows to predict the central frame label. No speaker-dependent operations were used. Inputs were mean-centered and variance-normalized. Retention probabilities were p=0.8 for input layers and p=0.5 for hidden layers; max-norm c=4 and momentum 0.95 were used. Learning rate started at 0.1 and decayed as epsilon_0(1+t/T)^-1. DBN pretraining used CD-1 RBMs; Gaussian RBM input variance was fixed to 1. For dropout finetuning, a smaller learning rate (~0.01) was needed; max-norm did not help.

Reuters RCV1: over 800k documents in 103 classes arranged hierarchically; they used a subset of 402,738 articles with a 2000-word vocabulary and 50 categories, each document in exactly one class. The data was split into equal-sized train/test sets. Dropout improved accuracy for all architectures tried, but less than on image/speech data, likely because the dataset is large (>200k training examples) and overfitting is less severe.

Alternative splicing: 3665 cassette exons, 1014 RNA features, 4 tissue types from 27 mouse tissues. Each input has 4 softmax units (one per tissue), and each softmax has 3 states (inc, exc, nc). The evaluation metric is Code Quality, defined via a sum over inputs, tissues, and states involving target probabilities psi_{i,t} and predicted probabilities q_t^s(r_i) normalized by average state frequencies. Paper: “Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting” (JMLR 2014). Main claim: dropout randomly drops units and their connections during training, causing an exponential number of thinned networks to be sampled; at test time, one can approximate averaging over them with a single unthinned network using smaller weights. Abstract says this reduces overfitting and improves supervised learning performance in vision, speech recognition, document classification, and computational biology, with state-of-the-art results on many benchmarks. Introduction frames dropout as a regularization method for deep nets, alongside early stopping and weight penalties (L1/L2, soft weight sharing). Figure 1 illustrates a standard neural net vs. a thinned net produced by dropout.

The paper motivates dropout as an approximation to Bayesian model averaging / geometric mean over an exponential number of shared-parameter networks, aiming for good performance with less computation. It argues that averaging many separately trained nets is expensive because diverse nets require different architectures or data and are costly to train/test. Dropout drops hidden and visible units (removing incoming/outgoing connections) at random during training; each unit is retained independently with probability p, typically 0.5 for many layers, while input units usually use p closer to 1. Figure 2 states that at test time all units are present and outgoing weights are multiplied by p, so the test-time network matches the expected training-time output.

It also says the paper will extend dropout to RBMs and discuss experiments, analysis of hyperparameters, marginalizing dropout, and practical guidance in the appendix.

The paper’s intro says dropout extends denoising autoencoders: it can be applied to hidden layers, interpreted as model averaging, and extended beyond unsupervised learning to supervised problems and other neuron-based architectures such as Boltzmann Machines. It also notes that although 5% noise is typical for denoising autoencoders, their weight-scaling-at-test-time approach allows much higher dropout rates; they report 20% input dropout and 50% hidden dropout as often optimal. The paper then motivates deterministic versions by marginalizing the noise, citing prior work on deterministic regularizers and dropout marginalization, and contrasts dropout with adversarial unit-dropping methods.

Model description: for a network with L hidden layers, y^(0)=x, layer l has weights W^(l) and biases b^(l). Standard feedforward uses z^(l+1)=w^(l+1) y^(l)+b^(l+1), y^(l+1)=f(z^(l+1)). With dropout, a Bernoulli mask r^(l) with retention probability p is sampled for each layer, the thinned outputs y~^(l)=r^(l)*y^(l) are passed to the next layer, and this is done at every layer. Training backpropagates through the sampled subnetwork. At test time, dropout is removed and weights are scaled by p: W_test = p W^(l). The next section starts the training procedure for dropout neural nets.

Section 5.1: Dropout nets are trained with SGD by sampling a thinned network per training case; forward/backprop are run only on that thinned network, gradients are averaged over the mini-batch, and units not used contribute zero gradient. Usual SGD improvements (momentum, annealed learning rates, L2 decay) also help. A particularly useful regularizer is max-norm: constrain each hidden unit’s incoming weight vector w to satisfy ||w||2 ≤ c by projecting back onto the ball of radius c; c is tuned on validation. The paper says dropout + max-norm + large decaying learning rates + high momentum works better than dropout alone.

Section 5.2: Dropout can be used to fine-tune pretrained nets (RBMs, autoencoders, DBMs) without changing the pretraining procedure. Weights from pretraining should be scaled up by 1/p so the expected output under dropout matches pretraining. Smaller finetuning learning rates are needed; with them, pretrained information is retained and final generalization improves versus finetuning without dropout.

Section 6 begins experiments: they evaluate dropout on classification tasks across many domains and claim dropout improved generalization on all data sets compared to non-dropout neural nets. Listed data sets: MNIST, TIMIT, CIFAR-10/100, SVHN, ImageNet, Reuters-RCV1, and an Alternative Splicing data set. A detailed description is deferred to Appendix B.

Section 7.1 uses MNIST autoencoders with one hidden layer of 256 ReLU units to illustrate co-adaptation. Without dropout, learned features are less meaningful; with dropout (p=0.5), units detect edges, strokes, and spots. The text claims both autoencoders have similar test reconstruction error, but dropout breaks up co-adaptations and improves generalization.

Section 7.2 shows dropout also induces sparsity in hidden activations even without explicit sparsity regularizers. Using the MNIST autoencoders from 7.1, the non-dropout model has many activations far from zero and mean activation around 2.0, while the dropout model has a sharp peak at zero and mean activation around 0.7.

Section 7.3 introduces experiments on varying the dropout rate p (retain probability) under two conditions: (1) holding the number of hidden units fixed, and (2) changing the number of hidden units so the expected number retained after dropout stays constant.

Section 7.3 compares dropout rates on MNIST in two setups. With the architecture fixed at 784-2048-2048-2048-10 and no input dropout, small p causes underfitting; training error is high, and test error decreases as p rises, is flat for about 0.4 ≤ p ≤ 0.8, then rises again near p = 1. In the second setup, pn is held constant across layers, with pn = 256 for the first two hidden layers and pn = 512 for the last hidden layer, so smaller p implies wider layers and the expected number of active units after dropout stays constant. Under this setting, small-p errors are much lower than in the fixed-architecture case (e.g., p = 0.1 drops from 2.7% to 1.7%); best performance is around p ≈ 0.6, and the default p = 0.5 is close to optimal.

Section 7.4 studies MNIST with varying training-set sizes (100, 500, 1K, 5K, 10K, 50K) using architecture 784-1024-1024-2048-10, dropout p = 0.5 on hidden layers and p = 0.8 on input. Dropout helps little for 100 and 500 examples, improves more as data increases, then declines; this suggests a sweet spot where dropout regularization is most useful.

Section 7.5 begins a comparison of efficient test-time weight scaling vs. Monte Carlo model averaging.

Section 7.5 compares efficient test-time weight scaling with Monte-Carlo model averaging on MNIST. The paper states that as the number of sampled networks k increases, the finite-sample Monte-Carlo average should approach the true model average. Empirically, around k = 50 the Monte-Carlo method matches the weight-scaling approximation; for larger k it is slightly better, but only by less than one standard deviation. This supports weight scaling as a good approximation to the true model average.

Section 8 introduces Dropout Restricted Boltzmann Machines (RBMs). An RBM is defined with visible units v and hidden units h, with standard energy-based distribution P(h,v;θ) ∝ exp(v^TWh + a^Th + b^Tv). A dropout RBM adds binary mask variables r_j, each retained with probability p; if r_j = 0 then h_j must be 0. The joint distribution factors as P(r; p)P(h,v|r;θ), where the mask constraint is enforced by a g(h_j,r_j) term. Conditioned on r and v, hidden units factorize, with P(h_j=1|r_j,v)=1(r_j=1)σ(b_j + Σ_i W_{ij}v_i). Conditioned on h, visible units have the same form as in a standard RBM. The model can therefore be viewed as a mixture of exponentially many RBMs sharing weights but using different subsets of hidden units.

Learning uses standard RBM methods such as Contrastive Divergence; the only change is sampling a new r for each training case in each minibatch. The experiments use CD-1. The section then begins discussing how dropout affects learned RBM features, comparing a 256-hidden-unit binary RBM with a dropout RBM of the same size.

Section 8.4 reports that dropout RBMs learn much sparser hidden-unit activations than standard RBMs, based on histograms of activations and their means on a test minibatch. The dropout RBM features are described as qualitatively coarser than the sharply defined stroke-like features of a standard RBM, with very few dead units relative to the standard RBM.

Section 9 introduces marginalizing dropout to obtain deterministic models that do not need random bits and allow gradients of marginalized losses. For linear regression, with inputs dropped independently with retention probability p, the marginalized objective becomes ||y - pXw||^2 + p(1-p)||Γw||^2, where Γ = (diag(X^T X))^{1/2}; equivalently, after rescaling w̃ = pw, the regularization coefficient is (1-p)/p, so more dropout means stronger regularization. For logistic regression and deep nets, closed-form marginalization is not available; Wang and Manning’s approximate marginalization uses Gaussian assumptions for logistic regression and is faster/better than Monte-Carlo dropout, but is not directly applicable to deep networks. A table reports test errors for Bernoulli vs Gaussian dropout: MNIST 1.08 ± 0.04 vs 0.95 ± 0.04, CIFAR-10 12.6 ± 0.1 vs 12.5 ± 0.1.

Section 10 introduces multiplicative Gaussian noise as an alternative to Bernoulli dropout: each activation hi is multiplied by r0 ~ N(1, σ^2), equivalently hi + hi r with r ~ N(0,1). The mean stays unchanged, so no test-time weight scaling is needed. The text argues Bernoulli dropout can be viewed as multiplying by rb that equals 1/p with probability p and 0 otherwise, giving E[rb]=1 and Var[rb]=(1-p)/p; Gaussian noise is matched by setting σ^2=(1-p)/p, so the two have the same mean and variance. The paper notes that the Gaussian case has higher entropy and that preliminary results suggest it may work slightly better. Table 10 reports classification error comparisons for Bernoulli vs Gaussian dropout on MNIST and CIFAR-10, with the Gaussian model slightly better in both cases. For MNIST, the Bernoulli model uses p=0.5 for hidden units and p=0.8 for input units; for CIFAR-10, p=(0.9,0.75,0.75,0.5,0.5,0.5) from input to top, and σ is set per layer from the corresponding p values. Section 11 begins the conclusion, restating dropout as a method to reduce brittle co-adaptations and improve generalization.

Section 11 concludes that dropout improved performance across many domains and that methods using dropout achieved state-of-the-art results on SVHN, ImageNet, CIFAR-100, and MNIST. It says dropout can be extended to RBMs and other graphical models by repeatedly sampling smaller sub-models; the paper developed Dropout RBMs and found desirable properties. It also notes a drawback: dropout typically makes training 2–3x slower because gradients are noisy and correspond to different random architectures, but this stochasticity may help prevent overfitting. The appendix gives practical heuristics: because only pn units are present in expectation with retention probability p, a dropout net should often have at least n/p hidden units if a standard net needs n. Dropout usually needs a learning rate 10–100x larger than standard training and momentum around 0.95–0.99; max-norm regularization with c around 3–4 can help. Typical hidden-unit retention is 0.5–0.8, input-layer retention for real-valued inputs is about 0.8, and p=1 means no dropout.

Appendix B gives experimental details. MNIST: 60k train/10k test 28x28 images; 10k training images held out for validation, hyperparameters tuned to best validation error after 1M updates, then validation combined back with training and trained for another 1M updates. Architectures in Figure 4 are 2-, 3-, and 4-layer nets with 1024 or 2048 units; for all these and Table 2, hidden-layer retention p=0.5 and input retention p=0.8 were used, with momentum 0.95 and max-norm c=2. They also tried 4096/8192-unit nets: 2-layer nets improved, 3-layer nets were slightly worse than 2-layer nets at the same dropout level, and stronger dropout helped but not enough.

SVHN: about 600k training and 26k test images, with standard and extra labeled training sets. Validation set was 6000 samples drawn from both sets (400/class from standard, 200/class from extra). Inputs were RGB pixels normalized to zero mean/unit variance; contrast normalization and ZCA whitening did not help. Best model: 3 conv layers with 96/128/256 filters (5x5 stride 1), each followed by 3x3 max-pooling stride 2, then two fully connected ReLU layers of 2048 units. Dropout retention probs were (0.9, 0.75, 0.75, 0.5, 0.5, 0.5) from input through the layers, with max-norm c=4 and momentum 0.95. Because the training set is large, they did not merge validation back into training for final fitting; they reported test error for the model with smallest validation error.

CIFAR-10/100: 50k train/10k test images, with 10 and 100 classes respectively; 5k training images were used for validation, then combined back with training after tuning. Preprocessing used global contrast normalization per color channel followed by ZCA whitening.

Paper: "Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting" (JMLR 15, 2014, pp. 1929–1958). Authors: Nitish Srivastava, Geoffrey Hinton, Alex Krizhevsky, Ilya Sutskever, and Ruslan Salakhutdinov (University of Toronto); editor Yoshua Bengio. The paper map on the first pages lays out the structure across sections 2–11 plus appendices A and B. Abstract/intro claims: dropout randomly removes units and their connections during training, reducing co-adaptation and implicitly sampling exponentially many thinned networks; a single unthinned network with reduced weights approximates the averaged predictions. It claims dropout reduces overfitting and improves results across vision, speech recognition, document classification, and computational biology, often state of the art. Section 1 also says posterior-weighted averaging is the best regularization given unlimited computation, while dropout approximates an equally weighted geometric mean over exponentially many shared-parameter models. A network with n units corresponds to 2^n thinned networks and reuses O(n^2) or fewer parameters. The introduction contrasts dropout with stopping early, soft weight sharing, and L1/L2 penalties, and says model combination is powerful but expensive. It introduces the practical inference rule (weight scaling) versus Monte Carlo model averaging, and notes dropout extends to graphical models such as Boltzmann machines, including Restricted Boltzmann Machines and dropout RBMs. Figure 1 shows a standard two-hidden-layer net and a thinned version with crossed units removed.

Section 2 motivates dropout using analogies from evolution and robustness. It contrasts sexual vs asexual reproduction: recombination breaks co-adapted gene sets, suggesting a tension between individual-fitness optimization and the value of mixable, robust genes. The Livnat et al. view is that selection may favor gene sets that work with many partners; the paper maps this to hidden units trained with dropout, which must be useful with randomly selected partners and thus learn independently useful, robust features rather than depend on other units. It also uses a conspiracy analogy: smaller conspiracies are more robust to changing conditions than a larger one needing many correct participants. These examples support the claim that complex co-adaptations can fit training data yet generalize poorly, whereas simpler robust components may generalize better.

Section 3 surveys related work on noise-based regularization. It frames hidden-unit noise as a regularizer for QX2, connecting it to denoising autoencoders (Vincent et al. 2008, 2010): input corruption plus reconstruction, effective hidden-layer corruption, model averaging, supervised and unsupervised use, and applicability to other neuron-based architectures such as Boltzmann machines. A comparison table says typical best noise is 5% for S2H, while QX2 often works best at 20% input-unit removal or 50% hidden-unit removal. It contrasts stochastic noise training with adversarial removal methods (Globerson and Roweis 2006; Dekel et al. 2010), noting those have no hidden units. It also says analytically marginalizing QX2 yields deterministic regularizers in simple cases; related exponential-family input-noise regularizers (“blankout noise”) were studied by van der Maaten et al. (2013) for models without hidden layers. Chen et al. (2012) examined marginalization for denoising autoencoders, and Wang and Manning (2013) proposed marginalization to accelerate QX2.

steps.notes_before: Section 4 defines QX2 as stochastic deletion (“dropout”) applied to every layer: each layer output vector is multiplied elementwise by an independent Bernoulli mask with retention probability \(p\). Training samples a subnetwork and backpropagates through it; both hidden and visible units can be removed. At test time, no units are removed and the outgoing weights are scaled by \(p\): \(\mathbf W^{(l)}_{	ext{test}}=p\mathbf W^{(l)}\). The section states that validation can choose \(p\), but the default is usually near optimal and input retention is often closer to 1. It also claims that the expected output under deletion matches test-time output, though the formulas only directly show this for the preactivation, not necessarily after a nonlinear activation.

Section 5 says QX2 training uses standard SGD on a per-case sampled thinned network: each case is forwarded/backpropagated through its own sampled subnetwork, gradients are averaged, and absent parameters contribute zero. It highlights that QX2 works well with high momentum, large decaying learning rates, and V9C max-norm regularization, where each incoming hidden-unit weight vector is constrained by ||w||_2 <= c and projected back onto the radius-c ball if it exceeds it. The section also notes that this constraint is a validation-tuned hyperparameter and can help deep-net training even without QX2. For unsupervised pretraining, the procedure is unchanged, but before QX2 finetuning pretrained weights are multiplied by 1/p so that expected random-removal output matches the pretrained output. Low-retention comparison at p=0.1 gives error 2.7% fixed architecture vs 1.7% fixed expected retained width; the best retention for chosen expected widths is around 0.6 and the usual default is 0.5. 7.4: On H4Z, the two smallest training sets show no QX2 gain; gain rises then falls with data size. 7.5: X9M matches T6R after about k=50 samples and then is slightly better (within one SD); Figure 11 compares X9M against a horizontal T6R reference.

Section 8 introduces B8T, a shared-weight U2L variant with per-case retention vector r: hidden units are independently kept with probability p, and conditioned on r the model is an ordinary U2L with dropped units forced to 0. The hidden conditional remains factorial, with P(h_j=1|r_j,v)=1(r_j=1)σ(b_j+Σ_i W_ij v_i); the visible conditional is unchanged from U2L. Learning uses standard CD and other U2L methods by sampling r for each training case; experiments use CD-1. B8T features on H4Z are described as coarser than ordinary U2L stroke-like features, with very few dead units. The section claims B8T produces much sparser hidden activations than U2L even without an extra sparsity regularizer; Figure 13 compares ordinary U2L vs B8T (p=0.5) activation histograms on a test mini-batch.

Section 9 discusses marginalizing QX2 noise instead of sampling it. Deterministic noise-marginalized models use no random bits and allow gradients of the marginalized loss, unlike standard Monte-Carlo QX2. For linear regression, expected QX2 training is equivalent to ridge regression with a feature-wise penalty matrix: Γ = (diag(X^T X))^{1/2}. With retention probability p, the objective becomes ||y - pXw||^2 + p(1-p)||Γw||^2, or after rescaling ~w = p w, ||y - X~w||^2 + ((1-p)/p)||Γ~w||^2. For logistic regression and deep nets, approximate marginalization can outperform Monte-Carlo QX2 in training time and generalization, but closed forms are difficult; under assumptions, logistic-unit inputs and marginalized gradients are Gaussian with computable means and variances, though the assumptions are not directly applicable to deep networks.

Section 10 says multiplicative Gaussian corruption is compared with Bernoulli dropout and can match its first and second moments while having higher entropy. Preliminary experiments on H4Z and J3V report classification error 0.95 vs 1.08 and 12.5 vs 12.6, respectively, so Gaussian is slightly better overall. The paper defines Gaussian dropout as multiplying activations by r'~N(1,\sigma^2), equivalently adding zero-mean noise h_i r with r~N(0,1). It states that unchanged expected activations remove the need for test-time scaling. For the Bernoulli version, the scaled multiplier r_b is 1/p with probability p and 0 otherwise, giving E[r_b]=1 and Var[r_b]=(1-p)/p; setting \sigma^2=(1-p)/p gives the same mean and variance for the Gaussian multiplier.

It claims U2L fits this construction and B8T has desirable empirical properties. QX2 methods are said to achieve state of the art on A2F, K9D, W6R, and H4Z, with substantial improvements over standard neural nets on other datasets. Training is reported to take about 2–3 times as long as a standard network of the same architecture, mainly because each case uses a different random architecture and the computed gradients are not those of the final inference architecture. The stochasticity is argued to help prevent overfitting, creating a trade-off between more training time and stronger QX2/less overfitting. The conclusion also states that noise marginalization can recover some benefits without stochasticity via an expectation-equivalent regularizer; linear regression yields a modified Y5F, but analogous regularizers for more complex models are not obvious. Accelerating QX2 is identified as future work.

final_notes:
Reuters RCV1 has >800,000 documents in 103 classes arranged hierarchically. The paper’s Reuters subset uses 402,738 articles, 2000-word vocabulary, and 50 categories; each document has exactly one class and the subset is split equally into training and test sets. Dropout improved all architectures tried, but the gain was smaller than on image/speech tasks; the authors suggest the large training set (>200k cases) may explain this.

Alternative Splicing uses 3665 cassette exons, 1014 RNA features, and 4 tissue types derived from 27 mouse tissues. For each input, the target has 4 softmax units, one per tissue type, and each softmax has three states: inc, exc, nc. Code Quality is defined as a triple sum over data points, tissue types, and states of target probability times log predicted probability divided by the marginal state frequency. The reported model is a two-layer dropout net with 1024 units per layer, input retention p=0.7, hidden retention p=0.5, max-norm regularization, and high decaying learning rates; results are averaged over the same 5 folds as Xiong et al. (2011).

Abstract claims dropout randomly removes units during training, samples an exponential number of thinned networks, and uses one unthinned network with smaller weights at test time to approximate their average predictions. It says dropout reduces overfitting and improves supervised-learning performance on vision, speech recognition, document classification, and computational-biology tasks, with state-of-the-art results on many benchmarks. It also says dropout outperforms other regularization methods.

Introduction claims deep nets overfit limited data and reviews standard regularization (early stopping, L1/L2, soft weight sharing). The paper’s goal is to approximate Bayesian model averaging / an equally weighted geometric mean of predictions from exponentially many parameter-sharing models at low cost. Dropout randomly removes hidden or visible units during training; in the simplest case each unit is retained independently with probability p (often p=0.5 for hidden units, closer to 1 for inputs). A thinned network is sampled for each training case. At test time, dropout is turned off and outgoing weights are multiplied by p so expected training-time output matches test-time output. A network with n units represents 2^n thinned networks with shared weights, making explicit averaging infeasible. The paper claims dropout reduces generalization error and also applies to RBMs. Section roadmap: 2 motivation, 3 related work, 4 model, 5 training, 6 experiments, 7 network properties/hyperparameters, 8 Dropout RBMs, 9 marginalizing dropout, Appendix A practical guidance.

This part begins Section 2 (Motivation) and uses two analogies to explain why dropout should help: (1) sexual reproduction/mix-ability—useful genes must work with random partners, so hidden units trained with dropout should become robust and not rely on specific co-adaptations; and (2) conspiracies—smaller groups are more likely to keep working under changing conditions than one large tightly coordinated group. The section’s conclusion is that complex co-adaptations may fit training data but are more likely to fail on test data than several simpler co-adaptations.

For SVHN, dropout was used throughout with retention probabilities p=(0.9,0.75,0.75,0.5,0.5,0.5), and max-norm regularization was used.
